en: Prosperity!
The Mahāvīracarita:
Bhāvapradyotinī.
I pay homage to Vīrarāghava, the granter of boons, who is filled with affection.
By which the great sacrifice of Viśvāmitra was indeed completed without obstacle.

Now, the venerable Bhavabhūti, considering the employment of correct words (*sādhuśabda*) to be a religious duty (*dharma*) based on such scriptural injunctions as, "A single word, rightly understood and properly employed... and so forth, [composed this work], thinking: "Poetry leads to fame, to the attainment of wealth, to knowledge of worldly conduct, and to the destruction of that which is inauspicious."

"Immediately leading to supreme bliss through instruction comparable to that of a beloved woman"—by this [verse], perceiving that the nature of poetry (*kāvyātman*) is a cause of abundant spiritual welfare, and desiring to describe Rāma alone—who is delightful in every quality—in the form of a poem according to the principle "if [the subject] has been trodden by predecessors," and having discerned the superiority of the dramatic work (*dṛśyaprabandha*) over the recitable work (*śrāvyaprabandha*), wishing to compose a *nāṭaka* because of its preeminence therein, and intending to relate the later life (*uttaracarita*) by means of the *Uttararāmacarita*, [he likewise intended to relate] the earlier life...

While composing the drama titled *Mahāvīracarita*, he composes the *nāndī*—the primary constituent of the *pūrvaraṅga*, which is itself a part of the *prastāvanā*—beginning with the words "atha" and so forth.
This word "atha" is auspicious.
As it has been said: "The syllable *oṃ* and the word 'atha'—these two were formerly the mouth of Brahmā."
"Having pierced the throat, both emerged; therefore, they are both auspicious.
This is the established doctrine of the grammarians (*śābdika*) that this [sound] is auspicious by its very nature, like the sound of a drum.
To the "Self-abiding One" (*svasthāya*), who, according to the Śruti, "is established in his own majesty," abides in himself alone.
The meaning is "to that which has no other support.
"To the eternal" means to that which is devoid of origination and destruction.

"To the one whose sins are destroyed" means to that which is free from the evils of old age, death, suffering, and so forth, and which, through its own connection, destroys the association with such evils in others as well.
"Because of the Vedic scripture stating, 'All evils turn back from here,' [it is said:
to Him by whom sequence and division have been abandoned—that is, to Him who has relinquished both succession (paurvāparya) and internal differentiation (vibhāga).
By virtue of His eternity and partlessness, it is intended that He has abandoned sequence and division."
To the light of consciousness;
for light is indeed illuminating—
to that light whose nature is consciousness.
By the word *caitanya*, there is the exclusion of the third element (*bhūtatṛtīya*).

Alternatively, it means "to Him whose light is consciousness"—that is, the knowledge produced by yoga and scripture which is the illuminator. Or else, it means "to the light of consciousnesses," that is, to the illuminator of cognitions.

"According to the Vedic scripture, 'That is the pure light of lights,' salutations to such a God— whose nature is radiance, who sports, who desires victory, who is worthy of praise, who rejoices, and who is the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān).
The etymological derivation of the word *deva* in these aforementioned senses should be understood through [the root] *div*, meaning 'to sport' and so forth."

By these words, the meaning of such scriptural passages as "This Self is free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light" has been kept in mind. This is an auspicious invocation in the form of a salutation.
As it has been said: "A benediction, a salutation, or a mention of the subject matter—these constitute its opening.
This is the *nāndī* consisting of eight quarters. As it has been said: "Because it is always employed as being joined with words of benediction..."
Therefore, it is designated as *nāndī* for [ceremonies concerning] gods, brahmins, kings, and others;
it consists of twelve or eight metrical feet.
Thus it is said.

By the phrase "to the god" (*devāya*), it is indicated that Rāmadeva—who is to be described in the upcoming passage, "he led [him] to Rāmadeva"—is the subject of description here. By the phrase "whose sins were destroyed" (*hatapāpmanaḥ*), it is indicated that the slaying of Vālin, Rāvaṇa, and others is the subject of description here.
For this very reason, it is indicated that the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is predominant.
As it has been said: "That in which either the heroic or the erotic sentiment is described as the primary element, and which is endowed with a well-known protagonist, is cited as a *nāṭaka*.
By the phrase "of the light of consciousness" (*caitanyajyotiṣaḥ*), the well-known status of the protagonist is also indicated.

By the phrase "to him who has abandoned the distinction of sequence," it is indicated that the subject of the poem is to be followed by [the sage] Jāmadagnya and others, through the non-perception of distinctions such as age, order, and caste.
By the word "to the god" (*devāya*), his sporting with Jānaki and so forth is indicated.
Thus, in this manner, the meaning of the poem is suggested both through its sense and its words.
As it has been said: "Even a slight indication of the meaning of a poem, whether by way of its sense or its words. (1)
Regarding the phrase "ending with the *nāndī*": this *nāndī* belongs to Nandin.
As it has been said: "The *nāndī* is the beloved of Nandīśvara."
"At the end of that," meaning at its conclusion, the *sūtradhāra* speaks;
the *sūtradhāra* is the master Bharata.
"Of the Blessed One," and so forth.

Of the Blessed One, who is full of sovereignty and the rest as described in the verse: "The term *bhaga* is said to refer to the six: complete sovereignty, valor, fame, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion";
[and] of Kālapriyānātha, the Lord of the Mother named Kālapriyā.
The reading "Kālapriyānāthasya," employing the word *priya* with a short vowel at its end, is frequently observed. Even there, the meaning remains as before;

for in the compound name *Kālapriyānātha*, which designates a specific Lord (Īśvara) of a particular sacred field (*kṣetra*), the optional shortening occurs by virtue of the rule: "In the case of feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp*, [shortening is] frequent in names and Vedic meters. (*Pāṇini 6.3.63*)
During the journey or the festival,
the noble sirs command and instruct.
He states that manner by means of the words beginning with "Great Person" (mahāpuruṣa), and so forth.
In whatever context or literary work there is a profound, unshakeable, terrifying, and fear-inducing—
this being a compound of two adjectives—
the "exertion" (*saṃrambha*) of the Great Man, that is, the steadfast effort of the *dhīrodātta* hero.
The word "to be explained" (*pratipādya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣa*).

Furthermore, in that literary composition (*saṃdarbha*) which possesses the quality called *prasāda* (clarity), as stated in the passage beginning "clarity, alliteration, clarity, evenness," it has been said:
"That which consists of words with well-known meanings is declared to be *prasāda*."

The remainder [of the sentence] is that speech (*bhāratī*) becomes both harsh (*karkaśā*) and of vast meaning (*vipulārthā*), possessing an abundance of objects of cognition (*prameya*) divided into the categories of the expressed (*vācya*) and the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).

Alternatively, "clearly harsh" (*prasannakarkaśā*) means having a composition of slightly soft meaning; it is of vast meaning and rich in the suggested, which is to say that the *vṛtti* called *bhāratī* comes into being.
As it has been said: "The *bhāratī* *vṛtti* is held to have a composition of slightly soft meaning. (2)

Furthermore, in a literary composition (*saṃdarbha*) where the characters are non-worldly (*aprākṛta*), meaning devoid of ordinary human speech, and who occupy specific roles such as Rāma or Paraśurāma (Jāmadagnya), the rasa that exists as the primary element to be employed—when tasted by the audience as the nature of unsurpassed bliss—is the heroic (*vīra*) permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*). This consists of an internal combustion of the mind provoked by an offense committed by an enemy; it is a form of anger (*krodha*) that is subtle when directed toward specific focal objects (*ālambana*) such as Vasiṣṭha or Viśvāmitra, yet becomes manifest through those very subtle means when directed toward focal objects such as Rāma or Jāmadagnya.
It is divided—that is, made possessed of distinctions—by means of manifest differences and specific states in each respective substratum, across all the aforementioned objects of focus;
that is to say, it is rendered characterized by mutual distinctness. ||3||
The connection with the preceding [text] is: "They command that this composition must be enacted.
Here, by the term "Great Man" (*mahāpuruṣa*), there is the exclusion of [other types of works such as] *prakaraṇa* and so forth;
by the phrase "the heroic sentiment" (*vīro rasaḥ*), there is the exclusion of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*).

By the word "serene" (*prasanna*), the inclusion of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and other sentiments is indicated; by the word "terrifying" (*bhīṣaṇa*), the inclusion of the fearful (*bhayānaka*) is indicated.
By the phrase "great person" (*mahāpuruṣa*), the renown of both the hero and the plot is indicated. Likewise: "Where either the heroic or the erotic is described as the primary [sentiment]..."

The meaning of the verse—"That is declared to be a *nāṭaka* which possesses a renowned protagonist"—is reflected here. Upon further inquiry into its specific details, it is concluded that the *Mahāvīracarita* itself is such a composition, due to its similarity in the aforementioned qualities and generally in its verbal expression.
This is what he states with the words beginning "the *Mahāvīracarita*," and so forth.
"By these venerable noble ones, it has been indicated— that is, commanded— by means of inference from the sense.
'Vaśyā' and so forth means 'one whose speech is submissive.'"

The speech of a poet who has attained transcendent vision and possesses mastery over the operation of his own words—that mass of sounds consisting of a collection of verbal and nominal forms—is what is to be represented; this is the ellipsis.
Furthermore, that narrative sequence, which takes the form of the poet’s speech and is characterized by command over language, concerns Rāma and is delightful through all its qualities;
it "becomes" [such], this is the ellipsis.

Furthermore, we have obtained—that is, reached—a person, namely the assembly of spectators, who serves as a touchstone for the purpose of testing the excellence of the "outflow of speech," which is the aesthetic flavor (rasa) such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) produced by that speech; this touchstone consists of the refinement involved in discerning the meaning.
[This is the ellipsis: "by us. ||4||
"So 'ham" and so forth.
"So 'ham" means "I, who have been commanded by the member of the assembly. This refers to the specific [work] such as the poet's poem that is about to be described.
"Exists," and so forth. "In the Dakṣiṇāpatha" means on the path (*pathin*) of the southern direction (*dakṣiṇā-diś*).
The suffix *ap* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) by the rule "ṛkpūrabdhūḥpathāmānakṣe."
The meaning is: in the region to the south of the Śarāvatī river.
The Taittirīyas are those who study what was proclaimed by Tittiri.
The Kāśyapas are those who are descendants of Kaśyapa.
The great teachers (*mahopādhyāya*) are the preceptors of those who study the branches [of the Vedas] (*caraṇa*);
they "purify the row" (*paṅktipāvana*), which is the understood completion of the sentence. They are "foremost" (*agrya*) among all the Vedas and all the expositions (*pravacana*).
"Those born in a lineage of Vedic scholars (śrotriya) are to be known as purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvana)," so says Manu.
Those who maintain the five fires—the Gārhapatya, Āhavanīya, Dakṣiṇāgni, Sabhya, and Āvasathya—are called "pañcāgnayaḥ.
Those by whom the vow (vrata)—consisting of the fixed duties to be performed as prescribed in the Śruti such as "His vow is..."—is maintained are described as "dhṛtavrataḥ."
"Somapīthinaḥ" means those who have drunk the Soma; "Udumbaras" is their name;
this is the name of their lineage.
The meaning is that those who discourse on Brahman—those habituated to teaching the Supreme Brahman who is to be known through the Vedāntas—are residing there.
Regarding the phrase "the son of such-and-such" (*āmuṣyāyaṇa*) and so forth:
the son of "that one" (*amuṣya*) is *āmuṣyāyaṇa*.

The suffix *phak* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *naḍādi* group. By the rule "āmuṣyāyaṇa-āmuṣyaputra-" and so forth, there is no elision (*luk*) of the genitive case-ending. One who is the descendant of those [ancestors] is *tadāmuṣyāyaṇaḥ*.
The meaning is "the son of someone belonging to him. The grammatical construction is like that of the phrase "Devadatta’s teacher's house.

He is the fifth descendant—that is, the grandson of the grandson—of such a venerable (tatrabhavataḥ), worshipful (pūjyasya), great poet who performed the Vājapeya sacrifice (vājapeyayājinaḥ), having offered the Vājapeya rite.
Of him whose name is well-grasped and whose name is to be celebrated— for it is said, "He is one whose name is well-grasped whose remembrance bestows happiness at dawn"—
the grandson of Bhaṭṭa Gopāla.

The son born of Nīlakaṇṭha, whose fame is purifying and whose glory is sanctifying—he who has the name Śrīkaṇṭhapadalāñchana (marked by the title Śrīkaṇṭha). According to the *Ratnamālā*, "lāñchana" means both "name" and "mark";
this is the name given by his father.

Bhavabhūti, who was learned in words, sentences, and the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and proficient in grammar, logic (*tarka*), and Mīmāṃsā, was given the name "Bhavabhūti" by the king—who was delighted by his composition of the verse beginning with "May Sāmba purify Bhavabhūti, whose form is sanctified"—because of that very verse.
He is the son of Jatukarṇī; "Jatukarṇī" is the name of his mother, and he is her son.
He is our friend's relative.
The meaning is "a friend.

In the section beginning with "The suffix *dheya* is applied after words denoting a portion, a form, or a name," the suffix *dheya* is added to the word *mitra* in its own sense by the rule "also after *mitra*. Let this be understood by the wise.
The meaning is "let them know.
Regarding the words "the best" and so forth: among the great seers (maharṣis), those of truthful speech, Aṅgiras is like Aṅgiras himself.
The teacher of this [author] was a treasury of knowledge whose name did not deviate from its true meaning—the most excellent among the supreme ascetics (paramahaṃsas) of the highest stage of life;
"he is," is the ellipsis to be supplied. ||5||
"By him," and so forth;
by that aforementioned Bhavabhūti.
Of those who harm righteousness (*dharmadruh*).
This [word] ends in the second case (accusative). It refers to the subduer (*damayituḥ*) of those who harm the Dharma, such as Rāvaṇa and others;
this [word] ends in the suffix *tṛn*.
Of Rāma, the delight of the Raghus, who is to be instructed;

he is a compound of adjectives meaning "he who is both a hero, wonderful, and beloved. His state is "heroic-wonderful-belovedness" (*vīrādbhutapriyatā*); by that [state], he is so described as one by whom the root of the three worlds' distress—the root of wretchedness, or the root of anger—has been uprooted.
The *Viśva* lexicon states: "The word *manyu* means dejection, sacrifice, and anger.

Thus, it is described as having "abundant" (*astoka*), meaning vast, heroism—that is, the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*)—and as having "weighty" (*guru*), meaning excessive, rashness—that is, terrifying action.
Furthermore:
the wondrous and marvelous deeds of the delight of the Raghus—beginning from the defeat of Jamadagni’s son and ending with the slaying of Rāvaṇa—have been composed;
that is to say, they have been set forth in a continuous literary work. ||6||
"May they fulfill [it]" means may they complete and purify it.
And this was stated by that Bhavabhūti, the son of a *śrotriya*— one who has studied the Vedas in their entirety— in the passage beginning with "Prācetasa," and so forth.
The offspring of Varuṇa Pracetas, a bull among sages and a lord of munis;
the word *vṛṣa* is derived as ending in *n* by the rule "kaniny uvṛṣi... and so forth.
He is the foremost of poets, the first among those of far-reaching vision—Vālmīki.

He has composed—that is, set forth in a literary work—the purifying and sacred life-story of Rāma, the Lord of the Raghus. In that narrative of Rāma’s deeds, even the words of me, a devotee full of devotion, though I am unworthy of such a task, have come together in harmony.
The use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is according to the rule "after the roots *gam*, *ṛ*, and *cchi*," and by the Vārttika "also after *ṛ*, *śru*, and *dṛś*."

The suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule "sarti-śāsty-artibhyaś-ca. Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the rules prescribing augments, there is an absence of the augment *āṭ*; or, because of the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahulam*) in the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there may be an absence of *āṭ* even outside of Vedic usage.
When these words of mine are impelled by devotion, may the virtuous, with delighted minds and compassionate hearts, being wise and learned, cultivate them with affection;
for it is said: "Devotion is defined as meditation preceded by love. (7)

The *pāriṣadas* are those who have shown favor and bestowed grace. A *pariṣad* is an assembly (*samāja*) of virtuous persons (*satām*) and wise counselors (*sanmantriṇām*); thus, "those belonging to that assembly" are the *pāriṣadas*. The suffix *ṇa* is applied to the word *pariṣad* by means of a formal separation (*yogavibhāga*).
Because of its unprecedented nature, because of its novelty;
a portion, a part, of the narrative— that is, of the historical account—
at the commencement, at the beginning of the composition.
One who is about to be initiated (*dīkṣiṣyamāṇaḥ*) is one who will enter the initiation for sacrifice on the following day.

[He was the son] of Ajakṣvāka, a descendant of Ikṣvāku; the elision of the suffix *ṭi* occurs according to the rule beginning with "dāṇḍināyana. He was one whose domestic priest (*purodhāḥ*) or family chaplain (*purohitaḥ*) was Vasiṣṭha.
And he is Viśvāmitra.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Vijaya":

[the sage] intends to cause the innate valor—the elder brother—of Vijaya (the conqueror of enemies) to expand and become exalted by means of weapons such as the *Jṛmbhaka* and others; and he is the seed, that is, the cause, of the benefit to the world, which constitutes the purpose of the Lord’s incarnation, namely the removal of thorns and other acts of assistance for the people.
And it has been said by Parāśara: "She is eternally inseparable from Viṣṇu and is the benefactress of the worlds.
[The word] "Maithilī" refers to Sītā;
[the word] "Rāmadeva" is to be drawn back [to apply to this as well].
Intending to bring Lord Rāma [to that place],
he led him— who was the vessel and recipient of praiseworthy auspiciousness and welfare through the destruction of the ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa) and the annihilation of Rāvaṇa’s lineage—
to Lord Rāma, who was accompanied by his two assistants, namely the bow and the younger brother (Lakṣmaṇa).
The word "his own penance grove" (svatapovana) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
Here, by the phrase "of Kālapriyānātha," the location is indicated; by the phrase "on the journey" (yātrāyām), the time is specified;
and by the phrase "the exertion of a great man" (mahāpuruṣasaṃrambha) and so forth, the purpose of the action is communicated.
By the words "asti khalu" and so forth, the praise of the poet is offered; by the words "tenedaṃ" and so forth, the praise of the poem is offered.

As it has been said: "The announcement of the subject matter to be performed, the specification of place and time, and the praise of the poet, the poem, the actors, and so forth, constitute the *prarocanā* (the prologue). ||8||
"Having been invited," and so forth.
"He" refers to the one who is well-known [Rāma], or the one introduced by the word "Maithila" in the preceding verse. "The Maithilī" refers to Sītā.

King Janaka, the lord of Videha, having undertaken the sacrificial initiation (*dīkṣā*), was invited—that is, summoned for the necessary performance of the sacrifice—by Viśvāmitra; he sent his younger brother, his half-brother.
The implication is that according to scriptural injunctions such as "one who is initiated neither gives gifts nor performs oblations," the arrival of an initiated person is prohibited.
That brother of Janaka, known by the name Kuśadhvaja, this king standing before us, approaches accompanied by Sītā and Urmilā.
The word "stage" (raṅgasthalam) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Here, the introductory element (prastāvanāṅga) called *prayogātiśaya* is mentioned.
As it has been said: "This is considered *prayogātiśaya* because of the introduction [with the words] 'This is he'. ||9||
Thus they both exit—
the actor and the stage-manager— onto the stage (the remainder of the sentence). This constitutes the *prastāvanā* (prologue).

The definition of that [opening] is as follows: "When the Sūtradhāra addresses the Naṭī, the Māriṣa, or the Vidūṣaka with striking speech that introduces the subject matter of his own work, that is the Āmukha;
or it may be called the Prastāvanā."

Now the act (*aṅka*) is introduced. As for the definition of an act: "An act is performed by characters present on the stage, preceded by the manifestation of the *bindu* (plot-continuity), and is the locus of various types of plot-constructions and aesthetic sentiments."
Then, "she enters," and so forth.
"Then" means immediately after the departure of the *sūtradhāra* and others.
"And the two maidens" implies that they enter as well.
"O long-lived ones," is a dual vocative addressing Sītā and Ūrmilā, who possess an extraordinary lifespan worthy of aspiration.
"By one who has faith"— meaning by one endowed with the faith consisting of the certainty that the result will inevitably follow— one should pay homage, that is, bow down and venerate them.
"Jaha" and so forth.
"Kaniṣṭhatātaḥ" means the younger brother of the father.
"Tathāstu" (so be it) is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Here, by the phrase "by one who has faith," the *upakṣepa* (the initial suggestion), which is a limb (*aṅga*) of the *mukha-sandhi* (the opening juncture), is stated; for it consists of the deposition of the seed (*bīja*), namely the effort in the form of Viśvāmitra’s undertaking of Sītā and Rāma’s marriage and so forth.
As it is said: "The deposition of the seed is the *upakṣepa*.
Regarding the term "fourth":
This Viśvāmitra is the fourth *medhyāgni* (sacrificial fire); he is the fourth *pariśuddhāgni* (purified fire).

While three fires are well-known, this fire surpasses even them. He is described as such because he is the cause of all prosperity (*abhyudaya*), because he is invincible, and because of his supreme brilliance.
And this is with reference to one who maintains the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*);
the word *hi* indicates well-known fact;
or alternatively (*api vā*).
The meaning is "moreover.
This Viśvāmitra is the fifth Veda;
while the four Vedas beginning with the Ṛgveda are well known, this Veda excels even them.
The characterization [of the Mahābhārata] as being of the nature of the Veda is due to its constant instruction in what is beneficial, being free from defects such as error and negligence.
And this should be understood as being [possible] through the non-perception of the Bhārata [as a separate work].
Or else—
This Viśvāmitra is a moving holy ford (*tīrtha*), one that wanders about, possessing sacred waters and being a field of merit.

For the lexicon states: "The word *tīrtha* is well known to denote scripture, sacrifice, a sacred field, means, a teacher, and a minister; as well as an incarnation, a rishi, water frequented by sages, and the menses."
Because he comes of his own accord and bestows prosperity independently of pilgrimages and the like, he is described as being "mobile" (jaṅgama).
The word "vā" means "or," that is to say, "alternatively."

This is the *mūrtisaṃcara*, meaning one who moves by means of a form (*mūrtyā*). [The word] *saṃcara* is derived from the root *car* preceded by the prefix *sam*, with the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134.
The compound is formed with the third case ending according to Pāṇini 2.1.32: "In a *kṛt*-derivative, the third case [is compounded] with the agent or the instrument, in many instances."

Dharma is that which is the unmediated means to the fruit, produced by the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, and consisting of the *apūrva*.
Since this well-known Dharma is imperceptible and thus susceptible to being mistaken for something else, it is metaphorically described as having a corporeal form.
In the first half of this verse, there are two instances of "double metaphor" (*anubhayarūpaka*).

The distinction, however, is that in the latter half there are two *adhikarūpaka*s (metaphors of superimposition). For Dharma, when made known by faultless means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), being embellished by the place and so forth—which assist its non-acceptance—and by fire—which assists its acceptance—accomplishes prosperity directly by itself. Thus, Viśvāmitra possesses a similarity to Dharma along with its attendants; it should be understood that four metaphors have been stated. ||10||
It is called Sāṃkāśya because it was established by Saṃkāśa;
the suffix *ṇya* is applied according to the rule "saṃkāśādibhyo ṇyaḥ. The word "nātha" (lord) is connected to Kuśadhvaja as its possessor.
"Indeed not," and so forth.
No other person, by virtue of greatness or venerability, is certainly not superior to the sage Viśvāmitra; that is to say, he is indeed not greater than Viśvāmitra.
"Of whom," and so forth.

This *traiśaṅkavam* belongs to Viśvāmitra, the son of Triśaṅku; it refers to the raising to heaven, in his own physical body, of Triśaṅku who had attained the state of a *caṇḍāla* due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha.
He whose tail (*śepa*) is like that of a dog (*śunas*) is Śunaḥśepa;
according to the rule "the genitive case is not elided after *śvan* when followed by *śepa*, *puccha*, or *lāṅgūla*," there is no elision of the sixth case-ending.
This [work] concerning Śunaḥśepa is called *Śaunaḥśepa*.
In both the preceding and the present case, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "this belongs to him" (*tasyedam*).
It concerns the saving of the life of Śunaḥkṣepa—who had been abandoned by his mother and father and had sought refuge—by means of the instruction of specific mantras.

Those who know the narratives—that is, those who know the texts recounting past events—declare that there is an immeasurable and unfathomable collection of wonders, a multitude of marvelous deeds, consisting of the paralyzing and the thwarting of Rambhā when she arrived for the purpose of breaking [Nala’s] asceticism by means of making her appear deformed.
Because the word *uttara* (subsequent) is independent of the word *tat* (that), this forms a single syntactical unit with the preceding sentence.
"In this," and so forth.
O,
not so!
Ā ba ā
Not born, not produced.
He is not indeed.

To him who was thus addressed, and who was requested—that is, entreated—for peace—the cessation of his anger—by Brahmā and the others, the four-faced ones and foremost of the gods, the teachers of the thirty [deities].
According to the list of verbal roots beginning with "nāthṛ nādhṛ yācñopatāpe," the root *nāth* signifies entreaty.

Here, one should recall the Puranic narrative that Brahmā and the other gods sought the favor of Viśvāmitra, who had set about agitating the world, saying: "I shall make another Indra, or the world shall be without an Indra."

He is so described because he is the abode (*dhāman*)—the locus—of ascetic power (*tapas*), which consists of the discipline of emaciating the body, and of spiritual splendor (*tejas*), which is the capacity to overcome others; and because he has personally attained (*upanata*) Brahminhood (*brahma*), rooted in his own asceticism, through the words of Vasiṣṭha.

Furthermore, he is so described because in this Guru, the seer of mantras, who is the dwelling place (*nivāsa*) of the fourteen branches of knowledge beginning with the Vedas, Viśvāmitra has established (*upahita*) the management of a household (*kuṭumbavyavahṛti*), including the duties of domestic life such as the giving away of daughters in marriage.
Among householders in this world, you alone are the praiseworthy householder (*gṛhamedhī*).
[The suffix] *ṇini* is applied here by the rule *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye* following the root *medhṛ* (to meet).
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *gṛha* may be used in the plural (*gṛhāḥ*) to mean houses; these two [forms] may also denote a dwelling or a wife."
This is called the *parikara* (elaboration), a constituent of the juncture (*saṃdhy-aṅga*), defined as the expansion of the seed (*bīja*) which consists of the sage’s exertion.
As it has been said: "The expansion of the seed is the *parikara*. (11)
You speak—that is, you utter—words that are *sūnṛtam*: true and pleasant.

"Possessing a future result that is excellent" (*prakṛṣṭakalyāṇodarka*) means that which has a future fruit (*udarka*) that is preeminent (*prakṛṣṭa*), surpassing all else, auspicious (*kalyāṇa*), and blessed (*maṅgala*).
Those whose association (*saṃgama*) or connection (*saṃbandha*) is of such a nature are described as such.
"The future result of time and its fruit shall be [theirs]," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
Those by whom Brahman—the Supreme Self—has been directly realized, that is, made the object of most clear knowledge, are so described.
In the analysis of the compound as "great ones and they are seers," it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

"‘The sages are speakers of truth’—here, by the words ‘O good charioteer,’ and so forth, the *saṃdhy-aṅga* (limb of the juncture) called *samādhāna* (resolution), which consists of the acceptance of the seed (*bīja*) in the form of the sages' exertion, has been stated.
As it is said: ‘The acceptance of the seed is *samādhāna*’."

"Tamāṃsi" (darknesses): even from a single conversation among these great sages, or even during a mere exchange of words, the "tamāṃsi"—the qualities of darkness (*tamaḥ*) that cause ignorance—of people are destroyed and perish.
Furthermore, abundant (*bhūyān*), extensive tranquility (*upaśamaḥ*), which is the cessation of the internal senses, matures and increases.
Moreover, both here and there, in this world and in the next, auspiciousness—the accomplishment of blameless and desired goals—spreads and increases.
Now, the word "atha" (now) marks the commencement of a new statement.
Their association—a specific kind of contact such as sitting together in one place—bestows or grants an indescribable greatness, an ineffable majesty.
The words of these people—who have become serene or who have attained serenity quite unexpectedly—beget and produce for the world immeasurable and indefinable fruit and happiness.
Here, the phrase "bestows greatness" alludes to the Vedic scripture: "He attains the greatness of Brahman.
In this context, because of the description of the qualities of the seed (the cause), the dramatic element called *vilobhana* (enticement) is stated. ||12||
"Harita," and so forth:
"harita" means dark green due to trees and the like; that whose surrounding vicinity (*parisara*) or immediate area is such is described as "tathokta. It is delightful by virtue of such a forest.
Surrounded and encompassed by the river Kauśikī,
there is seen the hermitage of that seer Viśvāmitra, known as Siddhāśramapada— the site of the Siddhāśrama— a sacred dwelling-place.
[He went] with himself as the third.

With the addition of himself to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, there is the state of Viśvāmitra being "the third including himself" (*ātmanātṛtīyakatva*). The non-elision (*aluk*) of the third case ending in *ātmanaḥ* is according to the rule "in the sense of completing [a number] with oneself. Kuśikanandana refers to Viśvāmitra.
If it is thus, then Viśvāmitra—
[the grounds] near the hermitage, meaning the areas in the vicinity of the hermitage—
must not be transgressed; they must not be touched even by foot.
Thus it is well known;
"whatever you command" is the sense, with the words "let that be so" understood as the remainder.

Regarding the term *rakṣoghnāni*: on an auspicious day (*sudina*), those [rites] characterized by the *rākṣasa* [oblation], which pacify obstacles and so forth, are called *rakṣoghnāni* because they destroy (*ghnanti*) the *rākṣasas*. The suffix *ṭak* is applied to the root *han* according to the rule *amanuṣyakartṛke ca*.

Auspicious rites—actions conceived as the causes for the attainment of desired goals that are beneficial to one's limbs—should be performed. Furthermore, the marriage—the ritual union of Vaidehī, the daughter of King Videha, and the scion of Raghu, the best of the Raghus—should be arranged and brought to completion.
The word "kalpyāni" (to be arranged) is understood here, modified by changing its gender to feminine and its number to singular to agree with the following nouns.
Furthermore, "in our family" means in our house;
according to the *Ratnamālā*, the word *kula* is used for a house, a body, a country, a common quality, and a lineage.

*Īkṣāpraveśaḥ* (entrance into initiation) refers to the entrance—that is, the initial connection—into the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that the sacrifice must be performed during initiation, [expressed as]: "I must perform this; here, the sixth case is used according to the rule *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā*.

Alternatively, *dīkṣāpraveśo dārakriyāmaṅgalāni ca naḥ kalpyāni* ("the entrance into initiation, the marriage rites, and the auspicious ceremonies are to be arranged for us") is a single sentence; in the word *kalpyāni*, there is a neuter collective remainder (*napuṃsakaikaśeṣa*) according to the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām*.
Because of the optionality of treating it as a singular unit (*ekavadbhāva*), the plural number is used.

Furthermore, those various and manifold wonderful deeds of the Blessed Viṣṇu—who is Rāma by nature and the enemy of the Daityas—consisting of events such as the destruction of Tāṭakā and her sons, must be relied upon by us; that is, they must be accepted as necessary for the welfare (*kṣema*) of the worlds, the auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) of the people, or for the protection of what has been obtained. According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *kṣema* is not feminine; it denotes auspiciousness or the preservation of what has been acquired."

Furthermore, there is the genitive case [in *asmākam*] according to the rule "the genitive may optionally be used for the agent of gerundives" (*kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā*). Moreover, in the phrase "we" (*vayam*) and "I" (*aham*), the plural number is used for the singular according to the rule "after *asmad*, the dual and plural [are used for the singular]" (*asmado dvayośca*).

Being *vyāprāḥ*—that is, being occupied (*vyāpṛtāḥ*) with the duties mentioned—the *Ratnamālā* states that "the word *vyāpra* means occupied or agitated. We rejoice; we become possessed of intense joy.
It is said that the limbs of the twilight [of passion] are characterized by joy and laughter. ||13||
Regarding the phrase "it was sent":
a verbal message was sent by me to Janaka, the royal sage of Mithilā.
To the question "What [was it]? he says: "Conduct," and so forth.
The sacrificer, even though he has begun but not yet completed the sacrifice— meaning, even though he is unworthy of arriving—
is addressed as "you are invited to the sacrifice" according to established custom.
Because an invitation is established by the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), the meaning is this:
although you were not worthy of coming since you had already commenced the sacrifice, you were nevertheless urged by me to come for the sake of my sacrifice.
However, it was further instructed that Kuśadhvaja, accompanied by Sītā and Urmilā, should be sent; this is to be connected with what precedes.
You should not come merely upon being invited; rather, Kuśadhvaja must be sent in your stead along with Sītā and Ūrmilā.

The two princes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, have been thus accepted as dear friends—that is, they have received the acceptance of friendship—by Janaka, the beloved friend. They are the descendants of Nimi and Janaka.
"Nimi and Janaka" is a designation for their progenitors. "In Videha" means in the country of Videha.
"Of them" refers to those [kings].

Sīradhvaja, whose name is Sīradhvaja, is an elder distinguished by his knowledge, age, and character; he is the heir of those royal seers born of Nimi and Janaka, and as such, he exists now at this time—this is the meaning. [He exists] for the sake of reviving whom, namely Sīradhvaja.
The dative case is used according to the rule: "And [the dative occurs] after a word that is the object of a verb whose sense is implied by another word ending in a kṛt-suffix.
Yājñavalkya is the sage.
Of Brahman—that is, of the Veda.
The meaning is "of the Śukla Yajurveda. He recited—that is, sang—the *pārāyaṇa*, the complete study.
In the subsequent [verse], the word "yat" (which) does not require the word "tat" (that).
"Of whom":
that well-known bow of Maheśvara, the bow of Śiva, which is worshipped in his house.
Now, "atha kim" is used here in the sense of acceptance.
"Regarding the Amarakośa entry: *'aṭagīkṛtau syād atha kim'*. It is heard:
there, in that house of Janaka."
"Yat" means:
"That this maiden was not born from a womb"—this is another marvel that is heard concerning her.
"Ayaṃ tu" means: "But this... [is as follows].
By that sacrificer, Sīradhvaja, who is engaged in the current sacrifice, this younger brother Kuśadhvaja has been sent to my house out of *vātsalya*—that is, from an excess of affection toward me.

[The word *vatsala* is derived from the root *vatseṣu sādhur vatsalaḥ*, meaning "kind toward calves," with the suffix *lac* according to the rule *vatsāṃsābhyāṃ kāmabale*; then, by adding the suffix *vyat* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇādi* class.
He has been dispatched to the home of one who is about to sacrifice—that is, one who is to perform a sacrifice.
Because the root *pra-iṣ* (to send) takes two objects, the "cup" (*graha*) is also an object. ||15||

Regarding the word *tat*: therefore, when this *rājanya* who is a *śrotriya*— one who has studied the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs— is present, there is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*) between the word *rājanya*, which denotes a caste (*jāti*), and the word *śrotriya*, according to the rule beginning with "poṭā-yuvati-".
By the rule "śrotriyaṃśchando'dhīte," the word *śrotriya* is prescribed for one who studies the Veda (*chandas*).
[This was said] by you two, dear ones, with excellent and affectionate humility.
"Thus" (*evam*) signifies acceptance.
Having gazed upon and contemplated;
for Amara states: "Nirvarṇana, nidhyāna, darśana, ālokana, and īkṣaṇa all mean 'seeing'.
Regarding the word *prakṛtyā*:
"By nature" means by its own essence (*svabhāvataḥ*).
The instrumental case is used according to the rule "an addition [should be made] for *prakṛti* and so forth.
"Possessing auspicious fortune" (*puṇyalakṣmīkau*) means possessing auspicious splendor (*puṇyaśrīkau*).

"By the rule *uraḥprabhṛtibhyaḥ kap*, the suffix *kap* is applied because [the word *uraska*] belongs to the *uraḥprabhṛti* group. The inquiry 'What are these two *kā*s? is an internal reflection. In that regard, he states the determination of the specific [gender] based on internal evidence with the words beginning 'It is known' (*jñāyate*) and so forth."
The two princes, having undergone the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), were indeed recognized—that is, they were made the objects of a cognition consisting of a presumptive identification.
The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis.
The meaning is that no specific distinction, such as their mother or father, was known. ||16||
Regarding the phrase "of the second":
this refers both to the second of these two youths and to the second of the colors.
The suffix *tīya* is applied to the word *dvi* in the sense of ordinal number according to the rule *dvestīyaḥ*.

It is beautiful with the kṣatriya caste, the first stage of life (the student stage), fresh youth, and childhood; the meaning is that it possesses the splendor derived from this triad beginning with the kṣatriya caste. "Aho" expresses wonder. ||17||
"Surely these two princes have undergone the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Thus he presents a sign (*liṅga*) for the previously mentioned point, beginning with "For instance":
"With the crest-lock. This means that on their backs—that is, all around the back—there were arrows whose feathers (*kaṅkapattra*) were touched, or joined, by the crest-lock (*cūḍā*).
The meaning is "of two parts.
He wears a pair of quivers, a yoke of two scabbards;
his chest bears a small, pure, purifying mark made of ashes, and he wears the skin of a ruru deer.

He was bound and restrained by a girdle and waist-band made of *maurva* grass; he wore a crimson garment dyed with *mañjiṣṭhā* below his chest; in one hand he held a bow, and in the other hand [he held] a staff of *aśvattha* wood—this is the meaning.
In the reading "another [staff] of *pippala*," the meaning is that it is another, distinct from the bow-staff.

In this regard, one should consult the statement of Āpastamba, "The bowstring of a Rājanya is made of *jyā* [sinew], that of a Rājanya is dyed with madder (*māñjiṣṭha*), and that of a Rājanya is of *raurava* [deer-skin]," as well as the statement of Gautama, "[The staffs] are of *āśvattha* and *paippala* wood.
Regarding the phrase "the *raurava* for a Rājanya," the *Ujjvalā* commentary states, "The *ruru* is a spotted deer.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is to be understood that the two princes had already undergone their initiation (*upanayana*). ||18||
These two, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, are indeed of gentle appearance. I salute them.
The meaning is: "By means of salutation, I shall cause blessings to be uttered. The word *diṣṭyā* is used in the sense of joy;
as Amara states: "The words *diṣṭyā* and *samupajoṣam* are used in the sense of joy."
The construction is as follows: "I see you, who are like an embryo—meaning one to be nurtured—and who have come to our home, as being well. The meaning of "embrace me" is that one should hug me.
"Even," and so forth.
Even he—the lord of Videha, Sīradhvaja—who had commenced sacrifices (pravṛttayajñaḥ), meaning one who had begun the ritual, and who was not far removed [from such activity], was happy;
that is to say, he possessed happiness.
The family priest of the Janakas was Gautama, the son of Gautama;
the suffix *aṇ* is applied here according to the rule *ṛṣy-andhaka-vṛṣṇi-kurubhyaś-ca*.
Śatānanda is also [to be understood as] happy; this is to be supplied [from the previous verse]. ||19||

The noble one’s eldest brother, together with the priest Gautama, is his very own friend; that is to say, Sīradhvaja himself is possessed of the highest degree of happiness. [This is according to the rule:
"In cases of censure, praise, constant connection, or intensity..."

"In the case of a relationship, when existence is intended to be expressed, the suffixes *matup* and others are employed. Thus, here the suffix *matup* is used in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyana*). For that Sīradhvaja, in the manner previously described, the household duties—the engagement in domestic tasks—had "followed after" him; that is to say, they had come upon him.
"Paṇamāmo" means we bow down;
"lāṅgaleti" means being scratched by a ploughshare— that is, being furrowed by the tip of a plough.
The word "yajñabhūmeḥ" is in the ablative case;
the meaning is that this furrow which has emerged [from there] is Sītā. ||20||
"May it be auspicious!
Thus has been stated this seed-syllable (*bīja*), which consists of the form of the seer’s grace.
"Aside to another" (*janāntika*)—thus [it is called].

According to the statement: "But the meaning [of an aside] is to be understood by one person alone; subsequently, it may be made known to others through the context. Having called that 'janāntika' (aside), one should employ it in poetic composition," the sense is that Lakṣmaṇa says something which is unknown to Kuśadhvaja, Viśvāmitra, and the others, and is to be understood by Rāma alone.
"Ārya" means venerable.
"An extraordinary birth" means a wondrous origin; this much alone is a marvel, this much indeed is a wonder.
The sense is: "Is there any other marvel besides?
To this, Rāma says with the words beginning "utpatti" (birth), and so forth.
A *devayajana* is a sacrificial field where the gods are worshipped; from that [field] comes his birth or manifestation.

His father was Sīradhvaja, a king who was a proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādī*)—one who teaches the Supreme Self which is "supreme in every respect" and superior to everything in every way—and who was established in the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) consisting of the protection of the kingdom, as befits the Kṣatriya order.
The form of her, which is exceedingly serene and possessed of supreme grace, inspires affection for this Sītā in me and generates longing.
This is the sentence beginning with "utpattiḥ" (origination) and so forth;
therefore, the singular number in "karoti" (inspires) is justified.
Here, there is the *gumbha* ornament, according to the definition: "The *gumbha* is a causal chain (*kāraṇamālā*).
Here, by the phrase "he shows affection," the commencement consisting of longing (*autsukya*) is expressed.
As it has been said: "The mere onset of eagerness leads to the attainment of abundant fruit.

Thus, through these two—the seed (*bīja*) and the onset (*ārambha*)—the *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture) is described by the connection of affection (*sneha*) and the wish for welfare (*bhadram astu*). ||21||
"Who [is] you? and so forth.
*Pratāpa* (majesty) is the power to afflict enemies while remaining in one's own place; *vikrama* (valor) is the afflicting of enemies by means of an expedition;
*dharma* (virtue) is the means for attaining supramundane welfare.

The meaning is: "Who are these two Kṣatriya students standing before you, having emerged as if their majesty and prowess were personified by placing Dharma at their head? Whose sons are they, and what are their names? ||22||
The answer to that is: Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa;
"the two sons of Daśaratha" means the two sons of Daśaratha. [The suffix] *iñ* is applied here according to Pāṇini 4.1.95.
Those two, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa;
having approached—
[the object of their approach is] Kuśadhvaja, as is understood from the context.
"O Guru!"— this address is used because he is both a father's friend and a teacher. It is also implied that this same designation applies to a father-in-law as well.
That "the father of one's wife is one's own father" is established by the *Smṛti*.
"Daśarathaprasūtiḥ" means the offspring of Daśaratha;
according to the *Ratnamālā*, "prasūtiḥ" refers to both birth and a son.

"Not elsewhere" means that the birth or origin of these two, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, is not similar to— that is, not of the same kind as— anything other than the lineage or progeny of the descendants of Raghu.
The meaning is that their birth from the Raghu dynasty is entirely appropriate.

Where else could the birth of the moon and the Kaustubha gem have occurred except from the Ocean of Milk? From what other ocean than the Sea of Milk? The meaning is: from no other. This is the figure of speech known as *dṛṣṭānta* (the illustrative simile).
For the definition states: "If the state of being an original image and its reflection constitutes an illustration, that is the figure of speech [dṛṣṭānta]. ||23||

Regarding the word *śruta*: this nectar for the ears (*karṇāmṛta*), which is about to be spoken and is as enjoyable to the ears as nectar, has been heard previously; that is, it was already heard before.
Regarding the phrase *prāptā* and so forth:

By the Lord of Kosala, the son of Daśaratha, through the services and honors rendered to Ṛṣyaśṛṅga— which served as the cause— sons possessing holy splendor and purifying glory were obtained with great difficulty and sorrow;
indeed, all four of them, who were further endowed with brilliance,
meaning they were filled with the light of knowledge.

The connection is as follows: "It has been heard before that those who desire the further shore—that is, those who seek the ultimate goal—of the Veda in its form as the supreme good, which is the means for attaining the goals of human life, or of the goals of human life themselves, practice brahmacarya; they perform and observe the vow for the purpose of studying the meaning of the Veda. ||24||
Regarding the word *tad*:
here, it refers to the *ariṣṭatāti*—the cause of well-being—for you two princes.
[The suffix] *tāti* is applied to the word *ariṣṭa* according to the rule: "After *śiva*, *śam*, and *ariṣṭa*, [the suffix *tāti* is used in the sense of 'instrument' (*kara*)]."
"Kṣemaṃkara, ariṣṭatāti, śivatāti, and śivaṃkara"—thus says Amara. "Riṣṭa may mean inauspiciousness, security, destruction, a sword, or sin"—thus says the Ratnamālā.
Riṣṭa means auspiciousness; its opposite is ariṣṭa.
The cause of that is well-being (*ariṣṭatāti*). We desire it; we wish for it.
This is the third person plural present indicative form derived from the root *śās* with the prefix *āṅ* in the sense of "desiring," as recorded in the grammatical lists.
Regarding the word *siddha*:
the excellence of the progeny—the offspring of the Raghus, the descendants of Raghu—and the preeminence of qualities such as valor are indeed *siddha*, that is, already accomplished.
Therefore, there is nothing further to be desired; this is an elliptical reference (*ākṣepa*) to the meaning previously stated.
He specifies the excellence of the preeminence with the words beginning "yān" (whom).
Vasiṣṭha is the son of Mitra and Varuṇa, hence he is called Maitrāvaruṇi. The form "ānaṅ" is applied according to the rule "devatādvandve ca."
The suffix *iñ* is applied because [the word *āmnāya*] belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* class.

Regarding the injunction (*vidhi*)—which is purified, cleansed, and faultless by the *āmnāya*, that is, the Veda, and which is itself faultless because it is revealed by the Veda—he instructs you, meaning he excellently informs you concerning what is beneficial and what is harmful.
The term *śaśvat* (constantly) connects with both the preceding and the following [phrases].

Vasiṣṭha is their constant domestic priest; this is the meaning. "Having another object" means having another support or refuge; that which does not have such [another] is "not having another object" (ananyaviṣaya).
The meaning is that he is not dependent upon any other king.

The *adhikāra* (authority) consists in the protection and preservation of the *viśaḥ*, that is, of human beings; the meaning is that their sole purpose is for the sake of others (*pārārthya*). [I am] eternally established in you who possess this.
The meaning is that he exists eternally.
You alone are the primary protectors;
we and others are those who pay tribute to you—this is the sense.
For it has been said: "This entire earth formerly belonged to those [ancestors].
[They were] those who had obtained their bodies—meaning, those who were born—in the lineage of Manu, the son of Savitṛ (Sāvitra), which is most great and most worthy of worship.
"Ātman, effort, fortitude, intellect, nature, Brahman, and body"—thus says Amara.
The majesty—the unsurpassed excellence of qualities—of you kings who possess sovereignty free from all limiting conditions, is never at any time within the range of these two: speech and mind;
that is to say, it is not their object.
Here, knowledge is stated by the first quarter;
conduct is stated by the second;
and noble lineage is stated by the third.
Thus, the meaning is that this immeasurable majesty of yours consists in the excellence of your lineage, your power, your freedom from obstacles, and your supreme state. ||25||

Regarding the term *aśrānta*: those whose meritorious deeds—namely, excellent rites such as the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*)—are *aśrānta*, meaning untiring and uninterrupted, are so described.
By the word *aśrānta*, there is an exclusion of those [rites] performed for the sake of specific desires (*kāmya*).
The term "meritorious" (puṇya) excludes both [ordinary] actions and prohibited rites (abhicāra).
By this, it is established that [the subject refers to] the performance of actions that are means to liberation.
This was sung by the Blessed One: "Indeed, Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone."
Those whose fame consists primarily of sanctity—that is, those whose renown for possessing virtues is abundant—are described as such.
By the word *prāya* (primarily), it is understood that their fame also possesses the quality of being enjoyable (*bhogyatva*).
For sanctity and enjoyability are well-known to coexist.
In this context, when the abundance of one quality is stated, the mere presence of another is established even if not explicitly mentioned.
Since that which is beneficial is more esteemed than that which is merely pleasant, it is described as "consisting mostly of purifying [qualities].
The meaning is that her fame removes the sins of the worlds and is itself worthy of being enjoyed.

They are "knowers of great fortune" (*mahābhāgyavidaḥ*) because they know—that is, they understand—the great fortune (*mahābhāgyam*), which is the state of being highly blessed (*mahābhāgatvam*), the fruit of the excellence of lineage, learning, and conduct previously mentioned, and which consists of a preeminent degree of luck.
Those who possess great fortune (*bhāga*) or luck (*bhāgyam*) are thus called "highly blessed" (*mahābhāgāḥ*).
As the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *bhāga* [is used] in the sense of luck, in the sense of a form, and in the sense of a fourth part or a single portion."

From the word *mahābhaga*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because it belongs to the *brāhmaṇa*-class [of nominal stems]. You who have become such as this are alone capable of praising those kings of the Raghu dynasty; that is to say, you are worthy of praise.
The meaning is that your statement, "It is never within the range of speech or cognition," refers to objects other than yourself. ||26||
The settlement of Kauśika’s hermitage, the dwelling-place of Kauśika.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *āśrama*—not feminine—is used for a sage’s station, a monastery (*maṭha*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and so forth.
And according to Amara: "*Saṃstyāya* means a multitude and a settlement."
The shadow of the *vaikaṅkata* tree is *vaikaṅkatacchāyā*.
According to the rule "the word *chāyā* is neuter when denoting abundance," it takes the neuter gender.
We sit down (*āsmahe*) in that [shadow].
"By sitting upon [the āsa]"—thus [it is] *aiṃḍuttama*.
Alternatively, this [wood] comes from the *viṅkata* tree, hence it is *vaiṅkatī*; [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "this belongs to that."
"One whose shadow is made of *vaikaṅkata* wood" is what is meant;
the meaning is "in such a place as this.
The rest is as before.

In the *nepathya*, which is the place where the company of actors (*kuśīlavavarga*) resides—it is said that "the stage for the troupe of actors is called the *nepathya*"—there is the respectful repetition of "Victory! Victory! (*jaya jaya*).
What then?
Because of her excellence in splendor and her resemblance to a deity, she is called a "deity" (devatā).
Regarding the passage beginning with "Ahalyā," etc.:
Aucathya is the offspring of Ucathya;
[the suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "from Ṛṣis, Andhakas, Vṛṣṇis, and Kurus.
Āṅgirasa is the offspring of Aṅgiras.
By the rule beginning with *ṛṣya-andhaka-*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied. He desired— that is, he lusted after— that Ahalyā.

Because of the statement "āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā" (Pāṇini 3.1.31), there is an absence of the *ṇiṅ* suffix. Therefore, in the sense of "one who leaps upon or carries off the wife of Gautama"—referring to him who, under the influence of his desire for Ahalyā, leaped upon or carried off the wife of Gautama—the suffix *ṇini* is applied to the root *skand*, which is listed [in Dhātupāṭha 1.589] as meaning "motion and drying," according to the rule "supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye" (Pāṇini 3.2.78). [The result is *avaskandin*]. [He went to] Indra.
"They know [him] as 'the lover of Ahalyā'"—this is an imitation of the Vedic text "ahalyāyai jāraḥ.
[The compound] "ahalyāyā jāraḥ" is a genitive tatpuruṣa.
To the word "they know," the phrase "those who know the Vedas" is to be supplied as the subject.

Then, immediately after the wife's assault, the Blessed Gautama [pronounced] a curse (*manyu*)—that is, anger—upon her, Ahalyā. By means of that evil—the sin of enjoying another man—he made her body undergo the state of wood, stone, and so forth, which is to be experienced in the specific hell named Andhatāmisra.

And so it is said in the *Bhāgavata*: "In this very way, he who deceives a person and enjoys his wife and other possessions falls into the hell of Andhatāmisra; while being cast down and situated in that place of torment, his mind is destroyed and his vision is lost through agony, just as a tree whose roots are being severed—this they call Andhatāmisra.

Thus, this Ahalyā was released from that aforementioned sin; she was liberated (*niramucyata*) from that evil. [The form is derived from] the root *muc* with the suffix *yak* in the sense of the agent (*karmakartṛ*), or with the suffix *yak* in the sense of the object (*karman*), in the imperfect tense (*laṅ*).
"By the splendor of Rāmabhadra acting as the agent, and by reason of the previous conjunction.
Regarding "How? and so forth: "How? expresses astonishment.
He whose majesty (*anubhāva*), power (*prabhāva*), capability (*sāmarthya*), and potency (*śakti*) are immeasurable (*aprameya*) and indivisible (*aparicchedya*) is so described.
According to Amara, "majesty" (*anubhāva*) refers to power (*prabhāva*).
This [bow] belongs to Vikartana, the Sun; thus it is *Vaikartana*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "tasyedam" (Pāṇini 4.3.120). Thus, "the youth of that family" means Rāma.
"Filled with wonder," it is said;
wonder arises from her liberation from Ahalyā’s curse, and passion from her extraordinary beauty.
"Having gazed upon her" means having looked at her intently.

Having set aside [the others]—meaning, having concealed them so that Viśvāmitra and the rest would not know—the majesty (*anubhāva*) of this [Rāma] is like the creation of a body; it is similar to, or commensurate with, the creation of a body endowed with unsurpassed beauty.
[Regarding the passage beginning with] "To Rāma," etc.:
the noble Janaka [speaks of] the *traiyambaka* [bow], which belongs to Tryambaka (Śiva) and is impossible to counteract or turn back.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tasyedam*. The augment *aij* is added by the rule *nayvāyāṃ padāntābhyāṃ pūrvāai tu tābhyāmaic*.
The "stake" (*paṇa*) refers to the wealth [to be wagered] through the stringing of that bow, which entails the fixing of the bowstring.
The meaning is that the bride-price (*śulka*) consisted of the stringing of the bow.
"If he had not done so" means if he had not performed it; the word "by him" (*tena*) is to be supplied as the subject.
By that Janaka, Sītā was given to the one of meritorious luster and purifying splendor;
Daśaratha, the son of Daśaratha, is like the moon— this is a *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison).

"To him who was suitable and worthy"—that is to say, to the son of Daśaratha, who was like Rāma himself, possessed of meritorious splendor, and equal to the moon; had she been given to him, it would have been as if she were already given.
Here, because the common attribute of "producing delight" is not explicitly stated, the compound is an *upamita-samāsa* (a compound of comparison).

Since it is stated that a compound is formed even when the principal member is dependent [on another], the qualifiers such as *rāma* are construed with the referent of the word *dāśarathi* through identity (*tādātmya*). In the two forms *abhaviṣyat* and *akariṣyat*, the conditional suffix *lṛṅ* is applied according to the rule: "The conditional suffix *lṛṅ* is used when there is a cause for the conditional mood (*liṅ*) and there is a failure of the action (*kriyātipatti*)."

And thus, in the absence of the stipulation regarding the stringing of the formidable bow, it follows that [the condition] is an obstacle to the gift of the son of Daśaratha, whose nature is Rāma. ||27||
A *tāpasa* is one whose nature (*śīla*) is austerity (*tapas*).
According to the rule "after *chatra* and others, the suffix *ṇa* [is applied]" under the heading of *śīla*, [the form is derived].
One who possesses all *māyā* is thus called *sarvamāya*.
On account of the king’s business—that is, for the sake of the task concerning Rāvaṇa—he wishes to see you. "Hum" refers to the rākṣasa;
"hum" is used here as a particle of deliberation.
The meaning is: for what purpose has the Rākṣasa come here?
"A source of curiosity" means a cause for joy.
"By my maternal grandfather."

The ten-faced Rāvaṇa, though being forbidden and restrained by his maternal grandfather—the Daitya named Mālyavat, the father of his mother—nevertheless chose to marry Sītā, the king’s daughter born not from a womb (*ayonijā*), for the purpose of taking her as his wife; the ablative case here is used according to the rule *lyablope karmaṇyadhikaraṇe ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.28), meaning "having set aside the forceful seizure. The sense is: having abandoned the act of seizing her by force.
The vowel *vṛ* is long by rule (*jhaṭo dīrghaḥ*).
He dispatched me toward the capital of the King of Mithilā, the city of Sīradhvaja. ||28||

There, in that capital city of Mithilā, the sacrificer— the king Sīradhvaja who had commenced the sacrifice— said: "I have followed, that is, I have arrived here, at his word— that is, at the word of Sīradhvaja."
Thus he walks around;
the meaning is that he walks around by means of the "wealthy" one.
Regarding the phrase "of which there is no number":
The meaning is that Rāma, who was mentioned first, [is directed] toward Sītā, who was mentioned first; and Lakṣmaṇa, who was mentioned second, [is directed] toward Ūrmilā, who was mentioned second.
"To himself" (ātmagatam) means within his own mind; the sense is that he reflects upon what is about to be said.
"What for? means by some such cause.
"Like a wick of nectar" means like a line of nectar-collyrium.
"Varti refers to the wick of a lamp, an ointment for the limbs, a jeweler's touchstone, a type of medicinal salve for wounds, and the lines of collyrium on the eyes. Thus says the *Ratnamālā*.
This Sītā and Ūrmilā are also bringing refreshment;
that is to say, Sītā [refreshes] Rāma and Ūrmilā [refreshes] Lakṣmaṇa, respectively.
Why does my gaze cling to this delight for the eyes?
"Why" (kimiti) means for what reason; "clings" (sajjate) means she becomes attached. This designation of "bliss" (ānanda) is applied to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa because they are the causes of bliss.

Thus, by the passage beginning with "Why is this... and ending with "...the gaze," the first stage among the twelve stages of love (*śṛṅgāra*), called "delight of the eyes" (*cakṣuḥprīti*), is described.
As it has been said: "That which is a gaze with reverence, let that be the delight of the eyes.
The grammatical connection is: "She, whose form was wonderful and whose beauty was astonishing, had previously been heard of by us many times as Sītā.
The effort of the god Rāvaṇa—his exertion in the undertaking of abducting her by force—is appropriate.
The meaning is "proper.
"Anāmaya" means health;
for according to the traditional law (smṛti): "One should ask a Brāhmaṇa about his welfare (kuśala), and a member of the Kṣatriya caste about his health (anāmaya)."
Those two, King [Daśaratha] and Viśvāmitra—
[the phrase] "toward the Rākṣasa" is to be supplied as the object— say:
"Welcome."
The meaning is: "Why is there no arrival of happiness here? "Please sit down" is the sense;
the word "by you" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Regarding the passage beginning with *api*:

because the word *yat* (in the relative clause) is independent of the word *tat* (the correlative), the phrase *tasya* means "of that which is well-known. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Is it well with your lord, your king Rāvaṇa? as well.
That Indra, the subduer of Pāka, honors and obeys the command and order of this Rāvaṇa with his head, even as his crown slips from it. ||29||
"May it be well with my lord.
This means "may it be well with Rāvaṇa.
The great king Rāvaṇa has sent this message to you.
The meaning is: "some words through my mouth.
The particle *ca* (and) conjoins [the inquiry regarding] his welfare.
He qualifies the message with the words beginning with "kanyā" (the maiden).
That which has no birth from a womb is *ayonijanma*.
That which exists therein is *ayonijanma*, a jewel of a maiden (*kanyāratna*).
According to the *Ratnamālā*, "the word *ratna* refers to both a gem and something excellent."
"It exists" means it remains for you, for yourselves.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "We," and so forth.
We, who seek our own [benefit], manifest to you the desire to give with ourselves as the intended object regarding that [matter].
Furthermore, if there were some jewel anywhere, or if some excellent object existed anywhere— even setting aside Indra himself (śakrāt),
using the ablative case in the sense of "omission of the verbal root lyap"— it would be found among us, that is, in me.
In the preceding instance and here as well, the plural number is used for the singular according to the rule "asmado dvayośca" (Pāṇini 1.2.59).

However, the prohibition "saviśeṣaṇasya pratiṣedhaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.2.64) does not apply to the case of a specific predicate. Having reached its ultimate limit through transformation, it finally comes to rest.

For it is well known that "the king is the taker of the jewel. Furthermore, the fact that a maiden exists for the sake of another—that she belongs to another—is indeed held and desired by the authors of the scriptures.
For it is well known that "a maiden is a possession belonging solely to another."

And here, by the phrase "birth not from a womb," it is stated that because you lack any connection to a physical body, you do not possess ordinary worldly ownership. However, if one were to claim ownership based merely on being born of the field (*kṣetra*), then if someone were to request it, it would necessarily have to be given to them.

Even in that case, since the act of begging turns one toward wretchedness, if I were to request it while being free from even a trace of the desire for such ownership, it must certainly be given to me.

Furthermore, according to the maxim, "The thief of jewels [is punished] for violating my request," that maiden would somehow belong to me alone. Moreover, since a daughter is intended for another, she must necessarily be given to someone.

Thus, by these reasons, even though it is only a portion of the compound *vṛddhivṛtti*—namely, the word *tasya*—"these ten royal elephants and his very horses"—the word *tasya* refers back to that jewel-like maiden.

By means of the cause that is giving characterized by excellence—namely, being preceded by a formal request—I, the great-grandson of Prajāpati, shall become (*bhavitā*) your kinsman (*bandhu*), O Kṣatriyas; that is, I will be your kinsman (*bhaviṣyāmi*).

The verbal suffix *tiṅ* in the form of *bhavitā* follows the agent of the transformation, according to the rule "the suffixes of the verb *bhū* follow the agent of the modification," and thus it is the first person in the *luṭ* (periphrastic future) tense.
Those for whom Pulastya and Pulaha are the *praṣṭhas*—meaning those who go at the very front—are described as such. The word *praṣṭha* is derived by the rule "praṣṭho 'gragāmini" (Pāṇini 6.1.159).
According to the *Ratnamālā*, "praṣṭha means a woman, one who goes at the front, or excellent."
"Relatives will come to be"—here there is both elision (*anuṣaṅga*) and modification (*vipariṇāma*).
The meaning is "will exist in the future. (30)
"Alas, what a pity!"— this is used for expressions of suffering and despondency. "Reflecting"—
that is, reflecting upon this entreaty of the Rākṣasa.
The word "reply" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Rāvaṇa, the lord of night-stalkers, entreats this lady; he solicits Sītā.
[He does so] because she is common [to all].
Because of commonality, because of being shared, because of the equality of all.
That which has a common support (*dhāraṇa*) is "possessing a common support" (*sadhāraṇa*).
*Sadhāraṇa* itself is *sādhāraṇa*.
The state of being that is "commonality" (*sādhāraṇyam*). The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied because it belongs to the class beginning with *brāhmaṇa*.
Even one other than Rāvaṇa—meaning even someone else besides Rāvaṇa—being "without affliction," that is, being fearless, begs or entreats for the maiden.

What more need be said? The meaning is: Rāvaṇa—the great-grandson of the four-faced Parameṣṭhin (Brahmā), the grandson of [Pulastya], the son of [Viśravas], the conqueror of the worlds, the victor over the universe—is asking for the maiden. ||31||
Kindness (*saujanyam*) is the state of being a virtuous person (*sujanatvam*) which serves as the cause for the manifestation of one's qualities.
Indeed, "exceedingly" (*ati*) means surpassed or excelled;
as Amara states: "The word *ati* is used in the sense of excellence and also in the sense of transgressing."

*Nisarga* means that which has become one’s own nature (*svabhāvabhūta*). One who possesses enmity or hatred (*vidveṣa*) to an extreme degree is called *nisargavairī*. The suffix *-in* is added to the word *nisargavairin* in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyanārtha*).
As for the prohibition "not after a *karmadhāraya*," it applies when there is identity of meaning with a *bahuvrīhi*.
This is said when one intends to express excellence and so forth.
Even toward that Rāvaṇa, there is great respect—that is, worship. He establishes this state of being free from enmity with the words beginning "he who... and so on.
Rāvaṇa, who through the subversion of the three Vedas destroys the path of the Veda— [his] *kṣātra-tejaḥ*, that is, the power belonging to the warrior class (*kṣatra*) for overcoming enemies—
as defined by the *Ratnamālā*: "Tejas refers to strength, majesty, and fire"—
he diminishes, that is, he overcomes.
Furthermore, it is well known that Rāvaṇa killed our king Anaraṇya—who was as firm as a mountain—indeed, he slew him.

Thus, despite Rāvaṇa’s extreme enmity toward us through both common and extraordinary acts of injury, the noble one’s goodness is even more remarkable due to his great respect for him; this is the intended meaning. ||32||
"Granted, he may be killed as an enemy.
The meaning is that because of his enmity, I too have authorized his execution.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "In the sense of authorization, 'kāma' is an indeclinable [used with] 'smara' and 'abhilāṣa'."
To the question "What here is not permitted?", he says: "But not," and so forth. *Ativīryam* means possessing excessive prowess;
as the *Ratnamālā* states: "Vīrya [is used] in the sense of prowess and a bride-price."

One of immeasurable austerity and boundless splendor, who is extraordinary and not of the common folk, yet appears like an ordinary man among the common; for Amara states: "The vulgar, the base, the lowly, the commoner, and the person of the people (*pṛthagjana*) are synonyms for *prākṛta*."
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "You ought not to speak thus, nor to designate [me] in such a way.
Of one who has discarded the conduct of a heroic man and abandoned the duty of a heroic man—do not say so!
Do not speak thus!
"Thus, let not the manner of your statement [be so]; that is to say, 'it is certainly not so.
As for the words beginning with 'yad'..."

In this context, "Rāvaṇa" and so forth means that Rāvaṇa, though learned (*vidvān*)— that is, though possessed of knowledge— and though born into such a distinguished lineage— the best among men, specifically born in the family of Pulastya— [acted] contrary to what is consistent with *dharma*, that is, not departing from righteousness.
The suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "not deviating from dharma, path, artha, or nyāya. Furthermore, *cyutaḥ* means "despised," as in "fallen" or "degraded";
for Amara states: "The word *garhā* is used in the senses of reproach, collection, inquiry, doubt, and possibility."
The phrase "even though he is learned" (*vidvān api*) is stated with the intention that the punishment for a transgression by one who knows is more severe.
The phrase "in such a noble lineage" (*tādṛśe 'py abhijane*) is stated with the intention of highlighting his fall from such a high station.
Regarding the word "fallen" (*cyuta*), what can we say? What words do we have to speak?
The meaning is that we do not say he has fallen away from the path of Dharma;
rather, falling away from the path of Dharma is something entirely different— it means nothing other than a fault.
All virtues, such as valor, conduct, and so forth, do not dwell together;
the meaning is that they do not abide in a single place.
He says "playfulness," etc., to show that while faults may remain, virtue alone is worthy of esteem.

But who is such a hero, equal to Rāvaṇa, as one who has achieved universal victory without obstacles and attained all triumphs without hindrance—save for the illustrious son of Jamadagni, Paraśurāma, whose sovereignty and other qualities are divine, who conquered the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya) through mere sport, and who vanquished Skanda without effort?
The meaning is: "None at all. [Note:
The suffix *yañ* in *Jāmadagnya* is applied because the term is treated as a *gotra* even though it refers to a descendant of a recent generation. ||33||
What is there to be deliberated upon here?
The meaning is: apart from the matter commanded by my master through my mouth, which other point is being considered as about to be stated?
"Drāk" (immediately), etc.
The daughter of the Earth, who took the hand of that husband Rāvaṇa—the hero of the world and the preeminent hero on earth—[possesses] this chest, which is described by the following:

"by means of the fragments (śakalaiḥ) or pieces of the thunderbolt (vajra), shattered or broken by a sudden (drāk) impact or collision (niṣpeṣeṇa saṃghaṭṭanena), it is set (pratyuptaiḥ) or inlaid with the knots (granthibhiḥ) or joints (parvabhiḥ) of scars (vraṇānām) that have grown or appeared.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "A knot (granthiḥ) is a joint (parva) or a specific type of tumor."
The sense is that in those [mountains], which were shining intensely and brilliantly,

the fragments of the thunderbolt (*dambholi-śakala*) appearing to be stuck upon the scar-like protrusions— which resembled rubies (*padmarāga-maṇi*)— were seen as if they were diamonds (*hīra-maṇi*) inlaid there.
It refers to that [place] where the effort and activity of Indra’s (*maghavan*) elephant’s tusks was broken, destroyed at the very outset, and rendered fruitless even though it had been undertaken.
"In the abode"—that is, the place—of garlands and wreaths fashioned and woven by the deities of Nandana, the garden-keepers of Indra.
According to the *Ratnamālā*, "abode" (*dhāma*) refers to birth, splendor, a location, power, or a house of happiness.

Regarding the reading "in that which has fashioned garlands and wreaths" (*viracitasragdāmni*), the meaning should be understood as: that [place] in which garlands (*srajaḥ*)—meaning flower-wreaths—and wreaths (*dāmāni*)—meaning necklaces, shoulder-straps, and so forth—have been fashioned and woven.

Let the glory of heroes (vīraśrī) rest upon the chest of that Rāvaṇa, as if she were the very Fortune of Heroism (vīralakṣmī). The meaning is: let her find repose there; what else, then, is there to be considered?
The figure of speech here is *upamā* (simile), as in "like the glory of a hero" (*vīraśrīr iva*).

Furthermore, through the two qualifiers beginning with "drāṅniṣpeṣa... and "nandanadevatā...", the fact that his chest is adorned with a jeweled necklace and a garland of flowers—attributes suitable for being a place of repose—is stated; thus, the figure of speech is *parikara*.
This is because its definition is: "The ornament *parikara* [occurs] when there is a significant epithet. ||34||
Invited to the sacrifice, summoned for the sake of the ritual,
they gather together, coming together with their sons and wives, along with their children and spouses.
"Confused" means turbid with the wailing and crying sounds of the infants.
Regarding the phrase beginning with "āntra": "large" means those [entrails] which are strung or woven upon the *āntras*, that is, the entrails (*purītat*).
The *kapāla*s are like the *nalaka*s, like the joints;
or rather,
it is a *dvandva* compound meaning "the *kapāla*s and the *nalaka*s."
"Śṛṅkha and asthi are [synonyms for] nalaka," says Halāyudha. "Krūra" means as they resound or jingle; that is, the bracelets (kaṅkaṇas), which are ornaments for the hands.
They are described as such because they possess many of these bracelets, which are essentially large skulls and bones (nalakas) strung together with entrails and which jingle cruelly.
Making the sky resound—that is, filling the atmosphere with sound—by means of the noises of their many, abundant ornaments as they were swaying and moving;
[she was] by means of a thick, dense mass of the mud of her actions that had been vomited forth in excess due to having drunk too much.
Commentators explain that the word *prāgbhāra* is conventionally used in the sense of a "mass" or "collection."

She is described as such because her body is terrifying (*bhairava*) due to the weight of those two breasts, which are fierce (*ghora*), fearsome, leaping up, springing upward, tossing about, and moving violently on both sides.
Who is this that runs—that is, moves swiftly—with pride, in a manner that is haughty and lofty?
Regarding the root *sṛ* (in the sense of "going"), the substitution *dhāv* is applied for swift movement according to the rule beginning with *pāghrāghmāsthāmnādāṇ*.
"Āntraṃ purītat"—thus says Amara.
"Prāyaḥ [is used] in the sense of age, death, equality, abundance, and fasting;
furthermore, the indeclinable *prāyaḥ* signifies abundance"—thus says the Ratnamālā. ||35||
"Seiyam," and so forth:
she is the daughter, the offspring, of Suketu— the Yakṣa named Suketu—
and the wife of the Asura Sunda.
The mother of Mārīca was a terrible and fearsome Rākṣasī named Tāṭakā; this is to be supplied from the preceding verse. ||36||
