"Hatāśā" is used in the sense of reproach.
"Mā bhaiṣṭam" means "do not be afraid; do not be filled with fear. "Bhaiṣṭam" is the second person dual form of the aorist (luṅ) of the root *bhī*.
There is an absence of the augment *aṭ* due to the rule "na māṅyoge.
According to Amara, "the chin is below" (*adhastāccibukam*).
The meaning is: touching Rāma at the lower part of the lip.
"Let her be slain!
Let this Tāṭakā be killed—let her be put to death.
The word "by you" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
This very Rāma, who is exceedingly delicate, has been commanded to perform this most difficult task of slaying Tāṭakā.
Reverend Viśvāmitra, this Tāṭakā is indeed a woman;
therefore, the meaning is that she is not to be killed.
"Has it been heard by you, noble elder sister?
The meaning is: has Rāma’s speech, namely 'she is indeed a woman,' been heard?
"The mental agitation of this Rāma refers to a particular intention."
"One whose face is turned away from killing other than [the one intended]" means he is thus described.
"Ajakṣvāka" refers to one belonging to the Ikṣvāku lineage.
The meaning is that because Rāmabhadra feels such loathing for the killing of a woman, his status as a member of the Ikṣvāku lineage is indeed true.
"This," and so forth.
This refers to *uttālāyās*, meaning "of one who has risen up" (*udgatāyās*) to the *tāla* [measure].
The compound is formed according to the rule: "Words such as *ati* and others, when used in the sense of 'surpassing' and so on, form a compound with a word in the accusative case."

Unshaken and unmoved even at the sight of that *tāṭa*— the portentous leap, or rather, the unbearable omen indicating the suffering inherent in Tāṭakā— he was appointed and commanded by Viśvāmitra (as the remainder of the sentence implies) for the purpose of her destruction, which means her slaughter.
[He was thus directed] because of his *straiṇa* nature— that is, his manliness in the face of womanhood.

According to the rule "strīpuṃsābhyāṃ nañsnañau bhavanāt," the suffix *snañ* is applied to the word *strī* to denote the abstract state (*bhāva*). Thus, *vicikitsati* means "he doubts," in the sense of being uncertain as to whether one should kill or not kill; as Amarasimha states: "vicikitsā, however, is doubt (*saṃśaya*)."
"This is that" is the connection [between them]. ||37||
"Hasten!"— the word "to kill" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"Saṃghātamṛtyuḥ" means the death of the aggregate.
The meaning is the death of many at one time.
The construction is like saying "the teacher's house of Devadatta" or "the collective death of the Brahmin people.
It is to the front, to the north, and to the south.

And thus, according to the maxim "one should sacrifice a single [individual] for the sake of the multitude," the meaning is that the killing of a single wicked woman for the sake of the great majority of the Brahmin people does not constitute a fault.
O venerable ones, you— who, in accordance with the definition, "He who knows the origin and dissolution of beings, as well as their coming and going,
and who knows both knowledge and ignorance, he is to be called Bhagavān"— know and consider it in the manner previously described.
"All" means:

because they are free from attachment—that is, because they are devoid of the defects of the speaker such as delusion, negligence, and the desire to deceive—all [your doctrines] have attained equality with the Self, that is, they have reached the status of being equal to the Vedas.
Your acceptances—your formal acknowledgments—regarding merit and demerit, or what ought and ought not to be done, are authoritative; that is, they are the causes of valid cognition.
The word "they become" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Therefore, the meaning is: "By your command, I shall slay Tāṭakā. ||38||
"Has departed":

because of the prohibition against the direct representation of a killing in the rule "A long journey, a killing, and a battle [are not to be shown]," the meaning is that Rāma has exited the stage for the purpose of slaying Tāṭakā. The circle of whirlwinds is an omen indicating misfortune.
*Hatāśā* means one of wicked intent. *Dhanurāsphālya* means having twanged the bow; *dhanuṣṭaṃkṛtya* is a variant of the same. *Āḥ* is used to express anger.
"Āstu may mean both anger and affliction," according to Amara.
"Tāta" refers to Kuśadhvaja. Regarding the phrase "hṛnmarmeti":
"Piercing the heart-marma" means those that pierce the center of the heart—that is, the chest—of the *hṛd*.
With such falling arrows, fierce and formidable, feathered with heron plumes (*kaṅkapatra*);
as Amara states: "The *śilīmukha* is an arrow feathered with heron plumes."

She is so described because at that very moment—the moment of falling—she was produced with, or possessed of, a breaking and destruction of her limbs due to *saṃvega* (agitation) and *saṃbhrama* (alarm).
According to Amara, "saṃvega" and "saṃbhrama" are synonyms.
A small hut is called a *kuṭīra*.
The suffix *ra* is applied according to the rule "kuṭī-śamī-śuṇḍābhyo raḥ. Thus, the nose itself is the "nose-cottage" (*nāsā-kuṭīra*).
Of its two cavities, that is, the two apertures.

According to Amara, "kuhara," "suṣira," "vivara," and "bila" all mean a cavity or hole. She [Tāṭakā] was as if already dead, for her stream of blood—a flow of blood characterized by an abundance of bubbles and accompanied by a roaring sound—was emerging simultaneously from both [orifices], like a pair of bubbles. (39)
The repetition is out of respect: "It is dear to us, it is dear to us.
Firm striking is the state of being one who delivers harsh blows. Or rather?
The meaning is "wonder-inspiring.
Regarding the address "Noble Lady" (Ārye):
the Rākṣasa, though himself aged, addresses Tāṭakā as "Noble Lady" because she is senior to him in terms of the passage of time.
This is death from human [causes]. *Alābvāḥ* means gourds (*alābūni*). The suffix indicating a derivative product is elided by the rule "phale luk."
"Both the *tumbī* and the *alābu* are the same," according to Amara;
for when dried, these possess such extreme lightness that they naturally float when cast into water.
Stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*), which are rocks, float—that is, they cross over—in the water.
For those [stones], due to their excessive weight, possess the inherent nature of sinking when cast into water.

Just as a reversal of the fixed nature of both of these is utterly inconceivable, so too this reversal of the natures of humans and *rākṣasas*—though utterly inconceivable—is rendered possible by the defects of the present age; such is the meaning.
It is the inherent nature of a human to be slain by a *rākṣasa*, whereas it is the inherent nature of a *rākṣasa* to be a slayer of humans.

Thus, the sense is that although these two possess fixed natures, today their relationship as "slayer" and "slain" has been inverted. And it is said: "Rākṣasas kill humans," and "stones float upon the waters"—this is a *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphorical identification).

Because the act of Rākṣasa being killed by humans—the object of comparison—is swallowed up by the comparison with the sinking of the gourd, which serves as the standard of comparison, this constitutes "Hyperbolic Metaphor" (*rūpakātiśayokti*), according to the definition: "Hyperbolic Metaphor occurs when there is a superimposition [of one thing] upon another through the swallowing [of the former].
Furthermore, since the standard of comparison here is impossible, the figure "Impossible Simile" (*asaṃbhāvitopamā*) is suggested, as in:
"Like poison from the orb of the moon, like fire from sandalwood..."
"Harsh speech is like a thunderbolt; it is compared to that which is not easily endured. Thus it has been said.
Now, as for the words beginning with "nanu":
O Lord of the Rākṣasas, the majesty of Rāvaṇa, whose very nature is to scorch his enemies, has indeed faltered today.
The meaning is that he has indeed fallen [from his status] today.
According to Amara: "The particle *nanu* is used in the senses of inquiry, non-permission, permission, conciliation, and address.
The phrase "the marvelous (*adbhutaḥ*), which is to be wondered at, the humiliation (*paribhavaḥ*) or contempt (*tiraskāraḥ*) of the human infant by the Lord of the Rākṣasas" is to be supplied.
The meaning is that he has come today to Rāvaṇa.
Furthermore, while standing—meaning while remaining steadfast for the sake of my master’s cause—I witnessed the slaughter of my own kin, the killing of the rākṣasas.
Wretchedness, which is the depletion of one's strength through begging, as well as old age and the decline of youth, restrain me and turn me back from the desire to retaliate.
"How shall I act? means "What shall I do? ||40||

This "Slaying of Tāṭakā" is indeed the destruction of all Rākṣasas, the killing of every demon from Subāhu down to Rāvaṇa itself; it is the study of the Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*). Because the study of the Veda is mandatory—according to the rule, "The Veda, along with its six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), should be studied"—and because it is a means to achieve the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), this destruction of the Rākṣasas is likewise presented as a form of Vedic study for the sake of making it understood that for the Kṣatriya Rāma, it too was a constant duty and a means to achieve the goals of human life. The *oṃkāra* is the form of the utterance of the *praṇava*.

Just as the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*)—according to the teaching: "One should always place the *praṇava* at the beginning and at the end of the *brahman*; for the *brahman* not preceded by *oṃ* slips away, and at the end, it falls apart"—serves as both the commencement and the stabilizer of the study of one's own sacred texts (*svādhyāya*), so too, the slaying of Tāṭakā serves as the commencement and the stabilizer of the impending slaughter of all the *rākṣasas*. Thus, she is metaphorically described as being of the nature of the *oṃkāra*.
[The phrase] "among us" refers to myself and my mistress.
The plural is used for the dual.
Regarding "here":
here, in the context of the message to Rāvaṇa which you have described beginning with "the jewel among maidens," Janaka, whose banner is the plough, is the knower.
The word "answer" (*prativacana*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
From the root *vid* in the sense of "to know," the suffix *luṭ* (future) is applied in the first person.
Regarding the statement that this Kuśadhvaja is to answer, he says: "the younger brother."
The meaning is that you yourself surely know that Kuśadhvaja is the younger brother.
To the objection that because the two brothers are joint owners (saṃsṛṣṭa), even the younger brother might speak [on behalf of the elder], he says: "Of her.
That Sīradhvaja is the father of this maiden.
The point is that, in the matter of giving away a daughter in marriage, the authority belongs solely to the father, and not to the paternal uncle or others.

This girl is his non-aureas (non-legitimate) daughter; yet, the proximity resulting from her being obtained through the husband’s field (*kṣetra*) remains established for both of them. To this, he says: "In the family... (*kuleti*).
That Sīradhvaja is the eldest in his family and lineage, superior both by age and by virtue;
he alone is the lord and master.
Since among Kṣatriyas sovereignty over the land belongs to the eldest alone, the implication is that even this land obtained through cultivation must be bestowed by him alone. ||41||
"He too," namely Sīradhvaja, "knows the reply"—this is the ellipsis. Therefore, with his consent, Kuśadhvaja must indeed give the reply; such is the intention of the Rākṣasa.
Now Viśvāmitra delays the giving of the reply by means of another method, beginning with the words "of this," and so forth.
The *jṛmbhaka* weapons are indeed divine missiles; this is the opportune moment, the time that has arrived, for the bestowal of these auspicious gifts upon Rāma.
He who is skilled in what is auspicious is called *maṅgalya*. The suffix *yat* is applied here according to the rule *tatra sādhuḥ*.
"Yāni" and so forth.
[The word "kṛśāśvāt"] is in the ablative case according to the rule "ākhyātopayoge" (Pāṇini 1.4.29), meaning from the sage named Kṛśāśva, who was full of the Lord’s wisdom and other qualities.

The conduct of the guru is *gurucaryā*, consisting of tasks such as fetching wood and water; these very duties are the *vratas*, the dharmas that must necessarily be performed. By means of these, [the disciple] has studied and acquired the *rahasya*—that which is accessible only through oral instruction, such as the *kavaca* and *pañjara* mantras—and the *prayoga*, the ritual application.
*Saṃhāraḥ* means withdrawal.

*Jṛmbhakāstrāṇām prayoga-saṃhārau* refers to the employment and withdrawal of the *jṛmbhaka* weapons. *Rahasyam ca jṛmbhakāstraprayoga-saṃhārau ca* refers to the secret [teachings] and the employment and withdrawal of the *jṛmbhaka* weapons; thus, they are the "secrets, the employment, and the withdrawal of the *jṛmbhaka* weapons."

The meaning is "together with them. Regarding the *pārāyaṇa*—the collection of texts to be studied without interruption from beginning to end—of the *divyāstramantras*, which are specific portions of the *Upaniṣads* that reveal the divine weapons (*divyāstra*): those which are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*), that is, the seed-syllables of the reality of knowledge, [are the seed-forms] among the limbs of the mantra (*mantrāṅga*) enumerated in the science of mantras, such as the seed (*bīja*), power (*śakti*), and pin (*kīlaka*). [The word] "become" (*bhavanti*) is to be supplied [at the end].

"By my grace," meaning by my favor; that is to say, even in the absence of the observance of the guru’s conduct and vows. "May they manifest"—that is, may they become directly perceptible—both in their objective form as the respective deities and in their verbal form as the nature of the expressive sounds.
By the rule "the *kṛtya* suffixes and the imperative (*loṭ*) are used in the senses of command, permission, and [proper] time," the imperative is employed here in the sense of an injunction.
Regarding the phrase "Brahmā and the others":

the ancient, primordial teachers (*guru*) and instructors of knowledge, beginning with Brahmā—the four-faced one and the rest—for the welfare of the Veda (*brahma*), or for the welfare of the Brahmins, [spoke] more than a thousand times (*paraḥsahasram*).
The compound is *sup-supā* (noun with noun), with the augment *suṭ* applied because it belongs to the *pāraskara*-class;
the inversion of word order occurs because it belongs to the *rājadanta*-class; and the singular number is used because of the rule: "Numbers beginning with twenty always take the singular."
For more than a thousand years— *śaradaḥ saṃvatsarān*;
according to Amarasimha, "the words *saṃvatsara*, *vatsara*, *abda*, *hāyana*, and *samā* (in the feminine) are synonyms for *śarat*"—
the accusative case is used here to denote duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*).

Although, according to the rule *apavarge tṛtīyā*, the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) ought to occur in instances of absolute connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*) when the attainment of a result is intended, nevertheless, it occurs only where the attainment of the result is intended to be expressed by the third case itself;
as in examples such as *ahnā krośena vānuvāko'dhītaḥ* ("the lesson was studied in a day or a *krośa*").
Here, because the attainment of the result is intended to be expressed by another word (*śabdāntara*), the second case (*dvitīyā*) is used solely for the sake of absolute connection.
Having performed—that is, having carried out—austerities which are actions that wither the body;
the expression "having performed" is used here as in the phrase "he cooks the cooking.
[The fruits] consist of austerity, having arisen from austerity.
Under the governing rule "tata āgataḥ" (derived from that), the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied according to the rule "mayaṭ ca.
These *jṛmbhaka* weapons are their own respective splendors and powers;
this is an attributive adjective qualifying the subject.
"Adarśan" means not seeing; it refers to the non-perception of ascetic powers and weapons due to the relationship between cause and effect. The root *dṛś* means "to see.
Because it is in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, the suffix *aṅ* is applied.
In the word *ṛdṛśo'ṅi guṇaḥ*, there is the substitution of the *guṇa* vowel;
in *tapomayāni*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). ||42||
"Diṣṭyā" expresses joy.
It is the sound of celestial drums (*devadundubhi*).
According to Amara, "the word *bherī* is feminine, while *dundubhi* is masculine."
"In the sky" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
"And a rain of flowers"— "of the gods" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
In the former case, the verb "is heard" (*śrūyate*) is supplied; in the latter, the verb "falls" (*patati*) is to be supplied.
They perform—that is, they carry out—acts hostile to the king, such as beating the drum, which are undesirable to Rāvaṇa.
The word "how? (*katham*) expresses astonishment, followed by "suddenly" (*jhaṭiti*), and so forth.

The quarters [of the sky] appear as if suddenly, at this very moment, sprinkled or drenched with gold—molten because it is intensely heated by fire and thus liquefied, possessing the quality of fluidity.
The ellipsis [to complete the sense] is "they become so.
This state of the quarters occurs because they are enveloped by the splendors of the deities of the divine weapons.
The day, because of its tawny or brownish hue—
Amara states that *kaḍāra*, *kapila*, *piṅga*, and *piśaṅga* are synonyms for this color—
is visible only when it has been obscured or hidden by the twilight, that is, by the glow of the evening.
Here too, the beloveds of the deities of the divine weapons are intended.
The sky—the intermediate space—is filled and pervaded by divine weapons and the deities of those weapons; it is as if covered or obscured by masses of blazing, radiant banners.
Furthermore, it is as if made tawny, endowed with a reddish-brown hue, by flashes of lightning moving in an unbroken, dense succession.
"Piñjara is neuter when meaning gold, and masculine when meaning a yellow horse," according to the Ratnamālā. (43)
The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Regarding the phrase "by means of splendors" (*tejobhiḥ*) and so forth: "in every direction" (*diśi-diśi*) means in all directions; "on all sides" (*viśvataḥ*) means in every location.
The suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of the locative case according to the rule *sārvavibhaktikastasiḥ*.

[The moon] was seized and swallowed, and then released and let go, by those [planets] which were blazing and shining, eclipsing—that is, striking against—the splendor of the sun, the solar radiance, and which were quivering as they moved rapidly in succession and order;
this is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) similar to the term *khañjakubja* ("lame-and-bent").
"Nāyana" means pertaining to the eye;
it is a secondary derivative formed with the suffix *aṇ*. "Mayūkha" means a ray. It "leaves," that is, abandons, its "efficacy"—the power to perceive objects.
The root *raha* in the sense of "abandoning" belongs to the curādigaṇa. ||44||
In Prākṛta, because there is no dual number, the plural is used in its place; this is established by the Prākṛta grammatical rule: "Success [is achieved] according to worldly usage."
It is difficult to approach and difficult to traverse.

It "coagulates" (styāyati), meaning it becomes a compact mass; this is derived from the root *styai* in the sense of "sound" and "compactness," with the present tense (*laṭ*) and the third person singular ending.
By that splendor, [he quelled] the fury of the duel—that is, the exertion for the combat.
"All," and so forth:
entirely, with his whole life-force and strength, in such a way as to be inclined, and in such a way as to be bowed down.

"Prāṇa [is] the breath in another body, [and] the life-force of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman); [it is] also [found] in lifespan, the senses, and the vital essence (sattva)," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
"The word *pravaṇa* means 'inclined' on a sloping ground, and 'humble' [in a figurative sense]," according to Amara.
This was released by Maghavan, the lord of the Indras;
this is a modifier of the *kuliśa* (thunderbolt);
the chest—that is, Rāvaṇa’s chest—is the object (*karman*).

Having struck and violently battered it, [the thunderbolt] is such that its large, thick fragments have been shattered and split apart due to the collision and the friction against Rāvaṇa’s chest; it is thus described as having fierce and formidable brilliance. The agent is the *kuliśa* (thunderbolt), which acts by means of thousands of lightnings consisting of its own fragments.
The sky, the very work of the heavens,
was thus made as if turned tawny by the brilliance of the divine weapons;

moreover, their previously existing faces were made brownish-grey by the fire of their mouths blazing like the fire of Vajra, while their boisterous, dry laughs were fueled by the wrath and anger of their lord, Rāvaṇa.
"‘Aṭṭa’ refers to a watchtower (*aṭṭālaka*) when it is filled and thoroughly dried; it is used in three genders," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
[The demon] acted thus toward the sky (*vyoma*).
The verb "he did" (*akarot*) is to be supplied, along with its grammatical modification.
Therefore, the connection is: "I have been reminded of the agitation caused by the pairs of opposites. ||45||
"Salute him; offer him salutation.
[The root] *vad* is used in the sense of both "speaking" and "saluting.
[He says: "O Brahman!"

Brahmā is the four-faced one; Indra, Upendra, or simply Indra; Draviṇeśa is Kubera; Rudra is Īśa; Varuṇa is Pracetas; and Prācīnabarhis is Surendra—or rather, Prācīnabarhis is the name of a Prajāpati. As it is stated in the *Purāṇaratna*: "The venerable Prācīnabarhis was a great Prajāpati."

Among these weapons—each one individually possessing the capacity and efficacy to shatter this world—their excellence is like that of ascetic powers (*tapas*), due to their unimpeded and unblunted splendors, radiances, or strengths, which are like the causes of such power; they belong to those supreme beings who are distinct from Marut (the wind), Kāla (Yama, the god of death), Agni (Anala, fire), and the *āmnāya-mantras* (Atharva-veda mantras) and *ātman*s (living souls) that constitute the vital breaths, and who are full of knowledge, power, and other attributes.
That which has destruction, protection, and preservation as its limits—its boundaries—is described thus;
"she becomes" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. ||46||
"Eṣa" means "I am humble," that is, I am bowed down.
"Divyāstrasaṃpradāya" refers to the initial bestowal of divine weapons; it means, in other words, instruction.
The intention is: "May it be with Lakṣmaṇa just as it is with me. ||47||
Instantly;
"oneself" means "me."

He is so described because his manifest knowledge—that wisdom which suddenly and swiftly blossomed through the illumination, that is, the direct realization, of *vidyā*, the science of weapons—is such that it penetrates all things.

Furthermore, he is one whose power—the capacities capable of accomplishing difficult tasks—is inconceivable, being beyond the reach of thought as something belonging to a different class [from ordinary things];
moreover, he is as if composed of light, abounding in radiance.
In the rule "tatprakṛtavacane mayaṭ," the suffix *mayaṭ* denotes abundance (*prācurya*). These are qualifiers of the predicate (*vidheya*). I think [thus].
The meaning is: "I determine. ||48||

"Rāma, Rāma!"—the repetition [of the name] is used here to express excess of affection, according to the rule: "The vocative at the beginning of a sentence is repeated in cases of envy, consent, anger, censure, and threatening.
Because of Viśvāmitra’s authorization—that is, by reason of Viśvāmitra’s consent—we extend our efforts toward you, O grandfather.
The meaning is: "We shall be dependent upon you.
According to Amara, *adhīna*, *nighna*, and *āyatta* are synonyms.
By the word *abhyanujñā* (permission), it is understood that the divine weapons' dependence on Rāma is natural.
The phrase "with your brother" connects both the preceding and the following;
the meaning is that we are dependent upon you and your brother.
Rule over us together with your brother.
"Let your brother Lakṣmaṇa command us as to what is to be done;

you too, command us as to what is to be done"—this is the meaning. [This is derived from] the root *śās* (meaning "to instruct") preceded by *pra*, in the imperative mood, middle voice, second person plural. ||49||
"The deities are conversing"—this is wonderful.
The root *matri* in the sense of "speaking in secret" belongs to the curādigaṇa and is conjugated in the ātmanepada.
[The term] "Bhagavantaḥ" [is used here].
"O Blessed Ones, you who are full of the power of knowledge and other attributes, the hosts of divine weapons, the multitudes of celestial arms"—this is the address.

"From Viśvāmitra, the friend of the universe, the friend of all, from Kauśika," [meaning] he who is the friend of the universe is Viśvāmitra. From him, through merits and well-performed deeds, [you have obtained these].
The lengthening of the vowel in the first member of the compound occurs by the rule *mitre carṣau*.
The masculine gender follows from the inherent nature of the word.
The ablative case is used according to the rule *ākhyātopayoge* (Pāṇini 1.4.29).

The etymological meaning of "friend of the universe" (*viśvasya mitram*) is useful for the process of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*), whereas in actual instances of usage (*prayogasthaleṣu*), it is determined by the speaker's intention (*vaivakṣika*).

For example, in the expression "the garland of the seven seers" (*saptasaptarṣayo mālā*), the word "seven" is used separately because the number seven is intended to be expressed as distinct [from the compound].

For this very reason, the venerable teachers maintain that there is neither tautology with the word "goes" (*gacchati*)—since the word *go* is derived from the root *gam* with the suffix *ḍo* in the sense of "going"—nor contradiction with the word "stands" (*tiṣṭhati*).
And here, the name Viśvāmitra is intended to exclude the etymological interpretation favored by rival people, namely that he is "the friend of all" (viśveṣām amitraḥ) for us;
rather, it means "having obtained everything" (viśvam āpya labdhvā).
Thus, Rāma has today achieved his purpose.
This is the speech of Rāma:
"I have today attained all human goals"—this is the meaning.

[It is so] because of you, who are worthy of honor in every way, by you virtuous ones who have been meditated upon, that is, by you who have been thought of for the sake of your presence at those various times.

"Saṃnidheyaṃ saṃnidhiḥ kāryaḥ": because the root is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). The form *siḥ* is explained as being used for distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) according to the rule "nityavīpsayoḥ."
The term *vīpsā* signifies pervasiveness and universal application.
The meaning is: "At whatever time I perform meditation, at that very time you must remain present before me. You all, go—depart—to your respective places.
The form *prāṇe* is the second person plural middle voice of the root *lī*.
*Vaḥ* means "to you. The dative case is used according to the rule beginning with *namaḥ svasti* (Pāṇini 2.3.16). ||50||
From the words of the Noble One, from the words of Rāma;
they have been interrupted, they have been concealed.
O treasury of great wonders, O treasury of great marvels!

"Jvalita... means one whose ascetic practices, such as the *kṛcchra* and others, are "jvalitāni," that is, shining; he is thus described. Of him, who is a mass—a collection—of splendors (*tejasām*) characterized by the capacity to overwhelm others, there are "mitāni," meaning immeasurable or innumerable, "ojāṃsi," which refers to knowledges (*jñāna*) and powers (*bala*). Regarding this, the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *ojas* [denotes] the quality of sound, knowledge, strength, pride, and manifestation. Thus, it refers to you, in whom there has been committed a "stutisāhasam"—an act of rashness regarding praise—with respect to your "niravadhau," that is, unlimited, "māhābhāgye," meaning great magnanimity. He is thus described as one who has engaged in such rash behavior toward the subject of your praise.
The meaning is that he proceeded to praise without due reflection.

The praiser, or the composer of the hymn, not finding—that is, not obtaining—in his speech (*vāc*) the capacity or power (*śakti*) related to a true knowledge consistent with the praise regarding the object of cognition; yet, while finding such capacity within his mind (*cetasi*), being one whose movement (*parispanda*)—meaning some degree of activity—is thus obstructed;
or alternatively, he is one whose composition (*racanā*) consists of such obstructed movement. Thus it is said.
According to Amara, "racanā" means "parispanda" (movement).

Having met with misfortune—that is, having encountered calamity—one is "ghṛṇīyate," meaning one feels aversion; for the *Ratnamālā* states, "ghṛṇā" refers to both disgust and compassion. In this world, having fallen into adversity, one experiences such [aversion]. The *Ratnamālā* also notes: "ghṛṇā" signifies both loathing and pity.
Alternatively, the meaning is that he censures himself, thinking, "I am one who acts without due reflection.

Or rather, the sense is that this wretched man, having failed to consider the power of the object [of praise], suffers when engaged in its eulogy; thus, he becomes an object of compassion for those who possess discernment. The form *ghṛṇīyate* is derived from the root *ghṛṇiṅ*, which signifies both anger and shame, by adding the suffix *yak* according to the rule *kaṇḍvādibhyo yak*, followed by lengthening the vowel and applying the Ātmanepada ending due to the marker *ṅ*.
Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root [jugups] functions in the senses of both loathing and compassion. ||51||
Regarding the word "tat" (therefore):

for that reason, [it is for] Rāmabhadra—who has been favored by you and who has become the object of the bestowal of the divine weapons—to be adorned, that is, to be graced; in other words, to be joined [with it].
"I envy King Daśaratha; I possess a longing directed toward Daśaratha.

[In this context,] the root *spṛh* (meaning "desire") belongs to the *curādi* class beginning with *kath*. Since it is designated as a *saṃpradāna* (indirect object) by the rule *spṛherīpsitaḥ*, the fourth case ending is employed.
As for us, however, we have been deceived by the noble Sīradhvaja, having been deprived of our human purpose (*puruṣārtha*).
The ellipsis "we shall become" is to be supplied. [The meaning is:
"We do not wish to be deprived of such a son-in-law, the husband of our daughter, who possesses incomparable power.
The connection is as follows: "If we are not united with him, then by reason of his making the wager of stringing the difficult bow, we have been cheated by Sīradhvaja."

The word *yuja* is derived from the root *yuj* belonging to the *divādi* class; the form is the third person plural present indicative (*laṭ*), and by virtue of the prefix *sam*, it carries the sense of "union.

Even now—meaning even after the slaying of Tāṭakā and the instruction on the *Jṛmbhaka* weapon—if we do not unite, this is a "possibility" (*saṃbhāvanā*) regarding the previously introduced impossibility, taking the form of a doubt with one side predominant.
[This refers to] "among us," meaning in me, and in Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
No, no;
the term "impossibility" is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
Regarding the word "of Śambhu":
"By the boon of Śambhu, O Rudras,
[this state] grants presence— that is, it grants arrival— merely through the thought of you;
the meaning is that its nature is to produce [its effect] by mere contemplation."
The suffix *ṇini* is applied here according to the rule *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye*.
Let the bow of that Śambhu, acting as the agent, manifest—that is, remain present—in front of Rāmabhadra. (52)
"Let it be as you have said.
By these [arguments] beginning with 'Niśvāsa', something entirely different and indeed contrary to our position has been introduced and set forth.
For how long? For how much of a protracted time?"
"I have been disregarded because no reply was given; I have been humiliated.
This is the response:
"Sphūrjat" (thundering).
By the splendors (*tejobhiḥ*), powers, or radiances of the *diviṣads*, the gods;
for Amara states: "The word *tejas* [is used] in the sense of power and also in that of light. It is *iddham*, meaning illuminated or radiant.
From the root *dīp* (in the sense of "to shine"), the suffix *kta* is applied to form *dīpta*.

The compound *tripura* refers to the collection of the three cities; he who brings about their end or destruction is *Tripurāntaka*. The underlying sense is that this is due to his fierce nature (*raudratva*).

The bow is the agent. It is described as that by which a thousand thunderbolts—*vajras*, or *dambholis*—that are *sphūrjatām*, meaning "resounding" or "becoming sound," have been *nirjitam*, that is, surpassed or eclipsed. The word *nirjita* is placed at the end of the compound because it belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class beginning with *āhitāgni*.
In the reading "nirmitam iva," it means as if created.
"Sthitam" means situated. It appears before Rāma; that is, it manifests in front of Rāma.

Having heard these words of Sītā—"I am now filled with doubt"—she was uncertain whether Rāma would indeed cause her to be mounted [on the chariot]. Immediately thereafter came the king’s words: "By a *kalabha*—a young elephant—the *śuṇḍā*, which is the trunk of an elephant (*karahasta*).
According to the *Vaijayantī*: 'The word *śuṇḍā* refers to an elephant's trunk and to wine.'"
While the term *alpa-* (small) is understood from the preceding context, the suffix *-ra-* is applied to the word *śuṇḍā* according to the rule *kuṭī-śamī-śuṇḍābhyo raḥ*.
Thus, the meaning is "a small trunk" (*alpā śuṇḍā*).
The *Trirūpakośa* states: "That which is called *śuṇḍa*, *śuṇḍā*, and *śuṇḍāḥ* [is the trunk]."
Just as a mountain is immovable, so too was that small staff-like arm of Rāma, though he was but a child;
the suffix *kan* is used here in the sense of "small. Upon that very bow being placed—that is, having been fixed—[he drew it].
Having heard these words of Ūrmilā—“May this indeed come to pass!”—[he reflects upon] this placing of Rāmabhadra’s staff-like arms upon the bow. Again, the King’s words: “With a roar,” etc.
In such a manner that the bowstring—the *maurvī*—was accompanied by the sound of the bow’s roar during the act [of stringing it], it was drawn with great effort;
the meaning is that it was pulled by the fastening of the string.
Having heard this, she was again filled with joy at her own offering to Rāma, yet ashamed due to her youthful innocence.
"By good fortune! expresses joy.
"We prosper," meaning we attain increase; this is again the King's speech. "That bow was broken and crushed"—the word "by the child" is to be supplied as the subject.

The elephant calf is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and the [human] calf is the object of comparison (*upameya*). In accordance with that, the suffixes *śuṇḍāra* and *dordaṇḍaka* are employed in the sense of "smallness"; this is for the purpose of proclaiming an extraordinary degree of wonder. ||53||

It is called *sarvakaṣa* because it scrapes away everything (*sarvaṃ kaṣati*). The suffix *khal* is applied according to the rule "after the root *kaṣ*, [the suffix *khal* is used] in connection with *sarva*, *kūla*, *abhra*, and *karīṣa*. *Prabhāva* means splendor (*tejas*).
By the two acts of the expulsion of Tāṭakā and the breaking of Rudra’s bow, everything has been tested.

Regarding the phrase "the sport of the arms": through the sport—that is, the effortless activity—of the two arms (doṣṇoḥ), the bending and breaking of the staff-like bow of Candraśekhara was achieved; this constitutes the drum-roll, the sound of a specific musical instrument that serves as a herald, for the manifestation of the preliminary introduction to the childhood exploits of the noble Rāma.

The sound of the *ṭaṃkāra*— the nature of which is a harsh, intense resonance massed together because it was suddenly overturned, shattered, and measured by its two halves like a skull-cup (*kapālasampuṭa*), or perhaps small and limited like a skull-cup (the term "limited" being used here in view of the preponderance of the sound)—

which roamed within the belly of the vessel characterized as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), and for that very reason possessed a concentrated ferocity— that sound does not rest, nor does it cease, even now, despite the passage of time.

"Aho" expresses wonder. "Katham" (how? expresses agitation; that is, the state of being distressed by the thought: "If this resonance continues without interruption for even a short time beyond this point, will there not be the dissolution of the phenomenal world? ||54||
Joy arises from obtaining a suitable boon;
madness is a delusion of the mind caused by the difficulty of the situation. "Come, come! [he says].
The repetition is out of respect. *Caraṇapuṣkarakadvaya* refers to the pair of two small lotus-feet;
the suffix *kān* is used here in the sense of "small" (*alpe*).
The kissing and so forth appropriate for the address "O child, O delight of the Raghus," and the saying "I carry [you]" and so forth appropriate for the address "O Rāmabhadra.
Yogins take delight in the infinite, true bliss that is the self of consciousness.
"Thus, by the word 'Rāma,' that Supreme Brahman is designated"—so says the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) of the term "Rāma.
It is well known that kissing on the head out of joy, lifting the feet out of intoxication, and knowing the nature of those who are asleep or angry [are all possible]. (55)

"From excessive fondness" (*ativātsalyāt*) means from excessive affection (*atisneha*). The word *vatsala* is derived from the root *vatsa-aṃsa* with the suffix *lac*, signifying "power of desire"; from this word, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), according to the rule for words beginning with *brāhmaṇa*. "Occasion" (*prasaṅga*) refers to the relevant activity of speech. The ellipsis is "it transgresses the boundary."
The meaning is that the guru is like a father;
"in the form of an embryo" means being like a son.
[The phrase] "by Rāma" [is used].
By reason of Rāma—the lord of the earth who is identical with Rāma—being your husband, Sītā’s blessings for you have been fulfilled; that is to say, they are complete.
At this very festival—the festival consisting of the stringing of the bow which was the cause for the giving of Sītā to Rāma—I gave Ūrmilā to Lakṣmaṇa. ||56||
To Indra, [it was] in the form of the giving of Sītā;
it was "suṣṭutaram," meaning more excellent or more appropriate. The suffix *tara* is applied to the root *sthā* when the word *su* is used as an upapada, according to the rule "avaduḥsuṣusthaḥ."

The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "suṣāmādiṣu ca. It is well (*suṣṭhu*) that Sītā was given to Rāma; it is well (*suṣṭhu*) that Ūrmilā was given to Lakṣmaṇa—thus [the compound] is semantically justified.
There remains something else yet to be said.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *śeṣa* [means] Ananta, Hari; in the three genders it means 'that which remains' after what has been used.
Thus, the sense is that "something indeed exists."
Regarding the word *te*:
*te* is in the accusative case;
*bharata-śūghnābhyām* is in the dative case.
*Tapasyataḥ* means "practicing austerity" (*tapaścarataḥ*).
The suffix *yak* is applied after the root *tapas-* according to the rule for the *kaṇḍvādi* class.
In the term *vanecarasya*, the seventh case ending is not elided (*aluk*) by the rule: "In a compound denoting a name, the seventh case ending is not elided after a word ending in *hal* or a vowel."
In the household of a Kṣatriya, *vaiyātyam* refers to the impudence or audacity of the Kṣatriyas.

The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied to the word *viyāta* to denote either the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the action (*karman*). As Amarasimha states: "One who is bold is called *dhṛṣṇu*, *viyāta*, and [so forth]."
It must be deliberated upon and scrutinized.
Regarding this matter—the act of giving Māṇḍavī and Śrutakīrti to Bharata and Śūghna—I am *paravān*.
According to Amara, "one who is dependent on another, subject to another, or under another's control is called *paravān*, even if he has a protector (*nāthavān*)."
"By whom?"—
the word "dependent on another" (paravān) is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
The word "tāvat" signifies sequence.
"Firstly, by the Blessed One himself"—
the meaning is "by you.
"Now" (*atha*) indicates immediate succession.
"Gautama" [is derived] from Gautama-putra by the rule "ṛṣy-andhaka-vṛṣṇi-kurubhyaś-ca," which prescribes the suffix *aṇ*.
I am the one who makes the announcement.
The meaning is that I shall be the one to enlighten the two of you so that you do not entertain any disagreement regarding this matter;
now he understands—
the words "the state of affairs" (arthasthiti) are to be supplied as the object.

Regarding the phrase "of the Janakas": for whom is the relationship between the descendants of Janaka—the Raghus who are devoted to the yoga of action—and the offspring of Raghu—the [other] Raghus who are devoted to the yoga of knowledge—not dear?
The meaning is that it is dear to everyone.
The detailed explanation, however, should be consulted in our commentary on the *Uttararāmacarita* entitled *Talasparsinī*.

[The term *pratibhūḥ* refers to one who is a guarantor of welfare (*kalyāṇa*) in a particular relationship; it means either a neutral party who ensures prosperity or a guarantor who brings about auspiciousness (*maṅgalakara*).
The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule: "After the root *bhū*, [the suffix *kvip* occurs] when forming a name or in other [specific senses]."]
"He who stands between the creditor and the debtor for the sake of confidence is a *pratibhū*," say the grammarians;
"the *lagnakas* are *pratibhuvas*," says Amara.
You are such a one.
The meaning is "you. ||57||
Regarding the term "ākāśa":

as it is said, "When one speaks with those who have not entered [the stage], it is called *ākāśabhāṣita* (speaking into the air). Because the character Śunaḥśepa has not yet entered, it is referred to as "ākāśa."
"Having uttered my words according to my instruction"— the ablative case is used here because of the elision of a word ending in the suffix *lyap*.
He states the manner of the speech with the words beginning "these," and so forth.

By me alone acting as the agent, in the house of Nimi—that is, in the house of Sīradhvaja—these four princesses, Sītā, Ūrmilā, Māṇḍavī, and Śrutakīrti, were given simultaneously and together to the four delights of the Raghu dynasty—Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna. Acting like Gautama, they were given by Śatānanda, the son of Gautama and family priest of Janaka’s lineage;
and acting like Vasiṣṭha, they were accepted by Vasiṣṭha, the family priest of the Raghu clan. "They became [the wives of the princes]" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
From the root *iṣ* in the sense of "desiring" (*icchāyām*), the suffix *kta* is applied after the prefix *prati*, resulting in the object form.
By virtue of the prefix, the meaning becomes "accepting" (*pratigraha*). An example of its use in the sense of accepting is found in the phrase: "Accept her, may prosperity be yours. (58)
Therefore; having summoned and called;
of King Sīradhvaja.
Those for whom the auspicious *godāna* alone has been performed and forgotten are so described.
*Godāna* is that in which the *gāvaḥ*—meaning the body hairs (*loma*)—are given away, that is, cut off;
from the root *do* in the sense of "cutting off" (*avakhaṇḍane*).
"They will marry; they will perform the wedding"—this is the connection with the preceding phrase "speak" (*brūhi*).
[The two] princes are Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.

The meaning is as follows: more dear, indeed exceedingly dear, than the giving of Sītā and Ūrmilā to Priya and Dāva [Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa] is the bestowing of Māṇḍavī and Śrutakīrti upon Bharata and Śatrughna, as well as the addressing of the Preceptor and Father.
"Non-separation" refers to the absence of separation while remaining in Videha.

The meaning is that [she is] the wife of brothers within a single household. Even now, at the time of the betrothal (*vāgdāna*), I have replied with words of dharma— words uttered with the praise of dharma alone, because they serve to avoid misfortune.
Alternatively, the meaning is that since it is a matter of dharma to give even a betrothed girl to another before the seventh step is taken, these words of mine are intended to prevent that;
for this [proposed] misfortune— that this girl Sītā be given to another—
is contrary to our purpose.
In the word *anaḥ*, the masculine gender in *eṣaḥ* is used because the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is predominant.
By the phrase "this girl," it is implied that he has no regard for Ūrmilā and the others.
The connection with the preceding clause is: "thus [he spoke] while listening to the words of dharma."
Regarding the word *paulastya*:

Paulastya is Rāvaṇa, the grandson of Pulastya. In this sense—that he "entreats," meaning he "prays" with humility and without arrogance—even toward that which is praiseworthy and worthy of celebration, there is disregard or a lack of respect, or even contempt. Furthermore, in whatever connection there may be with that Lord of the World, Rāvaṇa—namely, the relationship of son-in-law and father-in-law—there arises happiness and well-being.
In that regard, "no longing" means the absence of longing for that relationship.
Furthermore, even in the absence of Sītā being given to Rāvaṇa in any other way, they must certainly go to Laṅkā;
"certainly" (niyatam) is used here in the sense of a strong probability.
The meaning is "it must indeed be obtained"; the intention is that it has been stated, "And the king shall be the one who takes the jewel. Thus, on account of those reasons [previously mentioned].
Because it has been stated that "that which does not perish amidst all words is indeclinable" (*avyaya*), the attainment of plurality [is established].
The meaning is that [the state] is possible because of the cause of being one who never takes [anything], of being full of longing, and of being destined to go.
It refers to the prison of the city of Indra and of the celestial nymphs residing therein.
The phrase "for the sake of cessation" means up to that point.
The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: "May there be no insistence or force on your part here regarding Sītā; let it not happen"—these are the words of dharma. ||59||
"Who are these two? What are their names, and whose sons are they?"—this is the meaning of the question; "These two" is his answer. (60)
An obstacle to the sacrifice (*yajñapratyūha*) is an impediment to the sacrifice (*yajñavighna*).
The designation "impediment" (*vighna*) is applied to the cause of the impediment.
This is the figure of speech known as *hetu* (causation).
According to its definition—"Some declare that the identity of cause and effect is *hetu* (the figure of speech)"—this is *vikaṭa*, meaning "uneven.
For Tāṭakā died because she was a woman;
whereas, in the case of the two men, Subāhu and Mārīca, [the opposite occurred].
"What does 'how' mean? "Ah!
I consider that what has occurred is well-accomplished, as it were, and favorable to us.
The ritual procedure—consisting of the construction of the lake, the breaking of the bow, and the restoration of Sītā—if performed, would become "perverted," meaning it would turn out otherwise;
that is to say, if Rāma were defeated by Subāhu and Mārīca, everything previously mentioned would be rendered otherwise. Alternatively, the meaning is that "fate" (vidhi) itself would be altered.
Alternatively, the meaning is that fate (or time) might turn out otherwise;
or else, the meaning is that the Creator (the four-faced one) might act otherwise.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "Vidhi refers to ordainment, destiny, time, and also the lotus-born [Brahmā]."

Therefore, having observed that the matter—which has as its ultimate conclusion the occurrence of desired and undesired results—rests with Mālyavat, I shall inform my husband’s maternal grandfather (the king).

Here, by the phrase "I shall inform Mālyavat," the entry of the character Mālyavat at the beginning of the next act (*uttarāṅka*) is indicated; thus, this is called an *aṅkamukha*, a device for introducing the subject matter.
As it has been said: "Because the subject matter of the subsequent act is indicated by a character appearing at the end of the [current] act. (61)

"Being vigilant and attentive, may you conquer the negligent and inattentive one. The verb *ji* (to conquer) takes the ātmanepada ending by the rule *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ*. Previously, with Subāhu in mind, Viśvāmitra had said, "Let him be slain"; now, with Mārīca in mind, Kuśadhvaja has said, "Conquer the negligent one."
He has indeed departed along with his followers. O King Kuśadhvaja, come here, come this way!
Although you are indeed a king, nevertheless, there is no place for you here.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Do not go there. [The term] *sahānujasya* means "together with his younger brother";
the optional substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* is according to the rule *vopasarjanasya*.
Behold Rāma’s peerless and incomparable prowess;
for Amarasimha states: "pratimānam, pratibimbam, pratimā, and pratiyātanā" all mean a reflection or likeness.
Behold his valor!
For indeed, this Rāma destroys all those haters of Brahman— Subāhu and the others— who are like dogs to the Brāhmaṇas;
he slays them with a fierce and terrible Atharvaṇic rite of malevolent magic, as it were.
The meaning is that it destroys.
For the Atharvaveda consists of five Saṃhitās. As Vāyu said: "The Nakṣatrakalpa, the Vidhi of the Vedas, and likewise of the Saṃhitās..."
"The fourth is the *Aṅgirasāṃ Kalpa*, and the fifth is the *Śāntikalpa*.
These are the most excellent among the Atharvanic divisions (*vikalpaka*) of the *Saṃhitās*. Thus [it is said].
The *Nakṣatrakalpa* is the section concerning astrology (*jyotiṣ*).
The *Vedakalpa* is the procedure for the *brahmayajña* and other such rites; the *Saṃhitākalpa* is the procedure for the portion consisting of mantras;
and the *Āṅgirasa-kalpa* is the procedure for malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).

The term *śāntikalpa* means the ritual procedure for pacifying the eighteen great plagues (*mārī*) and so forth. By the phrase "of those who hate Brahman," it is stated that the purpose of the ritual of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) is solely the destruction of those who oppose the Vedas and Vedic injunctions. ||62||
Thus all have exited;
the phrase "from the stage" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Thus ends the first act.
The meaning is that the first act is completed;
according to Amarasimha, the word *iti* is used "in the senses of cause, section, manner, and completion."
Vīrarāghava, a descendant of Vādhūla residing in Mahīsāra,
has expounded the first act in the Mahāvīracarita.
Thus ends the first act in the commentary on the Mahāvīracarita, titled Bhāvapradyotinī, composed by Vādhūla Vīrarāghava, whose name begins with the syllable Aṇṇā.
The Second Act.
Now, beginning another act, he states its introductory summary (viṣkambha) with the words "Then, having promised," and so forth.
The definition of a *viṣkambha* is: "It is that which indicates portions of the story already occurred or yet to occur."
"The summary meaning, however, is that the *viṣkambha* (interlude) is performed by a middle-ranking character.
From which time— that is, from whatever period onwards—
from Sarvamāya, whose name is Sarvamāya.
The account of the events at Siddhāśrama, beginning with the slaying of Tāṭakā;
"tat" is an indeclinable used here in the ablative case.
The meaning is "starting from that point.
Regarding the word *dūrāt* (from afar):
[he saw] Mārīca, the son of Tāṭakā (*tāṭakeya*), who resembled a mountain (*dharaṇīdharābha*)—that is, like a mountain—and was the offspring of Tāṭakā.
"From feminine stems, the suffix *ḍhak* [is applied].

"Like grass" (*tṛṇavat*) means equal to grass; "even from afar" (*dūrād api davīyaḥ*) means that in which the action is extremely distant—that is how it is described. Alternatively, *davīyaḥ* is an indeclinable.
"From afar" means from a very great distance. "Vyadhūnot" means he cast [it].
That prince, the slayer of Tāṭakā and even of Subāhu, torments me in my heart. ||1||
Of his followers— that is, the companions of that Mārīca (as Amara states:
*anuplava* and *sahāya* both mean "companion")—
[Brahmā] fashioned with the excellence of the prowess, the superior strength, of the nectar-eating gods, that bow which the lotus-born, four-faced one created.
The phrase "of those who consume nectar" (*amṛtabhuja*) is intentional;
for nectar is the cause of extraordinary strength,
consisting as it does of the preeminent vigor of all the gods.
This belongs to Śambhu, hence it is *śāmbhavīya*.
According to the rule "the designation *vṛddha* should be stated for a name," the word *śambhu* receives the designation *vṛddha*; consequently, the suffix *cha* is applied by the rule *vṛddhācchaḥ*.
The meaning is "belonging to Śambhu."
The "duality of the bow" means its being divided into two parts; the suffix *dhamuñ* is applied according to the rule *dvitryośca dhamuñ*. Rāma performed this; he did it.

From the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *vi*, in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, because the *sic* suffix is *kit*, the substitution of *i* occurs by the rule *sthādhvoricca*; then, by the rule *hrasvādaṅgāt*, there is the elision of *sic*.
Rāma, who is immeasurable and inconceivable, [protected] Kṛśāśva, the son of Ṛkṣa, who was truthful in speech.
According to Amara, "the ṛṣis are truthful in speech."

From his disciple Viśvāmitra, he obtained—that is, received—the divine, praiseworthy Upaniṣad, which is the mother of victory and the bestower of victory, consisting of the secret portion of the Veda in the form of weapon-mantras. ||2||
Regarding the word *prasahya*: it means "by one who is bold" (*prauḍhena*) or "by one who is confident" (*pragalbhena*). The vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) occurs by the rule *prādūhoḍhoḍhyeṣaiṣyeṣu*.

By the sage Viśvāmitra—at the time appropriate for the slaying of Tāṭakā, while disregarding us, the messenger who was looking on—the sixth case (genitive) being used in the sense of "disregard" (*ṣaṣṭhī cānādare*), he forcibly overstepped the words of prohibition and performed a wonder consisting of the granting of missiles—something detested by Rāvaṇa and undesirable to him—unto Rāma; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. ||3||
"O Sītā!"—

the humiliation of King Sīradhvaja resulting from the forcible seizure of Sītā by means of abduction has been cast aside and disregarded. Furthermore, regarding us, the gods have shifted their status from being primary to being subordinate.
"Bringing to looseness" means it was rendered slack;
the sense is that there was now a dual sovereignty.
For (hi) because, at that time, by both the king and the gods, beginning with the presentation of the *nāndī*...
"Regarding the phrase 'one should perform the *nāndīmukha* at a wedding,' this refers to the *nāndī-śrāddha* and other such rites.
By the word 'and so forth' (*prabhṛti*), the sounding of divine drums and similar activities are intended to be included as having been performed.
Therefore, [the passage] beginning with 'Sītā's captor' is connected with what precedes it."

Whether everyone is capable or incapable, when majesty and prowess are being shattered—that is, when they undergo a distinction from their former state—they generally, or for the most part, undergo a transformation, reaching a condition contrary to their previous state.
The word "prāyaḥ" (generally) is used here in the sense of probability, according to the statement: "I think, I suspect, certainly, generally," and so forth. ||4||
She is called *vatsā* because she is a daughter's daughter (*dauhitrī*). She is described as such because her nails are sharp (*śarpavan-nakhā*).
Regarding this, although the suffix *ṅīṣ* is prohibited by the rule "after words ending in *nakha* or *mukha*, when they form a proper name," the suffix *ṭāp* is applied instead.

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "pūrvapadātsaṃjñāyām" (Pāṇini 8.4.3). Regarding the words *vārtāke* and *vartane*: "In the presence of a king (*rājasaṃnidhau*) or in the vicinity of Sīradhvaja (*sīradhvajasamīpe*), *vārtāka* refers to agriculture and the like; *vartana* also [refers to these]," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
They were "accomplished" (*nirvṛttāni*), meaning they were brought to completion.
In that city of Mithilā, at an auspicious time; the meaning is that it was offered as a sacrificial gift. *Māhendra* means belonging to Mahendra.
"Parārdhyāni" means the most excellent; as Amarasimha states: "parārdhya, agra, prāg-grāhara," and so forth.
These [qualities] culminate in, that is, reach their ultimate perfection in Rāma, the Brahmarṣi.
"Amogham" means that the weapon of the Kṣatriya— the weapon unique to the Kṣatriyas— and the favor shown toward Brāhmaṇas are unfailing;
that is to say, they produce their effects without fail.
In the compound "Amoghaśca Amoghaśca," the singular form is used according to the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyāmanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.69).
Furthermore, the splendor— the power to overcome others— of that Kṣatriya class which is conjoined with Brahman, that is, supported by Brāhmaṇas, is unassailable and invincible against a mere mortal,
that is, against one who is simply human.
According to Amara, "mātra" means entirety or restriction.
Regarding the word "utpattyā":
Rāghava, by his very birth—that is, by his very nature—in this world...
The instrumental case ending is used according to the rule *prakṛtyādibhya upasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 2.3.18).
"Adbhuta" means that which produces wonder, something indescribable, the well-known *bhūta*, the Supreme Brahman endowed with unconditioned existence (*nirupādhika-sattā*).
Here, the Śruti passage, "That great *bhūta* which is infinite or otherwise," as well as "Of this very great *bhūta*... is being evoked.
What is there to be lost by this Rāma being of such a nature, that is, by his being mortal or human?
The meaning is: nothing at all is diminished.

For the deeds of this Rāma are sung even by gods and asuras; moreover, the gods and sages—who are superior (uttara) through their reasoning (tarka), that is, through knowledge consisting of hypothesis and refraction regarding what ought and ought not to be done—bestow and accomplish eloquence, the capacity for the successful execution of difficult tasks, upon all things, that is, upon all entities characterized by mere existence.

And thus, the sense is that the conjunction of the power to be supported (*ādheya-śakti*) with the innate power (*sahaja-śakti*) results in an extraordinary performance of action. Brahmā is four-faced.

At the time of granting boons—specifically at the time of bestowing desired objects upon Rāvaṇa and others—he did not speak of fearlessness, that is, the absence of fear, from a mere mortal, from a human being who had been treated with contempt by him as "just a man.
The root *gai* (to sound) is used here in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
The meaning is that [Brahmā] granted Rāvaṇa immunity from being slain by gods and others.
Alternatively, "brahmā caturmukhaḥ" means "of us," referring to Rāvaṇa and his ilk;
the use of the word "us" (asmad) is made with the intention of including [Rāvaṇa] within the same category.
He spoke of fear—that is, dread—from mortals alone;

the intention is that, since he has granted immunity from death by gods and others through the remainder [of the verse], he has effectively granted the state of being subject to death only from humans.
Therefore, the connection with the preceding part is: "Do not say 'a mere human'. ||6||

To the objection that one should therefore simply form a friendship with that powerful Rāma, he replies: "By nature," etc. "By nature" (*nisargeṇa*) means by his own inherent disposition; the instrumental case is used according to the rule beginning with *prakṛtyādi*. He is the "protector" (*goptā*), meaning the guardian, of "dharma"—that is, the dharma taught by the Veda which is the means for attaining supramundane welfare; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
We, Rāvaṇa and the others, are "by nature haters of dharma" (*dharmadruhaḥ*), meaning we are those who have long been hostile toward the aforementioned dharma.
The word "we become" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Therefore, a conflict—arising from the very nature of things—between us and our powerful opponent, Rāma, has arisen; that is, a relationship of destroyer and destroyed has come into being.
This is the underlying intention.
From the verbal root *duh* in the sense of "desire to kill" (*jighāṃsā*), the word *droha* is derived;
and *jighāṃsā* is the desire for destruction.
From the verbal root *gup* in the sense of "protection" (*rakṣaṇa*), the word *gopana* means protection.
And that [destruction] is the establishment of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of its own counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), which is the destruction itself.

Thus, the relationship of the destroyed and the destroyer between destruction and its prior non-existence is prompted by the very nature of the thing (*vastusvabhāva*), and not adventitious (*aupādhika*).
For it is well known that the establishment of the prior non-existence consists in the destruction of the cause that produces the counter-positive.
Therefore, there can be no friendship between you two, like that between fire and frost.
And it has been said by Kāmandaka: "The seizure of a king’s wife, his station, his country, his kinsmen, and his wealth; likewise intoxication, pride, and sensual affliction;
the obstruction of knowledge, purpose, power, and virtue; and even fate itself [are causes of ruin]."
"Disrespect for one's own interests, the destruction of kinsmen,
the severing of favor toward living beings, the corruption of the circle of states, and an obsession with unjust matters— these are the sources of war. Thus it is said.
Here, the contradiction resulting from the obstruction of the Dharma has been stated. ||7||

The connection with the preceding clause is: "I know that he does not desist, even though his gaze is being drawn away by specific glances—that is, by specific movements of the eyes—and his sight is being led inward.
The underlying sense is that Rāvaṇa might even engage in physical combat due to the force of his wicked pride (*māna*).
Here, the cause of the conflict is stated to be what is called *māna* (pride).
"Worthy of veneration" (*vandyāḥ*):

those who are worthy of worship (*pūjyāḥ*), the creators of the universe (*viśvasṛjaḥ*)—the progenitors of the worlds—at the beginning of the ages such as Kṛta and the rest; the teachers (*guravaḥ*) or well-wishers who provide instruction;
the offspring of the Self-born (*svayambhuvaḥ*), known as the *Svāyaṃbhuvās*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*).
Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of a grammatical operation conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), there is no *guṇa* substitution; hence, *uvaṅ* is applied.
The word "they become" (*bhavanti*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
And being related to the Vaideha, the king of Videha, why are they not dear?
That is to say, they do not become dear.
"Aho" expresses amazement.
"Neither we nor Kumbhakarṇa and the others—why are we not dear, why are we not beloved because of our kinship, and why do we not become cherished as relatives?
In this regard, the following statement should be kept in mind: "The one of great splendor created Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and Vasiṣṭha as the seven mental sons."

Granted that our relationship with the Creator of the universe may somehow be undesirable; yet, how could such a thought have arisen in the heart—how could it have been produced—that even Rāvaṇa, the descendant of Pulastya, the Lord of the World who possesses sovereign power under a single umbrella over all realms, who is radiant with blazing splendor through difficult penance consisting of bodily mortification, and who is possessed of a flaming majesty, should suffer a deficiency? That is to say, how did he come to perceive in his mind a lack of noble lineage, ascetic power, and sovereignty, which serves as the cause for not bestowing his daughter upon him? ||8||
The word "athavā" (or rather) expresses a challenge to what was previously stated.
Regarding the phrase "in his desiring":

even though the desire of the powerful lord, the master Rāvaṇa—the desire for the maiden—was manifested today through the mouth of Sarvamāya, whereas it had never been manifested before, the attainment of the fruit does not occur; that is, the acquisition of the fruit in the form of Sītā does not take place.
By this, the cause of opposition known as "insult" (*avamāna*) has been stated.

With the word *pratyuta* ("on the contrary"), [the text] refers to one who acts in opposition to what was previously mentioned; that is, the son of Daśaratha, Rāma—who is performing a service for his own kinsmen (such as Tāṭakā and others) by slaying them, and who is engaged in conduct opposed [to Rāvaṇa]—is joined with, or united to, Sītā, that maiden sought after by Rāvaṇa.
Here, by the word *druhyat* ("acting inimically"), the cause of opposition consisting in the destruction of a kinsman is stated.
By the phrase "united with that maiden," the cause of contradiction in the form of a single-pointed attachment is stated.

Furthermore, how can the proud ten-faced lord of the world tolerate—that is, how can he endure—the excellence of his enemy’s honor (māna), which consists of respect or mental exaltation, as well as the excellence of his fame, which is the renown of his possession of virtues, and his jewel of a woman? This is the meaning.
The root *mṛṣ* is used in the sense of "endurance" (*titikṣā*) and belongs to the *daivādi* class, taking both voices (*ubhayapadī*).

Here, the cause of opposition in the form of pride (*mada*) is expressed by the word *dṛpta*, and the cause of opposition in the form of arrogance (*māna*) is expressed by the phrase *mānayaśasoḥ*. ||9||
Half-entered from the dressing room—
meaning onto the stage— is the doorkeeper.
The meaning is "a man appointed to the gate.
Amara states: "Dvāri means one who stands at the door (dvāḥstha) or a doorkeeper (pratīhāra). Vārtāharaḥ means a bearer of news.

In the sense of "one who brings news," the suffix *ac* is applied to the root *hṛ* by the rule *āṅi tācchīlye*. Thus, *vārtāhara* means "by that news-bringer"; *tamālarasa* refers to the juice of the *tamāla* tree.
According to the lexicon, "rasa" [denotes] passion, liquid, and joy.
For that palm-leaf is white;
the sense is that there, the dark blue tamāla juice possesses an excellence of secondary luster (*parabhāga*).
Having introduced it—that is, having placed it nearby—he reads or recites it.
From the root *vac*, belonging to the curādigaṇa, the suffix *ṇic* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*).

Regarding the word *svasti*: having stayed on the island characterized by Mount Mahendra—that is, the island of Mahendradvīpa—the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used according to the rule "when there is an elision of a *lyap*-suffix, [the case ending is used] for the object or the locus."
It honors and respects.
The term *prabhupada* refers to a statement concerning a lord (*prabhu*). Regarding the word *pada*: "The word *pada* [is used] for pretext, foot, footprint, place, portion, and mark."
"Regarding *vyavasāya* (exertion), *suptiṅanta* (inflected words), *sāyaka* (arrow), *vastu* (subject matter), and *vākya* (sentence)," so says the *Ratnamālā*.
*Duḥśliṣṭakrama* means having abandoned the proper sequence. "In the sense of power (*śakti*), *paripāṭya* and also *krama* [denote] a step or stride," so says the *Ratnamālā*.
Having written concerning the Great King, one should write concerning the Minister.
Here, by omitting Rāvaṇa and writing instead of Mālyavat, the established order of the letter has been abandoned; this is the intended meaning.
This very point is found in the letter sent to me.
A *māheśvara* is one for whom Maheśvara is to be worshipped; [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "this is his devotion.
Having greeted—that is, having praised—the Lord of Laṅkā, Rāvaṇa, he speaks.
The meaning is that he uttered these words.
Regarding the honoring of ministers, the honoring of the king follows by a fortiori (*kaimutika*).
Furthermore, there would be an insult if one’s name were explicitly mentioned in the written document.
Therefore, the underlying intention is that he has depicted me alone, setting aside Rāvaṇa.

He explains the manner in which the subject of the painting was executed with the words beginning "viditam" (known): "by us," meaning by me, [from] the devotees or attendants of the holy sites (*tīrtha*) of the Daṇḍaka forest—that is, from those who serve the sacred lands or the sacred waters situated within the Daṇḍaka forest.
This [verse] ends in the dative case.

According to the *Ratnamālā*: "Descent into water, the means of entering a guru's womb, the scriptures, sacrifice, water resorted to by sages, the eighteen [categories] beginning with mantras, holy ground, a worthy recipient, water, and the menses of a woman—these are the sacred fords (*tīrtha*)."
"Security" means the cessation of fear; that is to say, it has been promised—that is, it has been accepted as something to be performed.
"This is known" connects with what precedes.
In this regard, those who frequent the holy sites of the Daṇḍaka forest are acting contrary to the purpose we have pledged.
Having restrained Virādha and the others and turned them back, may they—out of regard for our devotion to Maheśvara established among you—desire [to remain].
[The form] *anurudhyantām* is derived from the root *rudh* meaning "to desire," belonging to the *divādi* class; here it is used in the active voice (*kartari*) with the imperative suffix *śyan*.
The implication is that if Virādha and others do not desist, our affection for you—which is desired by you—would be frustrated.
Regarding the word "brāhmaṇa":
the abandonment—that is, the cessation—of transgression or offense against brahmins belongs to you alone.
"For your own prosperity and for your ultimate welfare"—this is the ellipsis; it does not mean "for our security alone. You must perform the transgression against and the abandonment of the Brahmins.

However, the sense is that this must be done even out of a desire for your own welfare. Would Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni, truly be a friend to you? The implication is that by the word "and" (ca), your prosperity alone is the primary fruit, whereas our friendship is merely incidental.

Otherwise, even in this case, upon the transgression against a Brahmin, the son of Jamadagni will become *durmanāyate*—that is, he will have a troubled mind (*duṣṭamanaska*) toward one named Duṣṭanāmaka;
he will become angry. This is because the suffix *kvaṅ* is applied after the bahuvrīhi compound *durmanas* by the rule: *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca*.
There is the elision of the letter *s* and the lengthening [of the preceding vowel]. ||10||

The introductory discourse (*upanyāsa*), which is a composition of words, is characterized by a support that is slightly smooth, somewhat gentle, firm, and profound; it is deep, dense, weighty, and grand.

Its slight gentleness is due to the statement that friendliness (*maitra*) follows as a natural consequence of the opposite of dejection (*daurmanasya*), and because prosperity (*bhūti*) is said to be the primary goal.
The word "indeed" (*khalu*) indicates what is well-known.
The meaning is that he is well-known for the specific qualities to be described hereafter.
Regarding the word "abhijana": it means by his own, that is, his personal [lineage].
"‘Nijau’ means one’s own and ‘svīyau’ means indestructible," according to the *Ratnamālā*.

One whose pride has increased—meaning whose arrogance is fit to grow—due to the excellences or preeminences of lineage (family), asceticism (such as the emaciation of the body), learning (consisting of divine knowledge), valor (prowess), and action (such as sacrifice or battle).
The suffix *arha* is used here in the sense of fitness.

According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The words *mada* (intoxication/arrogance), *dāna* (gift/flowing rut-fluid), *garva* (pride), *harṣa* (joy), *retaḥ* (semen), and *mṛgamada* (musk) all signify 'intoxication' (*mada*).

Nevertheless, because he has abandoned all [worldly things] such as noble lineage, and because he knows them to be unworthy of regard as causes for being overcome by others, this son of Jamadagni—remaining inactive and indifferent toward the insults of others—somehow, in some manner, out of affection for Śiva (that is, due to the love prompted by his devotion to Śiva).
This means that, according to the previously mentioned method, there is a reversal of the primary and secondary states.
"Without reliance" means being devoid of dedication;
according to the *Ratnamālā*, "reliance (*āsthā*) refers to a vow, intent, a social circle, effort, or perception.
It "designates us" by saying such things as, "the bypassing of Brahmins must be avoided," and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding each task he himself desires, he becomes exceedingly harsh like a master;
the meaning is that, according to the saying "the king kills as if laughing," he becomes one who wields an extremely sharp rod of punishment like a king.
Alternatively, in the phrase "like a master" (*prabhuriva*), there is a word-division (*cheda*) as *aprabhuriva* (like one who is not a master).
Regarding the phrase *kārye kā*, there is a division as *kārye akārye*.

Thus, the meaning is this: out of indifference, he designates himself as somehow powerless or, as it were, incapable. But regarding *akārye*—that is, when an undesirable task such as the transgression against a Brahmin must be performed by us—he becomes exceedingly harsh; such is the sense. ||11||
"Yadi," and so forth.
If Rāma, the breaker of Śambhu’s bow—that is, the one who shattered the bow of Rudra—should come to know of, or become aware of, [the situation] regarding the disciple of Śambhu, namely Jāmadagnya;
here, the genitive case in "śiṣyasya" is used in the sense of a residual relation (śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī).

The meaning is: "If it should become an object of knowledge related to his disciple. Śambhu’s disciple, Jāmadagnya, does not *titikṣate*—that is, he does not tolerate; for the suffix *san* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*) according to the rule *tijeḥ kṣamāyām*.
The meaning is that he will not tolerate the insult to his guru.

If, due to the connection with the fury of their wrathful exertion in the field of battle—that is, in war—there should occur a mutual destruction between both Jāmadagnya and Dāśarathi, like that of Sunda and Upasunda, then that would be exceedingly dear to us; it would be our ultimate desire.
The word "syāt" (should there be) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. ||12||

Even if one or the other were victorious—even if each were to triumph over the other—if Paraśurāma, the slayer of kṣatriyas, should conquer or overcome Prince Rāma, then having slain this prince, his desired object would be accomplished and fulfilled.
The phrase "if [he were] Aja-kṣvāku" refers to an alternative to the previously mentioned position;
as Amara states: "In the sense of another alternative, *ced* or *yadi*."
Victorious, overcoming [all], devoted to Brahman, and a benefactor of the Brahmins, Rāma—the son of Aja and Kakutstha—should not strike the Brahmin-sage Bhārgava; he is not worthy of being killed.

Having attained the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) and being as good as liberated, this son of Jamadagni should not fix his mind upon, nor even think of, taking up a weapon that has been cast aside or blunted.
His attainment of the highest good is to be understood from his renunciation of weapons out of respect for Rāma and his commitment to asceticism (*tapas*).

Then, since there was defeat at the hands of Rāma Bhārgava, what distinction [could there be]? The sense is that, because both were fixed as targets in the combat, there was no difference in their status as enemies. First, he is described as one whose vow or rule consisted of [protecting] the forest-dwellers—those humans residing in the forest.
The suffix *vuñ* is applied according to the rule "araṇyān manuṣye" (Pāṇini 4.2.129).
Furthermore, he would remain exactly as he was, still observing the *āraṇyaka* vow;
the sense is that he would not wish to act against us merely for the sake of killing Rāma.
"He" refers to him.

"If" (*cet*) indicates an alternative position. "Praiseworthy" means excellent due to his virtues and other qualities. "The prince," namely Rāma, however, desiring to rise again—even after the slaying of Bhārgava—desiring to rise once more, being one who wishes to attain the highest excellence.
The sense is that this is because it has been stated: "Likewise, a kṣatriya is content.
Regarding *utsāha-śakti* (the power of energy), it refers to the power of steadfast effort until the attainment of the fruit;
for it has been said: "Energy is a firm effort."
"Most excellent by excellence" means most preeminent through its superior quality.

Rāvaṇa was preeminent; Kārtavīrya was more preeminent; and Jāmadagnya was most preeminent—this is the usage of the suffix *tamap*, prescribed for the selection of a specific object from among a class.
[He saluted him] who was victorious through righteousness.
By this, his status as a deceitful warrior is refuted.

If one conquers that Bhārgava, all the gods (nirjarāḥ) would know—that is, understand—that victorious Rāma is the most excellent of all. Due to Rāvaṇa’s prowess—by the valor of Rāvaṇa—the musical instruments of war were silenced; that is, the specific instruments used in battle were rendered inactive.
There is also the reading "nibhṛtakruddhāḥ" (secretly enraged).
They would "enforce" or "actively engage" against this Rāvaṇa by force.
For, from the "insult"—that is, the humiliation—of the gods who have conquered their vital breaths (the Asuras), there arises "popular unrest," meaning a rebellion within the kingdom.

"The minister, the kingdom, the fortresses, the treasury, and the army as the fifth—these are declared by those who know [statecraft] to be the constituent elements (*prakṛti*) of one desiring victory," so says Kāmandaka. "Constantly attached" means constantly following; therefore, the connection is that they would forcibly exercise authority.
Regarding the word *paulastya*:
