that sage Bhārgava, through the defeat—that is, the subjugation—of Paulastya (Rāvaṇa), performed the very act of concluding the narrative, the destruction of the mention of all *kṣatra* (the entire class of Kṣatriyas) concerning Kārtavīrya—the son of Kṛtavīrya, Arjuna—who was of fierce deeds and violent conduct; this very conclusion of the narrative, the accomplishment of the completion of the composition, was itself the prescribed rite (*vidhi*), the performance of ordained duty, serving as the preliminary auspicious ceremony (*prāṅmaṅgala*) for the sake of completing it without obstacle at the outset.
Even though the *Madhyāntavibhāga* [is mentioned] here, the word "previously" (*prāk*) is used in order to exclude that [work].
He performed—that is, he began—the *vadha* (the slaying), which serves as an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) for the sake of a completion free from obstacles.
The locative case in "Kārtavīrye" is used because one intends to express the locus of the action.
Even toward such a person as that son of Jamadagni, [the act] was brought about—that is, rendered appropriate and fitting.
The meaning is that because a Brāhmaṇa is unfit to be slain, it took the form of drawing his bow with [mere] power;
he is thus described as one who performed this subduing or instruction.

"Being capable" means being powerful; "having abandoned fear of us" means having relinquished apprehension of harm caused by us. He whose conduct—that is, his behavior—is "gentle" (saumya) through righteousness such as compassion and so forth, is described thus.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *saumya* may refer to a wise man, a brahmin, or one presided over by the Moon-god; it may also mean 'beautiful' or 'not fierce'."
The meaning is that Rāma, as the lord of the universe, ought to become the sole sovereign ruler. ||13||
In this dilemma:
the provocation, sharpening, and kindling of enmity on the part of Paraśurāma;
on the other hand, a great fault would arise for Rāma in slaying the son of Jamadagni.
The meaning is that there will be the great misfortune previously mentioned.
Even in that case—that is, even if Rāma should defeat the son of Jamadagni—we shall provide a remedy, taking countermeasures according to our power;
"by us" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
By the phrase "retribution in the form of banishment to the Daṇḍaka forest, the abduction of Sītā, and so forth through deception," the meaning of the fourth act has been indicated.
However, with the words "but rather" (*kiṃtu*), there is an abandonment of the second alternative and an adoption of the first alternative.
[The phrase] "those very same... refers to this.

Regarding the passage beginning with *rāmasya*: if those very elements (*bhūtāni*)—namely, the earth and other elements that constitute the body and are unique to Rāma—are present; as Amara states: "The word *bhūta* [is used] in three genders when joined with *kṣmā* (earth) etc., or when it means a living being, or when it signifies 'equal'."
If those very powers and if those capacities are common to the world, then we neither perceive nor ascertain the defeat of Paraśurāma by Rāma.

This is the sense: if the powers that constitute the beginning of Rāma’s physical form and the capacities common to other heroic men were indeed common to all heroic men, then the defeat of Paraśurāma by Rāma would certainly not have occurred.

However, according to the scriptural teachings such as, "The body of this Supreme Self is not composed of an aggregate of elements; His form is not material," and "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold," it must certainly be suspected that Paraśurāma was defeated by Rāma due to Rāma’s possession of a physical form and power that transcend the world.
Alternatively, those very same elements of Paraśurāma’s body might have remained in their prior state if they had not been drawn forth [into a new form].
The meaning is "the syllables.
If those very [syllables] are the powers—
meaning, if even the powers have not been drawn forth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Then Rāmāditya," etc., this is the underlying intention: if Rāma had not drawn forth the essential powers of the weapons from Paraśurāma, his defeat by Rāma would not have occurred.
If those powers had been drawn forth by Rāma, then his defeat by Rāma would certainly have taken place.
"What, are they the very same? and so forth.
Indeed, the very elements that constitute the body of Rāma become the constituents of the body of Paraśurāma;
for surely the powers residing in Rāma become those residing in Paraśurāma.
Since both are incarnations of the Blessed One, they are identical in their essential nature (*dharma*);
therefore, we do not perceive the defeat of Paraśurāma. This also suggests that there is a logical impossibility in the notion that "one cannot be defeated by oneself."
Therefore, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Arise in order to set forth for Mithilā," meaning to cause the son of Jamadagni to depart for Mithilā.

There, on Mahendra Island, the descendant of Bhṛgu—the offspring of Bhṛgu, Paraśurāma—is to be seen; the meaning is that he must certainly be seen even for the sake of prosperity through this present occasion.
Regarding the term "profound" (*gabhīra*):

he is profound and difficult to comprehend because of his majesty, his great exertion, his great fortitude, his great-mindedness, his possession of a great nature such as noble lineage, austerity, and excellence, because he is a portion of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and because of his great knowledge and his great body.
[As the lexicon states: "The word *ātman* is used for effort, fortitude, mind, nature, and the Supreme Self."

This son of Jamadagni, when seen—that is, directly perceived by living beings—is a bestower of happiness and a cause of well-being for all people, like the ripened accumulation of the merits and good deeds of every person, or like the excellence of their harvest ready to yield fruit. This is due either to the preeminence of his sovereignty as the sole lord of the world, or to the extraordinary power of his capacity suited for the accomplishment of all tasks; and it is also due to the purity and sinlessness resulting from the ultimate perfection of his austerities, such as the emaciation of the body. Furthermore, he restores the *sattva*—meaning the strength, the quality of goodness, or the very essence—of every living being.

"‘Sattva’ [is used] in the sense of a substance such as a *piśāca*, effort, and essential nature; it is a quality, life-force, strength, mind, and existence, but among living beings it is not feminine. Thus says the *Ratnamālā*.
It causes to prevail, that is, it increases.

thus, its connection with the preceding phrase is "it should be seen.

Here, because of the excellence of its sovereignty, by the statement "it strengthens the *sattva*," the meaning of the Vedic scripture—"The Great Puruṣa is indeed the Lord and the instigator"—is brought to mind.

The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used here to denote continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*).

For *tattva* is the single performance of an action for the sake of multiple primary objectives.

This has been established by the venerable Jaimini in the eleventh chapter of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā-sūtra*; it should be examined there.

"‘Cakra’ refers to a collection, a whirlpool of water, a wheel (the part of a chariot), a kingdom, and an army; it is neuter when referring to a type of vessel or a means of accomplishment, but in common usage it is masculine. Thus says the *Ratnamālā*.

This embrace of Vaidehī— cool, refreshing, smooth, and tender like yellow sandalwood and like the moon— and this very embrace of Sītā, repeatedly causing the suspension of consciousness and inducing a state of swoon,
holds him back from any other side or direction.
The meaning is that he effects a cessation of movement. [The suffix] *śnam* is applied after the root *rudh* (to obstruct) according to the rule *rudhādibhyaḥ śnam*. ||22||
"Hā" expresses sorrow;
this refers to Bhārgava.
"Dinakarālokaḥ" means the splendor of the sun.
*Prabhāparikṣepaḥ* means a halo of light. According to the statement in the *Amarakośa*, "The word *paraśu* [meaning axe] is used for two genders," the term *paraśu* is not neuter.
[The word *ḍāmara* here means] tumultuous by reason of the radiance of his matted locks (*jaṭāprabhābhiḥ*).
He is skilled in the *ḍāmara* (chaotic battle) and the *vipīlava* (destruction); the suffix *aṇ* is applied here in the sense of "skillful" according to the rule *kṛtalabdhakrītakuśalaḥ*.
Thus, the meaning is "one who causes fear.

With a violent impact—that is, a firm blow—from his two formidable, pillar-like thighs, which were cast far apart, extended long, and possessed uneven shanks, he caused the earth to tremble; having arrived, this great destroyer of all Kṣatriyas has indeed reached the battlefield like a great *rākṣasa*.

"This" refers to this particular individual standing before one. "The sole hero of the three worlds" means one who performs heroic deeds (*vikrama*) among the foremost (*eka*) in the three worlds (*tribhuvana*).
The word *vīra* is derived from the root *vīrayati*, listed in the *āgarvīya* group as meaning "to act with heroism," with the suffix *pacādyac* applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
If the analysis were *ekaś ca vīraḥ* (a single hero), the resulting form would be *vīraika*. That sage was the descendant of Bhṛgu.
The meaning is that the sage Bhṛguputra is well-known.
He who is this Bhārgava sage is great, unlimited, and difficult to approach; he is unfit for one to go near him, like a mass, that is, a collection, of splendors.
The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Furthermore, he is, as it were, the very embodiment—possessing a physical form and shining with brilliance—of the confluence, that is, the meeting of his majesty (the power to scorch his enemies) and his asceticism (the discipline of emaciating the body through penance).
Moreover, he has attained a state of solidification, having reached the condition of a mass, [and is] a most fierce and intense essence.

By virtue of being relished by the audience, according to the logic of the *sūpa-kaṭa* (soup and vegetables) analogy, it comes to be designated by the word "rasa" (*rasaśabdavācya*) by resorting to its future state—just as "heroism" (*vīra*) [is so called] or just as "anger" (*krodha*), which consists of the mind’s flaming up due to an offense committed by an enemy.
The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
In the first simile, the removal of obstacles occurs through mere proximity.
The second [type] occurs when the adversary is neutralized through a specific relationship;
the third is when the adversary is neutralized by means of physical action—such is the distinction. ||23||
Regarding the word "merit" (puṇya):
the phrase "this which" is to be supplied from the preceding context.
It refers to a specific place for the preservation and protection of vows and ascetic practices.
He who possesses power and capability regarding immeasurable and infinite tasks is so described; or alternatively, he who possesses immeasurable powers is so described.
He is also meritorious and most righteous.

"Regarding the three words *dharma*, *ambu*, and *puṣpa*, merit (*puṇya*) is [implied] when they are accompanied by the suffix *vat*," according to the *Ratnamālā*. This descendant of Bhṛgu, whose actions are formidable—that is, whose activities are terrifying—possesses a form (body) that is both pleasing and terrible (*abhirāmaghorām*), a compound of adjectives similar to *khañjakubja* ("lame and hunchbacked"). It refers to his physical body.
"Successively" means up to that point. "Bibhrat" means maintaining or holding. One who has studied the Veda proclaimed by Atharvan is an Ātharvaṇika.

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied because [the word] begins with "vasanta" and so forth. By virtue of the rule regarding the *dāṇḍināyana*-group, there is no elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant).
The sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) of an *ātharvaṇika* is called *ātharvaṇa*.
In the section beginning with "caraṇāddharmāmnāyayoḥ," by the rule "ātharvaṇikasyekalopaśca," the suffix *aṇ* is applied and the suffix *ika* is elided.
Since the word *āmnāya* (scripture) does not enter into the denotative range (*vācyakoṭi*) of the suffix, there is no tautology in expressions such as "the Atharvaṇa Veda.
[The phrase] "it shines" means it appears or manifests like a *nigama* (Vedic text), that is, like a *āmnāya*.
The suffix *laṭ* is used here from the root *cakāsṛ*, meaning "to shine.
In the object of comparison (*upameya*), there is holiness due to the favor shown to those who bow down, and terrible activity due to the suppression of adversaries.

In the object of comparison (*upamāna*), there is loveliness through its tone and color, while there is dreadfulness through the ritual of sorcery (*abhicāra-vidhi*) expressed by the verbal meaning; such is the distinction. 2cha.
"This one indeed" means this Bhārgava; and his lineage continues in the subsequent [verses].
Of the *kalpa*—the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) presided over by the day of Brahmā;
for the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *kalpa* refers to dissolution (*pralaya*), logic (*nyāya*), scripture (*śāstra*), the day of Brahmā, and ritual injunction (*vidhi*).

[He is] effecting—that is, bringing about—the state of being the fire of Kālarudra, which is affectionate (*praṇayi*) toward destruction (*apāya*, i.e., dissolution), because he consists of Rudra, who is the death of all beings.

There is a prohibition of the *num* augment [after the word *tigma*] according to the rule *nābhyastāc-chutaḥ*. "Tigma" means sharp. Being prepared and favorable for the destruction—that is, the crushing—of the entire multitude of worlds (*nikhilabhuvanastoma*), the whole collection of the universe;
as the *Ratnamālā* states: "The term *brahman* refers to the Supreme Self, austerity, the Veda, Brahmā, and the twice-born."
"Having become a heap" means having become a mass;
since power (*śakti*), being formless, cannot logically constitute a heap, the suffix *cvipratyaya* is used here to indicate the attainment of that state [which was previously absent].
"Of the God of gods" refers to Him who was praised by Indra and the other deities when they were oppressed by Tripura.

Therefore, "saṃrabdhasya" means one who possesses angry exertion. "Tripura" is a collective term for the three cities (*purāṇām*); there is no feminine gender because it belongs to the *pātrādi* group.

Of that victorious conqueror Rudra; from the root *ji* (to conquer), as taught in the rule "ji abhibhave," the suffix *inip* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule "jidṛkṣiviśyartīṇvamāvyadhābhyamaparibhūprasubhyaśca. It is like the essence—that is, the excellence—of the powers, meaning the capacities for destruction.
The word "becomes" (bhavati) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
There is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). In the phrase "under the guise of Brahman" (*brahmacchadma*), however, there is the specific figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment). ||25||
*Svacchandya* means acting according to one's own will (*svābhiprāyeṇa*).
According to Amarasimha, "will" (*abhiprāya*), "desire" (*chanda*), and "intention" (*āśaya*) are synonyms.

One whose will or intention is his own (*sva*), and who does not depend upon the world or the scriptures, is *svacchanda*; the word *svacchanda* belongs to the class of words beginning with *brāhmaṇa* (the *ākṛtigaṇa*), and thus the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied to form the abstract noun denoting the action of such a person.
The meaning is that its variety and manifoldness are marvelous.
Regarding the word "light" (*jyotiḥ*),
the verb "became" (*abhavata*) is to be supplied.

On the neck of the venerable Paraśurāma shines an axe (kuṭhāra), which is matted (jaṭila)—that is, possessed of matted locks—due to the mass (pracayena) or collection of the portions that have issued forth as the brilliance, splendor, and flames of the luminaries.
The suffix *ilac* is applied to the word *jaṭā* in the sense of possession because the word belongs to the *picchādi* group, which is an open class (*ākṛtigaṇa*).
The axe is the *paraśu*.
Furthermore, regarding "on the shoulders" (*aṃse*), it means on the tops of the arms; "quiver" (*tūṇīra*) means an arrow-case.
The word "shines" (*bhāti*) is to be supplied [to the verse], and it is modified into the plural form. By this, the sense "they shine" (*bhānti*) is obtained.

Although it is stated generally as "in his body" (*vapuṣi*), one should understand by implication that the matted locks appear on his head, the bow in his left hand, the bark garment around his waist, and the [sacred thread] upon his chest. Furthermore, in his right hand, an arrow flashes— that hand in which there is a trembling rosary of Rudrākṣa beads strung together.
Since it is thus, he is both fierce and peaceful, terrifying and beloved.
This is a descriptive compound (viśeṣaṇasamāsa), like the term "lame-and-crooked" (*khañjakubja*).

The artificial form produced by the previously mentioned axes and other instruments spreads a beauty that is a fusion—a blending—of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) and the peaceful sentiment (*śāntirasa*).
The meaning is that he spreads [his influence].
Here, the distinction is that his ferocity is indicated by the axe, quiver, bow, and arrows, while his tranquility is indicated by the matted locks, bark garment, and rosary of beads. ||26||

The plural number in "eta" (these) is used for the sake of honor. They are the gurus. The term "guru" is used because of his status as a preceptor through his connection to the lineage of Vasiṣṭha and his kinship with the father-in-law's family.
*Āvaguṇṭhana* means covering.
*Parāgata* means having arrived; that is to say, Bhārgava has come into one's presence.
The noble one is his father-in-law; since he is the son of that [father-in-law], he is designated as "husband" (*bhartṛ*), and thus this address is "Noble Son" (*āryaputra*).
What is intended here by "departure" (*pariāṇa*) is the absence of going into the presence of Paraśurāma.
"The Sage" (*muniḥ*).
This sage Paraśurāma is one whose nature is contemplation of the Supreme Self.
The word "atha" (now) introduces another quality;
this Paraśurāma is such a hero, a superhuman hero.
Thus, since this union of my sagehood and my state as a great courtesan is dear to me,
therefore, O timid one, O unsteady one, let your trembling, your quivering, cease— let it vanish.
(The *parasmaipada* ending is used here according to the rule *vyāṅparibhyo ramaḥ*.)
Furthermore, O timid one, you are a Kṣatriya;
that is to say, you belong to the Kṣatriya caste.
Therefore, the implication is that even for this reason, trembling is not appropriate.

In the absence of the optional *ṅīṣ* suffix and the augment *ān* [prescribed] by the rule "after *ārya* and *kṣatriya*, when the word refers to itself," the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied to the word *kṣatriya* because it has a vowel in the penultimate position (*yopadhāt*).
He explains what was stated as "that is dear to me" with the words beginning with "asceticism" (*tapasi*) and so forth:
"I am a Kṣatriya of the Raghus, born of the lineage of Raghu; [my arms] are 'itching,' meaning they abound in that itching which requires the act of rubbing."
In the case of *sidhma* and other such conditions, the suffix *lac* is applied to the word *kaṇḍū* according to the rule "from small creatures and afflictions.
He was capable—that is, he was able—of performing the service, meaning the attendance, of that [Parasurama] whose arms were [like] defects.
This is the meaning.
In this passage, the two qualifiers beginning with "tapasī" (ascetic) are applied to Paraśurāma, who functions as the object (*karman*) of the act of service;
whereas the two qualifiers beginning with "rāghavakṣatriya" (Rāghava-Kṣatriya) are applied to himself, who functions as the agent (*kartṛ*) of that service. This is the intended meaning.

The word *raghu* is derived from the root *laṅgh* (to leap) by means of the rules and vārttikas: "there is elision [of the penultimate vowel]," and "the letters *l*, *r*, or *v* optionally replace the final letter of the words *bāla*, *mūla*, *laghu*, and *aṅgulī*. Since the root *laghi* means "to go," and according to the principle that "roots meaning 'to go' also mean 'to understand,'" the sense of going implies understanding; thus, *laṅghate* means "he knows. Therefore, the fact that Raghu knows everything constitutes the basis for the application of the name *Raghu*, signifying his preeminence in knowledge.
And it has been said by Kālidāsa: "May this child reach the end of what he has heard.
Likewise, I possess the capacity for service toward a venerable object—one who is devoted to asceticism and whose birth is consistent with my own lineage of Raghu, which is superior in knowledge.
Furthermore, by virtue of being a Kṣatriya, I am capable of satisfying that object, which is afflicted by the itching of pride. This is the meaning.

Regarding the statement "Since [the formation] is already established by the inclusion of *prādi* in the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, the inclusion of *ku* indicates that compounds with *prādi* are only occasional (*kvācitkatā*)"—according to this grammatical dictum, there is no compound for *pari*.

Furthermore, because the term *vā* (or) is understood to carry over from the rule *paryabhibhyāṃ ca*, the suffix *tasil* is also absent. Thus, the two words *paricaraṇasamayaṃ* should be understood as separate.
The poetic figure is *śleṣa* (paronomasia). ||27||

The lack of self-knowledge—the state of being devoid of knowledge of one's own true nature—of this wicked-souled, evil-minded Kṣatriya boy, this Kṣatriya child, is truly astonishing; such is the meaning. "He was not terrified," etc.

By that young Kṣatriya, Rāma—the agent—who was breaking and shattering the bow (*dhanuścāpam*)—the term *ārujatā* is derived from the root *ruj* (meaning "to break") belonging to the Tudādi class, in the present participle (*śatṛ*) form; because the suffix *śa* of the Tudādi class is marked as *ṅit*, there is an absence of *guṇa* strengthening. By him, through the continuous, uninterrupted flow of compassion (*karuṇā*) toward all beings, [he surpassed] the Blessed One, who is full of the six divine attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*), the God worthy of worship by all.
"Lineage (saṃtāna) refers to descendants, family line, offspring, and celestial trees," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
He whose self (*ātman*) or heart (*hṛdaya*) is tranquil—that is, free from anger and other such passions—is so described; [I bow] to that Lord of Bhavānī, the husband of Pārvatī.
Bhavānī is the wife of Bhava.
By the rule "indravaruṇabhavaśarvarudramṛḍahimāraṇyayavayavanamātulācāryāṇāmānuk," there is the addition of the suffix *ṅīṣ* and the augment *ānuk*.
Śiva is her husband; therefore, [the word is formed].
The ablative case is used by the rule "bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ" (for words meaning fear or protection, the cause of fear is expressed in the ablative).

If "not terrified" (*na trastam*) signifies the absence of fear, then the suffix *kta* is applied to the root *tras* in the sense of a state (*bhāve*), according to the rule "gatyarthākarmaka... (Pāṇini 3.4.72). Regarding the word *nāma*, Amara states: "The word *nāma* [is used] in the senses of manifestation, possibility, anger, approach, and censure."

The meaning is: "Even if," for one possessed of compassion characterized by suffering at the suffering of others, there is an absence of apprehension regarding the misfortune dependent upon that [suffering] because of the non-arising of the suffering of others; this is what is intended by the word "yadi" (if).
The word "tena" (by him) is to be supplied.

By that Rāma, his son—that is, the son of that Lord of Bhavānī—on account of the slaying of Tāraka, the demon Tāraka, who was blinded by pride (*mada*) and thus devoid of discrimination between what ought and ought not to be done, an "offering of festival" (*dattotsava*) was made to all living beings of the universe, meaning he performed the act of producing joy for them.

The meaning of "gives" (*dadāti*) is figuratively "performs" (*karoti*); thus, there is no dative case after the word *viśva*. As for *skanda*, he is Skanda, who—compared to the previously mentioned compassionate Lord of Bhavānī—is distinguished by an excellence of sharpness resulting from his function as a commander-in-chief.
Amara states: "The particle *tu* may signify difference or emphasis."

"How was it not heard?"—the sense is: having heard that Skanda was such [a hero], how could Rāma not have desisted from breaking the formidable bow? Or rather, the sense is that in the absence of fear of Skanda, he is as dear to the Lord of Bhavānī as Skanda himself, and even more so because of his superior strength.
"I am a disciple of the Lord of Bhavānī who has mastered all branches of learning; have you not heard that I am even more powerful than Skanda?
Because my strength exceeds that of Skanda, I am not incapable [of this task].
Furthermore, according to the maxim, 'One should restrain those who revile the gods and gurus to the best of one's ability,' the disparagement of my guru must certainly be avoided by me."
Therefore, the sense is: "How is it that you disregarded me and crushed the bow of our preceptor? ||28||
The harsh consequence—the final result—of tranquility, that is, the cessation of anger, is of the nature of misfortune.
As for the word "yat" (that):
even over those Kṣatriyas who do not deserve it, sovereign power—that is, lordship—remains established by me even after the total destruction of all Kṣatriyas.
Furthermore, by those very same Kṣatriyas—who are unworthy of such honor—I have now, during my lifetime, seen their umbrellas once again held aloft.

Moreover, I have heard again the unrestrained and transgressive deeds of those Kṣatriyas whose minds were deranged by the intoxication of their own arms and the pride of their power; that this very thing is the result of my tranquility (*praśama*)—this is how it connects with what precedes. ||29||
Regarding the term *akalila*:

it is "not *kalila*," meaning not mixed with faults (*doṣa*). The word *kalila* is derived from the root *kāl* by applying the suffix *ilac*, according to the rule: "The suffix *ilac* is applied after the roots *sal*, *kāl*, *nīm*, *mahī*, *bhaḍī*, *bhaṇḍī*, *śaṇḍī*, *piṇḍī*, *taṇḍī*, *kukī*, and *bhū*. Grammarians state that *kalila* means both "mixed" (*mitra*) and "thick" or "impervious" (*gahana*).
In that [person] who possesses the greatness— the sovereignty— of austerity (consisting of the emaciation of the body and so forth), of splendor, of majesty, and of heroism and strength;
[this is formed] by adding the suffix *iman* according to the rule *pṛthvādibhya imanij vā*,
and the substitution of *r* for the vowel *ṛ* according to the rule *ra ṛto halāder laghoḥ*.

When the sage Paraśurāma—puffed up, that is, filled with pride, which is a real entity because of the presence of the previously mentioned causes such as austerity, and which is a treasury, an inexhaustible storehouse, for the renown of possessing the aforementioned virtues of fame—rushed forward in anger, arriving swiftly, [she thought: "My hand, grasped this very day, that is, just now, and thus not subject to loss... [the rest of the verse follows].

The bow, out of impetuosity—whether through joy or haste—stirs and proceeds toward the act of subduing the pride born of excellence in the knowledge of archery, as well as toward the service appropriate for his forgiveness and toward battle, by means of clasping the feet and touching them with salutation. The sense here is that it is fitting for Paraśurāma to have his feet clasped through ascetic power and splendor, while it is fitting for him to engage in battle through heroism and arrogance.
The word "pāṇiḥ" (the hand) is used in the singular to denote the class. ||30||
"But what [is the point]?"—
this refers to the fact that the customary practice (*ācāra*) intended to be performed, namely the execution of either combat or the clasping of the feet, finds no scope or occasion [in this case].
If one does not fight when it is time for battle, there would be fault.
Even in the act of grasping the feet of one desiring to fight, there would be the fault of excessive prostration;
therefore, the meaning is that performance according to one's desire is not appropriate today.
The words "O, O! and so forth have already been explained.
"O sir, here I am," and so forth; the meaning is clear.
Regarding the phrase "you are sought":

although you, a being of pure nature (*viśuddhasattva*) and pure heart due to your noble birth, are being sought—that is, hunted—by me for the purpose of crushing or destroying me, out of pride (*darpa*), that is, from arrogance regarding your prowess, you consider yourself to be the cub (*kalabha*) of a lordly scent-elephant (*gandhadvipendra*), a superior species of elephant distinguished by its ichor.
"Kalabha means a young elephant," according to Amara. "Kūṭāni" refers to the peaks of elephants—that is, the mountain summits.
"Kūṭaḥ" (masculine/neuter) [is used] for a mountain peak, a machine, a heap, a battle, and a fraud.
"In *anṛta*, *māyā*, *sīrāṅga*, *niścala*, and *pāpa* [the suffix -a is applied]. Thus says the *Ratnamālā*. "Kumbhas" refers to the cranial lobes;
"the two *kumbhas* are the two lobes of the head," according to Amara.
It is a crusher and a cutter of them;
the suffix *ṣākan* is applied to the root *kuṭṭ* (meaning "to crush") according to the rule *jalpabhikṣakuṭṭaluṇṭavṛndaḥ ṣākan*.
You offer yourself to that lion (*mṛgāri*), whose very paw is a thunderbolt (*kuliśa*). You offer yourself as if you were his own self.
The meaning is "you cause to reach.
From the root *ṛ* in the sense of "going," the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied;
by the rule "arti-hrī-vlī-rī-krūyī-kṣmāyy-ātām puṅ ṇau," the augment *puṅ* (i.e., *puk*) is inserted.
The *guṇa* substitution [of *e* for *ay*] occurs by the rule "pugantalaghūpadhasya ca.
Therefore, the connection with what precedes is: "Truly, you are an Ikṣvāku. ||31||
"May evil be stilled. This means: "May the sin of Rāma be pacified by the unpleasant words uttered by Paraśurāma.
The past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is used here according to the rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca* ("in the sense of wishing, it is treated as if it were past").
"May ill-omened misfortune be struck down. The meaning is: "May that which is contrary to auspiciousness, caused by the previously mentioned sins, be destroyed.
Here too, as before, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used.

Regarding "to himself" (*svagatam*): the term *svagata* is used when one reflects upon a secret matter by oneself. As it has been said: "That which is audible to all is *prakāśa* (public); that which is not to be heard is considered *svagata* (to oneself)."
Regarding the word *cañcit*: the root *cañcati* is listed among those meaning "to go" in the rule, *vañcu-cañcu-tañcu-tvañcu-mruñcu-luñcu-racu-mlucu gatyarthāḥ*.
Thus, it is stated that he whose crest-jewel—his ornament—is five tufts (*pañcaśikhaṇḍa*) is so described.
According to the *Ratnamālā*, "śikhaṇḍa" refers to both a crest and a tuft of feathers. "Mugdha" means fresh; that is to say, endowed with childhood.
"Pragalbhaṃ" means mature due to its power;
"mugdhaḥ" refers to one who is gentle, new, or foolish—according to the *Ratnamālā*.
This is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*).

His form—that is, his physical appearance—is described as such because it is profound, its nature indiscernible even by the wise, captivating, and delightful; and because it possesses innate, natural marks of glory and beauty (*śrī-lāvaṇya-lakṣmāṇi*) which are the characteristics of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) well-known in the *Sāmudrika* treatises.
[As for the word *rūpa*: "Form" (*rūpa*) refers to essential nature, to white and other colors, to beauty, and also to drama.]
"Regarding the forms *grantha* and *ākṛti*," so says the *Ratnamālā*.

This youth Rāma, who possesses and bears the onset of youth, though seen by me only this very day, captivates—indeed, brings under his own sway—the heart of even one like me who am an assailant; that is to say, he becomes a source of delight. He does so by means of the splendor and abundance of the essence of beauty, the pinnacle of loveliness.
Nevertheless, even though he causes such pleasure, it is accepted that "he must indeed be killed by me"—

the word *tu* is used here for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), and *nāma* is used in the sense of anger (*krodha*) or reproach (*kutsana*), according to Amara’s lexicon (*"tu syād bhedāvadhāraṇe" and "nāma prākāśyasaṃbhāvyakrodhopagamakutsane"*).
Fie upon the cruelty of the vow of heroes— the rule that one must engage in combat!
The meaning is that cruelty is censurable.
The accusative case is used according to the rule "in the presence of *dhik*, *upari*, and three others.
Amara states: "*Dhik* is used in the senses of reproach and censure. ||32||
"Prāk" means previously. That by which a blow (nisumbha) has been obtained— that is, experienced— is described as such.
The word *nisumbha* is conventionally used in the sense of "striking.
It refers to such a bow belonging to Śambhu, a fierce bow;
the suffix *aṇ* is applied after the word *śambhu* according to the rule *tasyedam*.
"By making twofold" means by dividing into two;
that is to say, by making two parts. The suffix *edhāc* is applied to the word *dvi* (two) according to the rule "edhācca."
Impelled by a surging and intensifying rage, Bhima—by the pillar-like arm of the formidable Bhārgava Paraśurāma—has hurled that flaming, firm, and unyielding axe;

let it become your guest for a moment upon your very throat, which shall serve as its seat. (According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *kaṇṭha* may denote a denotative term, proximity, the throat, or sound.")
The meaning is: "Just as a guest sits upon a seat, let this axe remain for a moment upon your throat.
By means of this aforementioned axe standing before him, even the Lord Hara—Rudra, who desires victory—is made known throughout the worlds as "Khaṇḍaparaśu," becoming famous by the name Khaṇḍaparaśu.

"May this axe fall upon your neck—you who have broken this bow, which has never before been broken by anyone other than Viṣṇu! Alternatively, "O Rāma who has not previously encountered Niśumbha" is an epithet of Rāma in the vocative case;

Ah, O son of Daśaratha!

Of one whose anger is non-existent and whose wrath is pacified. "Astra" refers to the practice of missiles, that is, training in archery and the binding of targets.

"How so? and so forth.

"By which," and so forth.

Alternatively, the plural number is used because of the multiplicity of the collection [of axes]. It is well known that Khaṇḍaparaśu (the axe-wielder) grew forth as Khaṇḍaparaśu; by that very axe won through victory—attained through victory over Skanda, the enemy of the stars (Tārakaripu)—your fame as Paraśurāma was reached. "Utpattiḥ" means: your birth, O Blessed One, worthy of worship, from Jamadagni—that is, from Jamadagni;

That is to say, [he is] the master of the science of archery (dhanurveda). The meaning is that everything indeed becomes preeminent in the world.
Why is the neuter gender used for the general term?

To speak in a manner that is delightful and pleasing to the heart; for the *dhātupāṭha* states: "The root *mantri* means to converse in secret.
Thus, [she calls out] "Rāma, Rāma!"

From the word *ramaṇīya*, the suffix *vuñ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) according to the rule *yopadhādgurūpottamād vuñ*.
"In every way"—that is, by all means such as beauty, virtues, and so forth—you are heart-stealing to me. The meaning is: you are dear even to my enemy.

In the section on the suffix *khac*, by the Vārttika rule "it should be stated that *khac* follows *gam* when a word ending in *su* is the upapada," the suffix *khac* is applied to the root *gam* with the word *hṛdaya* as its upapada; and upon the addition of the augment *mum* to the word *hṛdaya*, the word *hṛdayaṅgama* is formed. ||37||
"Herambeti": the word "rāma rāma" from the preceding [verse] is to be supplied here.

In this context, the word *bhitti* refers to a side that resembles a wall. The reading *ekabhakti* means "a single delineated part. According to the *Ratnamālā*, "the word *bhakti* may denote a part or service."

My chest, marked and scarred by the wounds of arrows,

The suffix *ṇini* is applied to the causative form of the root *grah* according to the rule *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye*. By means of that goodness, the state of being a virtuous person, [the mind] is purified, meaning rendered free from defect.
The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Alternatively, even though the excellence (*utkarṣa*), that is, the preeminence (*atiśaya*), of the qualities of others—which transcend all—is a reality (*tattva*), that is, possesses substantial existence (*vastubhūtatva*); [it is surpassed] by one who has reached the limit (*kāṣṭhā*) through grasping its measure (*parimāṇa*).
In this context, the suffix *ṇini* is applied to the root *grah* (to grasp) alone.

(The *Ratnamālā* states: "A *granthi* is a joint or a section of a disease").

The suffix *ṇvul* is used in the active sense (*kartari*).
"To peace" (*śamam*) is the ellipsis.
Favor should be shown even to those who have committed offenses when they offer a request.
"For the virtuous show favor even toward those who have killed their fathers"—such is the teaching of the scriptures.
What need then be said of [showing favor] to superior persons who have committed no offense when they make a request?
Or rather, it refers to your lack of malice (*adruh*), that is, your absence of enmity.
The root *druh* is used in the sense of "desire to harm" (*jighāṃsā*); the suffix *kvip* is applied in the abstract sense (*bhāve*).
They become supplicants (*yācakāḥ*).
The meaning is that they are entreating you to desist from your desire to harm Rāma. ||5||
All this that is being said by you is true;
however, the word "but" (kiṃtu) indicates an exception to the previously stated point.
As for the phrase "the root of the enemy":

The enemies are metaphorically described as "roots" because they are the cause of their regrowth; the sense is that, being Kṣatriyas, they are roots of enmity toward himself, and by breaking his bow, they are enemies toward his own preceptor.

"Without uprooting" means without extracting them. [This is derived] from the root *khanu* (to dig) with the suffix *lyap*, where the substitution of *ā* for *i* occurs optionally according to the rule *ye vibhāṣā*.

I do not venture, nor do I resolve, to see again Tryambaka, the three-eyed one; the Teacher, the instructor of the science of archery; and the Teacher’s wife, the preceptress Pārvatī. [The forms are derived] by the rule "ācāryādaṇatvaṃ ca," which prescribes the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, the augment *ānuk*, and the absence of the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*.
"Utsāhaḥ syād vyavasāyaḥ" (energy is resolve), according to Amarasimha.
Although those two are compassionate, the sense is that I am not worthy of seeing them because I have committed an offense against them. ||6||
If you are devoted to your gurus and possess affection for them—
[the root] *anu-rudh* meaning "to desire" belongs to the *divādi* class [of roots]—
then, for that reason of devotion to your gurus, take some heed even of these two, Vasiṣṭha and Śatānanda.
The meaning is: "Know that [he] is to be attended to for a moment. The root *cit* (in *citī saṃjñāne*) belongs to the *curādi* class.
He establishes his status as a guru with the words: "from Hiraṇyagarbha... and so forth.
Those three sages— Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras— were born from Hiraṇyagarbha, the four-faced one.
The word "in them" (teṣu) is to be supplied [as the object],
because the relative pronoun *yat* is invariably followed by the correlative pronoun *tat*.
For there is a constant syntactic connection between the words "yat" (that which) and "tat" (that). "Among them, he is Vasiṣṭha" means that Vasiṣṭha is the one who is well-known among them.

Among them, you are the delight of Bhrigu; that is to say, you belong to the lineage of one of those [sages], Bhrigu. This Śatānanda also belongs to them—he is the son of the grandson of Aṅgiras, who himself was the great-grandson of one of those [sages].
In the phrase "sa tvaṃ tasyāṅgirasaḥ," the words *tat* and *yat* do not function as correlative pronouns (*pratinirdeśa*).
This is because the word *tat* is not observed in relation to Bhṛgu.

If one were to supply the word *tat* as referring only to him (Bhṛgu), the compound *bhṛgunandana* would be grammatically untenable; therefore, it should be understood that the necessary supply of the word is *teṣu* (in them).
In this regard: "Then, as he meditated upon creation, ten sons were born to him who was endowed with the power of the Blessed One, serving as the causes for the continuation of progeny:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu," and so forth.

The statement from the *Bhāgavata*, "Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, and Nārada as the tenth," should be kept in mind. Furthermore, the following is also intended here: "Vasiṣṭha was born from the vital breath (prāṇa), Bhṛgu from the skin, Kratu from the hand, Aṅgiras from the mouth, and Atri from the eye."
From the immutable Hiraṇyagarbha came Aṅgiras; from him Ucathya; from him Gautama; from him Śatānanda.
Likewise, from the immutable Hiraṇyagarbha came Bhṛgu; from Bhṛgu came Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ.
From them, in succession, came Arcīka; from him Jamadagni; and from him Paraśurāma.

Thus, regarding the superiority of rank (*sthāna*), Śatānanda is superior to Paraśurāma because he occupies a higher position; however, Vasiṣṭha is superior to both in terms of both rank and age, as he is the eldest great-grandfather and is older. Therefore, they both occupy the status of gurus toward Paraśurāma.

Furthermore, since Śatānanda is the offspring of Aṅgiras—who is the elder and possesses the most excellent limbs—he too occupies the status of a guru toward Paraśurāma; the sense is that both of them must be respected. ||7||
Regarding the phrase "prāyaścittam" (expiation):
here, the vocative "viśvāmitra" is to be supplied.

O Viśvāmitra, because of your transgression—that is, your act of hostility—toward those who are venerable and worthy of honor, and specifically because of your refusal to grant the peace requested by you, I shall perform an expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) which serves to avert the resulting sin.
The taking up of weapons itself is a great vow, a means for achieving great power.
I shall neither defile nor violate that dharma which has been resolved upon as something necessarily to be performed—
using the causative form from the root *duṣ* (meaning "to spoil" or "to cause corruption").
The lengthening of the vowel is by the rule *doṣo ṇau*.

Here, according to the method previously stated, it should be understood that Vasiṣṭha and Śatānanda possess a status of venerability toward Paraśurāma, whereas Viśvāmitra’s venerability toward Paraśurāma arises from his being the father [of Paraśurāma’s mother] and his maternal uncle.

According to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), "One should generally recognize sin; its purification is *prāyaścitta*," the word *prāyaścitta* denotes a religious duty (*dharma*) that removes transgression (*pratyavāya*).
The augment *suṭ* is applied by the rule "prāyasya citticittayoḥ.
In this context: "One should not cause distress to an elder, such as a father who has begotten a son, nor even to a teacher;
nor should one address them with the singular form of their name, or use the vocative 'tvaṃ', or utter the sound 'huṃ'."
"To avoid those faults, one should observe the Nāciketa vow;
having performed twelve nights of *kṛcchra* penance and bathed with one's clothes on, one becomes purified through the grace of the Guru"—this is the statement from the *Skānda Purāṇa* intended here.
By the word "should cause pain," both the performance of what is undesirable and the non-performance of what is desirable are meant.

Although, according to the Yājñavalkya-smṛti rule "and there is a lapse regarding atheism," one incurs a minor offense (upapātaka) upon abandoning the vow of wielding weapons, nevertheless, when that abandonment occurs by the command of a guru, the transgression resulting from the violation of the guru's word does not arise. Furthermore, due to the traditional teaching: "These eight do not destroy a vow: water, roots, ghee, milk, sacrificial oblation, the desire of a Brāhmaṇa, the word of a guru, and medicine," the fault of violating the vow does not occur.

Therefore, the word "but" (*tu*) is used to dispel the doubt that one must abandon the very taking up of weapons out of deference to the teacher's command; rather, since the attainment of a great fruit results from the observance of the vow of taking up weapons, that very vow should be maintained.
The sense is that the fault of transgressing against the teacher can be rectified by means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Furthermore, according to the reasoning stated, Vasiṣṭha and others are teachers by birth alone, whereas the Blessed Lord Tryambaka is a teacher both by birth and by knowledge; he too was born even before Hiraṇyagarbha through Marīci and the other sages.
This is stated in the *Bhāgavata*: "Though restrained by the mind, that wrath of Prajāpati was instantly born from between his eyebrows; he became Rudra, the blue-and-red one.

Furthermore, considering the request of Tryambaka—who is a teacher in both ways, being a teacher through the instruction of the Vedas and a teacher through sacred knowledge (*vidyā*)—the word "great" (*mahat*) in the term "Mahāvrata" is used with the intention that any transgression against you, who are teachers by birth alone, is of no consequence.

And so, according to the aforementioned method, in the consideration of what is weighty or light, and in the consideration of what bears fruit or not, the vow of wielding the weapon alone must be observed, because it is weighty and possesses fruit.

On the other hand, the adherence to Vasiṣṭha should be abandoned because it is light, because it is devoid of any fruit beyond the avoidance of transgression, and because that transgression can be removed even by expiatory rites (prāyaścitta). This is the intention of Paraśurāma. ||8||
Let it be so; nevertheless, strive for that unsurpassed fruit characterized by the crossing over of saṃsāra through the practice of yoga previously described.

For the fruit of the vow of taking up weapons is indeed extremely small in comparison to that. Therefore, since the abandonment of weapons itself serves as a means to liberation by bringing about tranquility (*śama*) and other virtues, one should perform that very act; to this he says: "yataḥ" (from which). "Yataḥ" means by which, namely, by a particular natural disposition or inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
"Saṃsiddhi, prakṛti, svarūpa, svabhāva, and nisarga"— thus says Amarasimha. [The word] vimukteḥ means from liberation (mokṣāt).
By the word *api*, [the sense is] "from your kinsmen and from you. The ablative case is used according to the rule *pañcamī vibhakte*.

The protection—that is, the preservation—of honor (*māna*), which consists of an excellence of veneration resulting from valor, victory, and so forth, is dear and desired to me; behold my nature to be such as that.

Even though liberation is inherently beautiful, it is not merely the beauty of the object that is the cause for desiring it; rather, as the saying goes, "Food is the sustenance for humans, but nectar for the dwellers of heaven," there is also the nature of the enjoyer, conditioned by the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of experience and determined by the distinction between states such as divinity and humanity through the fixed order of what is to be enjoyed.
You should explain the cause for this.
Furthermore, you are kinsmen who seek to cast off your human condition.
According to Amarasimha, "sapindas are sanābhis.

The substitution of *sabha* for *samāna* occurs by the rule beginning with "jyotirjanapada-. Those related through a lineage formed by the physical body are the external relations (*bahiraṅga*), as are the bowstring (*maurvī*) of the bow (*cāpa*).
"Jyā, maurvī, bhūmi, and mātṛ" [are synonyms for earth], according to the *Ratnamālā*.
He is so described because he has scars, which are marks of wounds;
he is harsh and impetuous.
"Syāt karkaśaḥ sāhasikaḥ"—thus says Amara.
The *bhuja* is the arm; this arm, being employed for the sake of protecting honor (*māna*), is "internal" (*antaraṅga*) because of its direct connection to the body—meaning it is more intimate.
And so, according to the principle that "between the internal and the external, the internal is stronger," the protection of the honor cherished by the arm is indeed the more powerful factor.
The sense is that this indeed results in the destruction of the proof (māna) favored by you;
and my aforementioned nature is such that it becomes even more clear through the very marks upon my arms—this is the intended meaning. ||9||

"Fully honored" means that its greatness—its excellence in steadfastness and other virtues—is praised. For the vow of a hero, which is easily subject to hatred at every step and in every situation, I shall certainly not violate it without having uprooted the very root of my enemies. The meaning is that in many instances, even for the sake of liberation, the preservation of honor is dear.

Uttering—that is, making manifest—words that are the speech of Paraśurāma; "marmas" refers to the vital points within the body which, even by a slight cause, become the cause of death. The suffix *manin* is applied here according to the rule *sarvadhātubhyo manin*.
Those which pierce or strike are called *marmāvidhaḥ*.
The suffix *kvip* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
By the rule "na-hi-vṛti-" etc., there is also lengthening of the vowel in the preceding member.
The meaning is: even though they are causes of suffering, they are not so because of the activity of Rāmabhadra, which prevents their manifestation.
"They cause me—who am permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of heroism—to experience horripilation; that is, they make me possess bristling hair.

[This is formed] from the word *romāñcavat* with the suffix *ṇic* and the elision of the suffix *matup*, according to the rule: "The suffix *ṇic* is frequently applied after a nominal stem in the sense of a verbal root, and it is treated like the suffix *iṣṭhan*.

The meaning is: "It is true that they gladden me—who am permeated by the latent impressions of heroism—through the excellence of their speech and retorts, and through the outpouring of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*). (10)
"Brahman" refers to those who are distinguished and mixed; the word "mixed" (*miśra*) and the plural number are used here as a mark of respect.
And thus, the meaning is that Vasiṣṭha is worthy of worship.
Those whose minds are "ekatāna"—meaning their mental activity is focused exclusively on Brahman and on the tranquility, self-restraint, and other virtues appropriate for a Brāhmaṇa—are so described.
Amara states: "Ekatāna means having no other activity."
The meaning is that they are indifferent toward war and such matters.
The word *hi* indicates well-known fact.
Regarding the deeds of heroes—such as the preservation of honor and so forth—you, who are the ancient and eternal teacher and instructor, speak; that is, tell [us].

The ellipsis is "the determination of the meaning to be explained hereafter. By me— who, having been born in the lineage of Bhṛgu (so called from the etymology *bhṛjati aniṣṭam*, "one who scorches what is undesirable"), whose nature is solely that of tormenting the undesired, and who belongs to one [lineage] most abundant in purity such as firmness of vow— this weapon was taken up.
In this matter concerning the taking up and the renunciation of weapons, what is appropriate?
The word *atha* has the sense of a question; the meaning is:
"What is appropriate?"—this is what is being asked.
The sense is that the vow of taking up arms must be observed even due to the nature of one's lineage.

Regarding the word *bhṛgu*: according to the rule "there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and elision of the *s* in the roots *prathi*, *mrad*, and *bhrasj*," the suffix *ku* is applied to the root *bhrasj*, resulting in vocalization, the elision of *s*, and the change to *g* (via the *nyaṅkv-ādi* class).
Grammarians state: "Bhṛgu is so called because he scorches (*bhṛjjati*) with ascetic heat."
The root list states: "bhrasj in the sense of cooking. (11)
"Kāmam" means "indeed.
This Paraśurāma is great, excelling [others] by his qualities such as valor, heroism, and firmness in his vows.
"Kāmam" is used here in the sense of granting permission.
The meaning is that the greatness of his virtues is indeed approved by me;
according to the *Ratnamālā*, "the indeclinable *kāmaṃ* is used in the sense of desire and longing, as well as for permission.
Furthermore, the word *punaḥ* has the sense of the word *tu* (but/however).
"Punaraprathame bhedē" is Amara’s definition [of the term *punar*].
However, [the word *prakṛtyā* is used] by nature (*svabhāvataḥ*);
the instrumental case is employed according to the rule "The addition [to the list] of *prakṛti* and so forth."
"An asura is indeed an asura.
Because [the word] belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class beginning with *prajñā*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*).
The meaning is: "one who is predominantly of the nature of an asura."
Regarding this, he states the reason: "because of excellence" (*utkarṣāt*).

For (*hi*) because its activity (*vṛtti*) or operation (*vartana*) extends everywhere—that is, in all modes—therefore, by reason of that preeminent excellence, one becomes arrogant (*dṛpyati*), full of pride (*garvavān*), in such a manner that the action possesses all forms (*sarva ākārāḥ*), such as being mental, vocal, or physical.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "Arrogance (*darpa*) refers to self-conceit (*ahaṃkāra*) and the musical instrument *kaṃsya*."
The root *dṛp* belongs to the *divādi* class, meaning "to be proud" or "to be deluded by joy.
The meaning is that because of pride (*darpa*) induced by an excess of valor, heroism, noble birth, and so forth, he is of an asuric nature;
for pride is indeed the inherent disposition of an asura.

And so it was sung by the Blessed One: "Hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, as well as harshness, and ignorance—these, O Pārtha, belong to one born to the demonic nature (āsurī saṃpat). The meaning is that hypocrisy and the rest are its inherent characteristics. ||12||
"Child"— this address as "child" is used because he is the grandson of his sister.
I shall speak, that is, I shall say, this which is about to be told.
"Speak!"— when thus addressed, the meaning is "I speak this.
"In a single individual," etc.

Formerly, at an earlier time, you were transformed—having reached a state of agitation—by a certain anger arising from an offense such as the theft of a sacrificial cow; and having become thus altered, you brought about the destruction of the substrata, that is, the individuals who serve as the locus for the caste of *kṣatriyatva*, by means of a total eradication (*niranvaya-pramathana*)—producing a ruin from which there is no possibility of regrowth.
Destruction is of two kinds: destruction with a remainder (*sānvaya-vināśa*) and destruction without a remainder (*niranvaya-vināśa*).

In this context, the destruction of a lamp or similar object, characterized by the successive arising of subsequent flames following the cessation of preceding flames, is "destruction with a remainder" (*sānvaya-vināśa*).

However, destruction through extinguishing and the like—which renders the object incapable of producing further flames of its own kind—is "destruction without a remainder" (*niranvaya-vināśa*). By bringing about such a destruction without remainder, you have effected the very eradication—that is, the dissolution at all times and in all places—of the *kṣatriya* caste from the class of *kṣatriyas*.
The implied meaning is that since a universal (jāti) residing in a single individual cannot remain without a substratum once that individual perishes, the universal would necessarily be annihilated.
Furthermore, even a Kṣatriya born from the seed (śukra) of a Brāhmaṇa—meaning those who are Kṣatriyas born of Brāhmaṇas through Kṣatriya women—is still a Kṣatriya.
According to Amarasimha, "śukra" refers to both "tejas" (vital energy) and "retas" (semen).

The phrase "up to twenty-one" (triḥsaptāvadhī) connects with both what precedes and what follows. One should understand it as: "you brought about the destruction up to twenty-one [times]," and "it was extracted up to twenty-one [times]."
This is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) for the act of extraction (*uddharaṇakriyā*), meaning that the limit of the number seven is the defining boundary of that action.
Grammarians have indicated two positions: that the word *sapta* refers to the number seven either through its primary denotative power (*śakti*) or through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
The word *tris* ends in the suffix *suc*.
The meaning of that [suffix] connects with the act of extraction as delimited by the number seven; thus, "twenty-one times" is obtained.

This is because the suffix *su* (forming *saptakṛtvaḥ*) has the inherent nature of connecting only with a single action, and therefore it cannot connect with the number seven, even though it is proximate.
In the same way, it was extracted directly, just like a Kṣatriya.
The meaning is "destroyed. The words "by you" are to be supplied and modified accordingly. Furthermore:
"You were restrained—meaning you were constrained—by your own elders, such as Cyavana and others, who were superior in terms of status, age, and so forth;
and by your own kinsmen (the word *sva* meaning 'wealth' when not feminine, 'kinsman' in the masculine, and 'one's own' or 'self' in the three genders, according to the *Ratnamālā*).
Because of that anger produced by the offense of the aforementioned single individual, you desisted—you became free from it. This is how it connects with what precedes.

The sense is that because the vow of taking up arms was already completed previously, the consideration of the aforementioned results and non-results is here overtaken by an inopportune moment (*anavasara*).
In the word *vyaraṃsīḥ*, the Parasmaipada ending is used according to the rule *vyāṅparibhyo ramaḥ*; and the augment *s* and the *iṭ* are added according to the rule *yamaramanamātāṃ sak ca*. ||13||

"I have desisted. This means: "I have ceased, I have become one who has turned away from that great mandate concerning the slaughter of Kṣatriyas, which was prompted by the killing of my father and rooted therein.
And thus, the sense is that because the occasion (*nimitta*) has changed, it is indeed proper for me to feel anger and take up arms once again today.
In this context, *nihnava* means concealment or denial, occurring upon the cessation of anger provoked by the killing of his father.
As Amara states: "Denial (*apalāpa*), however, is *nihnava*.
[The word] *paraśuḥ* [is used].

Is he not, like a thunderbolt, fierce and sharp, a battle-axe that even performs the slaughter of Kṣatriyas—despite having abandoned and renounced the killing of Kṣatriyas? Has he not become the instrument for cutting—that is, the means of felling—the sacrificial fuel consisting of palāśa and other twigs measured at a span (prādeśa), as well as the logs of palāśa and other wood which are twice that size?
[The answer is: He has indeed become so. The word *vraścana* is derived from the root *vraśca* (to cut) with the suffix *lyuṭ* according to the rule *karaṇādhikaraṇayoś ca*.

Although Amara has stated that the words *samit* and *idhma* are synonyms in the verse "idhma, medha, and samit [are used] for firewood, with *samit* being feminine," nevertheless, one should understand that they are not synonymous here in accordance with the Smṛti: "The three—*samit*, *pavitra*, and *medha*—are measured at one span (*prādeśa*); however, the *idhma* should be made double that, and the enclosing stick (*paridhi*) is recorded as triple.
Furthermore, there is both a staff for times of distress and a bow-staff.

Does he not bear the likeness—that is, the comparison—to a venomous serpent (*āśīviṣa*), one whose fangs are indeed the silent and motionless arrows, and whose poison is like fire that has been extinguished and quenched?
The meaning is that he certainly does bear it.
The words "not" (*na*) and "what" (*kim*) are to be supplied [to the question].
Therefore, the connection with the preceding [verse] is: "What then is the concealment here?

Although, having begun with the metaphor (*rūpaka*) "the fang of the arrow," it was concluded as a simile (*upamā*) with the words "bears similarity," nevertheless, there is no fault because there is no absolute difference between metaphor and simile.
As it has been said: "Metaphor is considered to be nothing but a simile in which the difference is concealed. (14)
"Thus":
the two verses form a single syntactical unit;
[it was] by me, the agent, through the words and reasons of Cyavana and others.

In this manner, by the breaking—that is, the snapping—of the bow of Lord Rudra, the fire of anger and the axe, which had been restrained and turned back by Rāma, the son of Raghu, have now been truly and authentically raised up again; he is thus described as one who has committed such impudence (cāpalya), that is, such ill-behavior, in the same manner and by the same means as they were originally raised by the Blessed One.
Regarding the word *capala*, the *Ratnamālā* states: "The masculine *capala* refers to mercury or a monkey; it is feminine when meaning 'fickle,' 'ill-behaved,' 'swift,' or 'low.'"
Having forcibly—that is, by sheer violence—“*prasahya* indeed means *haṭha* (force),” according to Amara; having severed—that is, cut off—the head of the lone descendant of Raghu, Rāma.

[The absence of the augment *iṭ* in the form *kṛttvā* occurs] because the rules governing grammatical augments (*āgama-śāsana*) are not universally obligatory, as indicated by the rule “*kṛtī cchedane*” (the root *kṛt* is used in the sense of cutting).
"Mayi vanāya"— the dative case is used here according to the rule beginning with "kriyārtha-".
When [Rāma] has set out again for the forest, may the descendants of Raghu and the Janakas remain healthy and free from affliction for a long time.
"Let there not be, let it not happen, that an occasion for misconduct—such as the disrespecting of one's elders—should arise again by any means.
Here, by the phrase "the Raghus are the progenitors of one [individual]," the maxim "one should abandon an individual for the sake of the family" is indicated. ||15||
"Āḥ, śakti," and so forth.

According to Amarasimha, "āḥ" is used in the sense of anger (*kopa*) and affliction (*pīḍā*). It should be understood that the poet has here, through the mouths of Śatānanda and others, revealed the principle that "one must direct one's anger with all one's soul toward those who harbor hatred for the Blessed One, who is the supreme human goal."

Of one worthy of being sacrificed for—that is, one who ought to be made the object of a sacrifice; [the form] *yājyasya* is derived from the causative of the root *yaj* by means of the suffix *yat* according to the rule *aco yat*.
Even of the shadow (*chāyām*)—that is, even of that which is not heat (*anātapam*)—of one who is more beloved than the most beloved (*preyasaḥ*).
The phrase "even the vicinity" (samīpadeśam api) means up to that point.

The grammatical construction is: "Who has the power to *avaskanditum*?"—that is, to cry out (*ākranditum*). The suffix *tumun* is applied to the root *skand*, which signifies both "going" and "drying."
The meaning is: what need is there to mention who else would have the power to attack the son-in-law?
According to Amara, "the son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*) is the husband of one's daughter.
As for the word "we" (*vayam*): [it refers to ourselves].

In that [house], which has as its pillars—the supports that prevent it from falling—nothing other than good deeds (sucaritāni), which are virtuous actions whose authority is derived from the Śruti, Smṛti, and established custom;
"stambha" means a pillar or stiffness, according to Amara.

Here, the intended meaning is "the crushing of enemies and upright conduct" within the home of householders (gṛhamedhinām) who are devoted to the stage of life of the householder (gṛhasthāśrama), such as Janaka, Daśaratha, and others.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *gṛha* may denote houses in the plural, while these two [forms] refer to a house and a wife respectively.
Like us, Vasiṣṭha and the others, as well as Agni (*vahni*), become *gṛhya*, meaning submissive;
or, as with birds and deer, they become attached to a house—this is the implied sense.

"Regarding the *karmāvabodhaka*, [the term] *gṛhya* applies to those who are under one's own control among the three [classes]; *gṛhya* refers to the village boundary (*śākhāpura*), and *gṛhyāḥ* refers to deer and birds attached to the house. Thus says the *Ratnamālā*.

The suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *grah* [to form *gṛhya*] according to the rule "after the root *grah*, [the suffix *kyap* is used] in the sense of 'not independent' (*asvaira*), 'external' (*bāhya*), and 'belonging to a faction' (*apakṣya*)."
Furthermore, we have remained here for so long, and the fire likewise has remained for so long.
In this context, the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to what precedes, just as in the expression: "There is a jar in the house of householders; bring it.

If an insult from another—that is, a disparagement caused by someone else—should occur and persist, then even that penance consisting of a collection of rules such as fasting, though dearer than life itself, [must be undertaken].
"The word *tapas* [is used] for the observances (*niyamas*)," says Āpastamba. "Fie!"—
the meaning is that there would be a censure directed at the practice of austerity (*tapas*).

The meaning of the word *dhik* functions as the agent (*kartṛ*) in the action of "being" (*asti*). Alternatively, the indeclinable *astu* has the sense of "envy" (*asūyā*); and it should be understood that this envy is produced by the intention that asceticism and the like are of no avail.
Amara states: "In the expression of envy, [the word] *astu* is used."
Shame on the Brahminhood that is merely useful for the study of the Vedas and such;
shame on the Brahmin caste;
shame on the lineage of Aṅgiras!

"Fie upon the lineage of Aṅgiras, who was born from the mouth of Brahmā—specifically, as it is said, 'Aṅgiras was born from the mouth'! Fie upon his noble descent, learning, and conduct!"—this is the meaning. ||17||
"Gautama, son of Gautama":
he is so called because he has performed what was to be done.
The meaning is that although he himself is devoid of activity for the sake of the fruit, he nevertheless partakes of the fruit through your activity.
"No.
A *brāhmaṇa* is one who possesses primary *brāhmaṇya*.
Amarasimha states: "A *brāhmaṇa* is he who performs the six duties and is engaged in sacrifices and other such rites."
The learned one is always intent upon contemplating the means for your prosperity;
the suffix *kvasu* is used here according to the rule "vidaḥ śatur vā.
You belong to that Sīradhvaja (the Plough-bannered One).

One who protects and guards the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*) or the inhabited territory (*janapada*) is a *rāṣṭragopa*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied here in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule "from the root *gup*, meaning 'to protect'. According to the *Ratnamālā*, "the term *rāṣṭra* refers to the realm or the inhabited territory."
Such a person you shall become as a domestic priest;
the sense is that you will not only be a witness to the performance of Vedic and Smṛti rites, but also an observer in matters of statecraft.
The kingdom of that Sīradhvaja, being of such a nature, was not distressed by anything nor did it fear anything;
or rather, it was not "vyathate," meaning it did not undergo a reversal of its natural state.
For the root *vyath* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha with the meanings "fear" and "trembling."
"Vibration" (saṃcalana) is said to be the reversal of one's nature.
It does not perish, nor does it harm;
the words "mutually" are to be understood as the ellipsis.
Furthermore, the root list (dhātupāṭha) states: "The roots *ruṣ* and *riṣ* mean 'to injure' (*hiṃsā*).
Alternatively, by abandoning the aspect of impelling, the meaning is that one does not become a locus of suffering;
for injury indeed consists in the production of suffering.
It does not decay at an untimely hour, nor does it undergo laxity; for the root list states: "jaṝṣ and jhaṝṣ mean the loss of vitality. ||18||

By the Kṣatriya priests acting as agents, through the *brahmatejas*—that is, by means of the power (*prabhāva*) consisting of the capacity to overcome others employed by their Brahminhood—a manifestation occurred; that is to say, a certain activity took place. However, such a manifestation was merely among common folk (*prākṛta*).
"An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is a commoner (*prākṛta*)," according to Amarasimha.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied here by the rule "born therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*).

In this act (*aṅka*), the *vimarśasaṃdhi* (the juncture of deliberation), which consists of the connection between the *niyatāpti* (certainty of attainment) and the *prakari* (sub-plot), has been described.

As it has been said: "The reflection upon the purpose of the seed (bīja), which was established in the *garbha* juncture (*saṃdhi*), by whatever means whatsoever—that is intended as the *vimarśa* juncture. Because of the statement regarding the excellence of the certain attainment, its constituent parts (*aṅga*) are thirteen."
"In that regard,

there are thirteen [elements]: censure (apavāda), quarreling (saṃpheṭa), fleeing (vidrava), rushing (drava), power (śakti), splendor (dyuti), attachment (prasaṅga), movement (calana), resolve (vyavasāya), obstruction (nirodhana), encouragement (prarocana), agitation (vicalana), and seizure (ādāna)."

Likewise, there is the *vimarśasaṃdhi* (the juncture of reflection), which consists of the ascertainment of the effect in the form of Rāma’s welfare being free from obstacles due to the absence of misfortune (*apāyābhāva*) employed by Paraśurāma, together with a portion of the narrative involving Śatānanda and others that does not pervade [the entire plot] but is useful for that purpose. This is according to the definition: "The ascertainment of the effect through the absence of misfortune is the *niyatāptikā*; it is non-pervasive and constitutes the *prakarikā*.
The constituent parts (*aṅgas*) of this will be shown later.
"Anaḍvān-garvoddhata" is an indication by means of secondary figurative usage (*gauṇavṛtti*);
for a bull indeed becomes stiff with pride.
"O lowest of men, you who cannot endure the prosperity of others!

For the ability to endure the success of others is the mark of a superior man; the opposite of that is the state of being the lowest of men. [Regarding the phrase] 'though innocent,' etc.: the point is that even if someone has committed an offense by stealing the sacrificial cow and so forth, another person remains innocent."
The meaning is "causing distress" (*kadana*) or "causing dejection" (*vaiklavya*), or "causing deficiency" (*vaikalya*).
[The roots] *kadi*, *kradi*, and *kladi* are used in the sense of "dejection" (*vaiklavye*);
there is also a reading "in the sense of deficiency" (*vaikalye*).
Nandī states that all three [suffixes] are *anidit*;
therefore, there is no application of the augment *num*. [The form is] *mahāpātakin*.
The term *mahāpātaka* is both etymologically derived (*yoga*) and conventionally fixed (*rūḍhi*) in reference to acts such as the killing of a Brahmin.
From that [term], the suffix *ini* is applied.

Alternatively, when there is a desire to express an intensification—namely, that the great sin consisting of the killing of a Brahmin and so forth exists in an extreme degree—the suffix *ini* is applied to a *karmadhāraya* compound.
For excellence (*atiśaya*) is not obtainable through a *bahuvrīhi* compound;
therefore, the prohibition "not from a *karmadhāraya*" does not apply here.
And the "excessive Brahman-slaughter" refers to the form of the slaying of Kārtavīrya.

This was stated by Jamadagni in the *Bhāgavata*: "The killing of a consecrated king is more grievous than the killing of a Brahmin. The sense is that [the perpetrator] lacks the acceptance of the authority of the Vedas as recognized by the cultured (*aśiṣṭa*), due to his transgression of the prohibition against a Brahmin taking up arms.
The sense is that he has a deformed appearance because he carries objects contrary to the nature of a Brahmin, such as an axe, bow, and arrows, and because he bears scars from weapon wounds.
The vocative "O you whose deeds are loathsome" (bībhatsya) refers to one whose actions are to be reviled.
In the sense of "loathing" (*jugupsā*) regarding the word *vadha*, the suffix *san* is applied according to the rule *vadheś cittavikāre*.
From that, in the sense of the object (*karman*), the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *aco yat*. Thus, *apūrva-pāṣaṇḍa* means a "new heretic. [As it is said:
"Those who uphold the vows of worldly existence (*bhava-vrata*) and those who follow them accordingly..."

The sense is that this is because of the statement, "They are heretics (pāṣaṇḍins). The meaning is "one who wears the signs of sin," as stated in the passage: "Therefore, the sign of sin is called heresy (pāṣaṇḍa). And Amara also says: "Heretics are those who bear all [false] marks."
*Kāṇḍīraḥ* is the vocative form of one who possesses *kāṇḍas*, meaning arrows.
According to the *Amaraśeṣa*: "Sāyaka, pradar, kāṇḍa, kaṅkapatra, and śilīmukha [are synonyms for arrow].
The suffix *īran* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) according to the rule: "After *kāṇḍa* and *aṇḍa*, the suffixes *īran* and *īrac* [are applied]."
"Syātkāṇḍavāṃstu kāṇḍīraḥ" (one who possesses a shaft is called *kāṇḍīra*)—thus says Amara. A *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* is one who lives by weapons;
"śastrājīve kāṇḍapṛṣṭhāyudhīyāyudhikāḥ samāḥ" (for one who lives by weapons, the terms *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, *āyudhīya*, and *āyudhika* are synonymous)—thus says Amara.
Living by the profession of arms is forbidden for a Brahmin. You are being bold; you are acting with audacity. "Re" is a term used to address a low person.
"Is it not so?"—this is a statement of contradiction.
"Are you truly a Brāhmaṇa? In what country do you live, and what kind of Brāhmaṇahood do you possess?"—this is a sarcastic remark. "Aho! (expresses astonishment).
The conduct of the Brahmin is astonishing; this is the meaning. Regarding the word "of the mother":
The particle *eva* (only/just) emphasizes preeminence;
the sense is that while there is great sin in killing an ordinary woman, how much more so in killing one’s mother, who is the most preeminent?
Alternatively, it serves to exclude the doubt that—due to compliance with the words of a guru—the killing of a mother might not be a sin, by means of its restrictive sense (*avadhāraṇārthaka*).
The point is that compliance with the teacher's word is appropriate only in matters other than those involving mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), but not in cases involving a fall from caste (*patanīya*).

Accordingly, Āpastamba states: "One should remain under the authority of the teacher except in the case of acts leading to loss of caste," and "When told by the teacher, 'Kill this Brahmin, my enemy, in such a manner,' one should not do so"; for the *Ujjvalā* commentary explains it as referring to such instances. Likewise, since "the mother exceeds the father tenfold in terms of venerability," the killing of a mother—who is more venerable than the father—is certainly not justified even if it were based on the father's command.

The destruction of fetuses, the cutting [of limbs] along with pregnant women, and the killing of kings or Kṣatriyas who have been initiated for sacrifices and the like—this constitutes a slaughter equal to that of a Brāhmaṇa; thus, the conduct of the Brāhmaṇa is to be marveled at, which is the connection with the preceding [verse].
By the phrase "equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa" (brahmahatyāsama), an extension of the rules (atideśa) applicable to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa is intended.

And so Manu says: "Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very vow; as also for killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice, and likewise a woman who is an Ātreyī.
The term *ījānau* refers to those two who are in the midst of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for a sacrifice.
The commentators explain that [the woman referred to] is one born of the Atri lineage, who is pregnant and in her menses.

Viṣṇu also states: "The killing of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice, of a woman in her menses, of a pregnant woman, of a woman born of the Atri lineage, of an unborn fetus, or of one who has sought refuge—these are equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa.
Kāmandaka, however, maintains that "the equality to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa in the act [of killing such persons] is established by a *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument."
In this matter, the killing of one who is preeminent in virtue and has been consecrated as a king is generally more grievous than the killing of a Brahmin.

The killing of a mere king while he is situated in the midst of a sacrifice is equal to the murder of a Brahmin; the killing of a mere king who is not engaged in the initiation for a sacrifice is equal to one-fourth of the murder of a Brahmin.
Thus says Amara: "One-fourth of the murder of a Brahmin is recorded [as the penalty] for the killing of a Kṣatriya. (19)
*Āḥ* is used in the sense of anger.
One who lives by means of pronouncing blessings is called *svastivācanika*;
the suffix *ṭhak* is applied here according to the rule *vetanādibhyo jīvati*.
"Duṣṭadoṣayuktā" ends in the nominative case; alternatively, it is an adjective qualifying "sāmanta," meaning a neighboring king (*pārśvarāja*).
"Of one devoid of universal sovereignty," so much is meant.
"Purohita!"—
the particle *re* is used for addressing a low person.
The son of Ahalyā. The designation "son of Ahalyā" is used with the intention of censuring Indra's transgression; the absence of the elision (aluk) is according to the rule "ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe."
"I am your *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*," meaning, according to your view, one who lives by the sword. "O wicked one... [and so forth].
O Durmukha, you of harsh countenance!
You who bring reproach and infamy upon the descendants of Bhṛgu, those born of the lineage of Bhṛgu—
[the word *pāṃsana* is derived from the word *pāṃsu* (dust/infamy), with the suffix *man* added, followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*].
Since the suffix *matup* has been elided, the suffix *lyu* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule for the *nandy-ādi* group.
Regarding "the kings":
these are kings such as Daśaratha, Janaka, and others.
The preceptors are Vasiṣṭha and others;
