by their very greatness—that is, by their very magnanimity—they are exceedingly patient, abounding in the kind of forbearance that endures offenses. Let them indeed forgive, let them indeed endure the harshness of Paraśurāma.

The meaning is that forgiveness is appropriate for them because the great possess forgiveness as their very nature. Śatānanda, however, thinks, "I am devoid of that greatness which is the cause of forgiveness," and thus,
unlike Vasiṣṭha and others, he will not forgive at all.
The meaning is: "I shall inflict a punishment corresponding to the offense at the very next moment.
Here, the *vimarśasaṃdhi* (the juncture of deliberation) element called *apavāda* (defamation) is expressed through the mutual exposure of faults by Śatānanda and Jāmadagnya.
As it has been stated: "The proclamation of faults is *apavāda*."
Right here, the juncture-element (saṃdhy-aṅga) called *saṃpheṭa* is defined as mutual speech arising from anger;
as it has been said: "Mutual speech arising from anger is *saṃpheṭa*. ||20||
He touches with the water from his water-pot; he performs the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
According to Amara, "touching" (*upasparśana*) means "sipping water" (*ācamana*).
The instrumental case is used here because there is an intention to express the water-pot as the instrument of the action.
"Because of the rule that 'one must perform [the rite] having sipped water'";
"let him be propitiated"—
[this refers to] with a *dhavitra*, a fan made of deerskin.

" *Dhavitra* is a fan made of deer-skin," according to Amara. *Nirdhūtaḥ* means shaken or fanned for the purpose of causing it to blaze more intensely; *abhipraṇītaḥ* means consecrated or prepared through ritual refinement.
"The fire that has been consecrated (*praṇītaḥ*) is [called] *saṃskṛtaḥ*," according to Amara.
When words denoting a qualified entity are used in syntactic proximity with a word denoting the qualificand, they have the sense of the qualifier alone.
*Pṛṣadājya* refers to clarified butter mixed with curd;
as Amara states: "Pṛṣadājya is clarified butter together with curd."
"By sprinkling from all sides with the *abhighāra* (libation).
The word *ghāra* is derived from the root *ghṛ*, meaning "to sprinkle," belonging to the *bhvādi* class, with the suffix *ghañ* used in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāve*).
He is like the fire (*tanūnapāt*), which is terrifying due to its flickering flames that produce a crackling sound.
"Jātavedas" and "Tanūnapāt"—thus says Amara. "Samidhyamānam" means being properly kindled.
This is derived from the root *indhī* (meaning "to shine") with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized; the suffix *śānac* is used here in the passive (*karman*) present participle.

That which is fierce and terrifying is the splendor (*varcas*) or brilliance (*tejas*) of Brahman; this is *brahmavarcasa*. According to the rule "after *brahman* and *hastin*, [the suffix] *ac* is added to *varcas*," that very light (*jyotis*) which belongs to him is thus described.
There is no tautology here because of the relationship of general and particular between the words *brahmavarcasa* and *jyotis*.
Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: "one whose light (*jyotis*)—that is, splendor (*tejas*)—is that of *brahmavarcasa*," which is the excellence of conduct and Vedic study.
As Amara states: "Brahmavarcasa is the abundance of conduct and Vedic study."
"Let him be propitiated; let his anger be appeased.

[Grammatical analysis: From the word *prasāda* (propitiation), derived from the root with the suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *matup* is elided by the rule "from a nominal stem, in the sense of the verbal root-meaning," etc.; then, the imperative (*loṭ*) is used in the sense of the object.
"With agitation" (*sasaṃrambham*).
*Saṃrambhaḥ* is an effort accompanied by anger.
*Śāpodakam* is the water that manifests or reveals a curse—a cry intended for the harm of another.
Those who sit (*sīdanti*) in the assembly (*sabhā*) are called *sabhāsadaḥ*.
The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *sad* (to sit/sink) in the sense of the agent according to the rule "satsūdviṣa-" and so forth.
Regarding the term "sakrodha": [it refers to] the enemy of another, namely Paraśurāma.
"The enemy and the Supreme Self" (*paro'riḥ paramātmā ca*), according to the *Ratnamālā*.
"From assault," meaning from injury in the form of humiliation; "with anger and impetuosity" (*sakrodhaprasabham*), meaning with the force of wrath.
The lexicon states: "The word *prasabha* [denotes] both speed and joy."
I am one whose swift movement has arisen and manifested, and whose activity is rapid; such as I am, [I shall strike] your assailant who is intent on killing.
According to Amara, "an *ātatāyin* is one intent on killing.
By this, the scriptural injunction—"One should kill an approaching *ātatāyin* without hesitation"—is indicated.

By means of the cause of an upheaval—an inauspicious conjunction of living beings—I shall reduce this entire [host] to ashes, just as a tree is consumed by the fire of a thunderbolt or a lightning-storm when it is shattered and broken by a turbulent, surging wind.
The suffix *sāti* is used here according to the rule *vibhāṣā sātikārtsnye*.
In this context, because of the exertion toward slaughter, the dramatic juncture (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) called *vidrava* (flight) is indicated.
As it has been said: "The flight [of beings] due to slaughter, bondage, and so forth. (21)
Be gracious;
show favor toward one who has come to your home— the implication being that Paraśurāma has arrived.
The sense is that this is based on the Vedic scripture stating, "One should not refuse anyone lodging.
May the unassailable and invincible splendor (*tejas*)—the power to overcome others resulting from asceticism (*tapas*)—be pacified; may it become tranquil.
The phrase "having come to the house" connects with both the preceding and following parts of the sentence.
"Praiseworthy" refers to Paraśurāma and others.
Paraśurāma is praiseworthy— that is, worthy of commendation— on account of his qualities such as being a master of the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
Furthermore, this is the best of the twice-born, the most excellent of Brahmins;
furthermore, he is your own kinsman,
meaning a sapinda relative of your own.
"‘Nijau’ means one's own and indestructible," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
"Sagotra, bāndhava, jñāti, bandhu, sva, and svajana are synonyms," according to Amara.
When he has entered your house—that is, when he has come to your home—would such an act of reducing him to ashes be appropriate or fitting toward one such as Paraśurāma?
The meaning is that it is "not appropriate.
This Paraśurāma, although he is learned— that is, although he is a knower—
here the intention is to convey the principle that "there is greater severity of punishment for the transgression of one who is learned."

Regarding the fact that he has deviated from the path consisting of conduct conformable to devotion to Brahman: for that purpose, it is the *kṣatra*—the warrior caste indeed—that is suitable for his discipline and instruction. The word "tu" (but) indicates a doubt.
And that suspicion takes the form: "This is Paraśurāma; because he has transgressed the rules of conduct, he deserves punishment.
To this, the rebuttal is: "In this matter, only a Kṣatriya is fit [to punish], not a Brāhmaṇa.
Since this is so, O Śatānanda, you, the best of Brāhmaṇas, should resort to—attain—*śama*, the cessation of anger.
In this context, *śakti* (power) is said to be a constituent element (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) of the plot because it serves to reconcile contradictions;
as it has been stated: "The reconciliation of contradictions is *śakti*. ||22||
The remainder is: "May it be exactly as he has said.
Regarding the word "yat" (which):

we—myself, Viśvāmitra, and the others—mentally bring about, that is, accomplish through our aspiration, that auspicious welfare of Rāma which consists in the attainment of his blameless and desired goals.

Having been addressed as "O Jābāli," you should perform— do— *śānti*, which is a *homa* for the pacification of undesirable things, within the fire (*adhyagni*). This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of a locative case.

In the previous instance and here as well, the *ātmanepada* ending is not used because the fruit of the action does not accrue to the agent. That Blessed One—Vāmadeva, who is renowned in the Śruti for being filled with the sixfold divine attributes such as knowledge, as it is said: "Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realized," being accompanied by our disciples, [uttered these words] in order to overcome others, that is, to conquer them by means of those things that cause victory (*jaitrān*).
The suffix *tṛc* is used here because there is an intention to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Just as "conqueror" (*jetṛ*) is the same as "victorious" (*jaitra*),
the suffix *aṇ* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) because [the word] belongs to the class of *prajñādi*.

Reciting—that is, uttering in a low voice—the *sūktas* such as the *Śrīsūkta* and *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Sāmans* such as the *Rathantara*, and the *anuvākas* beginning with "śukrapravidhya" and "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ," let him chant them.
Here, the term "japati" (recites) denotes merely the effort of whispering, since the act of loud articulation is expressed by the verb "gṛṇāti.
In this context, the constituent element (*sandhyaṅga*) called "taking up" (*ādāna*), which consists of the gathering of the tasks to be performed, has been described.
As it has been said: "Appropriation is the grasping of what is to be done. ||23||
"Let him see"—
by the word "of the boy" (*baṭoḥ*), it is indicated that Śatānanda is younger in age than Paraśurāma.
However, his previously mentioned status as a preceptor (*gurutva*) is to be understood as being due to his position.
"Supported by Kṣatriyas" (kṣatriyāvaṣṭabdhasya) means relying upon Kṣatriyas such as Janaka and others.
The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* in the root *stambh-* preceded by the prefix *ava-* occurs according to the rule "avāccālambanāvidūryayoḥ.

[The term] "subsisting on the favor" (prasādam upajīvanti) of Daśaratha and Janaka, the lords of Kosala and Videha—meaning they live depending upon it—is formed with the suffix *ṇini* according to the rule "supyajātau... (Pāṇini 3.2.78).
Those for whom the seven continents and the great boundary mountains are their range and dwelling places are described as such.
This [phrase] connects with what precedes and follows.
"Or austerity," and so forth.

Among you, whichever Brahmin or Kṣatriya— here in this realm of Daśaratha and Janaka— practices asceticism (*tapas*), or performs an ascetic act intended to issue a curse, or wields a weapon, that is, a martial instrument or armament;

[it should be understood that] for the Brahmin, asceticism is the means, for the Kṣatriya, the weapon is the means, and for both, both may be employed according to their respective roles, whether taken as alternatives or in combination—
such a person "deals," meaning he speaks, using these as instruments for our prosecution.

Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, that man—excessively arrogant and even more so in his pride—being unable to endure our splendor and being intolerant of it, may he cause our splendor to stumble and fall away. The *loṭ* suffix is used here in the sense of "permitted action" (*kāmacāra*) or "proper time" (*prāptakāla*), according to the rule: *praiṣātisargaprāptakāleṣu*.

From the root *skhala* (meaning "to waver"), the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule *hetumati ca*; then, according to the opinion of King Bhoja, the short vowel is substituted because the roots *dali*, *vali*, *skhali*, *raṇi*, *dhvani*, *trap*, and *kṣapi* belong to the *mit* class, resulting in the form *skhalayatu*.
The use of the *loṭ* (imperative) mood in the sense of "acting according to one's will" indicates that nothing undesirable has occurred for us.

[In the phrase] "Paraśurāma [beheld] Arāmā," the word "rāma" (possessing joy) is absent; thus she is "Arāmā. According to the rule, "In the case of negative particles (*nañ*) used with words having the sense of 'existent' (*astyartha*), there is either an expressed meaning or an elision of the subsequent member," there is an elision of the word "vidyamāna" (existent). Thus, it means she was without joy.
The earth, the *jagatī*;
according to Amarasimha, "the *jagatī* is also called *ratnagarbhā*.

Having rendered it devoid of Daśaratha and Janaka—that is, having made it such that Daśaratha and Janaka are no longer present—by making it [a place] where the banners of the *sīra* (plow) have departed.

The suffix *cvi* is applied by the rule "upon connection with *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*" (*kṛbhvastiyoge-*). When the designation of a *gati* is established by the rule "the words beginning with *ūri*, as well as *cvi* and *ḍāc*" (*ūryādicviḍācaśca*), the compound is formed by the rule "a word preceded by a *kṛt*, a *gati*, etc. (*kugati-*); then, by the rule "in a compound where *nañ* does not precede" (*samāse'nañpūrve-*), the suffix *lyap* is substituted.

Being unsatisfied—that is, lacking the sense of sufficiency even with that much—he will subdue, meaning he will humble, even those humans who reside in the lineage and the household of his kinsmen, Janaka and Daśaratha.

The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here according to the rule "in proximity to the present" (*vartamānasāmīpye*), because [the action] is near the future. In this context, the dramatic element (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) called *dyuti* (splendor) is mentioned due to the act of threatening; as it has been said: "Threatening and alarming constitute *dyuti*."
The distinction is that intimidation is physical, while causing agitation is verbal. ||24||
"You are being smeared with pride; you become arrogant. "He is jealous of our arrogance" means that he manifests faults prompted by anger directed toward our pride.

The fourth case ending is used here according to the rule: "In the case of verbs meaning *kruddha* (to be angry), *druh* (to injure), *īrṣya* (to envy), and *asūya* (to find fault), [the fourth case is used] for that person toward whom the anger is directed.
The word *nāma* is used in the sense of contempt; thus, the meaning is that finding fault with one who is weak is itself contemptible.
According to Amarasimha, "nāma" is used in the senses of manifestation, possibility, anger, approach, and reproach.
And [the word] "sasaṃrambhaḥ" (with agitation).
"Praviśya" means having entered.
The word "said" (*āha*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Regarding the phrase "from the destruction of enemies": the agent is that *kṣātra*—meaning the splendor (*tejas*), the capacity for overcoming others, which is innate to victory and arises simultaneously with it, being unique to the Kṣatriya caste; [this agent] acts because, prior to the destruction of enemies, through the strength of his arms aided by the grace of the deities, he has utterly annihilated his foes.
Furthermore, it is by virtue of transformation (*pariṇati*) and in accordance with old age (*jarā*). [The root] *vaś* means "desire" (*kānti*); desire is longing (*icchā*).

Furthermore, regarding the *gṛhya*—the text composed by Āpastamba and others that makes known the ritual acts—the *Ratnamālā* states: "The *gṛhya* is that which makes known the ritual acts. Regarding the *tantras*—which consist of the practical applications taught therein—the *Ratnamālā* states: "'Tantra' refers to the administration of one's own kingdom, weaving, a covering, and also to the primary scriptures on the performance of sacrifices and established doctrines, as well as medicinal herbs."
Of vows (*vratānām*), that is, of observances such as fasting;
according to Amarasimha, "a vow (*vrata*) is a restrictive rule (*niyama*)," and it is not feminine.
By way of continuity, that is, through the absence of interruption.

Furthermore, the term "supreme" (*parama*) is used to exclude *pradhāna* (primordial matter), which is also a referent of the word "Brahman" only in a figurative sense, because it is only through the perception—that is, the direct realization by means of yogic vision—of the reality of the Lord, the supreme and primary Brahman denoted by the word "Brahman," in its unimputed form, that liberated souls attain liberation.
Indeed, it is heard in scripture: "O God, the supreme Brahman of the seers."

And it is recorded [in tradition]: "Of Vāsudeva, who has become the Supreme Brahman," and also: "O great sage, the word *brahman* is used in its primary sense only for that [Vāsudeva], because of its frequent application in the Veda and because of His connection with [the qualities of] the wielder of the Śārṅga bow."

"It is called the supreme *brahman* because it is vast (*bṛhat*) and it causes [all things] to grow (*bṛṃhayati*). "Because its qualities are vast (*bṛhantaḥ*) and because of its vastness and its nature as the supreme (*brahmaṇatva*), it is recited as *brahman*. And by such statements as "the *brahman* is all-pervading and sovereign everywhere," the etymology of the word *brahman* is established.

By the phrase "because of the perception of reality" (*tattvopalambhāt*), there is the exclusion of those perceptions of *brahman* that yield inferior results, which are taught in passages such as "one should meditate on the mind as *brahman*."
From this, it follows that [the cessation] was due to the direct realization of Brahman, which is the cause of liberation.
And thus, by these four causes, the Kṣatriya energy—the agent—ceased from actions such as war;
it has now arisen again, having attained its manifestation.
"Having reached the state of manifestation" means as far as that point.

"The bow" (kārmukam) refers to the weapon; it "urges" or "excites" for the sake of action—that is, for the action consisting of battle. [This is derived from] the root *tvar* with the prefix *ñi* in the sense of agitation (*saṃbhrama*). Because it belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group, it takes the *mit* designation; due to the *mit* designation, there is shortening of the vowel.

By the phrase "it impels one toward action" (*karmaṇe tvarayati*), the etymology "the bow is capable for action" (*karmaṇe prabhavati kārmukam*)—as stated in the rule *karmaṇa ukañ*—is recalled. ||25||
"You, sir! O Janaka, you are indeed devoted to Brahman;
it is well known that you are virtuous regarding the Vedas, the Vedic rites, and so forth.
The lexicon states: "Brahma, Tattva, Tapas, Veda, Brahmā, Vipra, and Prajāpati [are synonyms].
From the word *brahman*, the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *tatra sādhuh*.
Furthermore, you have reached full maturity.
Furthermore, you are endowed with dharma;
that is, you are constantly engaged in the dharma that is the means to liberation, as it has been said: "By dharma one dispels evil.
Moreover, the sage Yājñavalkya, the son of the Sun, [is your teacher].

"Having embraced them with knowledge, he said, 'O my sons! and "The giver of the Veda is a father more venerable than one's own father, for he begets him from knowledge"—from such passages, the disciple is perceived as a son; thus he is called the "son of the Sun. He taught—that is, enlightened—the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, which is the final and most excellent among the Upaniṣads of the Vedāntas.
The verb *śās* (to teach/instruct) is transitive, as seen in forms such as *dahyāt*.
The mention of it by the word "last" (acarama) is intended to show that its preeminence among the Vedāntas is understood from its very designation as the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*.
The word "iti" indicates a reason;
[it refers] to the fourfold reasons beginning with its being a Brāhmaṇa.

"Because of the conduct prescribed by the scriptures—such as 'you must comfort them with a seat' and so forth—you have been attended by me with humility and modesty; yet, for that very reason, out of delusion, through ignorance of the relative strength and weakness of yourself and others, being unaware of danger and ignorant of the calamities that lie ahead, you speak harsh and cruel words.
(Amara states: "The word *karkaśa* may mean one who acts rashly, as well as hard or rough. 26.
"The breaking of the egg is performed"—
the word "through arrogance" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. And "humility."
The word "is proclaimed" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The sense is that there is a mutual contradiction between the breaking of the egg and the speaking of humility.
[He says: "Listen!"
The word "you" is to be supplied as the subject.
Regarding the phrase "of Bhṛgu":
this Paraśurāma was born in the lineage of Bhṛgu.

Furthermore, for the reason that he was established in asceticism (*tapas*), even though he was hostile—nay, full of hatred—I have for a long time, throughout this entire duration, maintained only forbearance (*titikṣā*) toward Paraśurāma; that is, I have formed the resolve not to inflict punishment upon him in accordance with his offense.
The word *hi* indicates well-known fact. As for the phrase "when... (*yadā*):
The word "this" (ayam) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence].
This Paraśurāma, being *anibhṛta*—that is, being ill-mannered (*avinīta*).
According to Amarasimha: "The words *nibhṛta*, *vinīta*, and *praśrita* are synonyms."

The analysis of the compound is: "he does not remain quiet, thus he is 'restless' (anibhṛtaḥ). When, for whatever reason, he repeatedly—that is, again and again—shakes or agitates [us] like grass (*tṛṇavat*);
the word "us" (*asmān*) is to be supplied as the object.
Therefore, for that reason, let the bow—the agent—bow down, that is, become bent, even before this Brahmin Paraśurāma;
here there is an intention to express the agency of the instrument (the bow).
The reason for its absence [of bending] has already been stated previously.
There is no other course or alternative means;
the sense is that this can be accomplished only by force. ||27||
*Roṣaḥ* is anger; *hāsaḥ* is a smile; *ākṣepaḥ* is contempt.
"What do you say? means "What are you saying? The repetition of the word *dhanuḥ* (bow) as "dhanurdhanuḥ" is intended to convey the meaning of the term *kārmuka* (bow).
The two words *aho* and *āścaryam* indicate an excess of wonder. Alternatively, *aho* may be used as an exclamation.
Regarding the word *aho*, when it receives the designation of *pragṛhya* by the rule "āt," there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to the rule "plutapragṛhyāḥ."
"O Kṣattṛ!

[He says this] because he has been falsely puffed up—filled with the proclamation of our virtues—out of affection for Yājñavalkya; consequently, he has become arrogant and conceited. Furthermore, he is a "Kṣattrabandhu," a wretch of a Kṣatriya, worn out and weakened by old age.
Amarasimha’s statement, "The term *brahmabandhu* is used in a sense of contempt," serves as an illustration for the word *kṣattrabandhu* as well.
The word *bandhu*, when used in conjunction with the words *brahman* and *kṣatra*, denotes the lowest of Brahmins and the lowest of Kṣatriyas;
"Janaka" is the implied subject.

[He is] so described because his loud laughter (*aṭṭahāsa*) consists of nothing other than the prominent sparks of the fire of the Kṣatriya caste—which, having been agitated by the sight of that [Brahmin], has returned to its natural state.
"Attahasa is a great laugh that causes changes in the color of the face and so forth," say those who know the lexicons.
"Upon the whetstones in the form of the heads of enemies"—Amara states: "Śāṇa means a whetstone (nikaṣa) or a grindstone (kaṣa)."
"Śāta" means sharpened; as Amara states: "Now, *niśita*, *kṣṇuta*, and *śāta* mean whetted.
Even while looking at the axe, he speaks nonsense, being a laughingstock.
The meaning is that he speaks words that are purposeless.
Here, by the phrase "O base kṣatriya" and so forth, the sandhyaṅga (limb of dramatic juncture) called *calana* (shaking/disregard) is expressed through insult.
As it has been said: "Insult is *calana*. ||28||
With agitation and haste:
"What is the use of much?"— the word "by speech" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The sense is that action alone is the subsequent [factor].

Regarding the phrase "jyā-tihvaya" (the bow with the tongue of the string): *jyā* means a bowstring; that itself is the *jihvā* (tongue). By that [tongue], it is encircled (*valayita*), meaning a circle has been formed. It is so described as having fierce (*utkaṭa*) and elevated (*udagra*) tips (*koṭī*) which serve as its very fangs (*daṃṣṭre*).
Alternatively, "jyājihvā" is a *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison), meaning "the bowstring is like a tongue. "Koṭidaṃṣṭre" is also an *upamita-samāsa*, meaning "the two tips are like fangs.

Because this relies on a *bahuvrīhi* compound consisting of an *upamita-samāsa*—namely, "one whose two tips are like fangs, which are coiled and fierce"—the word "daṃṣṭrā" does not undergo *pūrvanipāta* (placement as the first member).
In the previous interpretation, there was a metaphor (*rūpaka*), whereas here there is a simile (*upamā*).
"One who has an outburst" (*udgārī*) means one who possesses an outburst; the sense is that [the emotion] has emerged without interruption.
The reading is also "udbhūri," meaning "abundant.

It is described as having a terrible, fearsome, dense, and loud *gharghara* resonance; such is this bow. May it be like that—having a vast, uneven, and protruding belly (*udara*) which imitates, that is, resembles, the gaping mouth of the laughing Antaka (Yama), who is intent upon devouring the world (*grāsa*). May it be so. ||29||
He strings the bow— the word "bowstring" (jyām) being understood as the ellipsis.
He is so described because he has continuously and incessantly bestowed thousands of cows (dhenūnām) in sacrifices, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites.
The sense is that [the action] must be performed with the right hand, because of the rule regarding the right hand (*dakṣiṇapāṇi-niyama*).

"Palita" refers to the whiteness of the hair and so forth caused by extreme old age; "purāṇa-dhanurdhara" (an ancient archer) is a compound of appositional agreement (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*) according to the rule beginning with "pūrvakāla-" (Pāṇini 2.1.49), meaning one who is a long-standing archer.
Your hand is upon this twice-born Paraśurāma.
"Pṛṣatka" means an arrow;
according to Amarasimha, "pṛṣatka, bāṇa, and viśikha" are synonyms for an arrow.
How does he touch [it]?
The word "to employ" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Here too, because it pacifies the contradiction, the juncture-element (saṃdhy-aṅga) called "Power" (śakti) is stated. ||30||

Regarding the address "Friend" (*sakhe*): By Vasiṣṭha’s statement in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, "Knowing him to be a former relative, I speak to you first," it is understood that Daśaratha was already Janaka’s friend; thus he is addressed as "Friend.

Furthermore, by the statement there, "This entire earth formerly belonged to all of them," it is shown that Janaka held the status of a mere king (*narapati*), whereas Daśaratha held the rank of a great king (*mahārāja*); thus he is addressed as "Great King."

"asmān iti" (us): "ayam ityādikam" (beginning with "this one," etc. means that this Paraśurāma may revile us—that is, he may utter harsh words regarding us. The use of the *loṭ* suffix here indicates freedom of action (*kāmacāra*).
The word *nāma* is used here in the sense of admission (*abhyupagama*).
According to Amarasimha, "the word *nāma* [is used] in the senses of manifestation, possibility, anger, approach, and reproach.
This insult uttered by Paraśurāma is *na kiṃcit*—that is, it is not anything at all.
Not even a trace of it causes suffering;
the sense is that there is no distinction between praise and blame.
When a twice-born man speaks harshly, to whom [does it matter]?
The sense is: "even for one who is established in Brahman.
"Disturbance of mind" (*cittabheda*) refers to a specific mental modification (*manovṛtti*) in the form of anger.
The sense is: "But for me, who am established in Brahman, there is no anger at all when insulted by a Brāhmaṇa."

But how can this wicked, evil-doing young boy Paraśurāma be endured—that is, how can he be forgiven—while shouting harsh and cruel words, contrary and adverse to the welfare and auspiciousness of my child Rāma, ringing in our ears?
[The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* in *viṣahyaḥ* is according to the rule "parinivibhyaḥ...";
the form *raṭan* is derived from the root *raṭ* (meaning "to revile") with the suffix *laṭ* in the present participle.]
*Paribhāṣaṇa* is a reproach accompanied by censure.

Here, however, because the object [of the act] is expressed by the word *kaṭu*, the root *raṭati* refers solely to sound. By this, it is shown that the scope of *titikṣā* (forbearance) consists in the endurance of self-reproach.
However, the distinction has been shown that for one who is intolerant, the object [of the offense] is the reviling of the Blessed One. ||31||

*Ā* is used in the sense of anger. "O evil-souled one! O wicked-minded one! O lowest of Kṣatriyas! O vilest of Kṣatriyas! [Regarding *apasadah*: Amara states, "The base, the outcast, the wretch (*jālma*) are called *apasadah*"].

In this context, because many characters such as Janaka and others, agitated by anger, address one another with mutual insults, the dramatic juncture-element (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) called *nirodhana* (obstruction) is stated.
As it has been said: "The mutual reproach of those agitated by anger is suppression. [He says: "Arise!
Arise!"
The word "for the sake of battle" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The repetition of the action is due to agitation caused by anger.
As stated by the grammarians: "In the case of activity prompted by agitation, usage in various ways as desired is generally established by tradition."
*Paraśu* means an axe. *Viśakalitāni* means specifically shattered or cut into pieces. *Yakṛt* refers to the liver; *kālakhaṇḍa* is a specific type of liver.
"Kālakhaṇḍa and yakṛt are both the same," according to Amara.
Kloma is the *tilaka*.
"Tilaka, kloma, and mastiṣka [are synonyms]," according to Amara.
The flesh at the tip of the kidneys;
"the flesh at the tip of the kidneys" (vṛkkāgramāṃsa) according to Amara.
Asra means blood.
According to the *Ratnamālā*, "the word *asra* [can denote] tears or blood.

That whose liver (*yakṛt*), lungs (*kloma*), kidneys (*vṛkka*), and blood (*āsra*) [are present] is described as such; he by whom the limbs (*gātra*) have their liver, lungs, kidneys, and blood shattered is thus described—this is an epithet of Paraśurāma. It is a separate compound consisting of a *bahuvrīhi* within another *bahuvrīhi*.
Furthermore, "snāyūnām" means of the sinews (snasā). As Amara states: "Alternatively, *snasā* and *snāyu* [are used] for the female gender."
By knots;
according to the *Ratnamālā*, "a knot (*granthi*) is [the joint] between the joints of a club.
And by the scales and fragments of bones.
According to Amara, *śalka* means "shred" or "bark.

*Vyatikaritā* means "joined" or "intermingled. *Jaratī* means "aged" or "worn out. [The form is derived] from the root *jarṣ* (meaning "decay of age") with the suffix *atṛn* according to the rule *jīryateratṛn*; because this suffix is marked with *u*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule *ugitaśca*.
"Kaṃdharā" means the neck; "in that neck"—as Amarasimha states: "Śirodhi and kaṃdhara [also denote the neck].
He is thus described as one by whom a "khaṇḍa," meaning a cutting or severing, has been given (datta). Being of such a nature...
"From the cutting of the head," meaning from the severing of the head; "rising up," meaning emerging.
This is an adjective qualifying Bhāra. "Of the throat," meaning of the neck.
"Kaṇṭha means the throat," according to Amara.
Regarding *dhamanīṣu* (in the vessels), *mahānāḍīṣu* (in the great channels), and *śirāsu* (in the veins):

although the words *dhamani* and *śirā* are synonyms—as in the statement "a *nāḍī* is indeed a *dhamani* or a *śirā*"—nevertheless, because they are used together here, one should understand them as referring to distinct sub-categories.
"Adhering" means bound together; "abounding in masses of foam" means thick with clusters of froth.
According to Amara, "ḍiṇḍīraḥ" refers to the ocean's scum or foam.
This is a descriptive characterization of a particular state of blood itself.
With a mass of blood—that is, a collection of gore—you are terrible and fearsome, like a beast such as a tiger, [torn] limb by limb at every joint.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *parvan* refers to a knot, the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight, a festival, the equinoxes, and so forth.
Thus, it means at every knot (*granthau*).
The suffix *śas* is applied according to the rule: "After a numeral and a word in the singular number, when repetition (*vīpsā*) is intended.

Although it has been stated that *śas* occurs only after a word denoting measure (*parimāṇaśabda*) ending in the singular—as in the example *māṣaśo dadāti* ("he gives by the māṣa")—nevertheless, even after a genus-word (*jātiśabda*) that denotes multiple objects due to the context of the meaning, *śas* occurs when repetition is intended. For instance, in accordance with the opinion of Vāmana—who accepts *śas* even after genus-words as seen in examples such as *khaṇḍaśo dadāti* ("he gives in pieces") and *vanaśaḥ praviśati* ("he enters forest after forest")—the form *parvaśaḥ* (by the joint) is indeed valid.
Since the phrase "from a *kāraka*" (kārakāt) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*), the suffix *śas* occurs after the *kāraka* of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
This word *parvan*, while denoting a finger-joint, is a term for measure; thus, even in this alternative interpretation, *śas* is indeed possible.
The meaning is: "May he destroy you, who are measured by [your own] joints."
Today;
from the agent of the action, the suffix *śas*;
as far as "let him hear."
The meaning is "he indeed injures.
The root *śṛ* is used in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsāyām*) and belongs to the *kryādi* class. The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *pvādīnām*.

In the reading "śṛṇāti," the meaning is "he will harm. The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here according to the rule "yāvatpurānipātayoḥ. However, in the former reading, the word *yāvat* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
"Yāvat-tāvat [is used] in the senses of totality, limit, measure, and restriction," according to Amara. ||32||
"Between Janaka and Paraśurāma" means in the midst of them.
Regarding "this":
this king Janaka, our friend, remains as he is; likewise, your own body also remains [as it was].
The sense is that, due to the mutual disregard of each other's words, not even a single limb of either was cut.
In that regard, concerning Janaka, we have been suffering—meaning we exist in a state of suffering—in every way and by every means, on account of his actions or his insults.
The particle *nanu* is used here for emphasis.

The sense is this: although Janaka does not feel distressed even when insulted by others because he is established in Brahman, nevertheless, the excessive insults directed at him by others become a cause of pain for us. ||33||
What then? Why is it that you cannot endure suffering? Furthermore, "it is not forgiven" means that because this insult causes pain, it is not tolerated by us. "You too... [and so forth].
By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "you also," Janaka is included.
"Another, like a powerful lord" means another master-like person; you "assail" him, which means you cause him distress.
The root *skand* means "to move" and "to dry up.
This is a figurative expression (kṣepokti).
You are the one to be restrained.
The meaning is that you are the director (*niyāmaka*). "Be mindful" means know. To the question "What? he says: "Eternal," and so forth.
By my very nature, by my inherent disposition, I am Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, eternally unrestrained and eternally unimpeded;
that is to say, I am the annihilator of the Kṣatriyas.
And you are a Kṣatriya.
Therefore, the relationship of slayer and slain is established even without being explicitly stated; this is the meaning.

Consequently, because you are a Brāhmaṇa and I am a Kṣatriya, you—who have strayed onto a wrong path—shall not be overlooked by me, but rather shall be subdued; such is the meaning of the phrase "of those who are difficult to tame."
"Of those who are difficult to subdue," meaning those who must be tamed with great difficulty because they are exceedingly haughty;
"the methods of subduing," that is, the prescriptions for training, "depend upon the Kṣatriyas," meaning they are contingent upon the Kṣatriyas.
The root *yat* preceded by the prefix *ā* (ā-yata) signifies being dependent or subject to another; as Amara states: "Adhīna, nighna, and āyatta [are synonyms for dependent].
You are difficult to subdue, and we Kṣatriyas are your instructors (*sāsitāraḥ*), that is, your tamers (*damayitāraḥ*). The word "we are" (*bhavāmaḥ*) is to be supplied.
"Immediately"—in this very moment; according to Amara, "sadyas," "sapadi," and "tatkṣaṇe" all mean "at that very instant. Be pacified—be one whose anger has ceased.

What else? What more? If you do not attain peace, there is nothing other than what is about to be said; rather, it is precisely that which is about to be said that will happen to you—this is the meaning.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "Of the one who is compassionate."
"You are being tamed; you are being trained.
Regarding the cause of training, which is transgression, he says: "Where [are] the *brahmāṇa*s?
Those for whom tranquility (*praśamana*)—that is, supreme peace (*prakṛṣṭā śāntiḥ*)—is the highest (*param* = *utkṛṣṭam*), are thus described as *brahmāṇa*s, that is, Brāhmaṇas.
"Brahmā, vipra, prajāpati"— thus says Amara.
"Kva" means in what manner or state they are situated.
Where, and in what manner, is the weapon that is to be wielded by a Kṣatriya?
The meaning is that there is a contradiction between being a Brāhmaṇa and wielding a weapon.
Therefore, the sense is: "Because you have taken up arms, you are difficult to subdue; you must be tamed by us, who are Kṣatriyas. ||34||
"Sanātha" means having a protector;
"vinetāraḥ" means instructors;
"kṣattriyāḥ" refers to kings who are protectors.
This is an instance of *kṣepokti* (ironical speech).
The meaning is: "I am not one who possesses a protector, nor are you instructors.

Here, regarding the relationship between the one to be instructed and the instructor between you and us, there is a delusion—that is, a misconception—arising from a state of confusion, wherein one mistakenly perceives the roles of the instructed and the instructor.
"Unknowing," and so forth:

either one who lacks knowledge—that is, one in whom there has arisen no cognition consisting of valid apprehension regarding the means and the visible or invisible fruits [of action]; or one whose cognition has reached, that is, attained, error—meaning a state where the object is an unreal property or where the subject is an unreal locus; such a person is described as being "of that kind."
The phrase *yadi ca* is a compound particle having the same meaning as the word *vā* (or).

For it is well known that error is twofold, by way of being an error regarding a property (*dharmabhrama*) or an error regarding a substratum (*dharmibhrama*), such as "the conch is yellow" or "I am fat.
[The subject] is either one who possesses both types of erroneous cognition.
And by "erroneous cognition" (bhrāntijñāna), what is intended is that which has as its object the means and results—whether seen or unseen [in this world or the next].
The word "atha" introduces a different alternative; according to Amarasimha, "atha" is used for auspiciousness, sequence, and so forth.

It is called *saṃdehadhṛt* because it bears (*dharati*) a cognition whose modes (*prakāra*) are various contradictory properties (*viruddha-nānā-dharma*) with respect to a single substratum (*ekasmin dharmiṇi*). The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*;
the augment *tuk* is added by the rule *hrasvasya*.
Doubtful knowledge (*saṃdehajñāna*) is also intended here as that which concerns visible and invisible fruits and so forth.

"The person" (*puruṣa*) refers to an embodied being (*dehī*) excluded from the animal realm, according to the principle stated in the sūtra: "But the scripture [is for] human beings, because they possess the capacity for qualification."

The visible fruit consists of the nourishment of cattle and children, as well as food, longevity, sensory faculties, and so forth; the invisible fruit consists of the results pertaining to the hereafter, such as heaven and liberation. He performs actions that are opposed to these two—actions that destroy them or yield contrary results—and carries them out as the cause for fruits to be experienced by himself.
By the rule "svaritañitaḥ" and others, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is used when the fruit accrues to the agent.
For that person previously described—who is characterized by non-arising, doubt, and error—the teacher (*guru*) is the preceptor who removes ignorance.
As it is said: "The syllable *gu* signifies darkness (*andhakāra*), and the syllable *ru* signifies its destroyer;
because he destroys darkness, he is called *Guru*.

The meaning is that, through protection, instruction, and so forth, by dispelling the non-arising [of ignorance] and other obstacles, he becomes the one who impels toward the human goals (purushārtha) pertaining to this world and the next, as well as their means, and who turns one away from their opposites.
The suffix *tṛc* is applied to the root *gup* (meaning "to protect") in the sense of the agent;
because it is marked with the vowel *ū*, the augment *iṭ* is optional.
Protection consists of both the attainment of what is desired and the avoidance of what is undesired.
When knowledge is free from doubt and error— that is, when it has transcended both the state of being doubtful and the state of being erroneous—

the meaning is that this occurs even though [knowledge] consists of valid cognition regarding both perceived and unperceived objects and so forth; here the designation emphasizes the abstract state (bhāva-pradhāna-nirdeśaḥ).

One whose activity or conduct (*vyāpāra*) is contrary—that is, opposed to both what is seen and what is unseen—is described as such; that person, indeed, "that person" (*puruṣam punaḥ puruṣam*), according to Amara’s definition: "the word *punaḥ* is used when there is no first [instance] or in the sense of distinction. If the king does not punish him, then from that absence of royal punishment, this "disturbance of the subjects" (*prajāviplavaḥ*), meaning the affliction of the people, has ensued. Therefore, you must certainly be punished; thus, one should not entertain the delusion of a reversal in the relationship between the punisher and the punished—this is the connection with the preceding [verse].

"One should instruct those who have gone astray due to weakness of their senses to feel world-weariness (*nirveda*). If they should persist excessively in their transgression, one should bring them before the king.
According to the degree of their strength, one should subdue them with restraints, excluding execution or slavery"—this statement of Āpastamba is to be kept in mind.
In this context, the mention of the guru is said to be the *saṃdhy-aṅga* named *prasanga*. As it has been stated: "The praise of the guru is *prasanga*. (35)
The great king Daśaratha.
Regarding the phrase "not yet arisen," [the commentary] begins with "O Bhārgava," and so forth.

O Bhārgava, if your knowledge—which consists of the valid cognition regarding the previously mentioned objects, both seen and unseen—has not arisen, that is, if it has not dawned, then serve the feet of Vasiṣṭha; attend upon him.
The sense is that through service to the Guru, as stated in such passages as "or by supreme service" and "know that through prostration, inquiry, and service," your perfect knowledge will arise.
If your knowledge is afflicted by doubt—that is, by a doubt concerning the same object and thus rendered devoid of practical application—then serve the feet of Vasiṣṭha.
The meaning is that, through his grace, doubt regarding the goal will cease.
Alternatively, this may be explained as an indication where the abstract state (bhāva) is primary: "that which, by virtue of being a doubt, is devoid of the power to bring about performance.
Even if your knowledge were erroneous—that is, if it consisted of the two kinds of delusion previously mentioned—nevertheless, you should serve the feet of Vasiṣṭha.
The meaning is that, through your grace, his erroneous cognition will cease.
Now, one might ask: "How can you cite the case of Paraśurāma, who was already possessed of [right] knowledge, as an instance where knowledge did not arise? To this he says: "Certainly" (*dhruvam*).
There is certainly a defect in his knowledge.
The meaning is that a defect consisting of non-arising, doubt, or error is inferred in his cognition.
Here, "bad conduct" (durācāra) is intended as the logical reason (*hetu*).
Thus, the formal structure of the inference is: "This person possesses a defect in his cognition because of his bad conduct, like a person whose [defect] is admitted."
Here, he dispels the suspicion that [the reason] is not probative by asking, "How?
The ellipsis is: otherwise, in the absence of the probandum—namely, the nature of a defect in knowledge—how could there be "misconduct" (durvyavahṛti), that is, bad conduct?
The root *hṛ* preceded by *vyava* denotes both physical activity and verbal activity.

In this context, there is a general causal relationship between cognition and its operation by way of a connection such as having the same object (*samānaviṣayatva*). By that very same connection, a specific causal relationship is observed between correct cognition and a correct operation, as well as between defective cognition and a defective operation. Thus, the point is that the very contingency of breaking the causal relationship between defective cognition and a defective operation serves to ward off the suspicion of [the argument] being non-conclusive (*aprayojakatva*).
[This concludes the section on] "in the case of purity."
The word "knowledge" (jñāne) is to be supplied [from the previous verse].

Even if there is purity of knowledge—that is, even in the absence of defects such as doubt mentioned previously—if you practice sin, meaning if you perform actions forbidden by the scriptures, kings do not tolerate it;
the meaning is that they do not endure it.
Because the punishment for transgressing against the learned is severe, kings would punish such a person accordingly; otherwise, that sin would fall upon them.
As it has been stated by Manu: "But a king, by failing to punish, incurs that very same guilt.
Thus, the sense is that kings do not tolerate such offenses. ||36||

Regarding the word *dharma*: the Blessed Lord Īśa Rudra is present in the following objects: in *dharma*—meaning the means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*) known solely through the Veda; in *Brahman*—the Supreme Self who is to be propitiated by *dharma*; and in the *bow*—the weapon used at the time of dispelling obstacles to *dharma*.
Because the specific sense of the locative case (as the locus) is intended here, the second case is not used, but rather the seventh case (*saptamī*).
"Me" means my; "śāsitā" means the instructor or enlightener.
The word "hi" indicates well-known fact.
Therefore, the sense is: "Thus, the fault lies with my knowledge."
"Of me, the destroyer of all kṣatriyas"—that is, the annihilator of the entire class of kṣatriyas; "nibarhaṇam" means "pramāpaṇam" (destruction).
In the present context, however, the suffix *lyu* (ana) is used in the sense of the agent because the word belongs to the *nandī* group.

How could the Kṣatriyas train in the Vinaya? How could they possibly do so? The potential suffix *liṅ* is used here with the sense of possibility (*śaki*). Therefore, it is said that the kings do not tolerate [it].

Regarding the term *vasiṣṭhamiśra*, the relationship is one where the most venerable Vasiṣṭha is the counter-correlative; this relationship is to be honored in the case of *jarā* (old age). The mention of *jarā* is illustrative; it also applies to *sthāna* (position).

When there is superiority in terms of status and age, he should be placed at the forefront for the purpose of serving his feet. The word "tu" (but) indicates the doubt arising from [his being] a great-grandfather or his seniority.
However, in the case of rivalry—that is, when there is competition based on knowledge or asceticism—he is not to be honored nor placed at the forefront.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Superior.
The meaning is: "Who else—whether Vasiṣṭha or anyone other than you—is superior or even equal to me in knowledge and austerity?
Therefore, the three statements made by Viśvāmitra—that one need not attend upon his feet for the sake of knowledge—are all refuted.
Here, the juncture-element (saṃdhyaṅga) called *drava* (softening), consisting of the disparagement of a superior, has been described.
As it is said: "Disparagement of a superior is *drava*. ||37||

The meaning is that it is our desire that there should be defeat, humiliation, or inferiority resulting from one born of Bhṛgu—that is, from a member of the Bhṛgu lineage. Since Bhṛgu is the eldest, being humiliated by one of his lineage who stands in the place of a grandson is indeed pleasing; the sense is based on the traditional teaching: "One should desire defeat at the hands of a son or similar descendant."
"By us":

because it is praiseworthy, worthy of protection through non-interruption by us who are its guardians, dear to us, ancient, and long-standing; and because the conduct [of the Brahmins] is not common to all Brahmins.
Behold the ruin and decline of the noble conduct rooted in the Vedas within our own household!
It is said to be "in our household" because of the ancient lineage of Bhṛgu and Vasiṣṭha.
The sense is: I do not grieve that this descendant of Bhṛgu insults me; rather, I grieve that a loss of dharma has occurred in our lineage, which is the upholder of dharma. ||38||
"Janaka," and so forth;
the word "they say" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
[This refers to] the ignoble and the unrefined.
"Without restraint" means one who breaks the Vedic order.
"Of the worlds" means in the eternal teacher, the perpetual preceptor of the worlds.

Regarding the term *nityasadātanasanātanāḥ*, Amara states that these are synonyms for "eternal. Furthermore, since Vasiṣṭha was born from the breath (*prāṇa*) of Brahmā, you are likewise unrestrained and fearless toward him—Vasiṣṭha being as dear to him as his own life-breath. You are "unrestrained" (*niraṅkuśaḥ*), meaning you have emerged beyond all restraint, like a "wild elephant" (*vyāladvipaḥ*), that is, a rogue elephant. As the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *vyāla* refers to a serpent, a rogue elephant, a beast of prey, or one who destroys; it is used in three genders [as an adjective]."

Since words denoting a specific quality, when used in conjunction with a word denoting the substantive, are intended to convey only the qualifying attribute, the word *vyāla* here refers solely to the state of being wicked.
You are being subdued—that is, disciplined—by us, many Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, after having been drawn near and entreated.
[The form *damyase* is derived from the root *damu* meaning "to pacify," followed by the causative suffix *ṇic*, and then the present passive third-person singular ending.]

In this matter, Vasiṣṭha is the eternal preceptor of the world by virtue of being the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the seven *vyāhṛtis*. Even if, according to your own stated logic that "in matters of dharma and Brahmanhood," Rudra may be your preceptor in dharma and so forth, nevertheless, because he is the seer of the seven *vyāhṛtis*—which are the primary cause of Brahmanhood and are most worthy of all honor—he is your principal preceptor. Thus, rivalry toward him is equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*). And so says Yājñavalkya: "Insulting one's gurus, reviling the Vedas, and the killing of a friend..."

"It should be known as equal to the killing of a Brahmin, as well as the loss of what has been studied. Your statement—"In matters of dharma, sacred knowledge, and archery, the venerable Lord is indeed my instructor; he is to be honored for his age, but not for competition"—is ill-spoken. Because Viśvāmitra, though a Brahmin, was included there among those to be protected by many, and because we feared a deficiency in Paraśurāma’s splendor due to his insulting a superior, we said that you must be subdued.
By this, the passage beginning with "of the destroyer of all kṣatriyas" is also answered. ||39||
"I am an Avadhūta; I have been insulted.
Regarding the word "internally" (*antar*):

my anger (*manyu*), which is wrath, having been compressed by the weight—the intensity—of *dhairya* (fortitude), specifically that particular state of mental composure which serves as the cause for the capacity to restrain anger, due to the words of the elders such as Cyavana and others, has been made into a mass. This means it has been subjected to an operation conducive to a state of condensation that obstructs its outward manifestation. Thus, it has been consolidated into a single lump.

Having become concentrated, and therefore like an arrow-head lodged in a vital organ (hṛnmarma), burning intensely—just like a fragment of an arrow lodged in a part of the body incapable of withstanding the pressure of the heart-region—he remains for a long time within the interior of my body even while staying in one place, causing torment all around. This very anger of mine, its stability shattered by the humiliation and the reproach inflicted by Janaka and others, having broken its bounds—"maryādā" meaning "limit," "support," or "stability"—according to Amara;
[it burns] at the end of the *kalpa*, the day of Brahmā, by means of the wind (*marut*).
The compound is formed by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of a rule) based on the term "saptamī.
He is like the submarine fire (*aurvānala*)—the fire of the mare (*vaḍavānala*)—of that ocean whose water has overflowed and spread abroad;
as Amara states: "Aurva, vāḍava, and vaḍavānala [are synonyms for the submarine fire]."
In this context, it should be understood that the word *aurva* functions merely as a specific epithet for the *vāḍava* (submarine fire), due to its co-occurrence with the word *anala* (fire).
"Now it flashes" means it exerts itself like a thunderbolt; the similarity consists in qualities such as possessing great velocity and being irresistible.
The intended meaning is that the word *ṭuāsphūrjā*, which is read in the lexicon as "the roar of a thunderbolt," is here used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to convey the aforementioned sense.
The particle *eva* (only/just) serves to indicate firmness or emphasis. ||40||
"Diṣṭyā" expresses joy. "Nikāram" refers to the humiliation or insult inflicted by Janaka and others.
According to Amara, "nikāra" means "viprakāra" (insult or mistreatment).
This axe has come into my possession; it blazes like death itself and possesses a fire favorable for consuming enemies.
It should be understood that the mention of receiving such insult is due to the presiding deity who takes pride in this divine axe.

On this earth, in the lineage of Daśaratha, there are kings—both those established upon the earth and those residing in the household of Daśaratha, such as Sīradhvaja, Kuśadhvaja, and others, as well as Daśaratha, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and so forth—who have arrived.
Since this is so, he is one who causes a festival—that is, one whose nature is to produce joy—for Kṛtānta (Yama) when he is provoked, that is, for Yama possessed of excessive anger.
[The suffix] *ṭa* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *ṭa* is used after the root *kṛ* in the senses of cause, habitual disposition, and favorability."
Twenty-two is *dvyadhikā viṃśatiḥ*.
According to the rule "dvyaṣṭanaḥ saṅkhyāyām" and so forth, the word *dvi* undergoes *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for *i*).
That which completes twenty-two is *dvāviṃśa*.
In the formation of that [term], by the rules *tasya pūraṇe ḍaṭ* and *tiviṃśaterḍiti*, there is the elision of the syllable *ti*.
The meaning is that previously there were twenty-one killings of Kṣatriyas, and this is another, the twenty-second.
The word *api* serves to include the preceding.

Like the dissolution of the world, this terrible dissolution of the phenomenal universe is terrifying even to me; it is the *parimara*—the slaughter—in which the *kṣatra*, the warrior class as a whole, perishes. It is called *parimara* because heroes (*vīra*) die therein. The suffix *gha* is applied in the sense of the locus (locative) according to the rule "the suffix *gha* is generally used for a masculine noun in the sense of a technical name.
Let it happen once more.
The imperative suffix (loṭ) is used when the time for action has arrived. ||41||
"As you wish.
This Paraśurāma is our own person, our kinsman (*svajana*).
According to Amarasimha, "kinsman," "one's own people," and "relative" are synonymous.
The word *kāmaṃ* is used here in the sense of granting permission.

Nevertheless, even though he is our own kinsman, out of arrogance he resolves upon—that is, determines as a duty to perform—a terrible and fearsome deed against Rāmabhadra and the others; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
"This one is certainly not dependent on us; how indeed might he become so? How might he come to be?
By all means, he must be made subject to our own will.
Otherwise, he would act according to his own resolve"—this is the meaning.

In that situation, as for the means to bring [the enemy] under one's own control: conciliation (*sāman*) would not be effective because of his arrogance; nor would bribery (*dāna*) be effective because of his dispassion;
and there can be no sowing of dissension (*bheda*) because he has no allies.
However, punishment remains.
With the intention that even this [punishment] is approved by me for a compassionate person on account of their relationship, he says: "by the corrupted one.
This Paraśurāma [was spoken of] as being "corrupted," having undergone a transformation in the form of anger.
The suffix *ṇic* is applied to the root *duṣ*, which is listed [in the Dhātupāṭha] as meaning "to become corrupted" (*vaikṛtye*).
Because the aspect of instigation (*preraṇāṃśa*) is abandoned, it becomes intransitive;
thus, by the rule "gatyarthākarmaka-," the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
*Vaikṛtya* means a transformation or a defect.

Alternatively, if he were looked upon even once by me—having been censured with the exposure of his fault, "He is venerable in his old age, but not for rivalry"—that glance would be a misfortune (*durita*) for that child of Bhṛgu, who is to be cherished due to his relationship as our great-grandson, who is worthy of compassion because of his youth, limited knowledge, and scant asceticism, and who belongs to the lineage of our eldest brother.
For since this is so, the connection is: "It is a pity."

In this context, the *bhāgavata* [author] has described the *saṃdhy-aṅga* called "wavering" (*vicalana*), because Vasiṣṭha manifests his own qualities—such as forbearance and compassion—even toward one who has done him harm.
As it has been said: "The manifestation of one's own qualities is wavering. (42)

As if devoid of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); as if empty of the excellence of good conduct, Vedic study, and recitation, which are the causes of the power to curse or bestow grace—according to Amara, "spiritual luster is the perfection of conduct and study";
and as if one whose capacity for weaponry—the power of wielding arms—has been shattered and fallen away.

"Śastra refers to a weapon and a bow," according to the *Ratnamālā*. "Jīvaloka" means the world that serves as the dwelling place for living beings (*prāṇin*). "Jīva [is used] for Bṛhaspati, breath, life, the self, and trees."
"In the three [worlds]—the earth, the atmosphere, and heaven—there exist both the living and the non-living within the bowstring made of murvā grass," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
"The word *loka* refers to the world and the forest," according to Amara.
Regarding the term *brahmakṣatra*:

O son of Jamadagni, although you are worthy of being protected by us on account of our relationship—namely, by virtue of your being the son of our sister’s husband, Jamadagni—you nevertheless insult (*ākṣipasi*) the assembly of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, that is, the community of those sharing the same dharma through austerity, study, and so forth. (Amara states: "The term *samaja* refers to animals, while *samāja* refers to others who share the same dharma.")
Furthermore, child Rāma, you are one of terrible intent and cruel purpose—
*abhiprāya*, *chanda*, and *āśaya* being synonyms according to Amara.

For by this transgression— which consists of the simultaneous insults against the assembly of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas and the desire to kill Rāma— you cause us pain, making us miserable by overstepping the boundaries of the Vedas and Vedic tradition.

From the word *duḥkha* (suffering), by applying the suffix *ṇic* according to the rule "that which performs it" (*tatkaroti*), there is the elision of the *matup* suffix because of the status of the *ṇi*-affix as having the nature of the desiderative (*iṣṭavat*).
Alternatively, [it means] "you cause us (*naḥ*) suffering," i.e., you inflict pain upon us;
here the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *ṇic* is used in the sense of performing that action" (*sukhaduḥkhatatkriyāyām*).
Regarding this: *ātaḥ ataḥ*.
Like the word *ataḥ*, the word *ātaḥ* also exists with a long vowel at its beginning, signifying "because" or "for that reason."
Because *viṣu* is listed among the indeclinables (*avyaya*) in the rule *viṣvag-devayoś ca ṭeradry-ekapade*, [the form *viṣvak* is used].
For me, who am angry toward you—that is, possessed of wrath directed at you—my right hand, becoming agitated, seeks out the water for the curse against you.

My other hand, the left one, by virtue of prior impressions (*saṃskāra*)—namely, in accordance with the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) for proficiency in archery derived from my status as a Kṣatriya prior to attaining the state of a Brahmarṣi through the power of asceticism and the words of Vasiṣṭha—[remains steady].
According to Amara, "grahaḥ" means "grāhaḥ," "vaśaḥ," and "kāntiḥ. Here, "kāntiḥ" signifies desire.
He seeks the bow.
The meaning is: "I restrain [him] by means of both a curse and a bow, which are conducive respectively to his present state of being a Brāhmaṇa and his past state of being a Kṣatriya.
Regarding the root *ṛṣ* in the sense of "going," it belongs to the *divādi* class; however, through the influence of a prefix (*upasarga*), it acquires the sense of "desire. ||43||

Regarding the word "thou" (*tvam*): if you were one who exists as one whose wealth is the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*), then the state of existing would be connected by way of having the splendor of sacred knowledge as one's wealth.

If you are endowed with the conduct, study, and prosperity appropriate to the status of a Brāhmaṇa belonging to this present time, then by means of a fierce austerity consistent with that Brāhmaṇahood, I shall burn—that is, reduce to ashes—your austerity that is inconsistent with Brāhmaṇahood. (The root *dah* is used in the sense of "reducing to ashes. Or else (*yad vā*), according to another interpretation: [the meaning is as follows].
If he should be an archer according to the custom of his own caste—that is, by the conduct (*samaya*) appropriate to his birth from a Kṣatriya father and a Kṣatriya mother—[then he may be so].
Amara states: "The word *samaya* denotes an oath, conduct, time, a philosophical system, and an agreement.
If he should be an archer [in that sense], [then he is fit].

In the alternative sense (*pakṣāntare*), the word *pakṣa* is derived from the root *pakṣati*, which is listed [in the lexicon] as meaning "to accept" (*parigrahe*). In this context, it refers to a specific conceptual acceptance (*parigrāhyakalpaviśeṣa*) characterized by the bow being the instrument (*dhanurupakaraṇatva*).
Let the axe (*paraśu*) perform the corresponding (*sadṛśa*), suitable (*anurūpa*) action, namely that of combat (*yuddhātmaka karma*).
The *loṭ* suffix is used here in the sense of free agency (*kāmacāre*).

Although there may be a dependence on me as the agent in the case of "asceticism" (*tapasaḥ*), there is no such dependence on me in the case of the axe (*paraśoḥ*); this is the intended meaning behind the difference in grammatical designation.
In this context, by praising one's own power, the dramatic element (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) called "determination" (*vyavasāya*) is expressed.
As it has been said: "Determination is the praising of one's own power. (44)
"A disciple of Kauśika" means a pupil of Viśvāmitra;
according to Amarasimha, "chātra" and "antevāsī" both mean "disciple.
Because the context concerns war, although he is designated as a follower of Vasiṣṭha, Rāma has addressed him here as a disciple of Kauśika.
"O descendant of Pulastya! [He says:

"I am able to conquer—that is, I can defeat—Paraśurāma, the enemy of the haughty Kārtavīryārjuna through his victory over the descendant of Pulastya (Rāvaṇa), and the vanquisher of the valor of other kṣatriyas, that is, one who overcomes the prowess of other warriors. [The use of the suffix] *taṅ* [the ātmanepada ending] is according to the rules: "after the root *śak*, the potential (*liṅ*) is used," and "after the roots *ji* preceded by *vi* or *parā*."
In the presence of his guru, he performs an expiation for the fault of manifesting his power with the words, "Homage be to you.
Alternatively, he entreats him, saying "Homage be to you," so that they do not restrain him out of excessive affection or groundless suspicion.
Here, Rāma’s intention is indicated: that victory over both Vālin and Rāvaṇa is easily attainable by me.
By this, the meaning of the four remaining factors has been indicated. ||45||
How was it obtained?
"How" is used here in a sense of wonder.
This is the slaying of the Destroyer of Kṣatriyas by the child Rāma.
"Excellent" means perfectly so.
"Hanta" expresses joy.
"Abhyanujānīta" means grant permission or give your consent.
"May Rāmabhadra be victorious"— the remainder of the sentence being "over Paraśurāma.
"This one," etc.

This Rāma, the lord of the world, is a hero who is the sole warrior, devoid of kinsmen and twice-born [adversaries]; he is the subduer and tamer of the arrogant. (The compound is formed by the rule of *bāhulaka*.)
This [word] ends in the suffix *tṛc*.

By the use of the plural "of the arrogant" (*dṛptānām*), it is indicated that he is the subduer even of Vālin and Rāvaṇa. He who is the leader and the sustainer is Vasiṣṭha; those [monkeys] belonging to him are thus described.
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rule "dhuro yaḍḍhakau.
We are all here guarantees (*pratibhuvaḥ*) for Rāma’s leadership;
as Amara states: "guarantees (*lagnakāḥ*) are [also] called *pratibhuvaḥ*."

In this context, by the statement "This is the destroyer of the arrogant," which describes a future benefit as if it were already accomplished, the *saṃdhy-aṅga* (limb of the juncture) called *prarocana* (incitement) is mentioned.
Thus it has been said: "The description of a future benefit as if it were already accomplished is *prarocana*. (46)
"nanvityādi": "nanu" is used as a vocative particle.
According to Amarasimha: "nanu is used in inquiry, determination, permission, conciliation, and address."
Although for Rāmabhadra— who possesses celebrated renown and well-known fame— fame itself is indeed renown, nevertheless, what is intended here is the "renown of renown.
For it has been said, "the fame of fame," referring to fame in the form of the widespread proclamation of one's virtuous qualities.
For the renown of possessing qualities consists in the well-known nature of those qualities being grounded in reality.
Indeed, it has been said in some instances that "fame is obtained through merits," even though fame lacks any such visible basis;
therefore, the phrase "of those whose fame is renowned" was stated in order to exclude that [latter case].
"Those by whom the vow of protection— that is, the rule of guarding the world— has been undertaken and maintained are referred to as such;
furthermore, [the word] 'vaḥ' (of you) refers to you who are worthy of officiating at sacrifices (*yājyānām*),
according to the rule *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā*, which allows for the genitive case in the sense of the agent."
Of such [persons]—
the word "of the Ikṣvākus" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He was well-born this very day in a virtuous house, that is, in a household abounding in excellence.

Although he was born through the *putrakāmeṣṭi* sacrifice performed previously, he is not merely "born" [in the ordinary sense]; rather, the meaning is that he possesses an auspicious birth because you have favored him just now with the excellence of a future victory, such as that of Paraśurāma and others.
Alternatively, the word *nanu* is an address to Janaka:
"O Rāmabhadra, you are truly well-born this very day in the house of your patrons—those of celebrated fame who have undertaken the vow of protecting [the world]."
The meaning is that no one has previously been born in our house.

For this reason, by means of the light of knowledge—that is, through the excellence of your wisdom—your powers (prabhāva), which consist of the preeminent natures (prakṛṣṭasvabhāva) of those beings who exist now, those who have passed, and those who are yet to be (bhavya), have been fully grasped and rightly known by you.
In the word *bhavya*, the suffix *yat* is applied to the root *bhū* in the sense of the agent, according to the rule beginning with "bhavya-geya-."
"‘Bhavya’ means true, auspicious, or fit; it is used in three genders for one who is capable or destined," according to the *Ratnamālā*.

The *brahmans*—the foremost of the twice-born, such as Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and others—even regarding Śiśuka (the Child), that is, Rāma who is exceedingly young, perceive—that is, they know collectively—that his leadership over Paraśurāma and others is something utterly unworthy of being even mentally entertained by me.
The root *vid* is listed in the *curādi* group with the meaning "to dwell in the narration of sensations" (*vedanākhyānanivāseṣu*).
Here, by the phrase "born this very day," etc., the certain attainment (*niyatāpti*) consisting of the certainty of the effect is stated through the absence of any obstacle (*apāya*).
Furthermore, the *prakarī*, which consists of a narrative that does not pervade [the entire plot] but concerns Śatānanda and others, is also stated.
Therefore, in this act, the entire *vimarśa-sandhi* (the juncture of deliberation) is described in its complete form. ||47||
"Come here, O Prince, you shall conquer the son of Jamadagni.
The construction is: "O Prince, you think 'I shall conquer the son of Jamadagni,' so come here.

According to the rule, *prahāse ca manyopapade manyater uttama ekavacca* ("and in jest, when *manya-* is the accompanying word, the first person [uttama] is used for the second person [madhyama], and it is treated as singular"), when the first person ought to be employed because of the root *manya-* being the accompanying word, the second person is used.

Since it is stated that "when the middle [person] of the verb *man* is to be employed, the first person should be used when irony (*prahāsa*) is implied," there is here the employment of both the first and middle persons in the phrase "I think you will conquer" (*manye vijeṣyase*).
Furthermore, the word "come" (*ehi*) indicates irony;
for this very reason, "Come, I think you will eat food" (*ehi manye odanaṃ bhokṣyase*) is cited as an example.
For in that case, there was a laugh directed at one who, being hungry, did not know that the rice had already been consumed by another.
Even though [the child] was the slayer of Kṣatriyas, his victory over the Kṣatriya children was a cause for laughter; intending this, the word "son" (putra) is used here.
He expresses this very laughter explicitly with the word "with a smile" (sasmitam).
"You shall not conquer him;
for the son of Reṇukā is difficult to subdue and will be your death. The middle voice (ātmanepada) of the root *ji* is used here according to the rule "viparābhyām... [Pāṇini 1.3.19].
Regarding the word *kṛtta*:
"Brahmastaṃbha" refers to the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
According to the *Ratnamālā*, "staṃba" means a thicket, a branchless tree, or a mountain.
By the word "staṃba," the world-eggs are expressed through secondary metaphorical usage (*gauṇī vṛtti*) due to their similarity in qualities such as verticality and so forth.
In their *nikuñjas* and *kuñjas*—
according to Amarasimha, "both *nikuñja* and *kuñja* mean a bower"— the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*) serve as the place of the creepers that constitute those bowers.
By this, the sense is that [the sound] pervades the multitudes of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*).

It is "heaped" (*puñjita*), meaning gathered into a mass; therefore, it is a "dense" (*ghana*) roar of the bowstring. By means of that, this formidable and terrifying bow—the agent—[is characterized]. From the caves (*kandara*) which are the very throats of the Kṣatriyas cut down (*kṛtta*, i.e., severed), there flow forth (*saradbhiḥ*) streams of *kīlāla*, that is, blood.
According to Amara: "In the sense of blood, *kīlāla* is used for water."
He is so described because his clusters and masses of flames (*śikhā-kalāpa-saṃghāta*) have been extinguished, calmed, and then rekindled.
According to the *Ratnamālā*, "The word *kalāpa* denotes an ornament, a peacock's tail, a girdle, a collection, and a quiver.
In the analysis of the compound as "those in which there are the humming sounds (*jhaṅkāra*) of such a fire (*hutabhuj*)," the suffix *ini* is applied according to the rule *ata ini-ṭhanau*.
By such arrows; "kalamba, mārgaṇa, and śara" are synonyms for arrow according to Amara. Of the gluttonous one, that is, the devourer of the world.
"An eater, a devourer, a consumer"—thus says Amara.
Let him practice, that is, perform repeatedly, the act of swallowing—the act of grasping—as Kālarudra, the Rudra of the time of universal dissolution (pralaya).
"Practice is repeated exercise"—thus says Amara.

Because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is optional according to the rule "the [suffixes] after a prefix [are used optionally] with the roots *as* and *ūh*, there is the active voice (*parasmaipada*). Here, the ornament is a specific type of *nidarśanā* (illustration) consisting in the function of word-meanings (*padārthavṛtti*), for its definition is: "Some call another [type of] *nidarśanā* that which functions through word-meanings.

Furthermore, by mentioning the bow instead of the axe, it is indicated that the bow is dearer even than that; thus, it is foreshadowed that in the subsequent act, Bhārgava, having been conquered by Rāma, will affectionately bestow the bow upon Rāma. ||48||
Vīrarāghava, a native of Mahīsāra and a descendant of Vādhūla,
has composed the third act of the Mahāvīracarita.
Victory now to our Guru, who is the eternal abode of Lakṣmī, who is to be served by all teachers without exception,
and who possesses a noble son here— the young Śrīraṅgarāja— by whom the neck of the horse of the Lord Śeṣa has been cast far away.
Thus ends the third act in the *Bhāvapradyotinī*, a commentary on the *Mahāvīracarita* composed by Vādhūla Vīrarāghava, whose name begins with the syllable Āṇṇā.
Act Four.

Now, the poet, intending to present the *garbhasandhi* (the development of the plot) once again through another means in the fourth, fifth, and sixth acts, first introduces the *viṣkambha* (interlude) of the fourth act with the words "O, O! and so forth.
Those who travel by means of a *vimāna*—a celestial vehicle—are called *vaimānikas*.
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "he practices by means of that.
Let auspicious things—such as showers of flowers and other virtuous deeds—proceed. The verb is in the imperative (*loṭ*) mood, used in the active voice (*kartari*).
He states the reason for this: "Kṛśāśva...

and so forth. The venerable sage Kauśika, a disciple and pupil of the Brahman-sage named Kṛśāśva—the first seer of the divine weapons such as the Jambhaka—triumphs, existing in a state of supreme excellence.
The underlying sentiment is that "the preeminence of a disciple brings glory to his teachers."
Now, in the lineage of the Moon—the Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa)—the Kṣatra, the warrior class, triumphs. Why is this so? To this he says:
"The Subduer. He is one whose wealth consists solely of the vow of granting fearlessness to the world, and who is the subduer—that is, the tamer—of Kṣattrāri, namely Paraśurāma.

Because it protects what has been acquired and because that which has not yet been acquired can be obtained, it is similar to wealth. Furthermore, the slaying of those who were thorns to the world, such as Vāli and Rāvaṇa, is also indicated here. He is the refuge of the worlds, being skilled (*sādhu*) in providing protection (*śaraṇe*).
"Śaraṇam" means protection or a house, according to the Viśva lexicon. The suffix *yat* is applied here according to the rule "tatra sādhuḥ.

By the phrase "granting fearlessness to the world," etc., the author intends to express both the bestowing of the fruits of the three aims of human life (*traivargika-phala*) and the destruction of their opposites.
By the words beginning with "the refuge" (*śaraṇya*), the removal of fear and the granting of liberation are intended.
By this, the bestowal of the lordships of Kiṣkindhā and Laṅkā upon Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa, as well as the slaying of their adversaries Vālin and Rāvaṇa—which are to be described later—are indicated.
Likewise, the granting of liberation to Jaṭāyu and Vālin is also indicated.

Thus, Rāma—the moon of the solar dynasty (*dinakarakulendu*), who brings joy to the lineage of the Sun—triumphs, existing in a state of supreme excellence. By the term *dinakara* (maker of the day), it is suggested that just as the sun, though a source of heat, removes distress like the moon, so too does Rāma dispel suffering. Herein lies the *Garbha-sandhi* (the "Womb" juncture), because of the search for the "seed" (*bīja*)—namely, Viśvāmitra’s efforts—which was previously seen through the defeat of Paraśurāma and subsequently unseen during the exile to the forest, yet serves as the cause for Rāma’s ultimate welfare.

As it has been said: "The embryo [of the plot] consists in the repeated searching for a seed that was seen and then lost. And in this juncture (*saṃdhi*), the *arthaprakṛti* known as the "embryo" (*garbha*) and the *arthaprakṛti* known as "hope of attainment" (*prāptyāśā*) must be stated.
Their essential nature is as follows: "The possibility of accomplishing the task arises through hope of attainment, characterized by apprehension regarding both means and obstacles."
It has been stated: "The *patākā* (subsidiary plot) is a story that pervades the story of the protagonist.
