Because the possibility of the accomplishment of the task (*kāryasambhāvanā*) has been mentioned through the apprehension of obstacles such as the hostility of Malyavat and others, and the apprehension of means such as the favor shown by Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, the "hope of attainment" (*prāptyāśā*) is expressed.
Furthermore, because the story of Lakṣmaṇa—which pervades the story of Rāma, the protagonist—has been described, the *patākā* is characterized.
And there are twelve constituent parts (*aṅga*) of this "embryo-junction" (*garbhasandhi*).
As it has been said: "Abhūtāharaṇa, Mārga, Rūpa, Udāharaṇa, Krama, Saṃgraha, Anumāna, and likewise Toṭaka and Bala."
"Agitation, flurry, and interruption are the twelve limbs in their proper sequence.
The specific natures of these will be demonstrated at their respective appropriate occasions. ||1||

He states the *viṣkambhaka* with the words "Then enter," and so forth. They are "agitated. Here, because of the mention of agitation (*saṃbhrama*), the dramatic structural element (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) called *toṭaka* is indicated.
As it has been said: "Speech characterized by anger and agitation is *toṭaka*.
This refers to the agitated speech resulting from the defeat of Paraśurāma, who had been emboldened by his own [powers].
His entry into the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) is for the purpose of ascertaining the activities of those traveling in such chariots.

Those for whom there is a single path (*ekamayanam*) as their basis (*adhikaraṇa*) are so described; in this sense, the suffix *ciri* is applied after the root *bhū* when used with the word *anekāyana*.
Furthermore, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *bhū* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Thus, [the term] *ekāyanībhāvaḥ* [is formed].
The meaning is that they have Rāma as their sole substratum (*ekādhikaraṇaka*).
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *ayana* [denotes] a dwelling place, a path, or the southern and northern courses of the sun.
The phrase "Was he seen? (*dṛṣṭaḥ kim*) should be construed with an interrogative intonation (*kāku*).
Indra and others;
by the word "others," the inclusion of Agni and so forth is intended.
The state of being a *bandī* is the status of one who recites hymns of praise.
"Bandins are reciters of praises," according to Amara.
This state of being a *bandin* is mentioned in reference to the verse beginning with "the pupil of Kṛśāśva.
As for the fact that they have approached [him] spontaneously, by their own will, this constitutes their "state of single-minded devotion" (*ekāyanībhāva*); such is the grammatical connection.
That which has been ascertained, deliberated upon, and concluded does not contradict [the truth] nor does it become otherwise.
According to Amara, *vipralambha* means "contradiction.

By the statement in the second-act *viṣkambhaka*, "May all the gods know him as victorious," and so forth, that which was ascertained by Mālyavat—and subsequently stated by Śūrpaṇakhā—has been determined by you.
This sequence, consisting of the attainment of the accumulated meaning, is called *krama*, which is stated to be a limb of the *saṃdhi*.
As it has been said: "The attainment of the accumulated meaning is *krama*.
Now, I am trembling.
Now, following the defeat by Paraśurāma—
what should be done here regarding this matter of Rāma?

In that regard as well, Mālyavān had generally promised a counter-measure in the event of Parashurāma’s defeat, saying, "I shall provide a response according to my power. That specific matter is now being asked about by Śūrpaṇakhā: "What is to be done here? As for the phrase "that which":
it refers to the two boons that were promised—that is, vowed.

They are called *varau* because they are chosen (*vriyete*) or requested (*prārthyete*). The root *vṛṅ* means "to choose" (*saṃbhakti*), and "choosing" here signifies requesting; she is so described because she possesses those two [qualities].
Amara states: "Acceptance, agreement, promise, and resolution are synonyms."
*Kaikeyī* is the female descendant of *Kekaya*;
according to the rule beginning with "kekayamitrayupralayānām," the initial *ya*-class vowel is replaced by the *i*-class vowel *ī*.
A *vārtāhāriṇī* is one who brings news or conveys information.
"From Ayodhyā" (*ayodhyātaḥ*):
the suffix *tasi* is applied to the ablative case according to the rule "and [the suffix *tasi* is applied] after [a word ending in] the ablative," etc.
"To Mithilā" (*mithilām*).
Because the root *preṣayati* (to send) is transitive with two objects according to the rule "gati-buddhi... etc., the word *mithilām* takes the second case.

[The form] *preṣitā* [is derived] with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the object, because it is stated: "For other roots ending in the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffixes beginning with *la* (i.e., *kta*) are considered to apply to the indirect object (*prayojya-karman*)."
By means of spies and secret agents—
Amara states that "a spy (cāra) is indeed a secret agent (gūḍhapuruṣa)"—
of that Mantharā.
Regarding the phrase "speaking into the ear":

as it is stated, "But that which is to be understood by one person alone and subsequently made known to others should be expressed in a poetic composition by saying 'thus, as if into the ear' (karṇe evamiva)"; thus, the speaking of a secret matter into the ear is what is meant.
And here, it will become clear later that of these two boons, one concerns Rāma’s exile to the forest and the other concerns Bharata’s consecration.

Here, because of the employment of a deceptive practice for the sake of the subject at hand, the *saṃdhy-aṅga* (limb of the plot) called "the fabrication of the non-existent" (*abhūtāharaṇa*) is mentioned—according to the definition: "The fabrication of the non-existent is the employment of a deceptive practice for the sake of the subject at hand.
[Kaikeyī asks: "What will Rāma do? Will he enter the forest?"
"What else will he do?
The meaning is that, abandoning his entry into the forest, he will rule the kingdom himself.
Here, because it expresses deliberation (*vitarka*), the dramatic constituent (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) called *rūpa* is stated.
As it has been said: "The form [of a statement] consists of speech that sets forth a deliberation.

In the houses of the Ikṣvākus, the noble conduct—meaning the proper behavior consisting of carrying out the commands of mother and father—is not broken; that is, it does not become divided, nor is it abandoned. This is the meaning.
In that context, the "seeker of victory" (*vijigīṣu*) is the cause.

The definition of a seeker of victory was stated by Kāmandaka: "One who is endowed with excellence, skillful, possessed of great energy, diligent in effort, and whose nature is to desire conquest—he is known as a seeker of victory."

The constituent elements (*prakṛti*) are also mentioned in that very same [work]: "Ministers, the kingdom, fortresses, the treasury, and the army as the fifth—these are declared by those who know [statecraft] to be the constituent elements of one seeking victory.
The sense is that the abandonment of good conduct should be avoided, as it is a cause for the displeasure of ministers and the subjects.
By the phrase "I am such a one," the possession of the ten-fold group [of qualities] is intended.
And the ten-fold group is as follows: "The punishment of the wicked and likewise the favoring of the virtuous;
the swift dispatch of spies and the winning over of both the army and the kingdom."
"Likewise, one should attend to the dharma and the artha, as well as the pay of the army, and the performance of daily rites; these are declared to be the ten duties. Thus it has been said.
In this regard, the sense is that if one neglects proper conduct (*sadācāra*), the loss of both the affection of the army and the kingdom, as well as the loss of dharma, would follow.
The fulfillment of one's father’s word—dharma understood from such passages as "by carrying out the command of those who are living"—is established here.
Because this expresses the excellence of the subject at hand, it is called *udāhṛti*, a constituent element (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) of the plot;
as it has been said: "The expression of the excellence of the subject at hand is *udāhṛti*."
"What follows from that?
means: what fruit will result for Rāma by his adherence to virtuous conduct and his fulfillment of his father’s command?
"Therefore, by this," and so forth.
Then:
the meaning is that when Rāma had fulfilled his father’s command;

by this—by what has been told into your ear by me—through the reasoning of the practice and application of the *yogas*, namely the means consisting of conciliation (*sāma*), bribery (*dāna*), sowing dissension (*bheda*), and force (*daṇḍa*), and through the determination of propriety as the cause for practicing those means with discrimination between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, in accordance with place, time, and other factors.
According to Amara, "yoga" refers to "preparation, means, meditation, conjunction, and application.
Furthermore, Amara states that it also denotes "the absence of error and logical propriety.
Alternatively, "Yogācāra" refers to a particular disciple of the Buddha; [the term here] refers to the method of restraint (saṃvaraṇa) taught by him.
The meaning is: by means of a particular punishment consisting of the employment of illusion (*māyā*).
"Of one brought to the *aṅka*—that is, the vicinity or presence—of the Rākṣasas.
[Regarding the word *aṅka*: it is used in the sense of an interlude in a drama, a name, battle, and ornament.]
"Nearby, in a figurative sense, in the mind, and as a mark on the lap"—thus says the *Ratnamālā*.
"In the Vindhya forests" means in the woods of the Vindhya mountains; "of one wandering who is ignorant of the land" means of one who wanders while being ignorant of the land.
The meaning is: of one who moves about without knowing the defects of the region.
"Attacks and oppressions would be easy indeed; they would be capable of being performed with ease.

The suffix *khal* is applied to the root *kṛ* (to do) in the sense of the object, according to the rule "after the words *īṣat*, *duḥ*, and *suṣu*, when used in the sense of difficulty or facility, the suffix *khal* is added.
[The word] "virādha... [is explained as follows].
"Fierce and cruel in the *satras* of the Daṇḍaka forest"—that is, in the forests known as the Daṇḍaka forest, the region of King Daṇḍaka which became a wilderness due to the curse of Śukra.
According to the *Ratnamālā*, "the word *satra* denotes a sacrifice, a specific type of sacrifice, a perpetual gift, and a forest.
Because it is a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*), there is no tautology.

One whose sovereign power (*prabhuśakti*)—consisting of the form of efficacy arising from the treasury and the army (*kośadaṇḍaja-tejorūpa-sāmarthya*)—has been lost or destroyed; that is, one who, even before [this], was deprived of the power consisting of the treasury and the army due to the loss of his kingdom and exile to the forest; such is the meaning.
The word "of Rāma" is an ellipsis [to be supplied].

*Utsāha* (energy) is the persistent effort toward what ought to be done; *śakti* (power) is the capacity therein. They are capable of deceiving—that is, of subverting through guile, meaning by means of deception consisting in the employment of *māyā* (illusion)—that power by means of secret execution, which takes the form of the application of trickery.
The sense is that they are competent [to do so].

In this context, the root *dadhāti* preceded by *ati-sam* is employed in the sense of destruction through deception. "Irreversible" refers to Rāvaṇa’s grasping of Sītā’s true character— that is, his persistent insistence on taking her as his own.
According to Amarasimha, "the planets, such as the sun during an eclipse, are called *nirbādha*.
[The term] *anivartanīyaḥ* means incapable of being turned back by any other means;
the word "is" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the verb.
"And that" means:

when such an employment of illusion exists, that persistence in accepting Sītā is "easily accomplished"—capable of being performed without effort—and "purposeful," meaning it possesses the attainment of its objective in the form of gaining Sītā.
The word "would be" (bhavet) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

When Mālyavān had whispered into Śūrpaṇakhā’s ear the series of statements ending with the resolution, "No one other than Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa alone shall follow as attendants," Śūrpaṇakhā asks: "What is the purpose of also deceiving and drawing away Lakṣmaṇa? Here, *atha* is used in the sense of a question: "Now, what is the necessity for Lakṣmaṇa’s assistance?"
Regarding the word *vīra*:

a hero (*vīra*) is one endowed with innate power who goes to the "other shore" (*pāram*), which is the ultimate limit or perfection of study; thus, from the root *gam* (to go), the suffix *ḍa* is applied in the sense of the agent.
From the root *pāra* (or *tīra*) in the sense of "completion of an action," the suffix *ghañ* is applied to form the noun.

The meaning is that just as Rāma is to be contemplated as a source of fear and a cause for apprehension, so too must the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, who has mastered all weapons, be contemplated as a source of danger.
For it was previously requested by Rāma, "May [the task] be accomplished together with Lakṣmaṇa.
The application of a deceptive punishment (*chadmadaṇḍaprayoga*) refers to the execution of a secret penalty.
"Daṇḍa is not feminine; it refers to self-restraint, injury, an army, a club, and the punishment of kings," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
As for "in one [place]" (*ekasmin*), the meaning is "in a single location"; the word "to be done" (*kārya*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
Likewise, it should be performed for two;
the meaning is that it should be performed for both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa. ||2||
Regarding the phrase "mama tu" (but for me): "incurable enmity toward women" (*apratisamādheyaṃ strīvairam*) refers to hostility instigated by women that cannot be reversed by any other means.
In the Prakrit language, the word *strī* is replaced by the substitute *itthiyā*.

The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: "the harboring of enmity by one who has no unbound enmity—that is, one devoid of enmity occasioned by any other cause—and that which is enmity toward women; these two [are the causes].
For enmity is indeed fivefold.
As it has been said: "Enmity born of a rival wife, born of material objects, born of women, born of speech, and born of an offense."
"Enmity is considered to be of five kinds by those skilled in the classification of enmities.
Thus [it is said]. "He, for his part"—the word *tāvat* here signifies sequence.
The meaning is that proximity is indeed appropriate, and thus it is examined first.
That Rāma, by virtue of being "immediately adjacent to the earth"—that is, because he is situated right next to the earth—is indeed close at hand.
It is intended that his proximity to the earth is in relation to Rāvaṇa.
And that consists in being situated within a circle surrounded by one's own circle.
As stated by Amarasiṃha: "The king whose territory is immediately adjacent is the enemy; beyond him is the friend.
"Immediately adjacent" means having the land directly bordering [one's own].

Since the term *viṣaya* in the phrase "a district (*nīvṛt*) and a country (*janapada*) are *viṣayas*" denotes a region, there is among the twelve types of kings one known as the *bhūmyanantara* (the immediate neighbor).

To explain: in the center is the *vijigīṣu* (the seeker of conquest); then his enemy (*ari*), his friend (*mitra*), the friend of his enemy (*arermitra*), the enemy of his friend (*mitraśatru*), and the friend of the enemy's friend (*śatrumitramitra*)—these are the five situated in front.

Then there are the rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*), the one attacked by him (*ākrānta*), the ally of the rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāhāsāra*), and the king situated at the side who is neutral (*madhyama*); and finally, the one situated outside of all these is the indifferent king (*udāsīna*). Thus, there are twelve types of kings.

This has been stated by Kāmandaka: "One who is endowed with [good] constituents, possesses great energy, has exerted effort, and is habitually desirous of conquest, is known as a *vijigīṣu* (an aspirant for victory). An enemy, a friend, an enemy’s friend, and beyond that, a friend’s friend..."
Now, the enemy, the friend, and the ally are the ones who precede the seeker of victory (*vijigīṣu*).
After that comes the rear-enemy (*pārṣṇigrāha*), and immediately following him is the one attacked (*ākranda*).
Furthermore, there are two reinforcements (*āsāra*) for these [latter two], situated behind the seeker of victory.

"The middle king is situated between the conqueror (*vijigīṣu*) and the enemy (*ari*), bordering their territories; he is capable of supporting them when they are united and of subduing them when they are divided. In this context, Rāvaṇa is the *vijigīṣu* from Mālyavat’s perspective, while the group of gods beginning with Indra is the *ari*, and the host of asuras is the *mittra* (ally), and so forth. Thus, through the appropriate conceptualization of these roles such as the *vijigīṣu* and others, Rāma becomes the *bhūmyanantara* (the immediate neighbor).
Thus, the proximity has been established.
Now, he explains the existence of enmity with the words beginning "sānucara":

because of the calamities—the form of one being killed and the form of the other being cast into the ocean—caused by Subāhu and Mārīca, the sons of Sunda and Upasunda along with their followers, Rāma, who is the neighbor of the earth, [was approached] by those whose marriage-alliances were not yet fixed.
Because of the killing of Tāṭakā and the harassment by Subāhu and Mārīca, Rāma is a neighbor on earth;
the meaning is that he is indeed one with whom enmity has been established.
And so it has been said: "Of kingdom, wife, territory, country, kinsmen, and wealth..."
Starting from "theft, intoxication, and pride" up to "these are the sources of conflict," otherwise [the situation] must be countered;
the meaning is that it is difficult to turn back [the enemy] without the employment of secret punishment.
He states that very same irreversibility of enmity with the words beginning "Behold" (*paśya*). The injunction "behold" is intended to signify his state as a sage (*muni*).
As for the word "to be protected" (*pālyam*):

The world is to be protected—that is, it must be guarded—by that Rāma; this is the ellipsis. As for us, Rāvaṇa and the rest, we are the constant, forceful, and coercive rulers and governors of the world.
The meaning is "we shall become.
Amara states: "Prasabha, however, means forceful compulsion (balātkāra) or violence (haṭha).
The sense is that there is a contradiction between the protection of the world and such violent compulsion.
To this he says: "Sāma" (conciliation).

This being so—given that Rāma and we ourselves are both intent upon the happiness and suffering of the world—how can there be conciliatory, sweet speech directed toward Rāma by Rāvaṇa, the agent, who is always (śaśvat) of a contrary nature, possessed of perverted intellect, and a doer of what is unpleasant?
That is to say, of what kind [could such speech possibly be]?
The sense is that even for one who has done something disagreeable, a word that is itself disagreeable is simply impossible; thus, the very nature of *sāman* (conciliation) is difficult to achieve.
According to Amara, "Sāma means conciliation (*sāntva*), O Sage, and it is also [the number] five," and "Sāntva is exceedingly sweet.
By this, it is stated that the method of *sāman* is not a cause for retaliating against an enemy.
He says that very thing: "Therefore, even giving does not exist here.
Here, in the case of retaliation for enmity, it does not exist;
the word "as a cause" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

In this matter, even regarding Rāma— specifically that very Rāma who was chosen as husband by the gods— there is no means of division (*bhidā*) for us, nor any remedial strategy (*pratividhihetu*) available to us. Even through the recruitment of troops by means of wages, the separation of the army and its members by the lure of offering higher pay is not feasible.
The sense is that, because they are for their own sake and due to their natural inclination toward attachment, it is difficult to effect a division among them. ||3||

Only punishment (*daṇḍa*) remains, because deceit (*māyā*) and indifference (*upekṣā*) are included within that very category, and because trickery (*indrajāla*) is included within stratagem (*bheda*).
This is because the fourfold set of means alone is accepted, rather than accepting the sevenfold set of means.
As it was said by Kāmandaka: "Conciliation (*sāma*), bribery (*dāna*), sowing dissension (*bheda*), and punishment (*daṇḍa*)—this is the fourfold [set]."

This punishment is of two kinds: open punishment (*prakāśadaṇḍa*) and silent punishment (*tūṣṇīṃdaṇḍa*). Among these, open punishment consists of execution, imprisonment, and so forth, by means such as the mobilization of an army; silent punishment, however, consists of secret execution and the like.
This very [punishment] is designated by such terms as "disguised punishment" (*chadmadaṇḍa*) and so forth.
In that case, since an open punishment is not appropriate when [the enemy] is powerful,
he states— beginning with the words "even punishment"— that silent punishment (*tūṣṇīṃdaṇḍa*) alone is suitable.
"Abhyadhike" means "exceedingly superior.

Kārtavīrya was superior; Paraśurāma was superior even to him; and Rāma is superior even to him—this is the intended meaning of the term "abhyadhika. When the enemy is Rāma, the manifestation of punishment—such as the marching of an army or execution—is not praised, nor does it possess merit.
However, the meaning is that because it causes the destruction of the speaker’s own nature due to his weakness, it is indeed faulty.
[In the word *śaṃsaḥ*], the root *śaṃs* (in the sense of "praising") takes the suffix *yak* in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*), resulting in the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*).

Praise is the naming of qualities residing in a virtuous person; however, against an exceedingly powerful enemy, silence or punishment (*tūṣṇīṃdaṇḍa*) should be employed—that is, it is what ought to be done.
The word "tu" (but) indicates the distinction from the "rod of light" (*prakāśadaṇḍa*).
And that [distinction] consists in the absence of causing the destruction of the agent's own nature.
This [action], such as entering the body of Mantharā, is the commencement—that is, the intentional undertaking—of that "rod of silence" (*tūṣṇīṃdaṇḍa*) on your part.
The word "occurs" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
According to Amara, "the commencement (*upakrama*) is the undertaking (*ārambha*) after having understood [the situation].
Here, because of the statement regarding conciliation (*sāman*) which is useful for the matter at hand, the *saṃdhy-aṅga* (limb of the juncture) called "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) is stated.
Thus it has been said: "The gathering [of allies] through speech consisting of conciliation and gifts that is useful for the matter at hand is called a limb of peace (*sandhyaṅga*).
As it has been stated: "Gathering [of allies] through speech consisting of conciliation and gifts that is useful for the matter at hand. (4)

That being so, the sense is: in the event of exile to the forest and the like, what else could he do—what other thing would he be able to do—as a result of Sītā’s abduction? That is to say, apart from what is about to be mentioned, he would be unable to do anything else. The suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility (*śaki*).
[The compound] *hṛtajāniḥ* means "one whose wife has been carried away."
In this context, "Rāma" and so forth [are used].
Rāma [was] by his enemies (arātibhiḥ), that is, by his foes (śatrubhiḥ).
Amara states: "Abhighātī, para, arāti, pratyarthin, and paripanthin [are synonyms for enemy]."
If he were one whose reputation was stolen or whose wife was taken away, then Rāma would be filled with shame;
the meaning is that, being unfit to look anyone in the face, he would become incapable of performing tasks such as battle.
Alternatively, death—his passing away—would be his refuge, his protector; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The word "tasyāḥ" (of her) is also to be supplied [after "tasya"].
The sense is that because she cannot endure even a moment's separation from him—she who is dearer to her than her own life—she would die at that very instant.
According to Amara, "śaraṇam" means both a house and a protector.
Otherwise, however, even in the absence of death at that very moment, [it] becomes softened— that is, made soft.

This is derived from the root *mṛdu* with the suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "making it so" (*tatkaroti*), where the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *r*, followed by the past passive participle suffix *kta* in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*).
"He would die" means that, his strength being exhausted, he would die gradually. The phrase "otherwise, however" is to be supplied [from the previous context].
Otherwise, however, even in the absence of death occurring in due order, he would be devoid of majesty because his kingdom has already been lost;
for, as Amara states: "Sapratāpa and prabhāva are the splendor (tejas) born of the treasury and the army.
Being thus tormented and distressed, he might strive toward peace.
The root *ghaṭ* is used in the sense of "exertion" (*ceṣṭā*),
where exertion means movement toward what is beneficial or harmful.
Alternatively, this collection of indeclinables (*avyayasaṃghāta*)— namely *yadi vā*— functions in the sense of *yad vā* (or) and should be construed with all the alternative possibilities (*kalpa*).
Peace (*sandhi*) is defined as the state of unity characterized by the establishment of terms between one who desires victory and another;
it is the first among the six measures of policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*).
"Peace, war, marching, sitting encamped, double-dealing, and seeking refuge..."
"Six qualities," according to Amarasimha;
and those six qualities have been defined as follows:

for one desiring victory (*vijigīṣu*), the establishment of a state of unity is peace (*saṃdhi*); opposition is war (*vigraha*); the march of the victor-seeker against the enemy is marching (*yāna*); the remaining silent while waiting for the right time when the two [parties] have their powers mutually obstructed is sitting (*āsana*); the verbal surrender of oneself by the weak to the stronger of two enemies is double-dealing (*dvaidhībhāva*); and seeking refuge with a powerful ally when being oppressed by an enemy is seeking shelter (*samāśraya*).
The meaning is that one should employ oneself in such a state of alliance (*saṃdhi*).
In this regard, four modes of conduct toward an enemy are established by political science (*nīti*).
These are stated as: "destruction, defeat, oppression, and likewise emaciation."
In that context, "shameful" refers to defeat; "death" refers to annihilation; "dead" refers to affliction; and "tormented" refers to emaciation. ||5||
He states another alternative: "uttiṣṭheta" and so forth.

Here too, "Rāma" and so on [are implied]. The sense is that Rāma’s wrath (*manyu*) was already kindled by the humiliation consisting of the abduction of Sītā; it became inflamed by the affliction of the sages, and it reached a state of intense blazing (*pradīptatva*) through the abduction of Sītā herself. The distinction is that it was initially provoked by the oppression of Indra and others, inflamed by the oppression of the sages, and finally set ablaze by the abduction of Sītā.
"Wrath" (*manyu*) is the blazing of the mind caused by anger (*krodha*), such as an offense committed by an enemy; this wrath leads to our destruction.
The word "not" (*naḥ*) should be construed with both "destruction" (*vadha*) and "contempt" (*paribhava*) according to the maxim of the central gem (*madhyamaṇinyāya*).
"If he should rise" means if he should exert himself [to attack].
The *ātmanepada* ending is used according to the rule "udo'nūrdhvakarmaṇi. According to Amara, "utthāna" means "human effort" (*pauruṣa-tantra*) as well as "emergence" (*saṃniviṣṭa-udgama*).
"Udadhi" refers to the ocean; "its flow" (*prasara*) refers to the departure from this [place] by that Rāma.
According to Amarasimha, "syād āsāraḥ prasaraṇam" (the word *āsāra* is a synonym for *prasaraṇa*).
The words *prasaraṇa* and *prasara* are synonyms.
[The subject] is not able—meaning, it is incapable—to restrain or turn back.
In the word "īśaniyamane," there is the elision (luk) of the suffix śap.
For [hi] because that Rāma possesses the vigor of the sun— meaning his majesty is like that of the sun—
the verb "bhavati" (he is) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
"Vīrya refers to strength and power," according to Amarasimha.
Even if Rāma were to rise up, we still possess the ocean as a watery fortress (*jaladurga*).
As it has been said: "The [fortresses] are those of water, mountains, trees, deserts, and likewise of plains."
"This is praised by those of excellent intellect who contemplate the advantages of water-fortresses. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, others have declared that among these, there are seven great fortresses:
the mountain fortress (giridurga), the forest-named fortress (vanadurga), the water fortress (saliladurga), and the mud fortress (paṅkadurga).
"Namely, Ajariṇa, Devadurga, and that called Miśra—thus it is sevenfold. Even so, this was of no consequence to Rāma;
the sense is that, like the sun, he possesses the power to dry up the waters.
Having thus refuted the position regarding the ocean as a fortification intended by Śūrpaṇakhā, he states his own view with the words "But rather... (kiṃtu).

By Bhīmaujas, who had previously accepted Rāvaṇa’s friendship through his earlier adoption of the role of Rāvaṇa’s friend; by one endowed with a strength that was a cause of fear even to Rāvaṇa—according to the *Ratnamālā*, "ājāḥ" [is used] in the senses of sound-quality, knowledge, strength, pride, and manifestation;
and by Hari, the son of Indra (the Vajradhara), a monkey who was a source of terror even to Rāma.

The result is that [it will be said], "O Vālin, Rāma, the enemy, will slay [ghāniṣyate] [you]. From the root *han* in the sense of "killing," the periphrastic future (*lṛṭ*) is used in the passive voice; by the rule beginning with "syasic... (*Pāṇini 6.1.40*), there is the substitution for *ciṇ* (resulting in *ciṇvad-bhāva*), which causes the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) and the addition of the augment *iṭ*.
Because of the rule "aciṇṇaloḥ," there is an absence of the substitution of *t* for the suffix *ciṇ*, as well as the change to *kutva*.
Here, the word "hariṇā" (by the monkey) is used to dispel the doubt: "How can the son of Indra be an adversary to Rāma, who is on the side of Indra?
The intended meaning is that due to his nature as a monkey (*kāpeya*), it is possible for him to oppose the side of his father [Indra].
The maxim intended here is: "This too is his monkeyishness that he pays homage to the sun.
To ward off the doubt as to how such a weakling could act as an adversary to Rāma, the term *bhīmaujasā* ("of terrible vigor") is used.
To ward off the doubt as to what the cause for such an excess of strength might be, the term *ghoreṇa* ("by the terrible one") is used.

The "terribleness" (*ghoratva*) consists in the fact that even all those who have risen up [to oppose him] have their strength increased by the extraction of [his own] power; therefore, the underlying intention is that he might even extract the power of Rāma.

Now, one might ask: "Even so, why would he perform the task of Rāvaṇa? To ward off this doubt, it is said: "by virtue of having accepted the friendship of Rāvaṇa. The sense is that he will certainly carry out his friend's business, according to the saying: "One should completely sacrifice body, wealth, and knowledge for the sake of a friend."

Now, one might object: "Even so, how could Rāvaṇa kill Rāma once he has formed an alliance with Vālin? To ward off this doubt, the word "previously" (*prāk*) is used. The sense is that since Vālin had already been befriended by Rāvaṇa in the past, it was impossible for him to form an alliance with Rāma, who was his foremost enemy.
Therefore, the intention is that this position remains free from fault.

Thus, it has been stated that among the six measures of policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), the last mentioned—seeking refuge (*samāśraya*)—is appropriate to employ. For seeking refuge consists in resorting to a powerful ally when one is being oppressed by an enemy. Here, because it follows as a means to achieve the desired end, it is called "Suggestion" (*ākṣepa*), which is a constituent element (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) of the dramatic juncture.
As it has been said: "The pursuit of the means to a desired object is *ākṣepa* (suggestion). ||6||

Even though the fear regarding the opposing side has been thus removed, [the author] anticipates the objection that there may still be fear regarding Rāvaṇa’s own side and refutes it with the passage beginning with "by this occasion" and ending with "there is no indifference. "By this occasion": the term *prasaṅga* (occasion/context) refers to the state of being unfit for indifference, which arises when something has presented itself as a subject of consideration due to the introduction of the fear of the opposing side. For *prasaṅga* is precisely the state of being unfit for indifference once something has been brought to mind.
The multitude of meanings that will be explained at great length should be connected with and examined.
"Beloved of Rāvaṇa":
she is called "kāryajñā" because she knows what must be done.

The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*. "Heartache" (*hṛdayakheda*) is "reported" (*āvedyate*), meaning it is told (*kathyate*) in such a way as to be "without hesitation" (*niḥśaṅkam*), that is, free from the fear of being disclosed to others.
The word "to you" (*tubhyam*) is to be supplied as the object.
In this context, there are three kinds of friends: the artificial (*kṛtrima*), the innate (*sahaja*), and the natural (*prākṛta*).
Likewise, there are three kinds of enemies: the artificial, the innate, and the natural.
Among these, an artificial friend is one who has become so through actions characterized by mutual assistance.

A friend born of the same body is a natural friend (*sahajamitra*); this is established by its very nature and essence, consisting of such persons as a mother’s sister’s son or a father’s sister’s son.
A friend devoid of the artificiality mentioned previously is a natural friend (*prākṛtamitra*);
this consists of the king whose territory is immediately adjacent.

Thus, an enemy produced by the act of doing harm is an artificial (kṛtrima) enemy; one born from the same body, such as a paternal uncle or his son, is a natural (sahaja) enemy; and one whose territory is adjacent is a common (prākṛta) enemy.
In that regard, Rāma was not a natural enemy of Rāvaṇa because they were both Kṣatriyas; rather, he was a common enemy due to the adjacency of their territories.
Furthermore, he became an artificial enemy through acts such as doing him harm.

Vibhīṣaṇa, however, being a natural enemy of Rāvaṇa yet closely allied to Rāma on account of the latter’s virtues, might do harm to Rāvaṇa; thus he presents him as a source of fear, stating "due to proximity to the earth" (*kṣiterānantaryāt*) and so forth.

Because Rāma is a Kṣatriya, by virtue of his proximity to the earth—that is, due to the aforementioned fact of being adjacent to the land—he is "fixed by nature," meaning established by his own inherent character.
In other words, he is *prākṛta* (natural).
Furthermore, there is the one who has done harm and the one who is being harmed; that is, the harmer and the victim of harm.
"Artificial" (kṛtrima) means up to this point.
An enemy is of two kinds, meaning an enemy characterized by the two modes of being natural (prākṛta) and artificial (kṛtrima).
The word "of Rāvaṇa" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

Regarding the term "kṣatriya": because there is no inherent enmity [between them], the kṣatriya Rāma is naturally constrained by the earth; thus, the construction is that he becomes a foe in two ways—as one who has done harm and as one who is being harmed.
The natural enemy of the Lord of Night (the Moon) [is Mars];
"because of brotherhood" is the ellipsis.
My third grandson—that is, my third daughter's son—is [Mars].
The meaning is "Vibhīṣaṇa.

Due to proximity—by virtue of quality through his closeness to Rāma, and by virtue of place and inheritance through his closeness to Rāvaṇa—he, like a snake sharing a single dwelling with another serpent, generates fear in us, that is, he produces apprehension of future misfortune.
Thus, the sense is that there exists a danger arising from our own side.

By the word *ahiriva* ("like a snake"), it is implied that the term *ahibhaya* (fear of a snake) is conventionally established to denote fear arising from one's own side, based on the etymology "fear as of a snake.
Amara also states: "The fear of kings (*mahībhujām*) arising from their own side is called *ahibhayam*.
Here, because of the mention of apprehension and terror, the dramatic juncture (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) named *saṃbhrama* (agitation) is indicated.
As it has been said: "Doubt, fear, and agitation constitute bewilderment. (7)

One might ask: "Why is Kumbhakarṇa not suspected? Why would fear of him not be averted by Vibhīṣaṇa? To this he replies with the verse beginning, "But Kumbhakarṇa... The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: because of his addiction to artificial sleep, because of the suffering of perpetual slumber brought about by the action of the Brahma-blessing, because of his lack of discipline, and because even when slightly awake he indulges in excessive eating and so forth due to being intoxicated with pride—he is like one who does not exist, despite being present. He explains why Vibhīṣaṇa is a cause for fear with the passage beginning, "But Vibhīṣaṇa... and so on.
As for Vibhīṣaṇa: the word "tu" (but/however) indicates his distinction from Kumbhakarṇa.
Those who are capable of approaching [the Lord] are called "ābhigāmikāḥ."
The suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "it prevails over battle and so forth. The meaning is that [these qualities] are the causes for being approached by ministers and others.
Because he is endowed with—and thus possessed of—such personal qualities, [one should approach] this aforementioned Vibhīṣaṇa.
In the case of subsequent reference (anvādeśa), the word *idam* takes the substitute *enad*.
The ministers are devoted to their original nature;
that is to say, they are loyal.

The word *evam* [is used] because the term *anu* receives the designation of *karmapravacanīya* by the rule *lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyāna...*. Consequently, the second case (*dvitīyā*) is applied by the rule *karmapravacanīyayukte dvitīyā*.

Furthermore, the group of qualities conducive to winning over [a person] (*ābhigāmikaguṇavarga*) is shown in the *Kāmandakīya*: "Good character, being a companion, courtesy, and promptness of action..."
Reliability, truthfulness, service to elders, gratitude, being endowed with good fortune, intelligence, having a retinue that is not mean-spirited,
having conquerable neighbors, and likewise firm devotion.

"Far-sightedness, enthusiasm, purity, magnanimity, humility, and righteousness—these are the qualities that cause a virtuous person to be sought after. One who is endowed with these qualities is clearly approached by others. Thus it is said.

"The minister, the kingdom, the fort, the treasury, and the army as the fifth—these are declared by those who know [the science] to be the constituent elements (*prakṛti*) of one seeking victory. Thus, the constituent elements are also shown in that very same [work]. As for "Kharadūṣaṇa and the others," etc.:
Those whose livelihood and subsistence are provided by the Saṅgha are so described;
that is to say, they are individually devoid of intellectual capacity.
They attend upon and serve the king, their master.

The verb *tiṣṭhati* takes the ātmanepada ending according to the rule "vā lipsāyām" (Pāṇini 1.3.65). For this reason—that is, because of that [fact]—by that community; the ellipsis is "as a cow by a calf."
They milk the king of his wealth.
The verb *duh* (to milk) takes two objects.
The meaning is that, having shown the assembly [of subjects] to the king as one shows a calf to a cow, they accomplish their purposes from the king just as one obtains milk from a cow.

The sense is that for those seeking their own interests, no restriction regarding their master is intended. Alternatively, it means that they obtain their own purposes from the king— who, fearing that they might at some point become independent by relying upon this natural enemy (Vibhīṣaṇa) as if he were a child, and so forth as previously described.
To the objection that, "in that case, let the subjects be alienated from Vibhīṣaṇa through another means," he replies with the words "upajāpitāḥ" (having been instigated).
The meaning is: once the subjects—the ministers and others—have been instigated, they in turn instigate [others];
that is, they should cause those very persons who would create dissension to be alienated by aligning themselves with Vibhīṣaṇa.
"Separation and instigation of discord" (*bhedopajāpau*)—thus says Amara.

The sense is that the subjects, who perceive the virtues of Vibhīṣaṇa, would cause even those capable of creating division to break apart by reflecting upon the faults of Rāvaṇa. "One who has not gained wealth is greedy; one who is proud is also [resentful] when insulted."
"One who is angry should be provoked, and one who is fearless should be terrified;
by means of desired objects, one should cause these four types [of enemies] to be divided. This is the method of sowing dissension as described.

In this regard, because Vibhīṣaṇa is endowed with the quality of being "generous" (sthūlalakṣya)—a trait conducive to seeking refuge—it is not possible here for anyone to remain without receiving a reward.
Because his retinue is not insignificant, no one in his retinue can be greedy; because he is disciplined, no one has ever been treated with contempt by him;
and because he is endowed with courtesy, no one has ever been provoked to anger by him.
Furthermore, because he is righteous, not even a single member of his retinue is afraid of him; thus, it is difficult to instigate a rebellion against him.
However, the underlying intention is that a counter-rebellion by those on his side is what is likely.
This is what [the author] means by "this very thing."

Therefore, for that reason, the royal household—the palace of Rāvaṇa—already shattered within by internal discord and mutual dissension among its own kinsmen, will break apart of its own accord as soon as it is attacked by Rāma; that is, as soon as he has marched forth for battle. The meaning is not that it was sowed with dissension, but that it will become divided spontaneously.
This is a construction with the agent as the subject (*karmakartari prayogaḥ*).
The intended meaning is that it would be stated [in the treatise] as "due to the distinctness preceded by clearly manifest disagreement.
Regarding this point, he cites the consensus of the *nītiśāstra* (treatises on statecraft) with the words "as it has been said," and so forth.

"Even a slight [laghu]—that is, even a very small—occasion for calamity (vyasanapada), a point of downfall (bhraṃśasthāna), or a locus of faults arising from desire and anger. According to Amara: *vyasana* means misfortune, downfall, or a fault born of passion or wrath.
By the term "locus of calamity" (vyasanasthāna), an internal distinction is intended.
"Of one who is attacked" means by an assailant;
this refers to the connection between the preceding and following [terms].
"The calamity of one who is attacked" means that for one who is attacked, it becomes difficult to overcome and must be remedied with great hardship.

"‘Sādhana’ is used in the senses of following and going, the penis, accomplishment, cessation, causing to obtain, the funeral rites for the dead, cause, wealth, injury, hellish torments, and a component of an army"— so says the *Ratnamālā*.
Here, the root *sādh* also functions in the sense of cessation (*nirvṛti*).

In this context, since there is a division, the word *avagraha*—which signifies a separation or a hiatus (*padaccheda*)—here refers merely to the state of being separated, namely the separation from Vibhīṣaṇa.
"Remedy" (*pratividhāna*) means a counter-measure (*pratīkāra*).
In that regard, it is not at all appropriate for the elder brother to employ conciliation (*sāma*) toward the younger one.
Nor can it be a gift, because of its composite nature;
furthermore, it has already been stated previously that division is not possible—this is the intended meaning when he says, "But that is the staff of light.
The masculine gender is used due to the predominance of the predicate.

That [refers to] the counter-measure; this is the meaning. Alternatively, the masculine gender of the word *saḥ* (that) is used with the intention of referring to the term *pratividhāna* (counter-measure).

According to the statement of the grammarians, "Pronouns bring about the identity between the subject and the predicate and assume their respective genders according to usage," there is a masculine gender even though [the word] is connected with *saṃrodhana* (imprisonment).
*Apasāraṇa* means expulsion from the city.

Among those four—[imprisonment, fine,] public punishment (*prakāśadaṇḍa*), and so forth—in the case of public punishment (*prakāśaṃ prakāśadaṇḍam*), how could they endure it or tolerate it, being bound by an inseparable relationship, that is, a relationship such as common ownership?
In the phrase "tijeḥ kṣamāyām," the suffix *san* is applied.

Even silent punishment (*tūṣṇīṃdaṇḍa*), when inferred by the wise who are skilled in reasoning and refutation and known through its indicative mark (*liṅga*), becomes a cause for the provocation of the subjects—namely, the ministers and others—and thus a cause for the inflaming of their minds.

Because of the usage in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Sūtra* "tatparayojakaḥ," and because the prohibition of a compound in the rule "tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari" is not absolute (*anityatva*), the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) "prakṛtikopakaḥ" (provoking the subjects) is grammatically valid.
Alternatively, it is a compound with a genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*).
When Rāma is the aggressor and has marched forth with his army, [the situation] would be "duranta"—that is, beyond remedy.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *anta* is not feminine; it means certainty, destruction, the front, proximity, or the interior."
Here, by the mention of the "inference of signs" (*liṅgādyūhana*), the dramatic element (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) called inference (*anumāna*) is stated.
As it has been said: "Inference is the deduction of signs.
[This occurs] in the context of "obstruction" (*saṃrodhana*).

When restraint has been established, they would undergo this transformation due to the cause of being overwhelmed; this connects with the statement "they would transform. The reason for this is "due to the unity of purpose" (*padaikamatyāt*).
Because they share an identical mindset with Vibhīṣaṇa, Khara and the others would also transform—that is, they would undergo a change in form such as anger and so forth.
The sense is that, therefore, that [position] is not tenable.

Consequently, since the harsh sounds (*khara*) and so forth are obstacles to the fourfold set beginning with *prakāśa* and *daṇḍa*, he states "therefore" (*tasmāt*) that they must be considered first;
that is, they must be considered right at the outset (*pura eva*).
The meaning is that they are to be suspected as being grounds for fear. ||8||
In this context, the utility of Rāma regarding Khara and the others is as follows—the remainder being that he shall become the cause for accomplishing the task we intend to perform.

Since Khara and the others have been slain by Rāma through some ill-spoken word, Vibhīṣaṇa’s departure and so forth are highly suspicious; therefore, it was our first plan that Khara and his followers should be caused to be killed by Rāma through strategic means. This is the sense: that Rāma is useful for our intended purpose.
In this context, the *saṃdhy-aṅga* (element of the juncture) called *atibala* (excessive force) is mentioned, consisting of the deception of a beloved person, such as Kharas and others.
As it has been stated: "The deception of a beloved person is *atibala*.
This refers to the state of being a subordinate (*anujīvita*) by virtue of being a minister, whose livelihood depends upon Rāvaṇa.
It is heavy indeed;
or rather, it is contemptible heaviness—
the suffix *kan* being applied in the sense of "contemptible."
It is contemptible because it causes inequality among kinsmen.
The state of being heavy is "heaviness" (gurukatā).
Oh!
The meaning is "wonderful.
The mutual relationship is equal;
the word "by you" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The meaning is: "given that the relationship with the maternal grandfather, the daughter's son, and so forth is equal.
Thus, the maternal grandfather contemplates the killing of the donkey and others by means of a stratagem;
the meaning is: "you are contemplating [this]."
The conduct and practice of sons of noble family, born of a virtuous lineage—even those who are extremely young—is indeed like this;
that is to say, they are renowned as being solely intent upon the service of their master.
[This applies] except for those headed by Khara.
The meaning is: in their absence, what resolution could Vibhīṣaṇa possibly take?

Indeed, that wise Vibhīṣaṇa—who is skilled in discerning the pros and cons—having himself observed the change [in the situation] and inferred my hostile intent, would surely depart from the city (this is the ellipsis).
But he is to be disregarded by us;
the word "but" (tu) indicates an alternative position.
Or rather, he is to be disregarded by us.
The meaning is that he is neither to be favored nor to be suppressed.

Furthermore, one must not think that there is danger from a biological son; rather, it must indeed be considered that even though Vibhīṣaṇa is a biological son and a kinsman, his fear—should he retreat while observing our own transformations—is of no consequence for one who is alone. This is the intended sense.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "Since" (*yataḥ*).
"From childhood" (*bālyāt*):

This Vibhīṣaṇa, from his very childhood—that is, beginning from infancy—possessed a firmly established friendship and deep-rooted affection with Bālin; and [he dwelt] on a portion of land, a specific area of the earth, which had been graciously bestowed as a gift of favor by Bālin.
*Kumārabhukti* means "that which is enjoyed by princes" (*kumāraiḥ bhujyate*).
The suffix *ktin* is applied to the root *bhuj* in the sense of the object (*karman*).

That which is called *kumārabhukti* is the maintenance (*vṛtti*) assigned to princes by kings. Because Sugrīva was the younger brother of Vālin, according to the maxim "an elder brother is equal to a father," Sugrīva held the status of a prince (*kumāra*) in relation to him; thus, the portion of land granted to him is designated as *kumārabhukti*.
The heart [of the matter] is this: Vālin’s running away was merely a pretext; it was through his very favor that he permitted Sugrīva to go to Ṛṣyamūka.
One should take refuge with Sugrīva, who is staying on Ṛṣyamūka.
The suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).
The word *dhruvam* is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).
Since the enmity with the elder brother was common to both of them, the meaning is that Sugrīva’s seeking refuge was a probable course of action. ||9||
He says that even so, there is no harm for us: "Staying there, he will be slain by Vālin.
The vowel lengthening occurs due to the *ciṇvadbhāva* rule.
To the objection that Vālin might overlook this weak one just as he did Sugrīva, he replies: "By Rāma."
Rāma, having had his wife abducted, might at some point arrive there alone out of friendship; then Sugrīva might take refuge with him, or Vibhīṣaṇa might seek refuge directly.

Consequently, by entering into an alliance with the powerful Rāma, Vālī should slay Vibhīṣaṇa along with Sugrīva even beforehand—because Vibhīṣaṇa is an enemy of his own friend Rāvaṇa, because he is a friend of his own enemy Sugrīva, and because he is a friend of Rāma, who is the enemy of his own friend Rāvaṇa. This is the underlying sense. He should not neglect [Vibhīṣaṇa] on account of taking refuge with Rāma—that is, by directly seeking refuge with Rāma, or by being in close proximity to Rāma through the mediation of Sugrīva.
"He ought not to be neglected"—
this is the ellipsis for "him.
Thus, Mālyavat, having anticipated the danger arising from his own side, has refuted it.
In this regard, Śūrpaṇakhā suspects otherwise, introducing an alternative view with the word "atha" (now).
"Vyāpādayati" means "he kills. According to Amara, "vyāpāda" is defined as "the thought of malice."
The root list (dhātupāṭha) states: "druha in the sense of wishing to harm.
By the phrase "like Paraśurāma," the seed of doubt is introduced:
Rāma will conquer Vālin.
The reason for this is that Paraśurāma is superior to Vālī because he was victorious over Jiṣṇu (Arjuna).
Similarly, the underlying intention is that Paraśurāma is superior to Vālī because he was the conqueror of Rāvaṇa, whereas Vālī was merely the conqueror of Kārtavīrya, who was equal to him.

The term "Rāghava" is used with the intention that Rāma—the scion of the Raghu dynasty, renowned for his vow to protect those who seek refuge—will slay Vālī in consideration of Vibhīṣaṇa and Sugrīva, who have both come to him for protection.
Here too, that which is called *anumāna* (inference) is stated as a constituent of the juncture (*saṃdhy-aṅga*).
"He" refers to: he who slays Vālī, by him we have been slain.
The word "we" (*bhavāmaḥ*) is to be supplied as the subject.
The term "certainly" (*dhruvam*) expresses a possibility.
Here, by the general statement "he who kills [is killed by him]," the intended inference is: "Rāma will kill us, Rāvaṇa and the others, because he is the conqueror of Rāvaṇa and the slayer of Vāli."

By that Rāma, when there is the destruction of all—that is, the slaughter of all [enemies] beginning with Rāvaṇa—the compound *sarvanāśe* is formed with the genitive of residue (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), because the rule "and in the case of the object" (*karmaṇi ca*) prohibits such a compound when both [agent and object] are present. May that single thread of the lineage—the subtle portion remaining of one who has perished—be adorned; may he live, may he remain endowed with life.
The *liṅ* [optative] is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).
May Rāma—who consists of dharma, that is, who abounds in dharma—grant sovereignty (*śrī*) over Laṅkā to this Vibhīṣaṇa.
The *loṭ* [imperative] is also used in the sense of a benediction.
Here, by the proclamation of the true meaning (*tattvārtha*), the juncture-element (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) called "the path" (*mārga*) is described.
As it has been said: "The path is the proclamation of the true meaning. (10)
Let it be so for now.
The word "api" (even/also) indicates the defect of being a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*).
The meaning is that while the death of Rāvaṇa is the primary course (*mukhyakalpa*), even in its absence, the death of Vibhīṣaṇa is to be wished for as a secondary alternative.
"Where you have been sent"— the word "to Mithilā" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"Easily accomplished" means this purpose, such as the entry into Mantharā's body and so forth, can be performed with ease.
"If Janaka... and so forth.

The connection is that [the matter] would be easy to accomplish if those two were not present. By this, it is indicated that among the four—Janaka and the others—who enter in the subsequent act (*uttarāṅka*), Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra will depart.
In this case, it should be understood that the *aṅka* (act) has concluded.
"Alas, mother!"—
the sorrow is to be observed.
The meaning is that [the world] will soon exist with Vibhīṣaṇa alone remaining.
"Alas, my children!"—
O children, Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and the others!
The word "you" (*yūyam*) is to be supplied [as the subject].
For me (*me*), who am full of sin—the cause of which is proficiency in crooked policies that instigate the killing of kinsmen—the genitive case is used according to the rule:
*kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā* ("the genitive is optionally used for the agent of verbal nouns ending in kṛt suffixes").
"Vadhyā" means "you are to be killed"; this is the second person plural form of the verb *as* (to be). "Hā" expresses suffering.
"Alas! In the pits of despair and grief"—thus says Amara.
Child Vibhīṣaṇa, you too, because of my own sinful deed—the deed of Rāvaṇa—from the place where I stand;
for the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *sthiti* denotes both place and limit."
"It must be abandoned"— the word "you" is to be supplied. The repetition of "hā hā" expresses an excess of despair.
"Vatsala" means affectionate toward me.

Regarding the word *vatsa*, in the context of grammatical derivation (*vṛtti*), the suffix *lac* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) to the word *vatsa*, which denotes affection, according to the rule: "After *vatsa* and *aṃsa*, [the suffix *lac* is applied] in the senses of desire and strength. Thus, *vatsa*.
The word *vatsa* (child) is used because he is a daughter’s son (*dauhitra*).
That was a great crisis, a crowded mass of suffering;
as Amara states: "The masculine *saṃkaṭa* means a crowded or confined space."
I see through the lens of logic and I conclude:
O child, daughter of my elder brother! Kekasī is the name of Rāvaṇa’s mother.
"You are destroyed!
The meaning is that there is a well-known proverb: "There is nothing greater than the birth or the loss of a son for happiness or sorrow.
Alas! You shall suffer grief before long—very soon—for your three sons: Khara, Kumbhakarṇa, and Rāvaṇa.
Khara is the son of Kekasī’s sister;
the suffix *kan* is used here in the sense of compassion (*anukampā*).
You shall see him.
The sense is that because those killed by Rāma go to your presence after death. ||11||
The mixed *viṣkambha*:
a *viṣkambha* consisting of both Sanskrit and Prakrit.
Now the act (*aṅka*) is introduced with the words "Then enter," and so forth.
The two kings, Janaka and Daśaratha; having embraced, that is, having clasped [them];
"by good fortune" (diṣṭyā) expresses joy.
You are prospering; you are becoming more fortunate.
Your good fortune arises from both your son and your son-in-law.
Such is your dear child—he who is the subduer even of Paraśurāma.
Because the son-in-law is almost like a son, there is affection toward him;
for the son-in-law, being a disciple of his father-in-law, occupies the position of a son.
Thus Dakṣa said in the *Bhāgavata*: "He has attained the status of my disciple, since he accepted the hand of my daughter."
"Like Sāvitrī, he [took her] by the hand before the fire in the presence of the Brahmins, acting like a virtuous man.
Regarding the phrase "extraordinary" (*aprākṛtāni*):

they are extraordinary, divine, continuous—that is, dense—with qualities such as knowledge, heroism, modesty, and beauty; they are supermundane, most highly esteemed, and productive of great results (*mahodayāni*), meaning they generate great fruits. It was said "of him" because of his current absence.

It is not that these wondrous deeds, which are the very form of their conduct, constitute auspicious blessings for us alone—namely, for the two of us—but rather that they are auspicious blessings for the entire world as well.
For auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is the accomplishment of desired goals that are beyond reproach. (12)
"By us" (asmābhiḥ) means "by the two of us" (āvābhyām).
The lineage of Rāma’s greatness—the connection with the excellence of majesty, opulence, and qualities—is not something to be merely wished for.
Why is this so? To this he says: "That" (yad).

By that Rāma, we have been made successful (*kṛtinaḥ*), meaning we have been rendered fulfilled; by his own relationship, characterized by his status as our Guru, we have been made partakers of the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*); and the worlds (*bhuvanāni*) have also been made fulfilled.
The word "kṛtinaḥ" (the wise) and so forth, which is connected [to the previous verse], undergoes a change of gender.

The meaning is: since our own prosperity depends upon Him, we should not pray for His prosperity; likewise, because the prosperity of others also depends upon Him, it is impossible for them to be the cause of His prosperity. ||13||

This is the majesty of Rāma; his majesty is preeminent and transcendent. It is so described because its material cause (*upādāna*) is the ripening of merit—the state of merit being ready to yield its fruit.
The word "becomes" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
As it is said, "He is the most meritorious even among merits," Rāma himself is essentially composed of supreme merit.
Therefore, the sense is that this majesty of Rāma is not dependent on anything else.
Regarding such a preeminent excellence, culminating in the victory over Paraśurāma—who are we? The meaning is that we are incapable of accomplishing it even through our prayers.
"Do not say so! It is not fitting for us to speak thus—'Who are we?'—this is the meaning.
[They are] the Ādityas."

The construction is as follows: "That you, the treasure-house of auspiciousness, have become gracious toward us; that you have bestowed favor upon us—this alone is the ripening [of our merit]. The term *ādityāḥ* refers to those of the Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśya).

According to the rule *dityadityāditya-* and so forth, the suffix *ṇya* is applied to the word *āditya* in the sense of offspring (*apatya*), resulting in *āditya*; then, by the rule *halo yamāṃ yami*, the letter *y* is elided.

Kings such as Dilīpa and others who preceded me worshipped with devotion—that is, they honored through the knowledge that he was to be propitiated—the sage Vasiṣṭha, the husband of Arundhatī, who is a mass of splendor, a treasure-house of majesty, and whose word is truth; who is like a family deity (kuladevatā) or like Śrī Raṅganātha; and who is the foremost of sages according to the maxim: "A word [denoting a quality] applies without distinction to the primary [subject], but especially to others. He is the husband of Arundhatī, of whom it is said: "She is a treasure-house of pure luster."
In this context, the Vedic scripture is recalled: "He whose devotion to the Lord is supreme, and who regards the Guru as he does the Lord.

Thus, even those blessings belonging to those of abundant austerity—those whose asceticism is vast and whose instructions are unfailing—find their fulfillment in him; "he becomes," is the ellipsis to be supplied. "Tāta" (O dear one) is a term of endearment.
Because the thing to be enjoined is primary, the word expressing the subject (the thing to be designated) takes the masculine gender in the form "this" (ayam). ||14||
"Such as this" means endowed with the majesty described by Daśaratha.
Regarding the phrase "yadvācām" and so forth: that greatness which belongs to speech and mind—that is, to words and to the intellect.
"Or (*vā*) [is used] in the sense of alternative (*vikalpa*), comparison (*upamā*), the meaning of *iva*, and also in conjunction (*samuccaya*)," says Amara.
"Region" (*viṣaya*) means a country (*deśa*);
"region and country" (*deśaviṣayau*), so says Amara.
"Having passed beyond," that is, having transcended. The suffix *ktvā* is used here according to the rule "and [it is used] in connection with 'the higher' (*para*) and 'the lower' (*avara*).
[This applies] when there is a compound preceded by the negative particle *nañ*.

The substitution of *lyap* occurs by the rule "ṛ-ktvo-lyap. The meaning is "beyond the reach of speech and mind. "That greatness" refers to the excellence that transcends all, surpassing everything in its preeminence.
The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied after the root *śī* preceded by *ati* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
The lengthening of the vowel occurs due to the irregular form (*nipātana*) "atiśāyana" in the rule *atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau*.
[The word *atiśayāt* means] from excellence by way of synonym.
According to Amarasimha, "paryāya" means "occasion" (avasara) or "sequence" (krama).
By the word *paryāya*, which denotes sequence, what is intended here is the excellence (*atiśaya*) expressed by another word signifying superiority.
Thus, the meaning is: "due to a pre-eminence that exceeds all limits" (*viśvāvadhika-prakarṣa*).

"Supreme" (param) means "excellent" (atiśayitam). The sense is that it is endowed with excellence exceeding all limits; that is, it possesses an excellence that surpasses whatever excellence exists beyond the limit of the entire universe.
By the passage beginning with "That which [is beyond] words," the superiority of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has been stated.

In that context, since speech and mind are by nature limited and have restricted objects, one might suspect that even after the removal of the limitation [imposed by them], the object of knowledge (*prameya*) itself might possess an inherent limitation.

Therefore, in order to demonstrate that there is no limitation even due to the nature of the object of knowledge, the sequence of synonyms such as "beyond" (*param*) and so forth is employed; furthermore, the successive mention of further limits is intended to convey that this excellence is absolutely and infinitely limitless.
By those splendors, meaning by those powers;
for Amara states: "Tejas refers to power and radiance.
Samiddham means thoroughly ignited.

From the root *indhī* in the sense of "to shine," the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule beginning with "roots meaning motion" (*gatyartha-*), and there is the elision of the letter *n*.
It is "immeasurable," meaning incapable of being delimited.
Here, because of the synonymy, there is an expression of the connection [of the word] with "beyond" (*param*).
"Immeasurable" is an expression of exclusion (vyatireka);
therefore, there is no tautology.
And by this, the notion that greatness is merely common is set aside; it is difficult to approach because of its extraordinary majesty.
O Brahmin-sage, even though we ourselves are unable to approach him, greatness—the excellence—shines and blazes in Viśvāmitra, who has attained the status of a great seer through his own asceticism.
(The root *jval* means "to shine" or "to blaze. ||15||
This [offering] belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa; thus it is *maitrāvaruṇa*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of a general relationship according to the rule *tasyedam* ("this belongs to that").
This is the awakening of Vasiṣṭha.
Regarding "Sanatkumāra":

although Sanatkumāra and Aṅgiras were his own elder brothers, the venerable teacher Sanatkumāra was the instructor of knowledge—specifically the knowledge of the supreme self (adhyātmavidyā)—to Aṅgiras through his asceticism, which consisted of the discipline of emaciating the body, and through his steadfast devotion to the contemplation of Brahman.
The sense is that you are one who is devoted to the cultivation of karma and a teacher of austerities, O descendant of Aṅgiras.
The word "you" (*tvam*) is to be supplied as the subject.
If you praise me in such a manner—that is, if you describe me as possessing virtues—then I am indeed worthy of praise; I am truly possessed of the qualities that justify being so described.

For indeed, because those words of yours are true, unfailing, appropriate to the actual state of their respective objects, pure, stainless, and free from inaccuracy regarding the portions they cognize—
the compound being like "lame-and-humpbacked" (*khañja-kubja*)—
[they] exist; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Praise, indeed, consists in the naming of qualities residing in one who possesses them.

Although such praise is not applicable to me, who am devoid of qualities, nevertheless—because your eloquent speech as a panegyrist is unfailing—it results precisely from this in my being endowed with greatness, just as I possess the status of a Brahman-sage; thus, the status of being worthy of praise is logically established.

Furthermore, in this context, just as Devahūtī and the Pracetasas [addressed] their own sons, Kapila and others, it is likewise appropriate that Sanatkumāra and Aṅgiras address Vasiṣṭha, their own younger brother, as their disciple.
This should be investigated in the Purāṇas.
For this very reason, the statement "and age is not a superior birth for those who are eminent" must be established as referring to other subjects. ||16||

The greatness of Rāmabhadra is not caused by me, for his greatness is established this very moment through your own words; rather, it is caused by his relationship with his father, Daśaratha. Thus he says: "But in the case of Rāmabhadra...
This greatness is neither a marvel nor something unprecedented.
For according to the rule *āścaryamanitye*, the word *āścarya* (marvel) is prescribed for a thing that is not permanent or previously known.
For since Daśaratha is his progenitor and father— the word "is" being understood—
therefore, by the power of his father, this majesty of Rāma is not unprecedented; such is the meaning.
"Directly" (*sākṣāt*):
they are worthy of being conceived as "as if they were actual accumulations of merit," meaning they have become manifest as heaps of well-performed deeds.
The word "as if" (*iva*) is used here in the sense of a conceit.

As it has been said: "When this initial element [of comparison] fails to be established through common worldly usage, then there is indeed *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), wherein the word *iva* is intent upon possibility.

Since the accumulations of merit belonging to the objects of comparison, though well-known in their essential nature (*svarūpa*) in the world, are not established in the world by virtue of having attained perceptibility [in the subject], the figure of speech is *utprekṣā*.

"Some rhetoricians have stated: 'Poetic fancy (utprekṣā) consists in the imagination of identity with the agent of an action. Here, there is this poetic fancy of identity with merit in those who perform meritorious deeds.
[The phrase] 'by what is desired by you' means 'by that which is pleasing to you.'"

In the reading "avekṣitena," the meaning is "by you having been seen. By "vidhinā" (by rule), it means by the procedure prescribed in the scriptures; [they are] "gopāyitāraḥ" (protectors) of the subjects, that is, people who have the habit of protecting the subjects.
The suffix *tṛn* is applied in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*) to the root *gup* (meaning "to protect") according to the rule *gupū rakṣaṇe*.
For this very reason, because the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* applies, the word *prajāḥ* takes the accusative case as the object.
They are described as such because their conduct and practices—which purify the world through mere remembrance and so forth—are themselves purifying.

"In the first, in the ancient [times]. Because the word *prathama* is designated as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) by the rule "prathamacarama-" and so forth, it takes the form *śī* for the nominative plural suffix *jas*; thus, this is the nominative plural.
The kings who were born—meaning they existed—in the lineage or dynasty of Vaivasvata, the son of Vivasvat, namely Manu; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The bearer of their burden—that is, the one who carries their external load—or the best among them, a hero, a bull among Kṣatriyas;
the meaning is "the most excellent of Kṣatriyas. As it is said: "In compound words, [terms such as] *vyāghra*, *puṃgava*, *ṛṣabha*, and *kuñjara* [are used to denote excellence]."
"Siṃha, śārdūla, nāga, and so forth, [are used] in the masculine to denote the meaning of 'excellent,'" according to Amarasimha.
This Daśaratha is the praiseworthy lord of the earth, a treasury—an inexhaustible repository—of virtues that are the cause of Rāma’s greatness.
"He is," is the ellipsis to be supplied. ||17||
"Ariṣṭa" refers to the well-known Maghavan Indra; the word *maghavan* is derived as an irregular formation (*nipātita*) by the rule beginning with "śvan-ukṣan-" and so forth.

Although he was the subduer of Jambha—that is, the slayer of the demon Jambha—and although he remained unharmed (*ariṣṭa*)—meaning free from misfortune—even during the act of killing the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, the divine architect (as Amara states:
*riṣṭam* refers to the absence of security or the presence of misfortune);
and although he is the Lord of All (*viśveṣām īśaḥ*), that is, the sovereign of the three worlds; [and] of the Maruts, that is, the gods or the seven classes of Maruts.
"Marutau pavanāmarau"—thus says Amara. *Nikāyasya* means of a collection or multitude;
"syānnikāyaḥ puñjarāśī"—thus says Amara.
Even though he is the husband,
this [word "pati"] also applies to both [the army and the demons] by way of the "central gem" (madhyamaṇi) maxim.
[He is] the leader of the army— one whose habit is training the army in maneuvers such as battle arrays— and the slayer of the asuras— one whose habit is the destruction of the asuras.
The word "satatam" (constantly) connects with both [the verb and the noun].
Due to its connection with a word ending in the suffix *tṛn*, the second case is used after the words "senā" and "asura.
He chose this hero, Daśaratha, in many battles (*samanīkeṣu*).

From the root *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing," the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is formed in the active voice; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule beginning with *svaritajitaḥ*. The word "as an assistant" (*sahāyatvena*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. ||18||
Regarding the word "sa" (he):
how could such a Daśaratha, who is worthy of being chosen by Indra, beget—that is, give birth to—such a Rāma, one who is dissimilar and unlike [himself]?
This word "īdṛśa" (such) refers to Rāma, the conqueror of Paraśurāma.
The sense is that, according to the maxim "a son is a hundred times his father," this Daśaratha begot a son who was a hundred times greater than himself, who was like Mahendra.
How can there be any wonder in this?
That is to say, how indeed could there be anything marvelous regarding Rāma?
The sense is that this is not unprecedented, as it is only logical for [the son] to be a hundred times superior to such a father.

Since this is so, he concludes with the words beginning "marutvantam" that everything has been conquered by him: "He who, in this world, [conquered] the ten-faced one"—that is, the Lord (Bhagavant), who is possessed of greatness or an excellence of valor.
"Regarding the word *bhaga*: 'It [denotes] fortune (*śrī*), desire, majesty, heroism, effort, the sun, and fame,' so says Amara.
*Devam* means either one who desires victory or one who is radiant; *marutvantam* refers to Indra. 'Indra is *marutvān*, *maghavān*,' so says Amara."
"Vijayate" means "he overcomes. [From the root] *ji* in the sense of "overcoming"; overcoming (*abhibhava*) means making inferior.
The *ātmanepada* ending is used according to the rule "viparābhyām-".
The present tense (*laṭ*) is employed because the subjugation of Indra by Rāvaṇa is still occurring even now.
That ten-faced one—[the king] Kārtavīrya Arjuna, the lord, master, and sovereign of the Haihayas, that is, the kings of the Haihaya country—in battle, in combat.
According to Amara, *samit* means "battle" and *ājisamit* means "armed for battle.
He conquered (*vijigye*), that is, he overcame;
the substitution of *k* [for *j*] occurs by the rule *sanliṭorjeḥ*.
The use of the *liṭ* (perfect tense) suffix occurs because Kārtavīrya is in the past.
[He refers to] the slayer of that Kārtavīrya, whose greatness was celebrated, and whose majesty was renowned for destroying all the Kṣatriyas twenty-one times.
"Tribhuvana" is the collective term for the three worlds.
Due to its inclusion in the *pātrādi* group, there is an absence of feminine gender.
[The word] "in that" (*tasmin*) is in the locative case used for specification (*nirdhāraṇa*).

"Mahāvīra" means one who, despite being within the three worlds, is endowed with a preeminent heroism that transcends the three worlds; alternatively, the locative case is used in the sense of location, and the construction is "one whose greatness is celebrated throughout the three worlds."
The meaning is "Paraśurāma.
The word "having conquered" is used, with "standing" understood as the ellipsis.
"By your child"—
meaning by Rāma— "what indeed has not come to pass?"

The word *kimiti* expresses censure (*kṣepa*). The meaning is that everything which was to be conquered has been conquered; it is used in the neuter gender because it refers to a general category (*sāmānya*).
The statement of exclusion (*vayyatirekokti*) is for the purpose of removing the possibility of negligence;
the word *iva* is used as a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*).
Here too, that which is called inference (*anumāna*) is stated to be a constituent element of the juncture (*saṃdhy-aṅga*). ||19||
Regarding the phrase "tatkim" and so forth:
"loka" means people;
the singular number is used here to denote a collective whole.
"That which is divided in two ways, split into two parts"—what is that?
The meaning is: "by what cause?
"This" refers to [the following].
"He approaches" means he is coming.
Therefore, it should be understood that the multitude of people parts in two to make way for those two.
"This one," who is this?
The meaning is "this one who is Rāma.

Regarding the phrase "by the glory of a hero" (*vīraśriyā*): he is resplendent by the glory of a hero—that is, by the abundance of qualities such as the valor characteristic of a heroic man—and by modesty, which consists of the absence of arrogance and the consideration of one's own excellence. He is bowed down, humble, before the venerable and worshipful sage; yet he is exalted and preeminent through his virtues, such as friendliness and the like.
The four *ca*s serve the purpose of aggregating those respective qualities.

Having committed a first offense against his guru, and having previously engaged in improper conduct, the disciple—just as one might feel toward a guru—bore shame before Bhṛgu, whose pride in heroism had been taken away and whose arrogance based on valor and the like had been destroyed; thus, bearing a contraction of heart induced by the thought of having performed an unworthy act, he approached him. This is the "assault" (*abhiṣaṅga*). ||20||
"Yad ityādi" and so forth.
O treasure-house of the Lord’s majesty! By the "proponents of Brahman"—those whose habit is to designate the Supreme Self as that which is to be known through the Vedānta—[your feet are worshipped].

For the proponents of Brahman are the most excellent of all; he whose feet are to be venerated even by some among those who are themselves worshipped by such [exalted beings] is described as such.
