In him, the inexhaustible repository, there is a storehouse of all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), cognitions (*jñāna*), ascetic practices (*tapas*), observances (*niyama*), and vows (*vrata*).

Although there is no difference between a *niyama* (observance) and a *vrata* (vow), nevertheless, a distinction is intended here based on their respective purposes: for the sake of knowledge and for the sake of liberation.

Regarding you, the most excellent (*variṣṭhe*) and best among those who shine (*tapatām*) by being unassailed by defects—I have, through fate (*daivāt*), that is, by the power of destiny (*vidhivaśāt*), committed an impropriety of humility (*vinayāpacāraḥ*), namely, an improper conduct prompted by a lack of discipline. Since this was done, for that reason, I offer this salutation with joined palms (*añjaliḥ*) to you;
the word "is bound" (*baddhaḥ*) is to be supplied.
It has been said: "The añjali is the supreme mudrā; it quickly propitiates the gods. To this he says: "prasiddhā" (well-known), meaning "abandon all impurity. ||21||
"What offense has been committed?
What transgression has been done? "Indeed, a favor was rendered."
The meaning is that a favor has indeed been rendered.
He states this very point with the words "puṇya" and so forth:
"O child Rāma, even a *mātrā*—that is, even a trace—of consciousness, which is correct knowledge."
"Now, *mātra* occurs in the senses of restriction and entirety;
*mātrā* [occurs] in the senses of a small portion, the measure of a syllable, an ornament for the ears and so forth,
and it also signifies a small dimension," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
"Carrying away"—that is, destroying—by means of this single, unaided disease of pride, the holy and righteous Brāhmaṇa caste;
for "holy" (puṇya) refers to that which possesses dharma, according to the *Ratnamālā*.
"Brāhmaṇa caste" refers to the Brāhmaṇas.
"Jāti, chandas, nāman, gotra, that which causes self-obstruction, uttara, sāmānya, and mālatī"—thus says the *Ratnamālā*.
The "quality" (*guṇa*) of the lineage (*anvaya*), namely the Bhṛgu clan, refers to the group of personal qualities such as humility (*amānitva*) and so forth;
for among the Brahmin lineages, the Bhṛgu clan is indeed most highly esteemed.
For this very reason, the *Pravarādhyāya* begins with the words: "We shall first explain [the lineages] of the Bhṛgus.
These—birth (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and conduct (*caritra*)—are such that one thinks: "My conduct is praiseworthy; it is to be practiced by me in accordance with my behavior, caste, and lineage.

Furthermore, in a copulative compound (*sahokti*) such as "this and that person" (*asau cāsau ca ādaḥ*), when the rule "tyadādīni sarvair nityam" applies for the retention of only one term (*ekaśeṣa*), the grammatical rule "puṃnapuṃsakato liṅgavacanāni" dictates that, because it is subsequent in order, the neuter gender is retained as the remainder among the pronouns beginning with *tyad*.
"Seized" means destroyed;
"were" is the ellipsis.

In the collective expression "seized (fem.), seized (masc.), and seized (neut.)", there is a neuter singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) according to the rule: *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām*.
The plural number is used because the treatment of a word as a singular entity is optional.

For it is well known that diseases such as *rājayakṣman* (consumption) destroy the three constituent elements (*dhātus*) consisting of wind, bile, and phlegm; thus, it is stated that this "pride-disease" (*darpāmaya*) likewise destroys the triad of caste and the other [social classes].

This very [pride], though being a single thing and even though it is without a companion, is "thick with many faults"—that is, difficult to approach—due to the specific qualities of its nature to be abandoned, such as anger, envy, and the like, which are instigated by itself.
The meaning is that it not only causes the loss of virtues, but moreover brings about faults;
"darpa" refers specifically to the pride induced by an excess of valor and other such qualities, which is itself a disease or affliction.
As Amara states: "roga, vyādhi, gada, and āmaya [are synonyms for disease]."

By you, who are affectionate toward brahmins, full of love, and especially fond of me—for the sake of security (*kṣema*), auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), and the preservation of what has been obtained—[may this be done]. According to the *Ratnamālā*, "the word *kṣema* is not feminine; it denotes auspiciousness and the preservation of what has been obtained. Here, the word *kṣema* refers to liberation (*mokṣa*).
And thus Āpastamba says: "The attainment of security through the awakening of the knowledge of expiation.
*Śamitaḥ* means destroyed.
The sense is that from this point forward, there shall be no obstruction to the increase of caste, qualities, and conduct.

By the phrase "dense with many defects" (*bhūridoṣagahana*), it is indicated that just as pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*) consists of a multitude of diseases, pride (*darpa*) consists of a multitude of defects.
Furthermore, by the phrase "taking away mere consciousness" (*caitanyamātrāṃ harati*), there is a similarity between this [pride] and disease due to both being destroyers of consciousness.
And it has been said: "Pride is like pulmonary consumption; it is a collection of passions."
And there is the saying: "Intellects arise in a mind that is healthy.

Regarding the phrase "out of affection for the Brāhmaṇas," one should keep in mind this [injunction]: "A physician should assist teachers, Brahmins, ascetics, and the distressed with his own medicines. (22)
"How was no offense committed? means "How was no transgression committed? "Up to the taking up of weapons" means "until the point of taking up weapons."
Due to the usage of the author of the Mahābhāṣya and other authorities, the accusative case is employed in connection with the word *yāvat*.
Amara states: "The words *yāvat* and *tāvat* are used in the senses of totality (*sākalya*), limit (*avadhi*), measure (*māna*), and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
This is a difficult grammatical construction (*duryoga*).
That by which a result in the form of good or evil is joined is *yoga*, meaning destiny (*daiva*). A bad *yoga* is adverse destiny;
that is to say, misfortune.
He has mounted and employed [the chariot].
This taking up of weapons is proper;
that is to say, it is appropriate.
In the rule "pari-nī-nī-ṇī-ṛ-dhū-stu-śru-vibhyaḥ karaṇe ca," the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefix *ni*.
The word "only" (*eva*) excludes those [means] employed through improper application.
Thus he says: "it is incurable."
The physician is the healer; "bhiṣaj" and "vaidya" both mean a physician, according to Amara.
Having ascertained that the affliction of the embodied being—the wound-like nature of karma—is incurable and irreparable by any means other than the taking up of the sword.

The *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *sādhana* [is used] in the senses of 'means' (*anugama*) and 'going' (*gati*), as well as in the senses of 'accomplishment' (*siddhi*), 'cessation' (*nivṛtti*), and 'causing to obtain' (*dāpana*).
For example, in the term *śastrapāṇiḥ*, he whose hand (*pāṇi*) holds a weapon (*śastra*) is so described.

The word *pāṇi* is placed last according to the rule: "After words meaning 'weapons,' the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) and the locative case ending (*saptamī*) follow. Thus, there is a posterior placement (*paranipāta*) of the word *pāṇi*.

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "for the purpose of removing the defects in the form of wounds. Likewise, the king appointed as the subduer of the Unsubduable (Durdama) will be one who, having discerned and determined that the embodied being—who ought to be subject to the scriptures—possesses defects consisting of the commission of what should not be done and the omission of what should be done, and who is otherwise incurable and irreparable even by means such as instruction in virtues other than the taking up of weapons, will become one who has taken up arms with weapon in hand for the sake of subduing the wicked.
Its future state is with respect to the act of delimitation (*paricchedakriyā*).
The meaning is that from the moment immediately following the certainty that the defect cannot be removed by any other means, one takes up the surgical instrument.
Passages such as "Just as a father performs the treatments of surgery, cauterization, and fire" should be considered here. ||23||
"Ka" refers to that action in which there is both speech and reply;
it is a compound formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group.
And "Tāta Janaka":
because Janaka is his father in relation to his wife, he is called "Tāta.
Intending to address the fact that two Kṣatriyas should not approach a Brahmanical sage, he says, "Or rather, peace! (śāntam).
Thus, the remainder of the sense is that the evil resulting from my speech [is meant].
"Śāntam" means "may it be pacified."
The suffix -niṣṭhā is used here in the sense of "expectation" (āśaṃsā) according to the rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca*.
Maitrāvaruṇa and Kauśika are Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra respectively. The meaning is that because of our superiority in learning and asceticism, it is logical that we should approach them.
This act of approaching Daśaratha and Janaka, or Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, which was previously performed by me, is now impossible for me at this time of humiliation;
the meaning is that it is difficult to perform due to shame. Yet, Rāma’s command is not to be transgressed.
Nevertheless, the meaning is that the command of Rāma is difficult to transgress. Amara states: "Nideśa and śāsana are synonyms; so too are śiṣṭi and ājñā."
"This very one... [means:

His victorious—meaning triumphant—command or decree was established even in Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni and slayer of kṣatriyas; that is, it became respected or endowed with the capacity to accomplish its purpose.
The word "was born" (*jātam*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Pratiṣṭhā [is used] in the sense of completion, dignity, the capacity for accomplishing a task, and the fourth meter," according to the *Ratnamālā*.

Because he is gentle—meaning he is as refreshing as the moon—he is "non-fierce" (*acaṇḍa*), that is, not harsh; yet this very Rāma is one whose commands are fierce (*caṇḍaśāsana*), meaning his orders are sharp.
The sharpness of the command [is such that] for those who transgress it, it leads to their own ruin and results in rebirth in miserable states of existence. ||24||
"Atīti" means a synonym for kindness (*saujanya*) and salutation (*namaskāra*);
its meaning is the non-transgression of that which has arrived in due order.
"‘Paryāya’ means ‘occasion’ or ‘sequence,’ according to Amara. [The suffix] *ghañ* is applied by the rule ‘*parāvanupātyaya iṇaḥ*’.
The sense is that since bowing before one’s teacher is prescribed, by performing it now, there is no transgression (*an-atipāta*) of that duty."
"They embrace" means they hug.
By the specific epithet "the sons of Jamadagni," together with the venerable Viśvāmitra and Kauśika, it is implied that even though I am wicked, my father should be looked after by you.
He states the very manner of his request: "O elders," and so forth.
The venerable masters are the agents; [the object] is Rāma, who has been tamed— that is to say, subdued— and instructed.
By the rule beginning with "vā dāntaśānta," the word *dānta* is formed as a past passive participle (*niṣṭhānta*) from the causative (*ṇic*).

For the sake of the purification (*nirṇiktaye*)—that is, the cleansing—of the great sin (*mahataḥ pāpmanaḥ*), which is equal to the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) and thus a mortal transgression (*mahāpātaka*), that was accumulated—that is, brought about—by my transgression (*atikrameṇa*), or overstepping, of you elders;
[the word *nirṇiktaye* is derived] from the root *ṇijir* (meaning "to cleanse") with the suffix *ktin* in the feminine to denote the abstract state (*bhāve*).
May they point out, instruct, or command that which is for the sake of purification—a means of mental reflection, an expiation, a determination of austerity, or an action that destroys sin.

Although the rule *prāyasya citticittayoḥ* prescribes the augment *suṭ* for the word *prāya*—which ends in *-ā* and signifies austerity, sin, or destruction—when followed by either *citti* or *citta*, which signify determination, purification, or connection respectively, nevertheless, because the *pāraskara*-group (*pāraskarādi*) is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), the augment *suṭ* is also correct when *prāya* is followed by the word *cetana*, which has the same meaning as *citti* and *citta*.
Thus, even the usage *prāyaścetayāṃcakre* by Murāri is correct precisely because the *pāraskara*-group is an open-ended class.
It is also said: "Prāya is declared to be austerity (tapas), and citta is said to be mental resolve.
The wise know that *prāyaścitta* is the conjunction of austerity and resolve. One should understand *prāya* to be sin, and *citta* to be its purification."
The root *cit* (in the sense of "perceiving") belongs to the curādigaṇa.
Since there is a rule that a failure to determine what is to be performed inevitably leads to misfortune, the performance [of that duty] is established as a matter of course.

However, they say that the meaning of the root *cetayati* is "purification" and "reunion," because verbal roots have multiple meanings; furthermore, since the word *prāya* signifies "destruction," actions such as *prāyaścitta* (expiation) which reunite a Brahminhood or similar status that has been destroyed are expressed by the term *prāyaścitta*.

Since the word *prāyas* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) and indeclinables possess multiple meanings, here it carries the sense of "sin" (*pāpa*). Consequently, the forms *prāyaścetanam* and *prāyaścetayāñcakre* are grammatically correct.
Likewise, the word *prāyaścitti* is also perfectly valid.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the rule *prāyasya citticittayoḥ* is intended to exclude forms such as *prāyaścitti*, which lack the augment *suṭ*.

O Teacher Vasiṣṭha, you alone were the original seers (*prāgdraṣṭṛ*) of Dharma—that is, of the means to supramundane welfare (*alaukika-śreyas*) which is accessible through the Vedas alone; whereas Manu and others, having attained the valid cognition of Dharma through your teachings and instructions, have propagated Dharma in manifold ways and set it forth in their treatises.
Alternatively, Manu and others, having obtained the authoritative knowledge of Dharma from you, propagated and made known that Dharma through various discourses in the form of instructional texts;
for the verb *nayati* preceded by *pra-* signifies "to establish" or "to expound.
Since they did indeed propagate it (*prāṇayan*), the connection is: "therefore, may you instruct [us]. (25)
"Child," [said he] at the time of seeking an expiation out of remorse for today; "ill-behaved one," [he said].

O child Jāmadagnya, while you are ill-behaved—having transgressed the conduct appropriate for the virtuous and being arrogant—we, the elders of the lineage, have become sorrowful, that is, we have come to experience grief. The word "abhūma" (we have become) is understood. Otherwise, had you been well-behaved, we would have become happy, that is, we would have experienced happiness.
The ellipsis is "may we be.
This refers to the state of suffering among one's own ill-behaved kinsmen and the state of happiness among those who are well-behaved.
Because the subject (the person) is primary, the masculine gender and singular number are used.
The "nature" (*nisarga*) refers to the innate disposition of elders—those men who are preeminent in wisdom, age, and character.

The word "hi" indicates well-known fact. Whatever is for one's ultimate good must be accomplished exactly so, according to the method you have described; thus, for you who are filled with remorse, this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is indeed achievable. (26)
"My child," [he says]. "O child, son of Jamadagni, we know—that is, we recognize—that your sin, incurred through the taking up of weapons and so forth, has been removed and destroyed by Rāmabhadra;
for he is a teacher of dharma, an instructor in righteousness."
"An *ācārya* is one who composes an exposition of mantras," according to Amarasimha.

Just as expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*, are said to effect the destruction of sin, so too do they declare that even royal punishment serves as a means of purification—a cleansing of the guilt of sin—even when meted out by kings for the purpose of correction.
The substitution of *man* for *mā* is according to the rule "pāghrā-," etc.

One should also consider the statement of Manu: "Men who have committed sins, when punished by kings, go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds"; and the statement from the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa: "He who inflicts punishment upon one deserving of it, and he who is punished as one deserving of it—both of them, having accomplished their respective purposes through cause and effect, do not suffer."
"What more [need be said]?"—
here "this honorable one" (*atrabhavān*) means "venerable. Grammarians state that the words *atrabhavat* and *tatrabhavat* signify respect.

Regarding the passage "Vasiṣṭha, in the presence of the protector of subjects," the following statement should be kept in mind: "A council consisting of at least three members—one who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and one who knows the Sāmaveda—should be recognized as authoritative for resolving doubts concerning Dharma.

Regarding the term "this venerable one" (atrabhavān), the following should be kept in mind: "That which one who is the foremost among those possessing knowledge of the supreme self (adhyātma) declares shall be the Dharma, even if he is alone."
"These" refers to the [mantras] beginning with "these,
indeed, are purified" and ending with "the Praśāstṛ," belonging to the Blessed Ones.

"The one who knows the origin and destruction of beings, their coming and going, as well as knowledge and ignorance—he is to be called 'Bhagavān'. The words and sentences of such seers (*ṛṣis*)—who possess the grounds for the application of the term "Bhagavān" as stated above; who have directly realized Brahman, perceived the Supreme Self, and directly beheld the scattered Vedas; and whose speech is truthful—are serene, capable of cutting through doubt, profound, unshakeable, purifying, and even by mere hearing, they remove sin.
This is the sense of the sentence.
The compound is a descriptive determinative (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), like "high and low" (*nimnonnata*).
By the two qualifiers beginning with "of the Blessed Ones" (*bhagavatām*), their state of seeing things as they truly are (*yathārthadṛṣṭitva*) is expressed;
by the word "of the sages" (*ṛṣīṇām*), their state of speaking things as they truly are (*yathārthavaktṛtva*) is expressed.

By the word *prasanna* ("clear"), its authoritative reliability (*āptatva*) is expressed; by means of this, its distinction from Vedic statements that require further investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) for the sake of resolving doubt is stated.

By the word *gambhīra* ("profound"), its distinction from deceptive traditional codes (*smṛti*) is stated, through the mention of its being rooted in the Vedas which are scattered [in various places].
And by the word *pāvana* ("purifying"), it is stated that it removes the sins of even the dull-witted that obstruct the attainment of the knowledge of the true reality (*tattvārtha*).
"O Blessed One! [He replies:
"By nature. "O Blessed One, son of Jamadagni, for you who are pure by nature—that is, pure by your very essence—and who purify others as well, what other means of purification could there be?"
The meaning is: "for what purpose?
"Tīrthodaka" refers both to water from a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) and to water frequented by sages (*ṛṣijuṣṭa*).

Due to the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word *udaka* (water), the term *tīrtha*, which denotes water frequented by sages, here functions solely as a qualifier meaning "the state of being frequented by sages."
Furthermore, neither fire nor the purifier (pāvaka) deserve purification—that is, purification caused by an object other than themselves;
the meaning is that they cannot tolerate it.
Therefore, the sense is that your statement, "Hence, prescribe an expiation," is not tenable.

This is the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration), according to the definition: "If there is the state of being an original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), that is the ornament *dṛṣṭānta*.

The mention of wood in relation to fire is intended in accordance with the saying: "The all-consuming [fire] is not a fault for those who are more powerful, just as [fire is not a fault] for fire itself. ||27||
"Bhagavatī" [is used here].

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of purpose (*prayojana*), as in the expression "he dwells for the sake of study" (*adhyayanena vasati*). It means: "for the sake of granting a cavity within herself," that is, for the sake of providing a dwelling place in a secluded spot for me—who, although my sins have been overcome by means of penance and other such acts, still possess unobstructed karmic effects.
"Be gracious; show favor!
[O] Blessed One, and so forth.
If you are pleased with us—that is, if you have bestowed your favor upon us—then "confidently," meaning in such a way as to inspire trust that these [beings] are no different from ourselves.

"Samau viśrambha-viśvāsau" (confidence and trust are synonyms), according to Amara. "Upaveśanāt" means from the seat; "paripunīhi" means purify completely; "asmadgṛhān" means our house. With the word "etad," he points to the seat with his finger—namely, that which is indicated by "yad."
To the disciple of Yājñavalkya, the pupil of Sūrya—a royal śrotriya, a kṣatriya who had studied the Vedic meters.
The compound *rājanyaśrotriya* is formed according to the rule "The caste [is compounded] with *śrotriya*, *adhyāpaka*, and *dhūrta*.
The dative case is used according to the rule "The one being pleased is [the object] of verbs meaning 'to please' (*rucyarthānām*)."
"Whatever is desired, whatever is pleasing— let that be," is the ellipsis. All sit down.
The meaning is that they are acting out the act of sitting down.
Regarding "janapada" and so forth, here [the phrase] begins with "jāmadagnya."

O son of Jamadagni, you [plural used for honor]. You are "forest-dwellers outside the inhabited lands" (*janapada-bahir-niṣṭhāḥ*), meaning you reside constantly in the forest situated beyond the inhabited lands such as Kosala; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

The meaning is: "May you become solely devoted to the forest. "We" (vayam) and "I" (aham)—the plural number is used for the singular according to the rule *asmado dvayośca* ("for the word *asmad*, the plural is used even when referring to two").

"Because of the maintenance of the household"—that is, because of our undertaking the householder's stage of life (gṛhasthāśrama) as characterized by the home—we are "distracted," meaning occupied or preoccupied with our own necessary duties such as the administration of the kingdom; the word "we are" is to be understood as the ellipsis. According to Amara, "vyagra" means "occupied," "engrossed," or "disturbed."
Because of that [fact], whatever union did not occur—that which had not come to pass—was desired and made the object of our *manorathas*, or rather, of our particular longings (*utkaṇṭhā-viśeṣa*).
This is a usage similar to the expression "cooking the cooking" (*pākaṃ pacanti*).

Alternatively, the term *manoratha* (literally "chariot of the mind") is a metaphorical designation based on the similarity [of the mind] to a chariot, insofar as it serves as the means for unimpeded movement.
The meeting with us is what has been desired and sought by you.
In the phrase "by us," the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the subordinate element (*apradhāna*), which highlights our own lowliness.
The term "by us" connects with both [the preceding and following parts].
Because of the ripening of well-performed deeds and due to the readiness of good karma to yield its fruit, we have reached it after a long time; it has been obtained by us after a long interval.
The word "abhūt" (it came to be) is to be understood as the ellipsis. ||28||
Regarding "and here":
the meaning is "in this assembly. Regarding "who is she?": [the answer follows].

He whose *dhāma*—his power or majesty—has *ativṛtta*, meaning transcended or surpassed, the *patha of praise*, that is, the way of eulogy; such is he. The ablative case in *stutipathāt* is used because one intends to express the sense of the source (*apādāna*) for the act of transcending. The suffix *a* is added to the word *pathin* according to the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ* and so forth.
"Regarding 'the abode, birth, splendor, station, power, and the dwelling of bliss,' this is from the *Ratnamālā*.
What praise could there be [for such a one]? The word 'might be' (*bhavet*) is to be supplied."

The meaning is that praise, which consists in the verbal expression of qualities, is not appropriate for you whose excellence of qualities lies beyond the range of words. The intention is that the maxim "teachers are to be praised when present" applies only to teachers who can be praised [in such ways]. What can be given to you, who grant the entire earth—including its islands and so forth—in the manner previously described?
The meaning is: "What object is worthy of being given?
The intention is that the phrase "with abundant wealth" refers to a different kind of occasion.
What is the use of your retinue to you—a sage who is peaceful, whose mind is restrained from sensual pleasures, and who is intent on contemplating the Supreme Self?
The meaning is that even service, which is normally accomplished by attendants, is not required here.
The sense is that the phrase "or by supreme service" also refers to other subjects.
This statement is made because of the intention to regard the son of Jamadagni as a guru due to his being the navel of Vasiṣṭha.
Nevertheless, even though he has no regard for praise, gifts, or attendants, Daśaratha, being together with his sons Rāma and the others, is today submissive to you;
that is to say, he is under your control.
The verb "is" (bhavati) is to be supplied.
The suffix *khac* is applied by the rule "priyavaśe vadaḥ khac.

Although the son of Jamadagni (Paraśurāma) has no need for praise or the like, because bystanders perceive that Daśaratha, along with his sons, is subject to the son of Jamadagni, Paraśurāma becomes one who has performed a great service.
This has been stated by those learned in political ethics (*nīti*): "Even a slight favor is rendered by everyone, because they are known to be his attendants"—this is the sense. ||29||
"What wonder is there in saying that you are such as this?
That Rāma and others, as well as the truth itself, are dependent upon Brāhmaṇas—this is nothing new; such is the meaning.
Regarding the word *preddham*: [it means "well-kindled"].

The sages, whose nature is to contemplate reality, recite— that is, they study— the Rig Veda verse concerning that Sun, whom they declare to be the intensely blazing, supremely radiant light (*dhāman*).

The excellence consisting in being rooted in the splendor of Agni and Soma is intended by the prefix *pra*; this very Lord, the treasury of lights and the inexhaustible abode of all radiances, is the Sun.
He is the master (*svāmī*) and the progenitor (*savitā*)—the one who brings forth—of your lineage (*yuṣmadvaṃśasya*).
The suffix *tṛc* is used here in the sense of the agent (kartari) derived from the root *ṣu*, meaning "to procreate" or "to exercise sovereignty."
The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Thus, what else other than this is a ground for praise—a locus of supreme eulogy—for the sake of prosperity (*bhūtyai*), that is, for the attainment of success? According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *bhūti* [is used] in the senses of prosperity, pride, erotic passion, origin, and ashes. What [else] is such a place?
"Nothing at all," he said.
"The Sun is the progenitor of your lineage"—this alone is the supreme ground for your excellence and praise;

that is to say, for you whose teacher is Vasiṣṭha, of immeasurable majesty and unsurpassed greatness, who, like the Veda, is eternal, non-human, and faultless, and who, like the Śruti, is the instructor in matters of dharma such as the obligatory and occasional rites—the means to supramundane welfare. He is the one who removes your doubts and other such obstacles.
The word "become" (bhavanti) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Those Ikṣvākus of such a nature, being devoted to sacrifice, were subjects of the sovereign of the Ikṣvāku country;
the suffix denoting offspring has been elided because he was their king.

Alternatively, the word *Ikṣvāku* is a specific name of a king, and its figurative application (*lākṣaṇika*) to his descendants justifies the use of the plural. Thus, "you are supreme royal sages" means that you possess the status of royal sages as an actual reality;
elsewhere, however, the term "royal sage" is merely metaphorical (*aupacārika*). This is the meaning.

The meaning is this: Sūrya is your guru by birth, while Vasiṣṭha is your guru by learning; therefore, for you who possess both forms of purity, it is nothing new that you are subject to the will of a Brāhmaṇa. ||30||
Regarding the phrase "in battles":

in the battles of the Lord of the Heaven-dwellers—that is, in the wars between the gods and the asuras—the bow (kārmuka) was the bestower of fearlessness, providing the cessation of fear from the asuras; [it was] the command (śāsana).
Amara states: "It is both a direction (nirdeśa) and a command (śāsana)."
The collection of the seven continents is "saptadvīpa. Due to its inclusion in the *pātra* group, it takes the neuter gender.
Upon that [earth] stand distinguished sacrificial posts (*yūpa*), which are wooden stakes for tethering animals, and sacrificial altars; for it is said, "One should sacrifice on level ground."

The various island-lands, marked by rows— that is, lines— of those places for the performance of sacrifices prescribed in such injunctions as "One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva on ground sloping toward the east," serve as the eternal foundation—
the cause— for his perpetual fame; for the word *śaśvat* signifies both "again" and "eternal."
The word *nibandhana* is always neuter in gender.
*Kīrti* is the renown of possessing virtuous qualities;
or alternatively, it is the fame resulting from the quality of magnanimity.

Alternatively, what is intended by "fame" (kīrti) is that which is defined by the following characteristic: "That action which truly delights the entire universe is called fame; if that [delight] has descended upon one's lineage, it is designated as 'glory' (yaśas). Because it brings peace (śam) to the universe, it is therefore termed 'glory' (yaśas). Thus, fame characterized by such a definition is what is meant here.
The Blessed One, most worthy of worship; Bhāgīrathī, the Gaṅgā associated with Bhagīratha; and Sāgara, the ocean dug by the Sāgaras.
And those various well-known and celebrated miraculous deeds of yours, the lords of the Ikṣvāku lineage—this refers to the vastness, that is to say, the majesty of you all.
They declare and reveal.

Here, in the communication of his majesty, the figure of speech is a specific type of *samuccaya* (accumulation), because the bow and other weapons are stated to be causes according to the maxim of the *khalekapota* (the pigeons on the threshing floor).
As it has been said: "When many [factors] accomplish a single task according to the maxim of the *khalekapota*..."
"The exertion of causes—that is the second collection. Thus, from the word *bahu*, which denotes abundance, the word *bhūma* is derived by adding the suffix *iman* to indicate state (*bhāva*). ||31||
"Setting aside," "setting aside":
the meaning is specifically toward Rāma and Jamadagnya.

This praise of the qualities of a Kṣatriya, uttered by Vatsa Rāma—the destroyer of Kṣatriyas—is intended to instruct the son of Jamadagni. "Grant your approval" means: please give your consent for his departure to the forest, and rejoice.
"May the venerable Vasiṣṭha, Daśaratha, Janaka, and others grant their permission; let them give their consent.
He states the matter for which permission is sought: "O Raghu and Janaka," and so forth, including the phrase "by me" and the rest.
By me, in the houses and dwellings of the Raghus and the Janakas—
according to the *Ratnamālā*, "the word *gṛha* (house) may be used in the plural, while it denotes both 'home' and 'wife' in the dual"—
[I have seen] those two whose form and nature were like that of an embryo.
The meaning is "of Sītā and Rāma.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *garbha* [is used] for a child, a juncture in drama (*nāṭyasaṃdhi*), the womb, the seed-pod of a jackfruit, an embryo (*bhrūṇa*), and a private room."

In this context, Rāma’s state of being an embryo, though he was already one whose sins had been destroyed, was based on his own will. Sītā’s state of being an embryo, however, arose from the non-differentiation [of her soul] from Rāma due to the intensity of her love, even though she was not born of his own loins (*anaurasa*).

"Intermingling" (*vyatikara*) refers to the matrimonial alliance with others; that itself is the auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), and its increase consists of the marriages of Lakṣmaṇa, Ūrmilā, and the others, which were experienced—that is, made objects of direct perception—producing happiness.

Furthermore, having congratulated my dear son Rāma— who is exalted by the victory of Paraśurāma, the Lord of Bhṛgu, and who possesses supreme triumph as he has already effectively conquered both Vālin and Rāvaṇa— and being thus happy and endowed with unsurpassed bliss (the suffix *ini* is used here in the sense of abundance),
may I return to and reach my home.
The connection with the preceding clause is: "May you, sirs, grant permission in this matter. The suffix *liṅ* in *upeyām* is used in the sense of a request (*prārthanā*).
The meter is *Puṣpitāgrā*.
As it has been said: "In the odd [pādas], after the *na*, *ya*, and *ra*, there is a *ya*; and in the even [pādas], *na* and *ja*, followed by *ja*, *ra*, and *ga*, constitute the *puṣpitāgrā*. (32)
"O child! Thus addressed, Kauśika, who is solely devoted to you, has set out;
that is to say, he has begun to depart.
"I am," [he says].
"O gentle one, you who are as pleasing to behold as the moon;
I alone am 'I'—that is to say, I am devoid of the necessity for the performance of the practices that are about to be described."

I do not venture to release you, nor do I resolve to do so—*utsāha* and *adhyavasāya* being synonymous according to Amara. However, what is meant is: the state of constant performance (*anuṣṭhāna-nityatvam*), that is, the quality of performing [the rite] perpetually or the necessity of its performance.
And what is intended here is that performance [of the rite] is the counter-positive of an absence which serves as the cause for the commission of a transgression (*pratyavāya*).
"Independence" (*svātantrya*) diminishes—that is, destroys—one's state of self-will (*svairāvasthiti*).
The meaning is that even if a state of self-will has been occasionally accepted, it becomes fruitless through the imposition of penance (*prāyaścitta*), which generates double the effort.
He explains this with the words "in times of distress," and so forth.
"Of those who have established the sacred fires" refers to persons who possess fires consecrated by the rite of *ādhāna*, as prescribed in the injunction: "One should establish the fires."

And this is an illustration of the obligatory rites (*nityakratu*) mentioned in such passages as "One should offer the *agnihotra* as long as one lives" and "One should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma* in the spring.

The householder—that is, the stage of life of the householder—is "beset with difficulties," meaning it is obstructed by transgressions—the faults resulting from the non-performance of duties rooted in one's own established state.
The word "is" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
For since it is so, therefore the connection is that the constancy of performance detracts from independence. ||33||
"From his own home" means that from the city of Mithilā, which is equivalent to his own home, he has the freedom to go to or come from his own home, Siddhāśrama;
"it is so," is the ellipsis.
The meaning is that the activity of moving at will consists in the purpose of going and coming.
"Moving at will" (*kāmacāra*) refers to an action (*cāra*) performed according to one's desire (*kāmena*), that is, by one's own wish.
"O Blessed One" (*bhagavan*).
O Blessed One, if you consent, if you so desire—
according to the Dhātupāṭha, the root *anu-rudh* means "to desire"—
then [come to] the site of Siddhāśrama, that place which is the very form of Siddhāśrama.
"Regarding 'tvām' (you):
the word 'I' is to be supplied.

Thinking, 'By going while placing you, the best of Brahman-sages, at my head, I shall become worthy of honor (*satkārya*) by the mother of Madhucchandas'—Madhucchandas being the son of Viśvāmitra, and his mother being the wife of Viśvāmitra—I shall be one who is to be respected."
The mention of Madhucchandas’s mother is intended to proclaim the extraordinary degree of respect due to her as the mother of a virtuous son.

The underlying sense is that her joy was even greater because she had obtained as a guest the most venerable Vasiṣṭha—who had previously wronged her many times but subsequently became her friend—and who bestows the status of a Brahmarṣi even upon oneself.
Why [is this so]?

Even for such a very slight command as coming to Siddhāśrama, you are my venerable one; therefore, do you not have authority over me? The meaning is: "Are you not my master? The two kings, Daśaratha and Janaka, are charming and pleasing.
The meeting—that is, the encounter—of the two Brahman-sages Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra was purifying, removing the sins of people through the mere sight, hearing, and so forth [of it].
"Mutually" means:
they were both aware of each other’s greatness, knowing one another's power; and they were such that their own true natures were unknown to others, being difficult for others to comprehend.
The phrase "of the two Brahman-sages" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
That even their enmity—that is, their mutual hostility—shines forth, meaning it is well known to shine forth preeminently as a cause for benefiting others;
and this quality of being a cause for benefiting others is evident in the cases of Triśaṅku, Hariścandra, and others.
But what need is there to speak of the affection between Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra?
The meaning is: how could it not be said that they shine forth?
The implication is that this is because they are the cause of benefit to the entire world.
"Here she is": Rāma’s wife, Sītā, pays homage to and salutes her elders, Vasiṣṭha and the others.
The "seers" (ṛṣayaḥ) are Vasiṣṭha and his peers.
Regarding the word "vīreṇa" (by the hero): O child Jānakī, [it means] by the hero who is the foremost in the world.
The status of being foremost is obtained through the statement: "A word that is non-differentiating [when applied] to the principal [subject] becomes differentiating for others."
That which has auspiciousness as its purpose is "māṅgalika. When there is victory, that which is auspicious is "vijayamāṅgalika.
The compound is formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* [allowing a compound] with the locative case (*saptamī*).

The meaning is that she obtained the auspiciousness consisting of the attainment of you, along with the incidental victory of Paraśurāma. "By her husband"—by Rāma, who possesses supreme excellence dependent upon you according to the statement, "For immeasurable indeed is his splendor, to whom that daughter of Janaka belongs"; when the great battles of Vṛtradruh (Indra) had been quelled—that is, brought to an end—in great conflicts, even Śacī, the consort of Indra, became *ūrjasvalā*, meaning powerful.
The word *ūrjasvala* is derived [as a nipātana] from the compound *jyotsnātamisrā*, and so forth.

Let her perform, with her mind—that is, mentally and without deceit—the honor and worship bestowed upon the wives of the foremost Kṣatriyas (the best of the warrior class), which is characterized by an excess of reverence. Alternatively, the term *kṣattraprakāṇḍagṛhiṇī* may be treated as a separate word, serving as an epithet for Śacī.
The "foremost of the Kṣatriyas" refers to Indra, the best among the warrior class.
As the Śruti states, "Brahman is Bṛhaspati; Indra is the Kṣatra; the Maruts are indeed the Viś of the gods," Indra’s status as a Kṣatriya is thus declared.
The meaning of the phrase "may his wife Śacī also offer abundant honor and worship" is the same as explained previously. ||35||
"Before long" means:
when the Rākṣasas, such as Rāvaṇa and others, have been "rubbed away with their very roots"—that is, destroyed along with their foundations—then this shall come to pass;
the meaning is that there will be great honor and worship performed by Śacī.
By the rule "nimūlasamūlayoḥ kaṣaḥ," when the word *samūla* is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied to the root *kaṣ*.
There is a subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) of the original root *kaṣ*.
Here, they say that because the state of being inherent [in the subject] is expressed, the non-mention of the manifestation (*prakāśa*) is due to boldness (*prauḍhi*).
"May there be well-being!
"Venerable Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, may you remain in well-being through such mutual affection; let it be as it is.
"Firmly."
May there be for you a firm tranquility, an unshakable and supreme peace through the mastery of the powerful senses, consisting of the internal restraint of the faculties.
(The *liṅ* suffix is used here in the sense of a benediction.
May the light of the inner self—the nature of the Self which shines by itself for itself—illuminate you.
The word "yogadṛṣṭyā" (by the vision of yoga) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
In this context, passages such as "O King, the light of the Self is within the vital breaths; that is the light of action" are to be considered.
By the word "light" (jyotis), self-luminosity is intended.

And since that [quality] exists even in the knowledge that has become an attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), it is called "inner" (*pratyak*). It is "inner" (*pratyak*) because it perceives itself (*pratyakṣati*).

By means of the prefix *prati*, which denotes the state of being, its nature as the residual illuminator is expressed; and that very same quality of appearing to itself is called "light" (*jyotis*) in order to exclude the doctrine of the Naiyāyikas who maintain that the self is insentient (*jaḍa*).
In this context, the mention of "tranquility" (praśama) is intended as an illustration for self-restraint (dama) and the other virtues.
By this, the meaning of the Śruti passage—"Having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, one sees the Self in the very Self"—is demonstrated.
May your internal organ—the mind—be such that its mental activity (saṅkalpa), which is non-different from and dissolved into Śiva, the source of auspiciousness, is thus disposed.
In the preceding [sūtra] and here, the suffix *loṭ* is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).
"My child," [he said].
"Come here first"—
this is the ellipsis for "you must come."
"Command me"—
the implication being, "What is to be done?"— "That which... [is as follows].
Because the kṣatriya lineage has been severed and the kṣatriyas have been destroyed, even though I am at rest and withdrawn, I maintain a state of total inactivity. ||37||

The axe (*paraśu*), however, has the purpose of felling or cutting wood such as fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and sacrificial fuel (*samit*); being thus described, the ellipsis is "let it remain with me alone.
Between the bow (*dhanus*) and the battle-axe (*paraśvadha*), since the battle-axe has a practical utility, let it remain with me.
But because the bow has no utility for me, while it does have utility for you, he says "puṇyānām" and so forth, [implying] "let this belong to you."

In that region where many sages dwell upon the banks and shores of the Daṇḍaka forest—of the meritorious and purifying rivers such as the Godāvarī and others—they sit or reside in Laṅkā; thus they are called *laṅkāsadaḥ*. The suffix *kvip* is applied here according to the rule beginning with "satsūdviṣa-".
"For destruction" means for the purpose of causing ruin;

that is to say, for the purpose of bringing about the downfall of the sages. "They roam" means they wander about; in the slaying of those Rākṣasas, the utility—that is, the serviceability—of that bow would be realized.
Now, along with this bow, this authority—the agency in the slaying of the Rākṣasa—rests solely with you, my child; it remains in you alone. (38)
"Thus he offers the bow":
the meaning is that having spoken thus, he gives the bow.
"Having prostrated": [this is the sense].

This command was issued by Paraśurāma; it is understood that "by me" [the speaker] has accepted this command for the slaughter of the Rākṣasas. This sequence, consisting of the attainment of the intended purpose through movement, has thus been described.
"O long-lived one!"—
the suffix *matup* is applied to the word *āyus* in the sense of abundance.
"Return."
The meaning is: "Enough of following me; turn back.
Having said this, he departed—this is the meaning.
"Perhaps" (api nāma) [indicates a wish].
"Should I set out by one way because of following Bhārgava, or even by another? The meaning is: 'Should I depart?
Here, the *saṃdhy-aṅga* (limb of the juncture) called *rūpa*—consisting of a sentence that expresses deliberation (*vitarka*)—is stated."
And how so? He for whom Rāma is dear is "rāmapriyaḥ.
The word *priya* is placed at the end [of the compound] according to the rule "vā priyasya."
"How could such a journey to the Daṇḍaka forest be for the sake of my elders?"—
the inference intended here is that "my elder is not the cause of my going to the Daṇḍaka forest because he is dear to Rāma.
Therefore, the dramatic element (saṃdhy-aṅga) called "inference" (anumāna), which consists of the mental deduction of signs and so forth, is stated here.
Regarding the word *nyasta*:
when Paraśurāma, the lord of the Bhṛgus, was one by whom weapons and arms had been *nyasta*— that is, laid down or abandoned—
the word *tathā* is used in the sense of similarity, because [the situation] serves as a cause for providing an opening for the *yātudhānas* (demons).

The meaning is as follows: those sages are so described because they are ones for whom austerity alone is wealth, which must be protected even more than their own lives from cruel, violent Yātudhānas and Rākṣasas who act as aggressors; therefore, out of fear of violating that austerity, they were unable to curse him.
"Utsāritāḥ" means driven away or expelled.
The word "become" (bhavanti) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. There would be *kaṣṭam*, i.e., suffering (*duḥkham*).
According to Amarasimha: "The words *kaṣṭam*, *kṛcchram*, and *ābhīlam* mean suffering. ||39||
Regarding the phrase "madhyamāyāḥ": O Rāma, "of our middle mother" means of Kaikeyī.
"Priyasakhī Mantharā" refers to the one named Mantharā; the word "is" (asti) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
This very Mantharā has come from Ayodhyā out of a desire to see you—that is, a longing to behold you.
This [word] ends in the fifth case (pañcamī) in the sense of the ablative (apādāna). It means "attained" (prāptā), that is to say, "come" (āgatā). ||40||
"Excellent!"—
referring to this news brought by Mantharā;
for Amara states that "vārtā," "pravṛtti," and "vṛttānta" are synonyms for news.

If this sorrow—the state of a troubled mind caused by our exile and our dwelling in another land—which we desire for both of us, our children, were to be severed, or rather, if it were perceived as non-existent, that would be excellent and proper;
therefore, bring it near, that is, cause Mantharā to approach. (The word "Mantharā" is to be supplied.)
"Thoroughly concentrated":
the word "task" (*kārya*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
The meaning is: "our task is free from distraction."
Having gazed intently—*nirvarṇya ālokya*;
according to Amara, "gazing (*nirvarṇana*) is the same as *nidhyāna*, *darśana*, *ālokana*, and *īkṣaṇa*.

By means of the acceptance—that is, the taking possession—of the abundance of complete and perfect beauty and fortune, [she is] an elixir (*rasāyana*) for the eyes, that is, for the eyes of the world; specifically, she is a particular medicinal drug known as an elixir.
"Rasāyana is that medicine which destroys old age and disease," says Vāgbhaṭa.
The meaning is: "The beauty of Rāma removes the defect of old age from those who behold him.
And it was said by Daśaratha as well: "I rejoice even while seeing [him], and having seen him, I become like a youth once again."
By this, Śūrpaṇakhā’s objection regarding the defect of her own old age has been answered.
"Saumyam" means relating to Soma;
the suffix *ṭyaṇ* is applied according to the rule "somāṭṭyaṇ."
"Saumya refers to a wise man or a Brahmin; it may also mean the deity Soma, or that which is lovely and gentle," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
"The formation of the body" (*śarīranirmāṇa*) means the construction of the body.
Regarding the passage beginning with "yad" and so forth:

this refers to the creation of Rāma’s body [for Sītā], even now that she is in extreme old age, due to the sorrow of long-term widowhood and the grief over her husband's death which has persisted for a great length of time.
It is clear from the later *Śrīrāmāyaṇa* that it was Rāvaṇa himself who killed her husband in the primordial era.

For such a person— meaning for me— the conduct (*cāritra*) consisting of the vow of fidelity (*pātivratya*), even though worldly happiness has been stolen away and destroyed, and the pleasure derived from association with women and men who have become the objects of attachment to the body, is as follows: [the rest of the verse follows].
This [word] ends in the accusative case.

Starting from the rule "The suffix *ṇitran* is added after roots beginning with *bhū* and *ṛ*," the word *cāritra* is derived from the root *car* by means of the suffix *ṇitran* according to the rule "After *car*, [the suffix *ṇitran* is added] in the sense of conduct (*vṛtta*).
Grammarians state: "Conduct (*cāritra*) is character (*śīla*)."
"He draws toward" and "stirs" in the heart, that is, in the mind; [the root] *kṣip* is used in the sense of "casting away.
Is all well?
The meaning is that one inquires after his welfare (*kuśalam*).
Amarasimha states: "The word *api* [is used] in the senses of censure, conjunction, inquiry, doubt, possibility, and also [in the sense of 'even'].
If *kuśalam* means well-being or happiness (*sukham*), [then the phrase means "Is he well?"].
*Kuśala* means that which is pleasing to the mind; *sukha* is the happiness of the self.

The distinction is that *kuśala* consists of wealth, grain, jewels, clothing, and so forth, while *sukha* consists of food, drink, health, and the like. As Amarasimha states: "The word *kuśala*, meaning security (*kṣema*), is not feminine," and "The words *śarma*, *śāta*, and *sukha* [are synonyms]."

The compound *sadāprasnutastanī* is a *bahuvrīhi*; its analysis (*vigraha*) is: "she whose breasts are always flowing," meaning her breasts are constantly streaming with milk due to maternal affection for her son.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule beginning with *svāṅgācca*. [The word *pariṣvajya* means] having embraced or clasped [her].
The two boons were promised with an oath, saying, "I shall give.

By the Prākṛta grammar rule *guṇe gā*, which means that words such as *guṇa* and others may occur in both the masculine and neuter genders, the word *vara* is neuter in Prākṛta and masculine in Saṃskṛta.

Alternatively, this word *vara* signifies "desired" (*iṣṭa*) and is neuter even in Sanskrit. As the *Ratnamālā* states: "The masculine *vara* denotes the grace of a god, a choice, or a son-in-law; it is neuter for saffron and for that which is excellent; as an indeclinable, *varam* means 'desirable'."
"In that regard" means for the purpose of making known the two boons.
"A messenger with a petition" refers to the manner of presenting a request to the Great King.

The word "iti" (thus) should be supplied immediately after "bhava"; its connection with the preceding is as follows: "bhava" means "command. A letter that makes known a task is a "kāryalekha" (letter concerning a task).
The meaning is that having spoken thus, he gives.
He causes [the other] to recite; he recites.
This root *vac* belongs to the *cur*-class (caurādika) and is here used with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in its own sense.
He states the meaning of the letter with the words beginning "astu" (let it be):

"By one boon," meaning by the first of the two boons previously granted by you; "Vatsabharataḥ" means Bharata, your son; "of your sovereignty" (*adhirājyasya*), which refers to the domain of protecting the entire circle of the earth as your royal duty;

[the term *adhirājyam* is formed from *adhirājasya karma*, meaning "the act of a sovereign king," where the absence of the *vṛddhi* vowel in the prefix *adhi-* is due to the non-universality of the rule regarding technical terms].
Alternatively, the analysis [of the compound] is *adhirājyam* as "excessive sovereignty" (*adhikaṃ rājyam*).
Or rather, the word division should be made as *ādhirājyam* itself. Let him be the enjoyer.
The suffix *loṭ* is used in the sense of a request (*prārthanā*).
"By another" is to be construed with "by a boon" (*vareṇa*); that is, by reason of another boon, setting aside any delay—that is, abandoning the wasting of time.
"Quickly" means as soon as possible.
Let Rāma go to the Daṇḍaka forest;
here too, the *loṭ* suffix is used in the sense of a request.
That Rāma was in that Daṇḍaka forest; here, as in the passage "The Great Self is higher than the intellect;
the Unmanifest is higher than the Great," there is a reference by means of the pronoun *tat* to the preceding qualifier.
Wearing rags and wearing bark garments—
according to the *Medinī* lexicon, [the suffix -in] is applied after the roots *su*, *śuṣi*, and *ci*, and the vowel is lengthened.
For fourteen *samās*, that is, fourteen years.
"Samāḥ [is used] for a woman, and 'sādhu' for all three genders when meaning equal"; thus says the Ratnamālā.
Let it be; that is to say, let her dwell.
Furthermore, "taṃ punā rāmam" means "that very Rāma.
"Sītā ca lakṣmaṇaśca" becomes "sītālakṣmaṇam"; this is a *dvandva* compound used in the sense of a collective whole (*samāhāre*).
"Sītā-lakṣmaṇam eva" means "only Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa. This is a compound according to the rule for *mayūravyaṃsaka* and other such terms. "Sītā-lakṣmaṇamātram eva" becomes "sītā-lakṣmaṇamātrakaḥ."
The suffix *kan* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). [The word *parijanāt* is derived from *parijana*.
The ablative case is employed according to the rule beginning with "anyārāditarartedikśabdāñcūttarapadājāhiyukte" (Pāṇini 2.3.29).
No other attendant should follow or go after him.
Here too, the word "iti" (thus) should be supplied;
it connects with the preceding phrase "he causes [the bridegroom] to recite. ||4||
The excellence of his serenity is a preeminent grace;
"aho" means it is truly wonderful.
Regarding the word "tatra":
the mind, which was eager for Daṇḍakā—eager to go there due to its preoccupation with the afflictions of the sages caused by the Rākṣasas—is situated there;
"is situated" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
In that very place, namely Daṇḍakā, the "command to go" (gamanādeśa)—that is, the order to depart—was issued; the word "was made" (kṛta) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The author of the Nyāsa states: "The root *diś* preceded by the prefix *āṅ* denotes the purpose of the one who directs."
Furthermore, has separation from his beloved and desired [brother] not occurred?
To the question "How so?", he says: "And he..."—that younger brother, the dear child Lakṣmaṇa, is both a follower and one who follows after him.
The word "instructed" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. ||42||
"By good fortune!
[He says: "I have been approved by the noble Rāma; I have been made an object of affection by my mother Madhyamā regarding the command to follow him to the forest.
"Noble one," [he says].
The use of the word "Ārya" is due to her being a dear friend of his mother.
Regarding the word "namaḥ":
since the dative case does not exist in Prākṛta, the genitive case is used for "saṃsārasya."
*Saṃsāra* is the phenomenal expansion for living beings; it is designated as "of the Blessed One" because it serves as the cause for the fulfillment of His own self-deception.
Such [beings] as Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who are endowed with an excess of faith characterized by the fulfillment of their father’s word and so forth, are like *kalpadrumas* (wish-fulfilling trees).
The metaphor of their being *kalpavṛkṣas* arises from the fact that by accepting the departure to the forest, they accomplish what is desired by Him.
"They sprout" means "they are born. The root list (dhātupāṭha) states: "The root *ruha* [is used] in the sense of the birth of a seed and in the sense of manifestation.
Regarding the word "mātula": [it is derived from *mātṛ*, with the suffix *ulac*].
Mātula is the brother of Kaikeyī. Lakṣmaṇa is addressed as Ārya by Bharata because of his seniority. Tāta refers to Daśaratha.
"By good fortune! and "Alas!"—
the meaning is that joy and suffering occur simultaneously.

To the question "Why?", he says: "Without embracing. Without embracing—that is, without hugging—Bharata, as I depart for the Daṇḍaka forest, I have no fortitude; the meaning is that my very existence will cease to be.
According to Amarasimha, "dhṛti" refers to both steadfastness and fortitude.
I do not venture, nor indeed do I resolve, to see this Bharata, who is afflicted by sorrow due to our exile— the departure of Lakṣmaṇa, myself, and him to another land.

The sense is that there is a coexistence of pleasure and pain: at the time of departure, there is joy due to the embrace of Bharata (which was taken as the object in the act of embracing), yet there is sorrow due to the sight of Bharata (which was subsequently mentioned as the object in the act of seeing). Thus, because of this subsequent mention (*anvādeśa*), there is no contradiction in the grammatical designation (*ādeśa*). 43.
"Having become unified"—that is, having come to abide in a single locus in the form of the desired object, namely the consecration of Rāma.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *ayana* [denotes] a dwelling, a path, or the southern and northern courses of the sun.
"All the subjects" refers to the entire guilds of the citizens.
According to Amara: "The constituent elements of the kingdom (*rājyāṅga*) are the subjects (*prakṛti*) and also the guilds of the citizens (*paura-śreṇi*).
Regarding the word *trayyā*:
he who is your son is the protector (*trātā*), that is, the guardian, of the *trayī*, which is the Veda.
The word "becomes" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
By that [person] of such a kind.
Considering that the quality of being a protector of the three Vedas (*trayīrakṣakatva*) and so forth is common to Bharata and others as well, he says: "by Rāmabhadra."
He is both auspicious (*bhadra*) and Rāma; thus, he is Rāmabhadra.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *bhadra* may denote 'auspicious' or 'mangala,' and when used as an adjective, it means 'charming' or 'excellent' in the masculine.
The inversion of the word order, placing *bhadra* last, occurs due to the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahula*) in the grammatical rule.

Alternatively, *Rāmabhadra* means "Rāma who is auspicious" (*bhadra*), formed as a compound according to the rule *upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ*. According to the *Ratnamālā*, the term *bhadra* also refers to a particular type of elephant.

By Your Majesty, the preeminent king, may all people be well-governed—possessing kings, resplendent, endowed with sovereignty, and having their desires fulfilled—meaning their aspirations are completely satisfied by the attainment of worldly objects.
These two phrases are adjectives [qualifying "people"].
By Your favor—that is, through the grace of You, the Supreme Lord—may these things come to pass. The verb *santu* (let them be) is used in the imperative mood (*loṭ*) to express a prayer.
The phrase "thus they inform" is to be connected with what precedes. ||44||
"Priyam" means "dear.
"Kalyāṇaḥ" means "bringing auspiciousness.
Those whose desire or longing (*kāma*) is such are described as "those [women]"; by them, meaning by those subjects acting as the agents.
The learned authorities maintain that bliss (*ānanda*) is the state of being favorable to oneself,
while auspiciousness (*kalyāṇa*) is the state of being favorably disposed toward both oneself and others without distinction.
We have been urged toward the consecration of Rāma, which is dear to us, dear to all, and supremely beloved.
The meaning is "instructed.
Since the root *cud* (to urge) takes two objects (*dvikarmaka*), the word *priyam* also functions as the presentation of an object.

However, even though that is the case, the sense here is: "In this region, there are no ones dear to Rāma (*rāmapriyau*) nor any who are dear to Rāma (*priyarāmau*)," specifically referring to Maitrāvaruṇa and Kauśika, that is, Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra.
The sense is that the very presence of those two is the cause of the delay. ||45||
Regarding the word *parokṣa*:
it means "in the presence of Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra.

In the analysis (*vigraha*) as "that which is beyond (*param*) the eye (*akṣṇaḥ*)," it is an *avyayībhāva* compound by virtue of the rule prescribing the compound-ending suffix [ṭac] in cases such as "pra-tipara-" (Pāṇini 2.1.59).
By virtue of the irregular formation (*nipātana*) "the *liṭ* [perfect tense] is used for the remote past," there is also the substitution of the vowel *u* for the initial [of the root].

The well-performed act—the ritual consisting of Rāma’s consecration—will produce joy and delight for those two, Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra. Therefore, the sense is that even in their absence, there is no fault.
To the question, "Who indeed should perform the duties of the domestic priest and so forth? he replies: "one who knows the mantras.

One who knows the mantras is one who knows those portions of the Veda that illuminate the matters to be performed in the form of consecration, as well as one who knows the secret injunctions regarding the purpose of consecration.
Amara states: "The term *mantra* refers to a specific division of the Veda and to secret counsel."
The Blessed One Vāmadeva was indeed present;
therefore, the meaning is that the office of family priest and so forth was easily obtained. ||46||

"If it be so"—that is, if the aforementioned manner [is applicable], then for that reason, this: "Let the auspicious rites be set in motion," which was previously introduced, means the following. The festival of Jāmadagnya’s victory—the celebration occasioned by Paraśurāma’s triumph—should be made to coincide with, or become a subsidiary part of, the great festival of consecration (abhiṣeka-mahotsava) already under consideration, which intervenes in its midst and consists of Rāma’s own consecration; that is, it should be made dependent upon it.
The intention is that the very rites constituting the limbs of the festival for Paraśurāma’s victory shall themselves become the limbs of Rāma’s consecration.
As it has been stated by the logicians: "Prasaṅga is the subsistence by one [action] upon the assistance produced by the performance of a subsidiary rite intended for another purpose.
This refers to the word "yaḥ" (which).
In this great festival—the great festival consisting of Rāma’s consecration—whatever living being desires something and is in need of a particular object, let that object be given to him.
(The compound is formed by the rule *tṛtīyā-tat-kṛta-* etc. The verb is in the imperative mood (*loṭ*) expressing an injunction.
And this is a distinctive feature of Rāma’s consecration.

Although garments, food, ornaments, and so forth are given even during the festival of the victory over Paraśurāma, there the giving occurs out of a desire to bestow; here, however, the giving is according to the requests of the supplicants—thus, this constitutes a distinctive feature.
"I" [says the speaker].
The word "tāvat" signifies sequence.
The meaning is: "Let others wait; I myself shall be the very first petitioner among those seeking [the goal].
As for the question "By what?"—
"By what?"—the word "object" (*vastu*) is to be supplied as the remainder. "That which... [and so forth].
That which is not far removed—the deposit consisting of the two boons—which has been set down once more as something to be accepted;
for Amara states, "A deposit (*nyāsa*) is a pledge (*upanidhi*) involving a person.
My mother Kaikeyī, acting as my mediator (*madhyamā*), entreats or begs for that deposit of the two boons, according to her desire, without overstepping what is wished for and distinguished.

The sense is: "Having generalized the two boons granted by you through the root *nāthṛ* (to seek) in the senses of 'request,' 'affliction,' 'sovereignty,' and 'blessing,' [the speaker] requests them by establishing them in their specific forms as desired.
O Father, we—myself, Lakṣmaṇa, and the others—are suppliants, full of expectation, through her grace and your favor;
[we] remain so, is the ellipsis. ||47||
"Truthful to their word" (*satyasaṃdhāḥ*): the Raghus, born of the lineage of Raghu, are those whose promises correspond to reality.
According to the *Ratnamālā*, the term *saṃdhā* refers to a limit, a boundary, or a promise.
The word "become" (*bhavanti*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The particle *hi* indicates well-known fact.
And it is said in the *Purāṇaratna*: "For those who come as supplicants driven by necessity never depart disappointed when they have approached the lineage of Kakutstha."
"But for those who seek [a boon], this vow of yours regarding the initiation into the river is praiseworthy; this lineage of yours is such.
Why do you hesitate in this matter? Are you full of doubt?
"Vicikitsā, however, is doubt," according to Amara.

O child, even though you are her messenger—even though you, who are as dear to me as my own life, are the bearer of Kaikeyī’s message—who would covet, or desire, even my life, which is the most cherished of all things?

(The form *dhanāyati* is derived from the root *dhana*, used here for the sense of *gardha* [covetousness] according to the rule: "The forms *aśanāya*, *udanya*, and *dhanāya* are used in the senses of hunger, thirst, and greed," where *dhanāya* is a prescribed present participle form.
The meaning is that because of the desire for him, I would give up even my life, though it is the very object of my own life's regard.
Even though it is not part of the formal categories, that which consists of deceiving beloved people is called adhibala (excessive force). ||48||
How so? It is something entirely different, something other than the consecration of Rāma as intended; it is a journey to the forest, unfit even to be contemplated by the mind.
The word "has occurred" (*apatitam*) is to be supplied here.
"We are destroyed. The word "by fate" is to be supplied. The exclamation "hā" expresses sorrow.
Regarding the word *ikṣvāku*:
it refers to the ornament of the Ikṣvāku lineage, the most excellent of the Ikṣvāku dynasty.
The word *tilaka*, which literally denotes an "ornament for the face," here has the secondary (gauṇī) sense of "most excellent."

She was the wife of King Daśaratha, the enjoyer of the fruits of the actions performed by him; the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the nasal *ṇakāra* are applied according to the rule "patyuno yajñasaṃyoge. Born in that pure royal family—the Kekaya lineage—she was known as Kaikeyī (this is the ellipsis). Being noble, she was virtuous.
"Regarding *gaurī*, [the term] *āryā* applies to three [senses]: one of noble birth, one who follows the right path, and one who is virtuous," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
"Something most grievous (*atyāhita*), which is unfit to be even thought of by the mind and strikes terror into the world.
Amara states: "*Atyāhita* means great fear and an action that disregards one's very life."
*Rākṣasakarma* means an action not common to *rākṣasas*. The suffix *aṇ* is applied to the word *rakṣas* by the rule *tasyedam* [Pāṇini 4.3.120].
How could one perform such an act?
The meaning is that it is not fit to be done.
This is a great wonder, a great marvel for us;
the word "exists" (bhavati) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. ||49||
Regarding "truthfulness":
"O Father," and so forth. This means:
if you remain true to your promise.
This is the second person plural form of the imperative (*loṭ*) from the root *sthā* (to stand).
The meaning is: "If you do not forget what was stated immediately following [the previous verse], namely, 'For Rāghava is true to his word.
Now, you are indeed dearer to him than even his own life.
"In separation from you, my life would come to an end;
therefore, in a situation where life is at stake, speaking untruth is not a fault—this is the established limit of the scriptures. To this, he says: "O Rāma! [meaning] if Rāma is dear to you.
The meaning is: "If it is desired.
The meaning of the phrase "even if you were my messenger," and so forth, which was stated immediately below, is that it should not be forgotten.
The underlying intention is: "If you do not grant me permission to go to the forest, Rāma himself will become difficult for you to attain."
The two occurrences of the word "vā" (or) indicate an alternative. "Then, be gracious to me; grant me your favor.
To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "O Mother."
This is the syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*).
May my mother, Madhyamā, have her desires fulfilled—that is, may she have her wishes completely satisfied through the attainment of the objects of her desire.
The *loṭ* suffix is used here in the sense of a prayer (*prārthanā*).
Because the word "me" (me) is a constituent part of the preceding sentence ["prasīdeta"], it does not constitute the beginning of a new sentence. ||50||
"Let it be so. This means: "Let it be in the manner stated by [the words] 'let it be by one,' and so forth.
What is the recourse?
The meaning is that without this, there is no other means for obtaining Rāma.
For if this is so, our recovery of Rāma may be possible at some point in the future;
otherwise, it would not be so—this is the underlying intention.
Regarding the word "putra" (son):

it has been transferred to the son because of the weakening of the [father's] physical basis; thus, it came of its own accord, rather than being deposited by them intentionally through the mind. This is the meaning.
The meaning is: "by those who possess such fortune (lakṣmī)," that is, by those described in that way.
The suffix *kap* is applied because the word begins with *uraḥ* and so forth.
According to the *Ratnamālā*, "Lakṣmī means prosperity, the goddess Ramā, and beauty."
The ellipsis is "it came to pass that the vow of the forest-dwellers was undertaken by the elder Ikṣvākus.

For it was only when these factors— the possession of sons by the ancestors, the enjoyment of the kingdom, and the onset of old age characterized by physical infirmity— were all present together that the undertaking of the forest-dweller's vow occurred.
But for you, even in the absence of any of those [qualities], the observance of the forest-dweller's vow has arisen; thus, a great distinction between you and them has come about.
By the word "vow" (vrata), there is an exclusion of improper conduct. ||51||
"Child!
[This is said] solely by the command of the guru, that is, by the command of the father-in-law. "Alas, child! [This is said.]

The address "O child" (*vatse*) is used with the intention of regarding her as a daughter, according to the statement: "But for us, the daughter of Janaka is indeed our own daughter. She is "wearing the bracelet," meaning she still possesses the wedding bracelet;
for, according to the *Smṛti* texts beginning with "When the auspicious rite has been completed," the removal of the bracelet is prescribed only after the completion of the auspicious ceremony.

However, because the accomplishment of the auspicious event was not understood while the bracelet was still on [her hand], the intensity of her grief—that she had been offered as a sacrifice to the Rākṣasas in the very midst of that auspicious occasion—is illuminated by the exclamation "hā" (alas).
Although it was stated in the second act that "the queens have gathered for the removal of the bracelets," the intent nevertheless lies in the extreme proximity of the time of the auspicious event.
As it is said: "Upāyana, upagrāhya, upahāra, and likewise upadā [are synonyms for a gift]."
"Atyāpanna" means having fallen into an extreme calamity. It is considered how—by what manner—this state of being afflicted will come to an end.
According to Amara: "The word *nāma* is used in the senses of manifestation, possibility, anger, approach, and reproach."
The sense is that an obstacle to my departure for the forest is likely to arise from the imminent loss of life of my elders. "In such a manner" means at the very moment of its occurrence.
"Even at that moment, there may be an initial onset," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
This means prior to the full realization of what is destined to happen.
"Agitation" (*saṃvega*) refers to the flurry caused by *karuṇa*—the sorrow arising from separation from a beloved person—as well as by *sneha*, the affection that is its cause.
This means "excess" (*atiśaya*).
According to Amara, "saṃvega" and "saṃbhrama" are synonyms.
The meaning is that such [an excess] is the cause of fainting and other such states.
"What is to be done here? What is to be done in this state of fainting?
The word *kim* is used in the sense of censure;
the meaning is that no delay in going to the forest should be made.
He asks "Why? and says: "It was forbidden.
By Ambā Kaikeyī, the delay of time—the procrastination regarding the departure for the forest—was forbidden;
that is to say, it was prohibited.
The meaning is that it is stated in the letter: "Let Rāma go to the Daṇḍaka forest by some other means, avoiding any delay.
In considering the relative strength of the father’s fainting fit and the mother’s command, the mother’s command is more powerful;
for according to the scripture, "A mother exceeds a father tenfold in terms of venerability."

For this very reason, in this section of the Rāmāyaṇa, there is the speech of Rāma: "Surely, Kaikeyī, you do not perceive any virtue in me, since you spoke thus to the King, even though you are my sovereign.
For the King is merely a master [in name].
The intention is that Kaikeyī is superior in power;
having this in mind, he says: "Therefore, enough.
"Tat" means "therefore."
The meaning is that the mother’s command is more powerful.
"Enough with this timidity born of affection" means that there is nothing impossible for one impelled by paternal love.
"Excellent!"—the repetition [of this word] indicates agreement.
"O you whose devotion (*niṣṭhā*)—that is, whose intent—is fixed upon conduct (*ācāra*), namely the performance of your mother's command": such is the vocative address to him.
"Niṣṭhā [is used] in the sense of destruction, accomplishment, end, intent, and request," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
"Excellent, excellent!"— the meaning is that you have spoken correctly.
"Non-human" (*amanuṣya*):

Your mental strength—the root of which is the investigation into the relative strength and weakness regarding what ought and ought not to be done—is the cause for abandoning your venerable elders who are otherwise difficult to forsake; it is like that of a non-human, being unlike that of a human.
That is to say, it is transcendent (*lokottara*).
According to Amara, "sāra" means strength and the solid core.

The repetition of "mātula, mātula" is used for contempt. This is a sarcastic remark by Kṣapaṇaka, implying that this which Kaikeyī desires is "fitting"—that is, worthy and appropriate—for your family.
The meaning is "not corresponding.

The two words *yukta* (suitable) and *sadṛśa* (similar) both function to express the meaning of the single term *anurūpa*. As it has been stated by the learned: "Correspondence (*anurūpatva*) consists in being excellent while possessing suitability, which is to say, similarity."
"Udbhrānta" means agitated or moved; the suffix *kta* is used in the active sense (*kartari*) according to the rule "gatyarthākarmaka... from the root *bhramu* (to wander/move).
"Saṃpramugdhaḥ" means I have fainted or am utterly bewildered.
The suffix *ka* is used as before.
"O child" (*vatsa*) is an address to Bharata.
"Lord" (*pati*).
"O sister-in-law," and so forth.
By this intention of granting two boons, her husband, her own master Daśaratha, "goes into the mouth of death"—that is, he will meet his end.
The use of the present tense (*laṭ*) here indicates proximity to the present moment.
This pair of sons, consisting of the two sons Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, acting as the agent—
[the phrase] "is going to the forest" is to be supplied;
the meaning is that they will go.

Regarding the statement, "I perceive no difference between Rāma and Bharata," the term "pair of sons" (*sutayugam*) is used with reference to Kaikeyī’s prior intention. Furthermore, the word *vadhūṭī* denotes one who has reached the onset of youth;
as the grammarians have stated: "The words *vadhūṭī* and *ciraṇṭī* signify a young woman."
"‘A young wife who supports her husband and remains faithful to her family is a woman who is not unchaste’—thus says the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*.
‘Varākī’ means pitiable;
the suffix *ṣākan* is applied to the root *vṛṅ* according to the rule beginning with ‘jalpabhikṣa-’."
The form [is derived] by adding the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* due to the presence of the phoneme *ṣ*; it means "Sītā. "From the *rakṣasas*" means from the Rākṣasas.

Because the formation of a compound with the word *bali* is prescribed by the rule "caturthī tadartha-" (Pāṇini 2.1.36) and others, the fourth case (*caturthī*) is used in connection with the word *bali*.
[The phrase] "like a *bali*" means like an offering (*upahāra*).
Amara states: "The word *bali* is masculine when meaning a tax or an offering; it is feminine when derived from a limb of a living being."
It has been directed and intended;
the word "cast" (prakṣiptā) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
The sense is that by the phrase "only Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa," Sītā was excluded from the prohibition against following Rāma.
Furthermore, the world—the people—is "without support" (nirālamba), meaning "without refuge" (nirāśraya);
the word "made" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
It is said to be "without support" in consideration of Bharata’s own nature, as expressed in the statement: "Both the kingdom and I belong to Rāma."
