Furthermore, why should our family be stained by infamy—that is, by a reputation contrary to the glory inherited through the lineage?
For it is said: "If that [glory] has come down through the lineage, it is called 'fame' (yaśas).
And as it is stated: "Resemblance, non-existence, otherness, and deficiency [are the grounds for comparison]."

Since it has been stated that "the meanings of the negative particle (nañ) are proclaimed to be sixfold: non-praise, contradiction, and so forth," the negative particle here carries the sense of the opposite.
"Enveloped" (parivṛta); the ellipsis is to be supplied as "it became pervaded."
The sense is that infamy has arisen for our lineage, which is renowned in the Vedanta as "Aśvapati, the Kekaya, is indeed my very self Vaiśvānara.
Because this is so, the wickedness—the evil intellect—of my own sister, born of the same womb, causes the entire world to become *viklava*, that is, utterly distraught.
Amara states: "The word *viklava* may mean one who is *vihvala* (distraught)."
In order to reveal your own fault, you did not say "my mother," but instead said "my sister. (52)
"By good fortune!
[said] by the noble father-in-law;
there is also a reading "by the noble mother-in-law."
"By my mother-in-law Kaikeyī"—this is the meaning.
She is called "Āryā" because she is the wife of his elder brother;
being accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa...
Regarding the word "eṣa" (this):

in this verse, amidst the sorrow of separation from us, "this father" refers to Daśaratha; and "the fathers" refers to Janaka and the others. They are so described because they have "dear ones"—that is, beloved offspring—namely myself, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā.
Sītā’s status as an offspring should be understood in the manner previously explained.
The mothers, Kausalyā and the others, are referred to in the plural because even Kaikeyī’s grief of resentment is unavoidable;
or rather, it is intended to include the remaining more than a hundred wives of Daśaratha.
They must be comforted by you alone.
The meaning is that they should be made to diminish their grief.
Now, as to why you offer consolation while saying "you must not depart," he replies: "We have gone.
The meaning is: "we shall not return."
Alternatively, he says "We have gone" in response to the question: "But surely Bharata and Śatrughna should be comforted?
Here, because Bharata and Śatrughna are incapable of performing the funeral rites, they are as good as having already departed. ||53||
"O Venerable One!
What shall I do now? Shall I follow him, or shall I do something else entirely?"—the meaning is: "In this state of doubt, please give me a decision.
[He addresses him as] "Rāmabhadra."

The meaning is: "Look upon me, who have followed you into the forest as your footman to serve at your feet, though you do not acknowledge me. The suffix *ṇvul* is used here according to the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām*.
[Therefore,] look upon me.
The meaning is: "Please grant your consent with a slight sidelong glance.
As for "nanu": *nanu* is used either as a form of address or for emphasis.
According to Amara, "nanu" is used in the senses of inquiry, determination, permission, conciliation, and address.

The "guru-niyoga"—the father’s command—regarding the protection of the *varṇas*, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others, and the *āśramas*, such as studentship (*brahmacarya*) and the rest, belongs to this Bharata.
The meaning of the conjunction is that just as there was a guru-niyoga for me to go to the forest, so too is there a guru-niyoga for Bharata to protect the *varṇas* and *āśramas*.
Regarding "of Lakṣmaṇa":
that refers to the protection of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama). What is the point here?

In this matter, regarding an object enjoined by the father, what is one's own preference? The meaning is: what arbitrary will can be a determining authority? The word "kim" (what) is used here in the sense of censure.
"Only this much" means: only in following you;
the sense is that elsewhere, my own inclination is not the motivating factor.
"It is possible":
while I remain alive and present, it is possible for you, or another such as Lakṣmaṇa, [to fulfill] the matter or the command of the father that was enjoined or ordered by him.
The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāve*).
The term *pitṛniyuktam* may end either in the accusative or the nominative case.
In the first instance, the meaning is that "transgression of the action enjoined by the father is possible.
In the second instance, it refers either to the object enjoined by the father or to the injunction itself.
The meaning is: "the object of the power of transgression.
In the word *śakyam* (possible), the negative sense is contained by means of an interrogative intonation (*kākū*).
Thus, for you too, following me would be difficult; and for Lakṣmaṇa and others as well, the protection of the castes and stages of life according to your will would be difficult.
It is said that this is because I am the wielder of punishment over the three who have transgressed their father’s command;
"ha!"— I have been abandoned!
The meaning is that [the departure] is forbidden because of the prohibition against following [him].
"Of little fortune" means one whose merit yields only meager fruit; the sense is that I am of little fortune because I have become an object of Kaikeyī’s greed for the kingdom.
"O child," [he says].
"Thus far," it is said;
this is a general indication of what is to be stated. "Having whispered into the ear" means speaking into the ear in a low voice.
"Afterwards, his light will shine forth.
'O Rāmabhadra'—
this Bharata will speak in the manner that is about to be described."

A pair of golden sandals—*tapanīyopānahau*, meaning "sandals made of *tapanīya* gold" (as stated in the *Amara-kośa*: "*tapanīyaṃ śātakumbham*")—was sent by the great sage named Śarabhaṅga, who was endowed with the excellence of knowledge described by the Blessed One in the passage beginning with "the origin and the dissolution... (*utpattiṃ pralayaṃ caiva*). [The word for the sandals is] *pādukā*.
"pādūrupānatstrī" (sandals are feminine), according to Amara.
"May my noble elder brother Rāma graciously grant me that pair of sandals"—the verb *prasādīkarotu* is used in the imperative (*loṭ*) in the sense of a request, meaning "may he give it as a favor.
This connects with the preceding phrase, "thus he makes his request."
"Tad" means that; having "unmucya" [removed] the pair of sandals, that is, having separated them from the feet,
"gṛhāṇa" means take possession of them.
"Alas, Noble Lady!"— the meaning is that he suffers, thinking, "Why do you dismiss me by merely giving me these sandals?"—
"Child!"— [he says].
"By touching my feet":
the suffix *ṇvul* is applied here in the sense of the verbal root's meaning, namely "one who touches. Thus, *spṛṣṭikā* means "touching."

"By means of touching my feet" (*matpādayoḥ spṛṣṭikā*) refers to the act of touching my feet. The meaning is: "If you persist in following me, then you are acting treacherously toward me; therefore, turn back on account of this—namely, by the cause of touching my feet. Alternatively, *matpādaspṛṣṭikā* refers to that oath-taking ceremony in which my feet are touched.

Because *āhitāgni* and others belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* words, the past participle ending (*niṣṭhā*) is placed at the end [of the compound]. The suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*). Thus, it becomes *matpādaspṛṣṭikā*.
The substitution of *i* [for *ai*] occurs by the rule "pratyayasthāt.
The meaning is: "by means of the act of swearing, characterized by touching my feet.
*Sapadi* means at that very moment.
"Immediately, at once, at that very moment"—thus says Amara. "Sambhāvaya" means "make them come into being"; the sense is: "prevent their non-occurrence."
Long since they have been utterly bewildered and fainted.
Regarding "in Nandigrāma":
the meaning is that until the noble Rāma returns, I shall wear matted hair and, having consecrated the noble one's sandals in Nandigrāma, I shall protect the earth. ||54||
"Baṣpastambham" means they simulate or imitate the state of being paralyzed by tears;
"nocchvasitaḥ" means they do not breathe out. In the word "śvasitaḥ," there is the augment *iṭ* for the *t* of the *laṅ* substitute [ending] according to the rule "rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke."
She fans him; that is to say, she acts out that gesture.
"Alas! Alas! [she cries].
"I am robbed; my purpose is destroyed.
Regarding "the vital breaths": my vital breaths depart, meaning they begin to go away.
Furthermore, I am shrouded—that is, pervaded—by *tamas*, which is ignorance.

Moreover, there are new (*apūrva*) and unprecedented (*nava*) pains (*rujaḥ*), that is, diseases (*vyādhayaḥ*), which cut into the vital points (*marmacchidaḥ*), piercing the seats of the life-breaths (*prāṇasthāna*).
As Amara states: "The words *strī*, *rug*, *rujā*, *upatāpa*, *roga*, *vyādhi*, *gada*, and *āmaya* all denote disease."
They spread forth, meaning they arise without interruption.
Since this is so, therefore place the moon of your son’s face—the moon of your own face—near my eyes; bring it close to my sight.
Furthermore, grant me your voice; speak these words: "I have desisted from going to the forest."
Furthermore, while I am suddenly and unexpectedly pained by the sorrow of separation from you, may you not be merciless—may you not be devoid of compassion toward me.
(The use of the *luṅ* suffix is in the sense of the optative [*liṅ*] according to the rule *māṅi luṅ*. ||55||
"Sonmādam" means acting out madness, which is a derangement of the mind; the meaning is that he enters while performing this. "Kva viśāmi? means "Where shall I enter? or "Into what shall I go?"
"Of meager fortune" means one of little luck.
According to Amara: "Daiva, diṣṭa, bhāgadheya, bhāgya, niyati, and vidhi are synonyms for destiny (feminine).
Being thus overwhelmed...
Regarding the word *ekībhūya*:

"O child Rāmabhadra, although [the world] consists of many flavors (*anekarasa*) and has diverse tastes (*bhinnaruci*)," according to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *rasa* refers to passion (*rāga*), fluidity (*drava*), and joy (*harṣa*)."
Having become one, having come to have a single taste, and having come to have a single desire with you, it was "destroyed"—
meaning, afflicted. It is described as such because the cry of lamentation— the sound of weeping— was released and uttered through a single action, that is, a single effort.
"Confused as to what this might be, [the place] where women and men—meaning females and males—are devoid of certainty; such is the meaning.
In the analysis of the compound *nāryaśca narāśca* (women and men), it is a *itaretarayoga-dvandva*.
By the rule of the *Śārṅgarava*-group, *nṛnarayor vṛddhiśca*, the word *nārī* is derived from the root *nṛ* by adding the suffix *ṅīn* and applying the vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*)."
This is because of the statement in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Where there is a distinction beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

For this very reason, even the usage "Hari consists of men and women" is correct. Furthermore, the city of Mithilā is called "your city" with the intention that "this entire city of yours is the sovereign power (*aiśvarya*) of the son-in-law. Thus, it is said that Mithilā is your city.
Alternatively:
the word *tvat* is a separate term ending in the ablative case.

This city, the city of Mithilā, having suddenly—that is, quickly—come about otherwise than it was, has become characterized by a state of grief that is distinct from the nature of joy produced by the festivities currently underway; thus it has fallen into calamity.
The root *pad* means "to go," but its function here is according to the stated meaning due to the influence of the prefix (*upasarga*).
In that city, [it was filled] with dense, thick tears—that is, eye-water;
for the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *bāṣpa* refers to eye-water and heat."
Although the word *bāṣpa* (steam/mist) denotes something specific, through its juxtaposition with the word *ambu* (water), it refers only to its qualifying attribute [moisture].
Regarding the word *kardamiteṣu*, it means "in those that have become muddy.
Amara states: "The words *paṅka*, *śāda*, and *kardama* are masculine or neuter [synonyms for mud]."
On the paths, that is, on the roads, there is foul weather; this is the ellipsis. "A day covered by clouds is called *durdina*," according to Amarasimha. ||56||
"O child!
means "be obedient," that is to say,
"desire [to follow my will]."
The suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle ending) is applied to the root *śam* according to the rule "āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca" (Pāṇini 3.3.132).
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because they are gurus.
They are to be followed by me for the purpose of following; they are not those who follow.
The meaning is that he is not worthy to follow me. He states another reason as well: "with himself as the third. The word "by me" is to be supplied [as the object].
"There are two others and I am the third;
I must go in such a manner"—this is the meaning of the mother's instruction.
The implication is based on the statement: "No one other than the retinue consisting solely of Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa shall follow."

By the two rules— the sūtra and the vārttika stating "and [the word] 'ātman'," and "it should be stated that [there is no elision] when 'pūraṇa' follows"— there is no elision (aluk) of the third case ending.
"What am I?"— here the word *kim* is used in the sense of censure.
The meaning is: "I am not going alone.
According to Amarasimha, "eka" means "principal" or "not alone. "Sabālavṛddhāḥ" means accompanied by children and the elderly.
By the rule "vopasarjanasya," the word *saha* undergoes the substitution *sa-* [for its initial *sa-*]. The *prakṛtis* are the citizens.
Regarding the word *skandha*:
"O child, those are the Sāketa residents of Ayodhyā.
These are great Brāhmaṇas, most venerable, and twice-born ones who perform the six duties (*ṣaṭkarmacarita*).
According to Amara: 'A *vipra* is a *brāhmaṇa*, one who is joined with the six duties such as sacrifice and so forth.'"

"Though they were elders" means that even though they possessed the threefold type of elderliness mentioned in the verse: "Those twice-born are considered elders in three ways: by knowledge, by age, and by spiritual power."

They were those upon whose shoulders rested heaps—that is, collections—of sacrificial vessels such as the *sruc* and *camasa*; they were those who carried the *gārhapatya* and other sacred fires held by their following wives; and they were those who had already set out the sacrificial cows (*homadhenu*)—cows serving as the source of the curds, milk, clarified butter, and clotted milk required for the oblations.
Because the cows were incapable of running, they were dispatched beforehand along with the Maithilas—the Brahmins whose ancestral home (*abhijana*) was Mithilā.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied here according to the rule "so'syābhijanaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.3.91) to the words *sāketa* and *mithilā*.
They are called "Sāketas" because of their arrival for Sītā’s wedding; thus it is said, "the Sāketas together with the Maithilas."
By means of their own umbrellas— those acquired through the *vājapeya*, that is, those obtained by performing the *vājapeya* sacrifice;
for it is established in the scriptures that those who have performed the *vājapeya* sacrifice must carry an umbrella.
They run—that is, they move swiftly—in order to ward off the sun’s rays so that they shall not fall upon you;
in the root *sṛ* (meaning "to go"), the substitution of *dhāv* occurs in the sense of swift movement according to the rule beginning with *pāghrā*.
The underlying meaning is that they even renounce the injunction, "One should not descend [from the bed] toward anyone for as long as one lives," for your sake.
This has been stated in the glorious Rāmāyaṇa: "These fires, mounted upon the shoulders of the twice-born, follow after you;
behold these umbrellas of ours, arising from the Vājapeya sacrifice, following behind us like clouds at the end of the rainy season."
"For you, who are oppressed by the sun and deprived of an unobstructed parasol,
we shall provide shade with our own Vājapeya umbrellas.
For our intellect, which constantly follows the Vedic mantras,"
"O child, it was for your sake that she was made to follow you into exile in the forest. || 57 ||
Regarding the term *mātula*:
it refers to elders such as one's father or maternal uncle. As for the word *guru*, it denotes a priest who performs the *niṣeka* and other rites, or the planet Jupiter (*bṛhaspati*).

"In the case of father and others, [the suffix *kha* is used] after words meaning 'great,' 'renowned,' 'difficult to support,' and 'light'—these three"—so says the *Ratnamālā*. This is because of the violation of the scriptural injunctions consisting of the duty to obey the words of elders and the obligation to follow one's elders, which are as firm as iron.
The ablative case is used according to the rule "bhītrārthānām... (Pāṇini 1.4.25).
"Be gracious; show favor.
He states the fruit of that [favor]: "Let it be turned back. "The great assembly" refers to the assembly of great Brahmins from Sāketa and Mithilā.
"Let [it] be turned back from me"— this is the ellipsis. Thus he bows down, seeking refuge.
The core meaning is that the characteristic of one who has come for refuge is indeed difficult for anyone to resist.
"Arise, arise!"—the repetition indicates urgency.
"Having awakened [him]" means...
The word "return" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "In some place" means in a location difficult even for the mind to conceive.
"You"—O mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa, I address you.
I also command you to follow me.
O daughter of the King of Videha, daughter of Sīradhvaja, I take my leave of you.

I am a sinner; having desisted from following [you], I—filled with the demerit consisting of the failure to perform the act of prostration to Rāma, which was the cause for my own desisting—now turn back from the pursuit.
May there be welfare for you two;
[this is expressed] in the optative mood (loṭ) used for benediction. ||58||
Having turned back while weeping—
here, "he said" is the ellipsis.
"Aho nu khalu bhoḥ" is a collection of particles expressing astonishment.
Regarding the phrase "in every manvantara":

this [conduct] is a purifier—that is, a cause of purification—for the worlds, beginning with Satyaloka; it pertains to *cāritra*, meaning virtuous conduct such as the fulfillment of one's father’s word.
The suffix *ṇitran* is applied according to the rule "after the root *car*, in the sense of conduct."
*Pañcikā* means expansion or manifestation.
The suffix *ṇvul* is applied according to the meanings of the roots *paci* (in the sense of expansion) and *paci* (in the sense of making manifest), as indicated by their respective verbal roots.
Femininity is established by the rule *strībhāvādāvaniktiṇṇvul*.

"In every Manvantara"—that is, at each successive Manvantara. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). The optional substitution of *am* for the case-ending occurs by virtue of the inclusion of the term "optionally" (*bahula*) in the rule *tṛtīyāsaptamyorbahulam*.

"A manvantara, however, consists of seventy-one divine yugas," according to Amara. By "beings" (bhūtaiḥ) is meant the classes of living creatures such as gods and others. "Bhūta" [is used] in the sense of what is right, what is equal, what has occurred, and also in the sense of the past and the factual.
"In the sense of a weak being, a piśāca, the earth, etc., or a living creature," so says the *Ratnamālā*.
Being given and being celebrated through the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa* and other works, it will "move about," that is, it will pervade [the world].
The word *prāyas* is used here in the sense of probability.
As it is said in such expressions as "I think," "I suspect," "certainly," or "most likely," *saṃbhāvanā* (possibility) is a doubt in which one alternative is predominant. ||59||
"How so?"—
the meaning is "to the one who makes his residence in the city called Śṛṅgavera.

The vowel lengthening (vṛddhi) occurs because the suffix *tavyat* is treated as having the marker *ṇi* by the rule "The suffix *tavyat* is added after the root *vas*, and it is *ṇit* when denoting the agent."
Of the Rākṣasa Virādha— the assailant and tormentor of the Niṣādas, the fishermen, and of Guha (by name), the lord of those bordering regions extending to Citrakūṭa;

[the genitive case is used] from the *karmadhāraya* compound "Virādha and he is a Rākṣasa," since the specific term functions as an adjective (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the general term, according to the rule "an adjective is compounded with the noun it qualifies" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*)."
The prohibition of a compound with a genitive case-ending when followed by a word in apposition refers specifically to compounds where the case-ending is already established.
"The wicked conduct" means the ignoble behavior of the Noble One has been described; this was reminded [to Rāma] by Lakṣmaṇa.
In that regard, Rāma’s speech begins with "tena hi," etc.
On account of that reason stated by Guha, for the sake of the destruction—that is, the death—of the one named Virādha, who was nearly slain;
[the word] "alpe" (in the case of a small amount) is used here in the sense of "kaḥ" (who?).
For the purpose of crushing, that is, for the purpose of killing.
" *Ghāta*, *unmātha*, and *vadha* [are synonyms for killing]," according to Amara.

He is so described because he possesses a "prayoga"—meaning a specific field—that is "sannikṛṣṭa," or situated nearby; and he is so described because his "mekhalās"—meaning slopes—along with which the Mandākinī is connected, are "pavitra," or perfectly pure.
According to the Viśva lexicon: "The word *mekhalā* may refer to the hilt of a sword, a girdle, or the slopes of a mountain."
The phrase "having approached Mount Citrakūṭa" is to be connected with what follows later.
Regarding the word "ṛṣibhiḥ":
it refers to that [river] whose sacred waters (tīrtha) are frequented and served by sages and seers for the purpose of destroying the rākṣasas. Such is her description.
Although the word *tīrtha*—meaning "water"—is commonly used by sages, here it refers solely to the substantive [the place].

Having reached Daṇḍakā, I shall go to—that is, reach—Janasthāna, which is characterized by the presence of the king of vultures, sequentially through the previously mentioned locations or simultaneously. The use of the optative (*liṅ*) expresses a wish.

Here too, because the character of the king of vultures, who is to enter at the beginning of the next act, is indicated by a character from the end of the previous act, this is called an *aṅkāsyaka*. (60)
Vīrarāghava, a descendant of Vādhūla residing in Mahīsāra,
has composed the fourth act of the Mahāvīracarita.
Thus ends the fourth act in the commentary on the Mahāvīracarita, titled Bhāvapradyotinī, composed by Vādhūla Vīrarāghava, whose name begins with the syllable Aṇṇā.
Act Five.

Now, the poet, describing the hope for attainment (*prāptyāśā*) through the form of the *patākā* (the secondary plot) consisting of the stories of Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa, as well as through the apprehension of disaster (*apāyaśaṅkā*) resulting from the slaying of Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and others, and the apprehension of disaster resulting from the account of Jaṭāyu, again describes the *garbhasandhi* (the juncture of development) with the fifth act. Therein, he first states the *viṣkambha* (interlude) with the words: "Then enters Saṃpāti," and so forth.
Saṃpāti is the elder brother of Jaṭāyu.
"Surely" (*nūnam*) is used here in the sense of a conjecture.
"The dear one, Jaṭāyu"—
he is called "dear one" (*vatsa*) because he is the younger brother.
"Malayakandara" refers to a cave in the Malaya mountains; according to Amara, "darī" and "kandara" are feminine terms for a cave. "Kulāya" means a nest, which is my own.
"Kulāya means a nest (nīḍa), not feminine," according to Amara.
He "approaches" (upāsīdati) means he reaches [it] by drawing near.
"By turn" (paryāyāt).
"In turn" means by succession; according to Amara, "paryāya" refers to an occasion or a sequence.
It refers to the contraction and expansion of the wings during the processes of dissolution and manifestation.
*Sam* is an indeclinable meaning "unification" (*ekīkāra*).
*Saṃvarta* means "contraction" (*saṃvartana*);
the result is "shrinking" (*saṃkoca*).

Those [rays] by which the quarters of the sky were seen for a moment and then vanished while unseen are so described. The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent according to the rule "ṇaśa adarśane" (Pāṇini 3.4.52) and "gatyarthākarmaka-" (Pāṇini 3.4.72).
"Being seen for a moment occurs when they contract; being vanished for a moment occurs when they expand."

"The intellect of discernment [perceives] the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) as the master of the directions among winged creatures. Furthermore, they are those by whom the lightnings—those which have been made like mist, rendered insignificant like snow-mountains, and released, distributed, shaken, and agitated from the clouds—are thus described as "flickering" or "moving" or "shining" clearly and manifestly (*vyakta-sphuṭa*).
When the clouds have been cleared away by the wind from his wings, the lightnings manifest their flickering due to being without support.
Moreover, they are scattered and dispersed from afar (*ārāt*).

In the word *kaṇāt*, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) to the root *kṛ* (meaning "to scatter"). The substitution of *na* for the final *t* of the past participle suffix occurs according to the rule *radābhyām*.
The term *kaṇāt* means "even from a tiny particle" (*leśāt*).
According to Amara, "lavaleśakaṇāṇavaḥ" [mean] particles, fragments, drops, and atoms.

Those [clouds] by which the rows—meaning the successions—of the heavy masses of rocks, that is, the mountain ranges, have been reduced to mere particles (kaṇīkṛta) and rendered into fragments (leśīkṛta), are described as such.
According to Amara, "acalaśailaśiloccayāḥ" [mean] immovable mountains and peaks.
Because they share the same meaning, the word *grāvoccaya* also denotes a mountain.
In the phrase "pāṣāṇa-prastara-grāva," the word *grāva* here signifies a stone.
*Śyaineya* refers to the son of Śyenī.
This is the meaning of Jaṭāyu’s words.
According to Amarasimha, "pattrī" means "śyena" (hawk/falcon).
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule "jāter astrī-".
The suffix *ḍhak* is applied according to the rule "from feminine nouns, *ḍhak*.
"The hawk gave birth to hawks and vultures of great splendor;
from him [Aruṇa] I was born, and Saṃpāti is my elder brother."
"Know me as Jaṭāyu, the son of Śyenī, O subduer of enemies"—thus indeed was it said by Jaṭāyu in the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*.
"The shaking of the great wings (patattra)—that is, the flapping of the feathers (pakṣa). According to Amara: "Garut, pakṣa, chada, patra, patattra, and tanūruha [are synonyms for wing]."
From the root *dhūñ* "to shake," listed in the *svādi* group, the suffix *ktin* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) to form the feminine noun.
They proclaim—that is, they cause one to infer—the arrival of Jaṭāyu.
There is also a reading: "they make known" (*prajñāpayanti*).
The inference based on signs (liṅgābhyūhana) is here called the dramatic element (saṃdhy-aṅga) named "Inference" (anumāna). ||1||
"Dūre" (far away):

[This refers to] that [ocean] whose waters are "ullolāni"—meaning extremely agitated, shattered, and driven from their places by the wind of the speed of Jaṭāyu’s great wings, as described in the verse beginning with "of the son of Śyenī, by the shaking of his great wings"; and which has its "vāḍava" fire—the submarine fire—surging or rising up intensely "dūram" (to a great distance), because [the ocean] is the friend of the Wind-god. This is the intended meaning.

The netherworld (pātāla) is being filled— that is, blown up— by the forceful wind generated by the speed of Jaṭāyu, which has entered through the cavities of the ocean, the gaps made manifest due to the depletion of its waters;
that netherworld, acting as the agent [of filling],
[was once] from the throat-cavity— the opening of the neck— of the Vaikuṇṭha-boar, the primordial Boar (Ādivarāha).
"Kuhara," "vivara," and "bila" mean a cave or hole, according to Amara.
"Sphāra" means extensive or abundant, as in "sphāraṃ bhūyaśca bhūri ca," according to Amara.
Like a roar—that is, like a sound—it resounds or makes a noise fiercely and cruelly, like a rain-cloud in an unseasonable night of universal dissolution (pralaya), falling unexpectedly.
The word *yat* (which) that has been mentioned does not require the word *tat* (that).
According to Amarasimha: "The word *kāṇḍa*—not feminine—denotes a staff, an arrow, a reed, a section, an opportunity, and water.
Two similes are employed here with the intention of expressing an excess of ferocity. ||2||
Regarding the word *kāverī*: he whose girdle—the slopes or hips (*nitamba*)—is encircled by the Kāverī is so described.
According to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *mekhalā* refers to the hilt of a sword, a girdle, a mountain slope, and the buttocks."
On this ridge, this plateau of Mount Malaya—[Amara states:

*snu*, *prastha*, and *sānu* are synonyms for a mountain’s tableland, used in the masculine and neuter]—I descend from the sky, from the atmosphere. On this ridge of Mount Malaya dwells my noble elder brother, the son of Kaśyapa; though separated by distance, he is my offspring according to the definition of the term.
From the word *kaśyapa*, the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* is applied in the sense of offspring;
*śakunta* means a bird; that is to say, Saṃpāti.
"Deprived of wings" means having one's wings clipped;
this qualification applies to both [the bird and the mountain].
"Another, like a lord of mountains," means he dwells like another mountain distinct from Malaya, which serves as his abode.
The meaning is that he stands like a mountain upon a mountain.
The reason for his wings being separated will be stated later. ||3||
"Relaxing [the wings]" means:

having grasped and reached the wings, she relaxes them—that is, makes them limp—due to the exhaustion of the effort of flying. "Distress" (ārti) refers to the pain caused by the intensity of the exertion for the purpose of flying; this has arisen even in me.
The word "api" (even/also) indicates that such distress is not normally appropriate for her.
For instance:
[it refers to] the "all-pervading" (vibhu), which possesses the causal power for the transformation, decay, and so forth of objects;
or else, it is called "all-pervading" according to the view that [space and time] are distinct from the Lord (Īśvara).
Alternatively, according to the statement "I am Time among those who measure time," the meaning is that of the Blessed One whose body is Time.
"Old age" (jarā) refers to a state of frailty resulting from the decline of vitality.
This is a metaphorical identification of the power (śakti) with its effect (kārya).

The remainder [of the sentence] is that *śakti*—meaning capacity—is the cause of obstruction for other capacities, such as the capacity for flying and so forth; it renders the production of the effect impossible. ||4||
Regarding the word "tat": in the *manvantaras*, he is ancient (*purāṇa*), meaning long-standing;
as Amara states: "A *manvantara* consists of seventy-one divine *yugas*."

Because of his arising and coming from that place, this king of vultures, Saṃpāti, is present here—the word "is" being understood as the ellipsis. Regarding the forms of pronouns: "the form *idam* refers to what is perceptible, while *etad* refers to what is very near."
Since it has been stated, "One should understand that *adas* refers to what is remote, while *tat* refers to what is beyond the senses," the word *idam* denotes what is proximate.
"Oh, how wonderful is this brotherly affection! How marvelous is the love for me, your brother!"—if one asks why this is so, he says: "In the city... and so forth.
This elder brother of mine, Saṃpāti, in a former kalpa—that is, in a previous day of Brahmā (as the *Ratnamālā* states:

"A *kalpa* refers to dissolution, logic, scripture, the day of Brahmā, and ritual")—practiced the art of leaping great distances; his "target-setting" consisted of taking the solar orb itself as his mark by drawing near to it.
"Khuralī means the practice of archery," according to Keśava.
That very thing is *kelī*, or sport; from the excessive engagement—that is, the extreme proximity—produced by that sport, [she felt] her limbs, which are the members of the body.
Regarding "limb" (*gātra*), the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *gātra* refers to a limb, the tip of a staff, the lower part of the leg, and also the body."

While [the sun] was scorching, thinking "he is but a child," he took hold of me out of compassion; grasping me with the affection felt for one who is a child—the cause of his own childhood—he spread his wings over me, and being thus above me with his two wings spread out, he protected me—meaning he preserved me whole and intact—from burning and from drying up.
This is the construction: "Therefore, the brotherly affection shown here is truly wonderful. (The verb *rakṣati* is used in the *laṅ* [imperfect] tense.)
By this, it is established that the withering of the wings resulted from the collision. ||5||
The repetition of "come, come" (*ehyehi*) is used out of respect.

By you—the heroic Garuḍa—just as Vinatā was by her son Garuḍa, so too was our grandmother; and by you, the sovereign emperor (*cakravartin*) of the vultures, our mother Śyenī became possessed of sons, endowed with praiseworthy offspring.
The word "became" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied.

The suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of praise. In this regard, one should keep in mind the following: "Vinatā had two sons, Garuḍa and Aruṇa; I was born from that Aruṇa, and Saṃpāti is my elder brother. (6)
"O child!"—this is said because of the lapse of time, that is, due to the passing of thirteen years.
One should understand the intonation (*kāku*) to be: "Has Rāma's grief for his father become diminished?"
Regarding the word "tasya" (of him):

for that Rāma, there was a conjunction—that is, a connection—with knowledge (specifically spiritual knowledge), with austerity, with self-restraint, and with the three kinds of elders; and his own steadfastness, which is to say, his fortitude, meaning his unshakability.

"Proper" means not deviating from justice; here, the suffix *yat* is used in the sense of "not departing from," according to the rule: "after *dharma*, *pati*, *artha*, and *nyāya*, [the suffix *yat* is added] in the sense of 'not departing from'. His authority and capacity for protection—that is, for the protection of the world—dispels and destroys his dejection, which is the sorrow caused by his father.
The sentences are distinct;
therefore, the use of the singular number for the verb is justified. ||7||
Regarding the word "tṛptaiḥ" (by those satiated): it means by those possessed of satisfaction caused by the flesh of Virādha;
the genitive case is used because the cause is intended to be expressed as a subordinate factor (śeṣatva).
He states the matters reported [by the messenger] with the words beginning "from Citrakūṭa," etc.
He approached (*upasedivān*), that is, he went near (*upasasāda*), the fire (*havyavāha*). The suffix *kvasu* is used here for the perfect tense (*liṭ*) of the root *sad*.
"The elision of the suffix *et* and the reduplication [of the root] from the verbal root (*dhātu*) has been explained. Thus, these two verses constitute a single syntactical unit. ||8||
"So be it.
This expresses Sampāti's agreement with what has been heard.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *bāḍham* is used in three senses: as an adjective meaning 'firm,' and as a neuter noun meaning 'agreement' (*anumati*)."

The collection of five banyan trees is Pañcavaṭī; he dwells, that is, resides, there. "A region on the bank of the Godāvarī" means a place on the shore of the Godāvarī. An abundance of objects—that is, a great number of things within the range of memory—and the distance of time—that is, the long lapse of the time since the experience—cause memory to be stolen away.

"Smṛti" (memory) is so called because one remembers by means of it; it refers to *bhāvanā* (cultivation), which "steals away" the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that produces memory, rendering it devoid of the capacity to generate memory.
He states both of these [effects] with the words beginning "at the beginning of the *kalpa*" and so forth.
At the commencement of this Brahma-*kalpa*, his foot—resembling a staff—is described as having the beautiful Gaṅgā as its banner-cloth (*patākā*), like a flag.
The sense is that it is like the banner-cloth on the flagpole of the Gaṅgā.

As far as Viṣṇu’s foot rose up—that is, ascended—so far, in the upper region above, was my acquaintance, that is, my specific understanding. Furthermore, the Lokāloka mountain—the circular range that serves as the boundary-limit for the luminaries such as the sun—is situated in the vicinity of this ocean, which forms its outer perimeter.
The word "as long as" (yāvat) implies "as long as he is settled. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "there was such familiarity on the surrounding sides.
Therefore, the connection is that both [the sight and the sound] previously mentioned cause the loss of memory. ||10||
Regarding the word "tatra":
*vṛṣasyantī* means desiring sexual union with *Rādhuvṛṣa*, the best among those born of the Ra[va] lineage. According to Amara, "a woman desiring a man is called *vṛṣasyantī*."
Regarding the word *anekā*: it belongs to her who lives for many yugas; her *tretā* is the Tretā-yuga.
According to the *Ratnamālā*, "The term *tretā* refers to the triad of fires and to the [second] yuga."

*Trayodaśī* means that which completes thirteen; the word *bhavati* (is) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. By the rule *tasya pūraṇe ḍaṭ*, the suffix *ḍaṭ* is applied; because it is marked with the *ṭi*-indicator, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.

That Śūrpaṇakhā, being lustful for Rāma—a calf who was a mere infant with milk still in his throat—desired him for sexual intercourse and felt neither shame nor embarrassment. Therefore, the connection [of the verse] is that her transgression of moral bounds is truly astonishing.

The meaning is that the desire of a woman who is slightly more than twelve *yugas* (approximately 172 years) old for Rāma, who is over thirty years of age, is utterly improper according to both the treatises on Dharma and the treatises on Kāma.

In the word *vṛṣasyantī*, the term *vṛṣa*—which ends in the suffix *kyac* expressing desire—undergoes the augment *as* by virtue of the two rules, the *sūtra* "aśvakṣīravṛṣalavaṇānāmātmaprītau kyaci" and the *vārtika* "aśvavṛṣayormaithunecchāyām"; thus, it has the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of "a lustful woman. (11)
Regarding the phrase "tasyām": Lakṣmaṇa [acted] toward her, Śūrpaṇakhā;
it is to be construed with the word "nyavīviśat" (he caused to enter).
Of the ears, nose, and lips—
this is a collective dvandva compound.
By means of cutting, that is, by lopping them off, he [Rāma] established, as it were, the fame of Rāma— the praise consisting of the humiliation of the ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa).

In the case of the root *niveśayati* in the *luṅ* (aorist) with *caṅ*, there is reduplication, and by virtue of the condition of *sanvadbhāva*, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel of the reduplicated syllable.
"Caused by that":
caused by that refers to a certain hostile act (*abhiyoga*)—a hostile seizure (*abhigraha*)—rooted in enmity, which had as its cause the making of Śūrpaṇakhā deformed.
Amara states: "An *abhiyoga* is indeed an *abhigraha*."
"Anubaddha" means produced or followed. By the word "anyone" (kaścit), the variety of causes, applications, and efforts is indicated. "By one" [is used].
The sense is that Lakṣmaṇa, however, was appointed to the protection of Sītā.
As for the word "caturdaśa" (fourteen),
it is due to the non-universality of the rule governing the application of compound-ending suffixes (*samāsāntavidhi*).
Because of the absence of the suffix *ṣa* [prescribed] by the rule "dvitribhyāṃ ṣamūdhnaḥ," the form is *trimūrdhānaḥ*. ||13||
"It is a marvel!
[This refers to] the son of Daśaratha, the great hero, the offspring of Daśaratha;
the sense is that this follows the maxim: "A son is a hundred times superior to his father."
From the word *daśaratha*, when there is the intention to express [him as] an offspring, [the suffix] *iñ* is applied according to the rule *ata iñ*. Regarding the word *mahat*:
the word *punaḥ* has the sense of "but rather" (*kiṃtu*).
"Furthermore, in the first division," according to Amara;
"a great and vast door of enmity"—the cause of enmity itself is the door.
This is a *śliṣṭarūpaka* (a punning metaphor).
"‘Dvāram’ [means] both a door and a means," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
Thinking that it was "uncovered" (apāvṛtam), that is, "opened," I have become utterly bewildered; I am deprived of the discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
[The root] *muha* is used in the sense of bewilderment (*vaicitye*).
Confusion is a lack of discernment.
At this juncture, at this very moment, they must not be released—that is, they must not be abandoned.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Of the father-in-law," and so forth.
Blinded by intoxication—the confusion between joy and delusion produced by wine and the like—one is devoid of correct cognition regarding what ought to be done and so forth.
As it has been said: "Intoxication (*mada*) is the confusion between joy and delusion produced by wine and the like.
Alternatively, one is blinded by pride (*mada*), that is, by the arrogance induced by valor and other such qualities.
According to the *Ratnamālā*: "Intoxication (*mada*) consists of [the rut of] elephants, pride, joy, semen, musk, and [the state of] being intoxicated.
A *māyāvī* is one who abounds in *māyā*; the meaning is that he is preeminent in deception and in the creation of wonderful weapons, missiles, and so forth, such as those of Śambarī.
The suffix *vini*, which conveys abundance (*bhūman*), is applied here according to the rule "after *asman*, *āya*, and *medhā*, etc. (Pāṇini 5.2.121).
The Lord (prabhu) is one who possesses a treasury, an army, and so forth;
according to the Ratnamālā, "prabhu" refers to those who are powerful or sovereign.
He is of immeasurable prowess (amitavīrya), meaning his valor is incalculable.

"Vīrya refers to valor and the white [virtues]," according to the *Ratnamālā*. The enemy who dwells nearby is the neighbor-state; the ten-faced Rāvaṇa is the immediate adversary. The word "sodaryāyāḥ" means "born from the same womb"; the suffix *yat* is applied here according to the rule "sodarād yat."
"Samānodarya, sodarya, sagarbhyā, and sahaja are synonyms," according to Amara.
[This refers to] the sister, Śūrpaṇakhā;
"bhaginī and svasā mean sister," according to Amara.
"Insult" (nikāra) means deformity;
Amara states, "nikāra would mean mistreatment" (viprakāra). How indeed does he endure it? How does he tolerate it?
By the word *iva*, it is suggested that even a mere semblance [of hope] is not a cause for endurance.
Likewise, in the same manner, toward his own people—that is, his kinsmen (*svajana*)—repeatedly, again and again.
According to Amara, "bandhu," "sva," and "svajana" are synonyms.
How indeed could he endure both downfall and slaughter?
And with the intent to kill Subāhu and Virādha, he spoke thus repeatedly.
"Alas! The children—Sītā, Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa—must be protected and guarded by us in a manner that is skillful and free from suffering."
The word "become" (*bhavanti*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
The sense is that kinsmen and others are causes for opening the door to enmity.
The definition of an immediate neighbor (*bhūmy-anantara*) has already been stated previously.
In this world, the desire for attainment is made manifest by the apprehension of both gain and loss;

herein, the limbs of the juncture (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) are said to consist of the path in the form of proclaiming the truth, the form consisting of sentences that set forth deliberation (*vitarka*), agitation (*udvega*) in the form of fear of harmful persons, and apprehension (*saṃśaya*) in the form of alarm and terror. ||14||
"I too," he says.
"Having performed my daily rites and bathed, I shall contemplate—that is, meditate upon—the *śivatāti*, the thing that brings about auspiciousness (*śiva*).
According to Amara, *śivatātiḥ* means "that which brings about auspiciousness."
Here, the pursuit of the means to achieve a desired object is called the *ākṣepa* (allusion), which is stated to be a constituent element (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) of the juncture (*saṃdhi*).
[The phrase] "having enacted the act of traveling through the sky" implies the intention of reaching his own abode.
"Here I am.
Here I am, [driven] by the fierce—that is, the intense—wind of dissolution, from the wind of the cosmic destruction.

Regarding the word *caṇḍa*, the *Ratnamālā* states: "The term *caṇḍa* refers to a particular class of demons and to Yama’s servant; in three genders, it denotes those who are fierce or intensely angry."
With *raṃhasā*, meaning with speed (*vegena*). According to Amara: "The words *raṃhas* and *taras* denote *rayaḥ* (velocity) and *syadaḥ* (swiftness).
It is described as such because its *prathimā*—its breadth or vastness—has been *saṃkṣipta*, that is, contracted or diminished.
The suffix *iman* is used here in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule *pṛthvādibhya imanij vā*.
Being as if drinking the atmosphere— the sky—
it is said that he is "as if drinking" because, considering the clarity of the atmosphere, it possesses a resemblance to water.
From Mount Malaya, I have arrived—reaching it as swiftly as possible—at the cluster of trees, the grove of forest trees, which is joined with that mountain, the abode of my dwelling. ||15||

"This" refers to [the mountain] whose vicinity (*parisara*)—that is, the surrounding region—is dense, lush, and shimmering blue, being uninterrupted by clusters and masses of forest trees; such are the forests that encircle it. It is a place where the caves (*kandarāḥ*) have their openings (*mukheṣu*) joined by the Godāvarī river. [The word] "abhiṣyandamānaiḥ" means pervading or overflowing.

In the word *syandu*, derived from the root *syand* with the prefix *abhi*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs according to the rule: "The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* in the roots *syand* and *nat* occurs after *anu*, *vi*, *pari*, *abhi*, and *ni*, when the subject is not a living being.
It is described as such because its blackness (*nīlimā*), that is, its dark-blue color, has been made dense (*amedurita*) or doubled by the clouds.
Regarding the word *dūram*:
Rāma was led far away by the illusory deer; "it came to pass," is the ellipsis.
Lakṣmaṇa goes by that same direction—the direction taken by Rāma.
Thereupon, immediately after that, the wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*), a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*)—
as Amara states: "A mendicant (*bhikṣuḥ*), a wandering ascetic (*parivrāj*), and a follower of the path of action (*karmandī*")—
[approached] the *uṭaja*, the leaf-hut.
"Parṇaśālā and uṭaja are feminine nouns for a leaf-hut," according to Amara.
He has entered—that is, arrived.
This mendicant of manifest form is the Ten-necked one (Rāvaṇa).
The word "born" (jātaḥ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Fie! is used here in the sense of censure.

In this context, because of the employment of a disguise for the sake of what is relevant to the matter at hand, the dramatic juncture-element (saṃdhy-aṅga) called "the concealment of the non-existent" (abhūtāharaṇa) is stated. ||16||
"Negligence" (*pramāda*) means my lack of attention toward Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa. "Aho" signifies something wonderful; the repetition [of the word] expresses censure.
"By thousands" means those that are beyond thousands (*paraḥsahasrāṇi*); by them.

Those whose faces are like those of *piśācas* are described as such; yoked with these donkeys, and surrounded on all sides by them, this wicked Rāvaṇa is going somewhere after having placed the blameless bride Sītā upon the chariot.
"A young wife who remains in her family while her husband is still living is a woman who brings disgrace," so says the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*. (17)
"Paulastya," meaning "one belonging to the lineage of Pulastya. This epithet is used with specific intention.
He states that intention with the words, "the upholders" (dhartr̥raḥ).

They are the lords and sustainers of all branches of knowledge; during the periods of dissolution, when there are no students, they are the upholders—that is, the preservers—of the Veda, the venerable scripture that makes known all human goals and their means of attainment, for the purpose of setting it forth at the time of creation. This is the sense.
"Pulastya and others" is the subject; "are [born]" is the ellipsis. Of them, [it is the lineage-banner] of the banner of the family (the dynastic emblem).

"Of him who makes that known" means, in short, of him who has performed the ritual bath (*snāta*) through Vedic observances (*vrata*), such as the *Śirovrata* of the four Vedas and the *Prājāpatya*, and who has thus completed his vows. "Those whose dwellings are in the netherworld" refers to the Kālakeyas and others whose abodes are located specifically in the subterranean regions (*adhastala*). [The Lord] is the conqueror (*jitṛ*) of those who possess such dwellings;
because the word ends in the suffix *tṛn*, the form *vaitalasadmanaḥ* takes the second case ending.

How, and by what means, did that evil-mindedness—the cause of the descent into, or the transition toward, wicked deeds and evil actions—arise in you, who are a king radiant with asceticism (*tapas*), shining, a ruler who delights his subjects, and a lord?
The sense is this: lineage, learning, austerity, valor, majesty, and so forth, stand as adversaries here to the theft of another’s wife through robbery.
Here, because of the use of words identical in form to those relevant to the subject at hand, the *saṃdhy-aṅga* (limb of the juncture) called *saṃgraha* (collection) is stated. ||18||
How so? Out of contempt—that is, with disregard arising from [his] being a bird—he does not listen; the words "my speech" are to be supplied as the object.
The word *iva* is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).
*Āḥ* is used in anger. "O evil-souled one, O wicked Buddhist! O lowest of Rākṣasas, O vilest of Rākṣasas!"
"Niḥhīna-apasadaḥ" [is defined] by Amara.
"Tiṣṭha tiṣṭha" is a reduplication used in anger. "Tuṇḍa" [etc.]...

From the cavities—the apertures—of the skulls (the bones of the head) of those pierced and perforated by my snout (my mouth), [the entrails] were drawn out and extracted, quivering and moving. (Regarding "skull": Amara states, "The word *karoṭi* is feminine and denotes the bone of the head.")
These two qualifiers are to be understood as part of a *dvandva* compound ending in the word *mālā*, which itself functions as the final member of a *bahuvrīhi*.
"The skin is the blood-bearer" (*tvaco'sṛgdharāḥ*);
Amara states: "In the feminine, *tvak* and *asṛgdharā* [are synonyms for skin]."
"Vasā" means "medas" (fat). According to Amara, "medas, vapā, and vasā [are synonyms for fat].
Furthermore, the reading "sphuratprasphuṭa-" is found in some places.
The *kloma* is the *tilaka*.
Amara states: "The *tilaka* is the *kloma*.
The *plīhā* is the *gulma*.
"According to Amarasimha, *gulma* (the spleen) is masculine;
*yakṛt* is the liver;
and according to Amarasimha, *kālakhaṇḍa* and *yakṛt* are synonymous."
The blood (rudhirāṇi) is liquid, having become fluid, and hot, possessing a warm touch due to the heat of battle-rage; the sinews (snāyavaḥ) are the tendons (vasnasāḥ).
Regarding "tendons," Amara states: "Now, *vasnasā* and *snāyu* [are synonyms] in the feminine."
"Āntramālā" refers to the entrails; "purītat" means the intestinal coil.
According to Amara, "āntra" and "purītat" are synonyms.
He who possesses such [entrails] is so described; this [term] is to be construed with "of you" (te) and "with these limbs" (asya cāṅgaiḥ).

With claws as fierce and sharp as a *krakaca*—a specific type of saw known as *karapatra*—he [performs] an *utkartana*, which is a thorough cutting or splitting. (Amara states: "krakaca" is not feminine and means "karapatra"; "nakha" is not feminine and also means "nakhara").
The word *kṛtī* is derived from the root *kṛt* (meaning "to cut") with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*).
They are so described because their *kīkasas*—that is, their bones (*asthis*)—resound or make a noise;
for Amarasimha states: "Both *kīkasa* and *kulya* mean bone."

"Khaṇḍitāḥ" means severed. "Grīvāṇām" refers to necks; as Amara states: "The word *kaṃdhara* is also used for the neck (*grīvā*) and the head. [They were] those whose vessels (*dhamanayaḥ*)—that is, veins (*śirāḥ*)—were [severed].
According to Amarasimha, "nāḍī, dhamani, and śirā" [are synonyms for a vessel].
By your limbs—that is, by your members as instruments—the son of Śyenī, namely the vulture, [is meant];
that is to say, I myself.
"May she be satisfied; may she attain satisfaction.
This is the imperative mood used when the time for an action has arrived.
Here, the dramatic element (saṃdhy-aṅga) called *toṭaka*, consisting of speech characterized by anger and agitation, has been described. ||19||
"He has departed" refers to Jaṭāyu;
it is called a "pure viṣkambhaka" because it consists solely of refined Sanskrit.

The meaning is that this is because the episodes already narrated, such as the slaying of Virādha, Śūrpaṇakhā, Khara, and Dūṣaṇa, as well as the episodes yet to be told, such as the story of Jaṭāyu, have been recounted in brief.
Now, the fifth act is introduced with the words "Lakṣmaṇa enters," and so forth:
"Noble brother!"
The meaning is "O Sītā.
She is addressed by the word *āryā* because she is the wife of her elder brother.
*Kaṣṭam* means that which consists of suffering, namely the ten states such as anger and the rest.
"Ten states are of many kinds," according to Amara;
"transformation" means change,
as in "transformation is change," according to Amara.
The enemy of Mārīca experiences—that is, he suffers—the consequence of killing the illusory deer; this is the sense. He refers to him with the words "this one."

He stands like anger incarnate, possessing form; he should be conceived as a moving, wandering being, like fire manifest before one’s eyes—an excess of mental inflammation provoked by the offenses committed by enemies.

He should be conceived as an excess of suffering born from the separation from beloved ones and other such causes, comparable to fire because it is the cause of burning. In both cases, there is the poetic figure of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
This noble "hṛllekha" refers to a particular kind of loathing (*jugupsā*).
According to the rule *hṛdayasya hṛllekhayadaṇlāseṣu*, the word *hṛdaya* undergoes the substitution *hṛt*.
It is called *hṛllekha* because it "scratches" (*likhati*) the heart; the word *lekha* here ends in the suffix *aṇ*.
*Hṛllekha* here refers to a state of mind characterized by loathing, prompted by the perception of the fault in abducting one's wife.
*Lajjā*, on the other hand, is the contraction of the mind; through these two causes, [the mind] becomes *saṃveginī*, meaning agitated.
According to Amara, "saṃvega" and "saṃbhrama" are synonyms.
He sustains—that is, maintains—his slender body with great difficulty and suffering. ||20||
He clarifies what was stated previously by means of an illustration, beginning with "tathā hi" (for instance).
This means "in that very same way.
[The term] "ābhugna" (bent) [is used].
The word "eṣa" (this) is to be supplied [from the previous context].
"Ābhugnayoḥ" means of the two that are curved or bent;
Amara states: "ābhugnam means curved."

Similarity is intended by means of qualities such as loftiness. By "ghaṭanayā" (through conjunction), meaning through mutual union, that which is indicated—manifested—is "stambhitaḥ," meaning checked or obstructed by an inner-shining fortitude characterized by immovability; nevertheless, he is "durvyavasthaḥ," one whose regulation or restraint is difficult to maintain. For this very reason, he is "vitataḥ" (extended) and "viśīrṇaḥ" (dispersed). He is described as one whose fire-like anger is "proccaṇḍaḥ," meaning exceedingly intense. Consequently, there is a "madhye uddhūmāvaliḥ," a column of smoke rising from the midst [of that fire].

"Jvalandīpyamāna-vāḍava" refers to one who possesses a submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*) that is blazing and flaming; "sa eṣa āryaḥ" means this noble one; "vidyutā vyañjito vajro dambholir garbhe 'ntar yasya" means he whose interior (*garbha*) contains a thunderbolt (*vajra*) or *dambholi* manifested by lightning—such a one takes on, or rather bears, the "chāyām," meaning the luster or beauty, of that "jalada," meaning the cloud. In this passage, the figure of speech is *upamā* (simile), because the eyebrows and the streaks of smoke, as well as the wrathful fire and the submarine fire, are non-different through the relationship of the original object and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*), thereby serving as common attributes (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

Thus, because the eyebrows and lightning, as well as the fire of anger and the vajra, are non-different through the relationship of original and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*), there is the figure of speech *upamā* (simile). Furthermore, since this is animated by that [simile], there is the figure of speech *nidarśanā* (illustration) consisting in the function of word-meanings (*padārtha-vṛtti*). This constitutes a *saṃkara* (commixture), according to the statement: "Some say there is another *nidarśanā*, which consists in the function of word-meanings."

Here, because the excellence of the pigeons is described, the description of the excellence of the subject at hand is called the *udāhṛti* (illustration), a constituent element of the juncture (*saṃdhy-aṅga*). ||21||
Regarding the word *nyakkāra*:
"The humiliation arising from the abduction of my wife is like a *vajrakīla*—that is, an unbearably piercing *vajra-śaṅku* (thunderbolt-stake)—in my heart.
According to the *Ratnamālā*, "The word *kīla* occurs in two senses: flame and a stake; the word *śaṅku* [occurs] in the sense of a stake and a porcupine."
Being intense and unbearable, it quivers and moves;
its similarity [to darkness] arises from its being beyond remedy.

Furthermore, the mind—contracted by shame due to having entered an improper state—is closed up and diminished, [falling] into a terrible, blind darkness that is both fearsome and conducive to ignorance.
The word *andha* is derived from the root *andh*, meaning "to impair vision," with the suffix *ac* added according to the *pacādi* group.
The compound is formed like *khañja-kubja* and similar terms.
It means "as if sinking into darkness."
The meaning is that it becomes devoid of application toward duties that ought to be performed.
Furthermore, the term *tātavipattijaḥ* means "born from the calamity of my father," specifically from the death (*vipatti*) of Jaṭāyu, who was my father’s friend;
the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *jan* according to the rule *pañcamyām ajātau*.
Grief is the agent;
it burns me, reducing me to ashes.
[The root] *daha* means "to reduce to ashes."
In this matter, there is simply no remedy for the grief born of the father’s misfortune;
however, the heart’s intent is that there *is* a remedy for insults and the like.
Furthermore, compassion toward the wretched and miserable Sītā is a state of suffering that exceeds even the foundation of Sītā’s own sorrow.
"Furthermore, in the first division," according to Amara;
"marmāṇi" refers to the vital points where the life-breaths reside.
The neuter gender [of the word] is established by the rule: "tirīṭaṃ marma yojanam."
She cuts [me] as it were.
And it was said by Hanumān: "This is she, for whose sake Rāma suffers with four things:
with compassion, with kindness, with grief, and with love."
"Compassion arises because [the husband thinks] 'my wife is lost'"—this is mentioned here because of its predominance. ||22||

Those whose actions transcend the world and whose conduct is supreme in the worlds do not become deluded in times of hardship or distress; they do not fall into confusion. Delusion (*pramoha*), however, is a lack of discernment (*aviveka*).
Here too, the *udāhṛti* (illustration) has been mentioned as a constituent element of the *saṃdhi* (transition).
[The address] "O child" (*vatse*)— [End of excerpt]
A change in tone (*kāku*) is intended here, meaning "Are they supramundane?
He explains this with the words "by whom":
by those kings through whom the worlds were protected and guarded, such that they became free from fear, devoid of any cause for dread.
In the analysis of the compound *nāstibhaya*, it is a *mayūravyaṃsakādi* compound [meaning "one for whom there is no fear from anywhere"].
Those whose reins (*abhīśu*)—that is, rays (*kiraṇa*)—are great are so described.
According to Śāśvata, "the word *abhīśu* refers to a bridle and a ray."

Those former kings of the solar lineage—the descendants of the Sun—who were like banners (*ketavaḥ*) shining like standards, have been insulted by me; they have been brought to humiliation by me. Furthermore, that Jaṭāyu, who is steadfast even at the end of kalpas—even at the conclusion of the days of Brahmā—being virtuous and devoted to the service of others, has been sent by me to heaven, led to another world.
Moreover, [I am the one] acting as the instigator (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) in the abduction of Sītā committed by Rāvaṇa, having caused my wife to be lost in the forest.

The meaning is that Rāma’s deeds are "world-transcending" (lokottara) because he has performed those very actions that worldly people have not performed. Alternatively, Lakṣmaṇa spoke of them as "world-transcending" with the intention that they are the best in the world.
Rāma, however, repeats those very words for the purpose of conceiving a different meaning: "Child, they are 'transcendent' (*lokottara*).
With the intention that they are called "transcendent" because they carry people across or transcend the world (*loka*), it was said that they were previously treated with contempt.
According to the maxim "the king [represents] the kingdom," the word *loka* here refers to that king.
Furthermore, they are called *lokottara* because they "transcend" (*uttaranti*)—that is, they cause one to reach with excellence—the world (*loka*), namely the world beyond (*āmuṣmika-loka*).

Just as in the expression "he crosses over the Vedānta," the root *tṛ* (to cross) has the sense of "reaching" (*prāpti*) with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized, followed by the suffix *ac*.
With this intention, it was said that Jaṭāyu was made to go to heaven.

Furthermore, with the intention that "supramundane" (lokottara) means transcending the worlds, he said, "That which was not done by the worlds has been done by me. Therefore, the meaning is that you have rightly stated that Rāma's deeds are supramundane. ||23||
Of one who has become a *tīrtha* (a sacred ford), like a teacher, who instructs for one's welfare.
Amara states: "The word *tīrtha* refers to a watering place, a source [of a river], water frequented by sages, and a teacher.
Ratnamālā states: "The word *bhūta* means what is right or proper, and 'equal'."
The syntactical connection is: "Where is its origin?
I seem to behold the final state, the ultimate condition;
there is a similarity between this and actual seeing due to the clarity of memory.
"Yāmiti" refers to this verse from the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa.
O long-lived one!

The suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of abundance; that is to say, [abounding] in the long life being prayed for. [He found] that Sītā, who was like the *mṛtasaṃjīvinī* herb—the herb that restores the dead to life—in the great forest (*mahāvane*), because that vast forest is a place where even rare herbs are likely to be found.
For a medicinal herb is indeed to be sought within the forest;
one who seeks it searches for it.
That Sītā, who revives the world, is both my Sītā and my very life-breaths.
The neuter gender is used because it denotes a collective sense.
The meaning is that [the city] was seized, brought [to destruction], and ruined by Rāvaṇa;
both actions are intended to be expressed through the single word (tantra). ||24||
Regarding "iti": "vīralokān" refers to the worlds to be attained by heroes slain in battle; its status as an object is established by the rule "adhiśīṅsthāsāṃ karma."
It was said "to the world of heroes" by way of worldly convention,
because of the granting of the unsurpassed worlds in the words, "Go to the unsurpassed worlds.
[The address] "my child" [is used].

In the analysis of the compound *hṛdayamarmāṇi vidhyanti* ("piercing the vital points of the heart"), the vowel of the word *marman* is lengthened by the rule *nahivṛtivṛṣivyadhi...* and so forth. The "introduction" (*uddhāta*) to a narrative is its "prelude" (*prastāva*).
As Amarasimha states: "The beginning (*abhyādāna*) may be called an introduction (*udghāta*)."
Now, *atha kim* is used here in the sense of acceptance (*aṅgīkāre*).
As for *kim*:

the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "What indeed will be done—that counter-measure which would be equal and appropriate to the excessive humiliation, that is, the extreme degree of contempt?"
"Even before," etc.
Even prior to the abduction of Sītā and other such events, my mind—that is, my will—was already set upon the slaughter of the Rākṣasas.
For this reason, since those Rākṣasas were destined for death by many infallible causes, such as the massacre of the sages and Janaka’s son, they were indeed to be slain.
Therefore, the connection is that "the intellect has already moved forward.

Hereafter—that is, subsequent to the arising of the cause for the abduction of Sītā and so forth—it is not possible to perform any remedial action (*pratividhāna*) other than the pacification of the family; nothing other than the destruction of the Rākṣasa clan is possible.
But here, regarding the causes such as the abduction of Sītā, there is only that—merely that, little, merely that, merely that.
The destruction of the race of Rākṣasas is indeed too little;
even when that has been accomplished, how could there be peace for me—the cessation of my [enmity]—from what cause would it arise? This is the implied meaning.
Therefore, the connection [of the verse] is: "What indeed will they do? ||25||
"Thus indeed" means because a corresponding remedy is difficult to find. "Fierce," etc.

Fierce, exceedingly intense, and concentrated—having attained a state of dense massing—it is a compound like *khañja-kubja* (lame-and-bent). Directed inward with a hidden movement, as if drinking me up again and again, suddenly blazing aloft with its crests of flames, it stands as if issuing forth or emerging outside; this wrath (*manyu*), unable to find an internal object to consume and finding no other substance to burn since the destruction of the Rākṣasa clan is so insignificant as to be almost non-existent, consumes and reduces me to ashes, just as the submarine fire (*vāḍava*) consumes the ocean.
Therefore, may you protect me from this pride;
"may you" is the ellipsis.
The meaning is: "May you protect me by providing me with a suitable bridegroom and other such things."
The ablative case [in *bhītrārthānām*] is used according to the rule "of those [roots] meaning fear.
This very state is the supreme pinnacle of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*).

Here, fire—first existing in a state of coiled power within cow-dung balls and the like, with its activity stilled and subtle within; then subsequently blazing upward; then thereafter pervading all directions with flames; and finally, due to the absence of any other substratum, burning its own very substrate—this well-known behavior of fire, though not the subject at hand, is what is referred to by the statement "that which... ||26||
Considering that he had obtained a suitable servant, Lakṣmaṇa, believing that creating a diversion was his only means of protection, said: "These...
[referring to] *mṛgayūthāni*, which means herds or families of deer (*hariṇajātīya*).
As Amarasimha states: "A *kula* or *yūtha* of animals refers to those of the same species; for lower animals, these terms denote a group of males or both sexes."

By "families" (*kulaiḥ*) is meant groups (*samūhaiḥ*) of predatory beasts (*śvāpada*), which are evil creatures. [The long vowel in *śvāpada*] is due to the rule "the long vowel for *śvan* when used as a name" (*śuno daṃṣṭrā* etc.). Being characterized by the southern direction (*dakṣiṇayā diśā*), they proceed toward the southern quarter and remain there in succession.
Because of the designation *karmapravacanīya* according to the rule "abhirabhāge," the second case ending is used in connection with it.
"Vibhāvayāmaḥ" means we investigate.
"Vatsa" (child).
"Never seen before" means never seen at any time previously.
"Nanu" is used here as a particle of emphasis.

[He was] the son of Aruṇa; [the suffix] *iñ* is applied according to the rule *ata iñ*. Having said, "Therefore I am born from Aruṇa," he [the father] committed him to the fire, made him entirely composed of fire, and consecrated him by means of cremation.
The suffix *sāti* is applied according to the rule "vibhāṣā sāti kārtsnye.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is with the phrase "having departed from the hermitage of Pañcavaṭī.
Some time has passed.
A long time has passed. The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here because of its proximity to the present. He states the reason for this with the word "since" (*yataḥ*).
"Separated far" means they have reached their conclusion. "Boundaries" refers to the limiting grounds. "And just as... [and so forth].
*Pratibhayam* means fear that confronts one;
thus, for that reason, I certainly infer. According to Amara, *nūnam* is used in the sense of "certainly," "inevitably," or "for sure."

To the west of Janasthāna, situated in the western direction, is the place known as Kuñjaravān. It was [occupied] by Danukabandha, who—due to being the son of Danu and because his body was headless—bore the name Danukabandha.
As it is stated in the Śrī Rāmāyaṇa: "O Lakṣmaṇa, know that you have slain the son of Danu, who was resplendent with beauty."
"Due to Indra's wrath, this form was assumed upon the field of battle"— thus it is said.
"It should be seen" refers to the frog from the forest.
The meaning is that he is unable to depart from the forest. Just as a frog remains only in the water, so too does he remain only in the wilderness; this is the intended sense.
He is to be seen;
the meaning is that he is desired to be seen because of his altered appearance.
"Ho there! Who is here?"
"It exists" is the ellipsis.
"May you protect me"— "you" is the ellipsis.
Regarding the phrase *ahaṃ hi*:
in the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound as "she who is both a Śabara and an ascetic" (*śabarī cāsau tāpasī ca*), it is a *karmadhāraya*.
The masculine form is applied by the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye*.
She is the resident of Mataṅga’s hermitage, the dweller;
she is the perfected one, possessed of spiritual accomplishment. ||27||
Regarding the verse beginning with "priye," he describes the intensification of Rāma’s grief due to the absence of any other distraction following Lakṣmaṇa’s departure.
"Madhurām" means the beloved wife;
as Amara states: "The words *madhura* and *priya* both mean sweet (*svādu*)."
"Scatter your speech"— speak again and again with the desire to express each respective meaning.
The word "atha ca" (and then) serves as a prohibition of what was previously stated.

Even for those who have been defeated and humiliated, the diversion of lamentation—such as the wailing "O beloved, alas, alas! Where are you?"—and even the lightening of sorrow through such expressions, is difficult to obtain; yet Rāvaṇa, the descendant of Pulastya, remains irreproachable and wanders at will, being beyond censure because his wife was not forcibly abducted.
For me, however, there is only public scandal and reproach on account of my having had my wife taken away.
The word "sthitā" (remained/established) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
For, by this Rāvaṇa (the agent), when hostility— that is, enmity— had become rooted, that is, had arisen.
The meaning is "beginning with the slaying of Tāṭakā.
It was repaid in such a way as to be manifold and superior;
that is to say, a counter-action was performed.
And here, by means of such acts as obstructing [the path], he has retaliated in accordance with the hostility and the desire to cause distress;
by the abduction of Sītā, he has retaliated twofold;
but by the killing of Jaṭāyu, he has retaliated manifold—this is the intended meaning.

Indeed, the killing of Jaṭāyu was even more grievous than the abduction of Sītā. Thus spoke Rāma: "O gentle one, O scorcher of foes, the sorrow born of Sītā’s abduction does not affect me as much as the destruction of the vulture on my account."
"Ṛ" means this:
the word *guṇa* here signifies repetition (*āvṛtti*).
In this context, it indicates an excess—as in the expressions "repetition of the bowstring," "repetition of the belly of Vṛkodara," or "repetition of the senses with respect to form and so forth."
"In the case of [the qualities] beginning with *sattva*, at the junctures [of the day], in acts of renunciation, and when not predominant, there is excellence. Thus says the *Ratnamālā*. 28.
Regarding the word *tad*: "cruel" (*krūra*) means harsh (*karkaśa*).
As stated in the *Ratnamālā*: "In three genders, *krūra* refers to those who are harsh, hot, pitiless, angry, and terrifying."
The teeth themselves are the saws (*karapatra*);
as Amara states, "the saw is *krakaca*, not feminine, and is a *karapatra*.

With those [teeth], living beings (*sattva*) are cut and severed; from the multitudes of those creatures, blood (*asṛj*) flows and streams forth, soaking and moistening the very tuft of hair (*kūrca*) between the eyebrows.
According to Amara, "kūrca" refers to the space between the eyebrows (*bhruvormadhya*).
Thus, [the term] means that which has a cluster (*guccha*) or bunch (*stabaka*) at that location.
Alternatively, it means that which has a cluster or bunch belonging to the *kūrca*, i.e., the space between the eyebrows.

According to the *Ratnamālā*, "A *guccha* refers to a cluster, a stalk, a type of necklace, or a bundle. The face and the deformed body of Kabandha—the long-armed one whose arms were a league in length—were not seen by you because you were disguised as a Rākṣasa, desiring to see the true form of the Rākṣasa while appearing in a deceptive guise.
Lakṣmaṇa’s regret is indicated by his remark: "That evil-souled one was certainly to be seen," implying that he did not see him [in his true form]. ||29||
The word "atha" (now) is used here in the sense of a question. "In our search" means in the search for me;
for her statement was, "She has arrived seeking Rāma."
"You hear.
This means "indeed you hear. Who does not hear it?
The meaning is that everyone in the world hears him as he is well known.
The word *kim* is used in the sense of censure.
And he is Vibhīṣaṇa.
"By fate" means by the power of destiny;
"at that very time" means immediately after the slaughter of Khara and the others; "for some reason" means for whatever cause.
"In the case of *nimitta*, *kāraṇa*, and *hetu*, all [six] cases are shown.
Thus, the genitive case is used according to the rule "the sixth case [is used] in connection with the word *hetu*.
The meaning is: by means of the relatives' imagining of a transformation of mind within themselves.
For Mālyavat said: "This wise man, having himself perceived the change, will surely withdraw. "Having restrained [him] from his kinsmen" means having separated him;
*avagraha* signifies separation.
The ablative case is used for the source (*apādāna*);
[it is used here] because of the reason of friendship with Sugrīva.
This too was stated by Mālyavān in the passage beginning with "from childhood" (*bālyāt prabhṛti*).
The meaning is that, having said, "This is a letter from Vibhīṣaṇa which offers himself up and reveals his intention that his own burden should be seized by you," he hands over the letter.
*Ātmasamarpakaḥ* means "one who offers himself up"; the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*).
Therefore, the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied in the sense of "he causes to speak," and the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the agent;
this very [suffix] is called the "final resort" (*carama-samāśraya*) in the case of *saṃdhyā* and other such forms.
As it has been said: "For one being pierced by an enemy, seeking refuge with a powerful protector is 'samāśraya' (seeking shelter).
He causes [the name] to be recited; he recites it.
"May there be well-being! he says.
The word "let it be" is understood.
Regarding "Rāmadeva":
this term *deva* denotes one who is supremely venerable.
"Rājā, bhaṭṭāraka, deva"—thus says Amara. Regarding "viśiṣṭa":
those whose fortune (bhāgadheya) or luck is distinguished—that is, surpassed—are so described.
In the rule "bhāgarūpanāmabhyo dheyaḥ," the suffix *dheya* is applied to the word *bhāga* when it signifies a portion (*bhāgya*).
For those like us, there is a "pair" (*dvayī*), meaning the two things that will be described hereafter.

Because the substitute *ayaj* [for *tayap*] in the rule "dvitribhyāṃ tayasyāyajvā" is treated as the original by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied to the word *dvaya* according to the rule "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ... and so forth.
The "supreme" means the state that surpasses all others; the ellipsis is that it becomes the means for accomplishing one's desired goal.
To the question "Which is this twofold [state]?", he says: "Dharma."
Or, "dharma" refers to that which is being drawn forth as transcending all else;
or, it refers to the means for attaining the supramundane good, untainted by even the scent of fault.
The sense is that the Śruti, beginning with "One dispels evil through dharma," concludes with "Therefore, they declare dharma to be supreme."

Are you the protector and guardian of Dharma—the one who ensures the existence of Dharma through its essential nature, its author, its place, its time, its accessories, its results, and its means—or are you the omniscient, omnipotent, and sovereign Lord, the compassionate one who has become the Supreme Brahman?
The word "you" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied. This alternative expressed by the word "or" (*vā*) is a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*).
For it is the established limit of the Mīmāṃsakas that "Dharma is being investigated";
and it is the established limit of those proficient in the Upaniṣads (Trayyanta) that "you are the protector of Dharma.
This is evident from the two Brahma-mīmāṃsā sūtras: "Jaimini [holds that] Dharma [is the subject]," and "The fruit [arises] from Him, because that is logical."
Furthermore, "Is dharma being excelled?"—this is the boundary for those who are disputants.
"Are you the protector of dharma?"—this is the boundary for those who have come for refuge.
