"Aṅgīkṛta, āśruta, and pratijñāta" are synonyms according to Amara. "Mahātmānaḥ" means those of great intellect. "Viśvavyāpakam" means pervading the universe, spreading throughout the three worlds.
*Lupyate* means it would be cut off or destroyed.
This is the *yag* (passive) *ātmanepada* ending used in the sense of the agent being the object (*karmakartṛ*).
The *liṅ* suffix is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).
Disrepute (*apayaśas*) is the opposite of fame (*yaśas*); it is the extensive and abundant proclamation of faults.
According to Amara: "Prabhūta, pracura, prājya, adabhra, bahula, and bahu [all mean 'much'].
Here, in this conflict, the resolution (*samādhāna*) is the pacification of the contradiction between two tasks.
"He fights" means he engages in combat.
"Renown" (prasiddhi) means fame (prakhyāti).
"In that very same way."
"Incapable" means impossible for Rāma;
"convincing" means that which produces the conviction of equality in strength.
Is there indeed anything that is truly incapable?
The meaning is that the notion that "nothing is impossible" is truly astonishing.
According to Amarasimha, "nāma" is used in the senses of manifestation and possibility.
"Āviddha" means cast or hurled.
"Contemptuous" (*sāvajña*) means accompanied by disregard due to extreme insignificance.

"Some slight indication" (*kiṃcit-pratyāyana*) refers to that which produces conviction regarding the cause of one's own humiliation. Through the possibility of being deemed worthy of only that much, it brings about one's own defeat; thus, "endeavored" (*samīhita*) means desired. Such speech is a statement requesting an indication that serves as a cause for contempt.
"By that which is joined with fault" means by that which is accompanied by transgression (*pratyavāya*). "Regarding the cessation of battle" means with respect to the withdrawal from combat.
"Upright" means not crooked.
This is what will be stated hereafter.
Preceded by such words as "Worthy of worship by the world," which indicate great respect,
[the term] *sakhya* means friendship (*maitrī*).
"Whether as a virtue or a fault"—
this refers to the encouragement (protsāhana) that generates the resolve to engage in battle with Rāma. According to Amara, "utsāha" means "vyavasāya" (resolve).

The path of actions is "karmapatha"; the compound ending is formed according to the rule "ṛkpūrabdhūḥ" and so forth. [He is] one who abandons friendship with Rāvaṇa, that is, one who renounces his alliance with Rāvaṇa.
This is Vālin.
Of that Rāma—

[there is] the connection or occasion for the two of them, namely, welfare pertaining to this life and the next, which is to be experienced in this body and which is to be experienced in another body.
*Garīyaḥ* means "heaviest. The suffix *-īyasun* is used here for the purpose of selecting one from among three. As for the phrase beginning with *na ca*, etc.:

The meaning is that, because of his desire to communicate with contempt, there is no occasion for a lack of trust in the form of suspicion regarding treachery toward a friend— due to Rāma’s turning away from him and his failure to carry out Rāvaṇa’s task.
This is because [of the reason] beginning with "yataḥ" (since),
namely, that in comparison to everything else, such as the maintenance of friendship with Rāvaṇa.
Truthfulness of promise means the fulfillment of one's pledge;
by the phrase "by Hariścandra and others," Daśaratha and others are included by the word "and so forth."

By the phrase "the state of being a Caṇḍāla woman's slave" and so forth, the word "and so forth" (ādi-padena) includes everything from the entire kingdom that has not been seized, up to [the state of] being under the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
"Not this" means:
this is a request for the communication of contempt.
"The cause of provocation" means the cause of being provoked.
Of that Rāma;
of the great-souled ones, whose nature is characterized by forgiveness;
[and] of those like me, even animals.
By that very pretext—that is, by means of a deception consisting of a request for a contemptuous response—he says:
"I shall depart. I shall cast off and abandon this friendship, this alliance with Rāvaṇa, which is worthless, fruitless, and leads to hell, resulting in rebirth in the infernal realms.
"Let them fall from their own feet, from their own places—let them tumble down, perish, or be destroyed!
Yet Rāvaṇa, the beloved of Mandodarī, is dull-witted by his very nature, devoid of discernment; his mind is deluded and his heart is led astray by Mālyavat.
By the mention of "Mandodarī" and so forth, it is suggested that such is the extent of her power to ensure his well-being.
Due to a delusion of intellect, he engages in enmity—that is, he creates hostility—with the Great Hero Rāma;
[the suffix] *kyaṅ* is used here in the sense of the instrument according to the rule "śabdavaira-," etc.
Here, what can we do regarding Rāvaṇa’s improper act of creating enmity with Rāma?
The meaning is: "We are wise; we shall not harbor enmity toward Rāma. ||51||
"Svalpāntarālam" means having very little space. "By the acquisition of a great hero" (mahāvīralābhena) means by the acquisition of you, who are a great hero; such is the sense.
The accusative case in *etāvantaṃ kālam* is used to express continuous duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*).
*Saṃprahāraḥ* means battle.
*Pratyayaḥ* is the certainty regarding the equality of strength.
According to Amarasimha, "pratyaya" refers to dependence, oath, knowledge, and the cause of trust.
Regarding the phrase "among the trees": with a mind that is "praṇihita," meaning attentive and focused, [he perceives] that which is "ābhogayukta," meaning endowed with fullness or perfection.
"Abhogaḥ paripūrṇatā"—thus says Amara. Discharge that sharpened, keen arrow which possesses a deep and firm strike;
let his chest be pierced, or even if it should allow the passage [of the shaft] and cause the spreading of blood and other fluids.
"Prasara means spreading," according to Amara.

Alternatively, "pravyatheta" means he might tremble; thus, when the apprehension of defeat and the doubt regarding inferior strength have been dispelled and removed, immediately thereafter he becomes one of equal strength—this is the meaning of "iṣṭo bhavet. ||52||
"Vīrabandho" means a contemptible hero.
Like the terms "brahmabandhu" and "kṣattrabandhu," the word "vīrabandhu" also intends to express contempt for the subject at hand.
"Tṛṇaprāyam" means resembling grass.
A great offense is a harmful injury.
An indifferent person is one who is not engaged in combat, being either incapable or powerless.
Slander is the public proclamation of faults.
Regarding the word *manoh*:
"of renowned fame" means those whose glory has descended through a well-known lineage; as it is said: "If that [glory] has come down through a lineage, it is called 'fame' (*yaśas*)."
The conduct and behavior of these lords of the earth do not fall into reproach—that is, they do not incur the spread of blame.

Disregard and neglect for that which is the sole progenitor—the primary cause—of powerful, widespread censure throughout the *trilokī*, the aggregate of the three worlds, pains the mind and causes it distress. (53)
"Offense against the deity" means doing harm to another deity.
"Alas," and so forth.
"Disagreement" refers to the lack of conformity between our two respective cognitions.
"In this Rāma" means by the vision of him as the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) and through the realization of him as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
The meaning of the contradiction is that there is only the perception of this Rāma’s supreme excellence, and not a perception of inferiority.
Therefore, [he acts] with the perception of excellence toward me, with the conduct due to one's own kin, and with the thought of me as a kinsman.
What do those who possess discernment and wisdom examine?
They do not examine it at all;
the meaning is that the power of burning is too well known.
"By my word" means having delivered my message; the ablative case is used here with the elision of the suffix *lyap*. "In the middle of the road" means in the midst of the path.
The compound is formed according to the rule "pāremadhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā" (Pāṇini 2.1.18).
*Vilamba* means the delay or passing of the time for meeting.
*Āsphālayan* means shaking or moving.
"Drāgiti" means immediately.
"Pratibhaṭasya" means of the adversary or enemy. "Prāgalbhyasya" means of boldness or audacity.
"Without breaking," and so forth.
According to Amarasimha: "Dhṛṣṭa, dhṛṣṇu, viyāta, and pragalbha [are synonyms for one who is bold]. ||54||
Regarding the word *dṛpyat*:

the agent, the profound and unshakeable essence—meaning the strength—of my two pillar-like arms, [is being compared] with the thunderbolt (*dambholi*), which is accompanied by a crackling, resonant roar and flashing, towering lightning; and with my own arrows (*madiṣu*), which vie with and rival that thunderbolt. Since it is stated that "the word *iṣu* [can denote both genders]," its feminine form is used here.

When the mountains, which had served as Vālin’s weapons, were struck and shattered in various ways, the massive boulders of those peaks—mountains that had been turned into weapons by Vālin and destroyed by my arrows—were further broken by the swift-moving forces of those [demons].
(Regarding "boulders": Amara states, "upala, aśman, and śilā denote stone.")
By the breaking of the Vindhya-egg through a firm blow—that is, by the bursting of the two Vindhya-eggs—of that which expands and increases;
for the middle voice (ātmanepada) conditioned by the anudātta-it suffix is not mandatory. Let it be the cause of the sound *bhāṅkāra*.
The imperative suffix (*loṭ*) is used when the time for action has arrived. ||55||
"With a former notion" means with the notion that I am worthy of worship.
"Is being considered" means is being doubted.
"Agitated" means distressed.
"Whether it be total aversion to battle or facing toward it.
Thus, all exit.
He who is a resident of Mahīsāra, a descendant of Vādhūla, and a scion of the Raghu lineage, has composed the fifth act of the *Mahāvīracarita*.
Thus ends the fifth act in the commentary on the Mahāvīracarita, titled Bhāvapradyotinī, composed by Vādhūla Vīrarāghava, whose name begins with the syllable Aṇṇāya.
Act Six.

Now, the poet again describes the *vimarśasaṃdhi* (the juncture of deliberation) in the sixth act: therein, because of the description of the story of Agastya—which does not pervade [the entire plot]—and of the excellence [of the plot] through the slaying of Vālin, as well as the absence of any obstacle (*apāya*) and the attainment of certainty (*niyatāpti*) regarding the accomplishment of the task, the *vimarśasaṃdhi* is established.
As it has been said: "The reflection upon the seed-meaning that was established in the *garbha* juncture—this reflection by means of any cause whatsoever is intended as the *vimarśa* juncture.
Because of its statement regarding the excellence of the certain attainment, it has thirteen constituent parts (*aṅga*s)."
Therein, he composes the *viṣkambhaka* with the words: "Then enters the monkey named Saṃpāti," and so forth.
The term "monkey" is used to distinguish him from the vulture Saṃpāti who appeared in the *viṣkambhaka* of the previous act.
"I have been instructed" means I have been commanded.
"To seek" means to search for;
"anveṣitaṃ gaveṣitam" (sought, searched for) according to Amara.
[He remained] hidden, having approached the battle out of the apprehension that his brother's fame might perish, fearing the ill-repute [that would arise].
The meaning is: "by means of the knowledge that the fame previously acquired would perish.
Seeking—that is, searching for—his brother Vālin, he wanders, meaning he moves about everywhere.
This is expressed by the mouth, that is, by the words issuing from his mouth, of the root *aṭ* (to go).
"Thus" means:
in the manner of the words of Aṅgada previously shown.
"Thus" means: [as described].
In the manner indicated by Rāma’s words:
"I shall inform" (*nivedayiṣyāmi*)—meaning "I inform" (*nivedayāmi*).
The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here according to the rule: "The *laṭ* is used after the particles *yāvat* and *purā*."
"With the bowstring drawn up to the middle" means with the string fixed upon the center of the bow.
"Parivāram" means a retinue or equipment;
as Amara states: "The word *parīvāra* may denote a moving vehicle, the scabbard of a sword, or personal belongings."

"Having sent him to Kiṣkindhā"—this is a transitive verb with two objects (*dvikarmaka*). "Alone" means solitary. "Without looking back" refers to an action in which there is no subsequent gazing or waiting.
And this follows from the [previous] arrival:
"It is Vibhīṣaṇa.
Because of the absence of Vibhīṣaṇa, this is not Sugrīva.
The meaning is that this one is Vālin because he is separated from his followers.
He states that separation from followers is the cause of his being Vālin by saying, "On the previous day," and "And on the following day, he remained alone."
The repetition of "he must not be killed" is due to agitation. "Error" (viparyaya) is the delusion of mutual identity.
"In one direction alone" means in a single direction.
In all compound formations (vṛtti), a feminine pronoun takes the masculine form;
thus: "I am Vibhīṣaṇa, and so are the others.
[The word] *amogha* means "unfailing" or "not fruitless."
The target is the mark. "An arrow" is the ellipsis; it should not be discharged.
"In a thicket of trees" means in a cluster of trees.
Regarding how one should act toward an innocent deer, he says: "by hunting.
Amara states: "Ākheṭa and mṛgayā [are synonyms] for hunting, used in the feminine."
Dharma alone is indeed conduct alone. With vigilance, meaning free from other distractions;
by the word "species of deer," the individual instances that serve as the substrata for the genus are expressed.
"He flees" means he goes elsewhere. When the root *i* (in the sense of "going") follows, the *r* of the prefix *parā* is replaced by *l* according to the rule *upasargasyāyatau*.

Because this deer, who was previously mentioned as the agent of fleeing, is now taken as the object of the act of killing, the form *enam* is used as the *enādeśa* for the purpose of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*).
Because the visibility of death is prohibited by the passage beginning with "a long journey, slaughter, battle," etc., he says: "having exited.
Here, the mention of slaughter implies a flight (vidrava). "Alas! (hanta).
"Vaiśasam" means the fault of violence. "Mayā" (by me):
he is the "dharaḥ," the sustainer, of that form of Vālin—that is, the body of Vālin—characterized by the dimensions of the king of mountains, the size of the best of peaks. ||1||
"Or the sage... and so forth.

A "sage" (*muni*) is a deity whose nature is contemplation (*manana*), possessing the power to bestow curses or favors; superior even to him is Jambhāri, Indra; and superior even to him is the creator of beings, the lotus-born Lord Brahmā, born from the navel-lotus. Among the glories—the greatnesses—of these [beings] starting from the aforementioned sage up to the four-faced one, what excellence whatsoever could prevail before me, who am myself favored by you at the end of my body? It would not be able to stand.
The sense is that the liberated one is heard of in the scriptures as possessing a power that surpasses even that of Brahmā and the other gods.
Here, the resolve consisting of the praise of one's own power is stated. ||2||
Regarding "ka":
it is not cognized, nor is it uncognized.
There is no elision of the *n* of the word *na* due to its being in a compound.

The referent of the word "mind" (manas) is the inner reality that has been transferred through curiosity—that is, the locus of the transfer performed by joy. It becomes clear; it becomes serene. ||3||
"O Vasundhara," and so forth.
"O Lord of Vasundharā, O Sovereign of the Earth, Rāma, you who are the restrainer and leader of the mighty forest-dwelling monkeys."
"Vaneti" indicates a distinction from village-dwelling, common monkeys.
"Vālya-ham.
To the question, "How is this state of being a deer [attained]? he says: "Madeti."

Through that state of blindness caused by intoxication and pride—the lack of discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done—I have incurred, or attained, the condition of a *mataṅga*, namely the state of being a deer (*kuraṅgabhāva*). ||4||
He clarifies what was stated previously with the words beginning "purā kila" (formerly, indeed), etc.
"Maryādām" means the established rule or boundary.
"Tadīyāśramasya" refers to the hermitage belonging to Mataṅga.
*Parisare* means in the vicinity;
*vikṣiptavān* means he has scattered or released;
*paryukṣitam* means sprinkled all around.
"By *vīradarpa* [means] by the pride of heroism; the term *vīra* is used here with the abstract quality as the primary referent.
By *atikrama*, [meaning] by an offense characterized by the transgression of established boundaries."
It was contrary to, or in opposition to, the conduct of a heroic man, which consists in dying in battle according to the dharma of heroes.
He showed favor— that is, he bestowed grace—
and states the purpose of that favor with the words beginning "vedānta."

That supreme person whom the wise man— having attained proficiency through the study of the multitude of Vedāntas, such as the Chāndogya and Taittirīyaka Upaniṣads, and through the practice of determining their purport by means of the reasons contained within the words of the Brahma-sūtras and their supporting expositions—
has realized through the hearing [of scripture] and reflection;
he is one whose state of being is non-dual and whose heart is not directed elsewhere.
The meaning is that one is engaged in meditation that does not involve the mental representation of anything else.
By this, *nididhyāsana* (reflective contemplation) is expressed.
"Free from obstacles" means devoid of impediments to liberation, such as the desire for heaven and other worldly goals.
"Vighna, antarāya, and pratyūha" are synonyms according to Amarasimha.

By the mention of the word *antarāya*, the following statement from the *Ratnapurāṇa* is illuminated: "O Maitreya, for one whose mind is fixed on Vāsudeva through chanting, oblations, worship, and so forth, even the fruit of the status of Indra is an *antarāya* (obstacle)."
He knows and sees; for there is the Vedic scripture: "But then, meditating, he beholds Him who is partless.

By that Supreme Person—who is most difficult to grasp and impossible to conceive without His grace—He has favored you with the promise: "At the end of the body, upon the destruction of the physical frame, you shall attain that which is otherwise unattainable and difficult even for the gods to reach. This is the connection with what precedes.

In this context, "intoxicated with pride" (*madāndha*) constitutes *apavāda*, which consists in the proclamation of a fault; "O evil-souled one" (*durātman*) is *saṃpheṭa*, which takes the form of angry speech;
and "disregarding the bounds of propriety" (*maryādām anavekṣya*) is *drava*, which consists in the contempt of a superior.
"Curse him" refers to flight in the form of execution, imprisonment, and so forth;
"he was conciliated" refers to the power in the form of the pacification of conflict;

and by the verse beginning with "the web of Vedānta," the incidental discussion (prasaṅga) in the form of the praise of the Guru is mentioned—thus the constituent parts of the *vimarśasaṃdhi* (the juncture of reflection) have been stated. ||5||
"This very thing is the curse.
The grammatical connection is: "That he has fled—this very thing is the curse.
"This very thing is the favor."
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "That which is yours"—namely, the thought "I have attained sovereignty over the unborn"—is itself this very favor (*anugraha*).
"Upanatam" means obtained or arrived.

The eternal state is the place of liberation. [He was] one who had performed the subsequent rites—that is, one for whom the funeral ceremonies (*aurdhvadaihika-karma*) had been completed. [This refers to] one who was shown the calamity of his brother’s death and was tormented by the grief of his brother’s passing.
For the sake of consolation and for the alleviation of suffering;
being attended to and having service rendered to him;
"for fourteen years"—these are two words.
The second case ending is used to express continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). In the phrase "in four months" (*māsacatuṣṭaye*),
since "months are indeed fortnights," the number four refers to two months, namely the months of Leo and Virgo.
Alternatively, because the months of Libra and Scorpio are also unsuitable for extensive travel, they are considered part of the rainy season (*vārṣika*).
It is with this very intention that it was said, "The four months of the rainy season. Regarding the phrase "in conversation about that":

For him, the diversion consists solely of conversation with his friends—the very exchange of questions and answers that recount past events—and this serves to lighten the sorrow of his separation from Sītā; for he is both distracted and absorbed therein. "The [enemy] is indeed slain" means that since Vālin, the leader of the monkey host, has been killed, the manly strength (*pauruṣabala*)—the power pertaining to a man—of Rāvaṇa, the lord of the night-stalkers, is destroyed.
The meaning is "the strength of friends.
"Hata" means destroyed or ruined.
The word "tāvat" indicates sequence.
The meaning is that between the power of human effort (*pauruṣabala*) and the power of illusion (*māyābala*), this power of human effort has first been destroyed.
Even the mere mention—the word "carnivores" (*kravyāda*)—has been destroyed by my wrath; it is as good as vanished.
The verb "to be" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied.
The qualifier "entire" (*kṛtsnam*) is used with the intention of emphasizing the excessive slaughter of asses and other animals.

Here, the dramatic element (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) called "Resolution" (*vyavasāya*), which consists of the praise of one's own power in the form of the thought, "Even my wrath has perished," is expressed. ||6||
Illusion (māyā) is indeed nothing but illusion;
and "illusion" refers to sorcery (śāmbarī) and the like.
It consists of both the creation of what has never existed before and deception.

"For the sake of counteracting that" means for the sake of avoiding that. Here, the "taking" (*ādāna*) which consists of grasping what is to be done is stated as a limb of conciliation (*saṃdhy-aṅga*). "Having thoroughly discerned" means having reflected skillfully.
Regarding the word "yat" (which):
by me, [the acts] such as the slaying of the Yātudhāna and so forth; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), the slaying of Vālin is included.
"Adhiṣṭhitam" means determined as something that ought to be done. ||7||
"It is known to you" means that it is indeed already known. "By one whose intellect is impelled" means by one whose intellect is prompted by the power of our asceticism.
"By mere resolve," that is, by the mental activity alone.
"In such a way as to produce conviction" means that Viśvāmitra gave the instruction, "May such be your conviction"—this is the connection.
"This one... [refers to the following].

This Rāma, by means of the excellence of the abundance of his physical beauty and the splendor of the weight of his bodily grace—resembling desire itself and equal to the God of Love—produces joy for the eyes even of those whose intellects are dull-witted.

This Rāma, through a mind possessed of the sense of "mine-ness" yet turned inward by the totality of yoga, expands—that is, extends—the bliss of self-realization, which is the supreme glory and unsurpassed abundance of the self-luminous bliss of consciousness (cidānanda). This is that bliss of the Self, which has long been familiar to him and made the object of his meditative absorption (samādhi), and which is beyond the reach of speech and mind, as established in the *Ānandavallī* by such passages as, "from which words turn back. The meaning is that he generates the bliss of direct realization occurring in the state of liberation, together with the abundance of bliss experienced during the stages of yoga. ||8||
Regarding "māyābalam":
O Rāma of great strength, one should not entertain even the slightest—indeed, not even a minimal—thought of rivalry or opposition toward a master of illusion; it is not proper to think so.
The use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) here denotes fitness or propriety. ||9||
"Thus": divine means capable of perceiving objects that are remote.
"What do you see?"
The meaning is: "What is this account of Laṅkā that you are seeing?
The account of Laṅkā begins with "Rāvaṇa" and ends with "surely the duty of a man is highly esteemed.
[It was seen] by all the subjects, including the ministers, generals, and so forth.
He *mantrayate*, meaning he speaks secretly regarding what is to be done;
the root *matri* is used in the sense of "speaking in secret" according to the *curādi* class.
The repetition of the word *mātāmaha* is due to agitation.
"By you":
whatever task was performed by you through deceitful means—that is, as a stratagem for deception—all of that has turned out contrary [to your intent] due to ill fortune (*durdaiva*).
The sense is that the actions against Virādha and others, though employed for the purpose of killing Rāma, became instead the cause of the very slaying of Virādha and the rest.
Your supreme human prowess was such that he who approached you for battle was swiftly slain by your power. ||10||
"Ours" refers to Vālī, the king of the monkeys;
"the destroyer of Kṣatriyas" refers to Rāma [the son of Daśaratha] and Paraśurāma. ||11||
"Once" means on one occasion;
according to Amara, "nivaha," "avasara," and "vāra" all mean "occasion.
The accusative case is used here to denote continuous connection (atyantasaṃyoga).
The meaning is "once.
A silent punishment (*tūṣṇīṃdaṇḍa*) is a means of killing consisting of deception.
"Dependent on fate" (*daivāyatta*) means subject to fortune (*bhāgya*).
The "open assault" (*prakāśadaṇḍa*), however, consists of war through a manifest military expedition.
He describes what was reported by spies and envoys with the passage beginning "on Ṛṣyamūka" and ending with "will dwell.
"Separated" (*viprayuktau*) means parted.
"Paraspara...

etc. If there is mutual assistance between these two and they do not become separated—that is, if there is no disjunction—then the employment and execution of a deceptive punishment (*chadmadaṇḍa*) will be successful; it will come to pass.
This is from the root *bhū* in the periphrastic future (*luṭ*). ||12||
The phrase "of what kind" and "of what nature" is to be connected with the term *chadmadaṇḍa* (guileful punishment).

He explains the varieties of guileful punishment with the passage beginning with "When first... and ending with "...to be conquered. [In this context,] "he will fall into delusion" means he will reach a state of fainting.
By the cessation— that is, the destruction— of the purpose for which the war was undertaken, namely the recovery of Sītā, it will come to pass; that is, it will happen,
regarding one's own people, meaning regarding one's kinsmen.
And the logical sequence regarding this downfall is as follows:
"Accidental" means when a downfall has occurred unexpectedly, having arrived quite suddenly and at an improper time.
When the foot is stepped upon by a glowing coal, as if it were not stepped upon at all— according to Amara’s lexicon, "vā" may be used for either an alternative or a comparison—
the mind of even an exceedingly steadfast man becomes agitated and devoid of composure. ||13||
It was created and fashioned by the illusory power (*māyā*)—the capacity for deception—of Vidyujjihva, who is known as Vidyujjihva; it was to be deposited and placed [there].
The grammatical connection is that this was to be done "even before [he could find] consolation.
This was due to the manifest offense, namely the visual act of performing an evil deed consisting of the seizing of Sītā’s head.
By the word "pratyakṣa" (evident), the abduction of Sītā is excluded.
"Dviguṇita-kopa" means possessing a wrath even greater than the wrath felt at her abduction.
"Tadavastha-dhairya" means their steadfastness remaining exactly as it was; "saṃnidhānam" refers to their proximity.

The "rākṣasa-force" (rākṣasabala) refers to the rākṣasa army. According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *bala* is neuter when it denotes an army, stability, semen, power, or bulk. [This concerns] Kumbhakarṇa.
The word "asleep" is to be supplied [to the previous sentence]. As for "where": it means hidden or concealed.
"While awake" means while it is manifest; and this [phrase] connects with what follows later. "Into the mother's womb," etc.
Liberation from great death—even from the death of death—is the going forth.
Indifference is the state of being devoid of the execution of punishment.
For heroes, it is [attained] through dharma, which is the means for achieving the highest good, by means of the blows inflicted by enemies.
Death means dying;
and here, as well as in the general category of punishment,
it refers to the "silent punishment" (*tūṣṇīṃdaṇḍa*).
"In its accomplishment" means in its completion;
that is to say, when silence has been achieved on the part of the staff, or rather,
while it remains unknown to others.

In a battle characterized by the staff of light (where weapons are clearly visible), death—that is, dying—and fame—the renown for steadfastness in the dharma of heroes—and the highest good—the attainment of the desired goal consisting of reaching the world of heroes, are eternal (*śāśvatam*).
The meaning is that these are certain.

Regarding the compound *śāśvataśca śāśvataṃ ca śāśvaṃ ca*, since they are mentioned together, the rules "the neuter [remains] with a non-neuter" and "it becomes a singular [form optionally]" apply, resulting in a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) and a singular form. ||15||
But in the case of indifference, or in the application of ordinary punishment, there would be death—a miserable end—and misfortune, namely, exclusion from the world of heroes.
Even if the sin of stealing Sītā were expiated through execution, the world of heroes would still not be attained; this is the sense.
"As we have stated" means as I have said.
Without exceeding the application of punishment and killing. An avyayībhāva compound is used in the sense of not exceeding the meaning of the word.
"Victory," so it is said.
One of the two is inevitably unavoidable.
This application of both types of punishment is my view; it is what I desire.

When the object is an enemy—that is, a foe—the agent’s indifference, which consists in the non-application of punishment, does not bring about mental composure, nor does it achieve the cessation of doubt.

In the case of non-action—that is, remaining indifferent by not applying punishment—calamity and death are constant and certain. Otherwise, if punishment is indeed applied, calamity is uncertain and doubtful.

Thus, since the application of punishment at that time involves uncertainty regarding calamity, the human virtue of exertion—the effort to apply punishment which is the very nature of a heroic man—is highly esteemed; indeed, it is truly praiseworthy.
Thus was the account of Laṅkā directly perceived. ||16||
Trust is knowledge of reality.
"Be victorious" means "be triumphant. The middle voice (ātmanepada) is used here according to the rule *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ*.
The *Ādityahṛdaya* is that which is called the "Heart of the Sun"; therein, the sun is the subject. "Uprooting" (*unmūlanam*) means destruction along with the root.
"Inseparability" (*avinābhāvena*) refers to a fixed proximity.
All this is the activity of the *māyā* of a *rākṣasa*.
"Rākṣasī" means belonging to a *rākṣasa*.
It is by virtue of the *rākṣasa* species, that is, in accordance with the state of being a *rākṣasa*.
"Is this not the conduct of a Rākṣasa?"—this is because it specifically prohibits the actions of a Rākṣasa.
"Sannaddham" means ready or prepared; as the *Ratnamālā* states: "The words *sannaddhau* and *sajjau* mean 'clad in armor'."
Having descended to the world of mortals (*bhūloka*) in the form of a monkey, he reached the earth. "The army of the gods" (*devatānīka*) refers to the host of the celestial forces;
according to Amara, "the word *anīka* is neuter when meaning an army."
"Let it be commanded; let him be informed by word of mouth.
"Hanta" expresses joy.
And the phrase "by you now" is to be connected with what follows later.

"Laṅkā": by you, the entire race of night-stalkers residing on the island of Laṅkā shall be defeated; it will be conquered very soon. The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here to indicate proximity to the present time.
The same applies to what follows.
"Diṣṭyā" expresses joy.
"Vinirdhūyate" means it will be destroyed or eliminated.
The exultation and intense joy of the mind of Indra, the lord of the gods, will be further increased;

here, "increasing" (*upādhāna*) means generating. By you—who possess the nature (*śīlana*) of perfect protection and preservation according to the rules—the happiness of the worlds shall be established as your duty.
Here, the element of the juncture of deliberation (vimarśasaṃdhi) called *prarocanā*—consisting of the statement of future welfare as if it were already accomplished—is described. ||17||
"Attahasa" refers to great laughter;
according to the lexicon, "attahasa is a great laugh that causes changes in the color of the face and so forth.
The directions are the east and others, and the intermediate directions are the southeast and others; these [laughter-sounds] will tear asunder, that is, split them apart.
"Bibhyat" (fearing):

the two qualifiers mentioned in the two halves [of the verse] are adjectives for the previously mentioned "loud laughter" (*aṭṭahāsa*). [The demons were] those by whom the sound of the thunderbolt (*dambholi-aśani*) was eclipsed—that is, surpassed—by the intensity of the terrifying quality (*bhīmabhāva*) produced by the downward fall of infants (*arbha-ka*) situated within the split or torn wombs (*garbha*) of the female Rākṣasīs (*kauṇapavadhū*), who, being terrified, had embraced the earth and fallen to the ground.

Those by whom the enemy of Jambha (Indra) was rendered such—that is, one whose mass of darkness (intense grief) was accumulated and produced through the attainment of celestial enjoyments (the acquisition of heavenly bliss), which was accompanied from the very moment of his birth by the commencement of dissolution (the onset of death), conceived as a failure in sacrifice, an obstacle to the rite, and a source of terror for the *rakṣas*—[such were they]. (Amara states: *bhreṣa* means *bhraṃśa*, i.e., a falling away from what is appropriate.)
"Darkness (tamas) refers to Rāhu, a quality, gloom, or sorrow," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
The sense is that even for those who cause obstacles to sacrifices, the bliss of heaven has arisen; thus Indra experienced sorrow.
The connection is that such [beings] will rend the cardinal and intermediate directions, such as Aṭṭahāsa and others. ||18||
"And this" means:
"And this is your bow"—this is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).
"Manifested," etc.

He has sustained—that is, held fast—by means of the abundance of your own powerful arm, which is rich in strength, that mental cultivation (bhāvanā) which destroys the power and sovereignty of the vast Saṅgha, those opposing forces that have arisen against the true reality;
for "dordōṣā ca bhujā bhujaḥ" is the *Dvirūpakośa*.

"Accompanied by" (saha) means together with the "terrifying state" (bhairava-bhāva)—that is, with the fear-inspiring quality—of your "arising and rising brow-furrow" (bhavad-bhrū-bhaṅga-bhaṅgī), which is the manner of your knitting the brows;
for the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *bhaṅgī* denotes a manner.
Thus, it is appropriate that [the word] is joined [with *saha*].

The connection of the sentence is as follows: this bow of yours—whose interior is filled with a mass, a multitude, of deep, dense, formidable, long, abundant, and increasing, terrifyingly resonant, and fearsome twanging sounds—will adorn the space between the corpses of the night-stalkers. ||19||
He who was a resident of Mahīsāra, a descendant of Vādhūla, and the son of Vīrarāta,
he [Bhavabhūti] composed the sixth act in the *Mahāvīracarita*.
Thus ends the sixth act in the commentary on the Mahāvīracarita titled Bhāvapradyotinī, composed by Vādhūla Vīrarāghava, whose name begins with the syllable Aṇṇā.
Thus ends the seventh act.
Now, the poet introduces the *nirvahaṇa-sandhi* (concluding juncture) with the seventh act.

And its nature is as follows: "The elements such as the *mukha* (opening), which possess seeds and are scattered according to their respective places, are brought together toward the final purpose (*ajakārya*) where that indeed is the *nirvahana* (conclusion). Because of its conformity with the purpose of attaining the fruit, it has fourteen subsidiary parts."

"Reconciliation (saṃdhi), conflict (virodha), the plot-knot (grathana), the resolution (nirṇaya), dialogue (paribhāṣaṇa), favor (prasāda), joy (ānanda), the occasion (samaya), composition (kṛti), speech (bhāṣā), the embrace (upagūhana), the prior state (pūrvabhāva), the conclusion (upasaṃhāra), and the eulogy (praśasti)— these are the fourteen [elements]. Thus it is said.

Here, because of the description of the *arthaprakṛti* consisting of the action—characterized by Vasiṣṭha’s activity and serving as the means to accomplish the result—and the attainment of the result itself, which consists of Rāma’s consecration on the royal throne together with Sītā, this constitutes the *nirvahaṇasaṃdhi* (the concluding juncture).
The definition of its constituent parts (*aṅga*) will be explained at their respective occasions.
Therein, he introduces the *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) with the words "Then enters," and so forth.
By means of an aerial vehicle; that is to say, by means of a celestial palace (vimāna),
or by traveling through the sky.
The desire—that is, the longing—has been fulfilled;
the meaning is that it has reached its specific limit in the form of the slaying of Rāvaṇa and so forth.
Regarding the word "having slain" (*hatvā*):
"Hanta" expresses joy.
"Sānvayam" means together with his lineage. "Straiṇam" means having abandoned the multitude of women.
The meaning is: having set her aside as the object of the act of killing.
*Tarasā* means with speed or force.

Then, immediately thereafter, when the Fire (*jātavedasi*), the proclaimer of truth, had become the speaker of the truthful matter characterized by Sītā’s purification, he took back his beloved Sītā from that Fire.
After the root *dā* preceded by the prefix *ā*, there is the elision of *sic* in the *luṅ* tense.
By the fire that carries the oblation;
"favor" means grace;
"himself" means his own self.
The word *ātman* here refers to fire (*vahni*).
That state which belongs to this [fire] is described as such; [she is addressed as] "her who remains as she was before.
Regarding the phrase "of the worlds":
Rāmacandra is like the moon;
who would engage in that which is adverse and brings about what is undesirable?
The meaning is that no one at all would so engage.
"Or who would not proceed when it is favorable?"— the meaning is that everyone indeed proceeds.
Here, the dramatic juncture (*saṃdhy-aṅga*) called "contradiction" (*virodha*), which consists of the search for what must be done, has been described.
"By relying on his manliness," that is, by taking recourse to Rāma’s prowess.
"In this manner" refers to an excellence of manliness, an excellence surpassing even that of Bāla and others.
"Only this much" means that which is about to be said is just this much.
"Having reached the forest-dwelling from the hermitage-dwelling":
the ablative case is used here with the elision of the suffix *lyap*.
Together with this Rāma— who, by means of security consisting in the protection of his own portion [of the kingdom] along with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa—
is such that Dharma alone is his sole and primary objective.
The word "eka" (one) excludes [other goals] such as sovereignty and the like. Furthermore, its connection occurs later [in the sentence]. Regarding the word "purā" (formerly):
By that sequence of speech—the orderly progression of words—of such a Kaikeyī;
for Amara states, "paripāṭī means anukrama (sequence).
[He was] dependent, being under her control.

"Puraṃdhrīsadhryaṅ" means one who goes or moves together with Sītā, the matron of the household; for Amara states, "A *kuṭumbinī* is a *puraṃdhrī*," and by the rule "the substitute *sadhri* is used for *saha*," the form *sadhryaṅ* is derived.
The meaning is "accompanied by Sītā. By this [statement], it is shown that Rāma has occupied (*adhyāsita*)—that is, dwelt in (*adhyuṣita*)—this deep place, a forest region, from Ayodhyā.
The verb is transitive according to the rule: "The objects of the roots *adhi-śī*, *adhi-sthā*, and *adhi-ās* are [the karmakāraka]."

Seeing this Rāma, who is well and has returned again to the city of Ayodhyā—himself transformed into a man, a transformation of the Supreme Person—I consider him to be a person of virtuous conduct, a collection of the merits of all the worlds, born again; I believe him to have descended once more.
(In the word *imam*, there is no substitution of *enad* because the subsequent reference is not intended. ||2||

"You speak thus. The relationship between you and Rāma as father and son—the bond of progenitor and offspring—conceals, that is, covers up, the greatness and majesty of Rāma; [the root] *gup* means "to conceal.
Here, the dramatic element (*saṃdhyaṅga*) called "the hiding of the seed" (*bījopagūhana*) is stated.
Those who protect the assembly are called *sāmājikāḥ*;
[the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied to the root "to protect" (*rakṣati*).
The meaning is: "Hasten for the consecration of Rāmacandra."
"Out of a desire to see," that is, out of a longing for a vision;
he "waits for" or awaits the city of Sāketa, the city of Ayodhyā, which is situated nearby, in its vicinity.
Regarding the phrase "by Mahendra":

In such a manner that the full weight of affection—that is, an excess of love—was attained during the act [of sitting], he sat upon half of the seat, occupying an equal portion of his [the king's] lion-throne. "Half of a seat" is *ardhāsana*;
this is a compound according to the rule "the word *ardha* is neuter."
"Mahābhāga" means one whose fortune is exceedingly great. "Surapariṣadā" means by the assembly of gods; "udgītavibhava" means one whose majesty is loudly sung.
"Mahānanda" refers to a bliss comparable to liberation (mokṣa).
"Mukti" means liberation, which is supreme bliss; such is the glossary (*nighaṇṭu*).

Its "overflow" is its increase, and its "flood" is its current. By the weight—that is, the intensity—of that [bliss], the Great King Daśaratha, whose heart was entirely dependent [on it], stands like the sun (*dyumaṇi*) itself, manifest before our eyes through his radiance, awaiting [his son] in the midst of the sky.

This is the connection [of the sentence]. Here, the *saṃdhy-aṅga* (limb of the juncture) called *grathana* (the knitting together), which consists of the introduction of the action to be accomplished, has been stated. ||3||
Vasiṣṭha, the husband of Arundhatī, having urged the group of ministers and other officials, causes them to take their seats— that is, to sit down— in that place abounding in jewels.
Therefore, let auspicious rites—those which avert obstacles and bring about the fulfillment of what is intended, such as singing, dancing, and so forth—be commenced and performed.
"O Gandharvas! [means:
in a manner that is sweet, through musical compositions (*āgama-bandha*) that are profound with wealth and firmly bound with passion (*rāga*).

Alternatively, let the Gandharvas sing with sweetness—that is, in such a manner as to be full of passion—according to the *nāṭyarāga*, which is the first among those [musical modes] beginning with *nāṭyagaula* and *varāli* because of its preeminence; and let them sing with lovely tones, that is, with charming sounds.

Let the Apsarases, skilled in the performance—that is, the execution—of the fourfold acting (*abhinaya*), consisting of the *sāttvika*, *āṅgika*, *āhārya*, and other types, which indicates profound emotions (*bhāva*) and aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) through subtle inference, dance with dexterity.
May the Vidyādharas, moving swiftly and with great speed, scatter and rain down radiant flowers.
May the divine drums and kettledrums dwelling in heaven, possessing deep resonance and thick sound, raise a tumultuous clamor.
Here, because the effect is proclaimed in accordance with its cause, the dramatic element (saṃdhyaṅga) called *nirṇaya* (determination) is stated.
As it has been said: "The determination [of a matter] is the manifestation of an effect that conforms to its cause. ||4||
"Diṣṭyā" expresses joy.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "Vasiṣṭha and others," Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, and so forth are included.
The meaning of "divine garlands" and so forth is clear.

Here, the dramatic juncture (saṃdhy-aṅga) called "Joy" (ānanda), which consists in the attainment of what was desired, has been mentioned. Regarding the terms "conduct" (ācāra) and "festival" (utsava): the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭa) must be followed, and a festival is not to be prohibited; this is the reason.
The investiture with the turban (*paṭṭābhiṣeka*).
The meaning is that, as in the case of another king, sovereignty over the kingdom is not established by means of an investiture with a turban.
By this [act], they were supported—that is, taken under his protection—by Rāma.
"As for me first": "First, having slain my enemies, I shall be established in the kingdom of heaven. (5)
Regarding "sugrīva": *avāpitaḥ* means "caused to reach" or "brought to.
This is a verb with two objects (*dvikarmaka*).

"Impossible for anyone other than Rāma, even in thought"—the word "vā" (or) suggests another means. Here, the *saṃdhy-aṅga* (limb of the juncture) called *paribhāṣā*, consisting of mutual conversation, has been described. ||6||
"Until the end of the kalpa" means:

by means of infinite millions of multiplied and repeated objects, riches, and accomplished sacrifices—numerous rituals—he [propitiated] the divine ones such as Indra and the others, as well as the non-divine ones dwelling on earth, that is, all the gods without exception; the meaning is both the gods and the "gods upon earth" (brahmins).

May he remain until the end of the aeon— that is, until the final limit of the kalpa— bringing joy and attaining bliss, cherishing his own kṣatriyas with incessant and constant gifts of sovereign power, pleasing them like sons, and experiencing a succession of our blessings.
"May he remain" is the meaning.
The *leṭ* [suffix] occurs in the sense of benediction. ||7||
"Ālokāloka" means:

by swallowing—that is, eclipsing—the majesty and power of the guardians of the quarters, Indra and the others, with his own exceedingly great and surpassing rays of fame, he has marked (añcitām) the earth, from the Ālokāloka mountain up to the very edge of the Lokāloka mountain.
The root "añc" is used in the sense of "distinguishing" (viśeṣaṇe) and belongs to the Curādigaṇa.

"Establishing"—that is, effecting—by mere command (and not by war), even all those enemies, the kings whose splendor has been seized and who have been overwhelmed, you cast them down and expel them from the earth;
may you enjoy the stability and firm foundation of supreme sovereignty over the entire world as long as the moon and sun endure. (The use of the *loṭ* suffix here expresses a benediction.)
Here, the dramatic juncture-element (saṃdhy-aṅga) called "the act of securing what has been obtained" (labdhasthirīkaraṇa-kṛti) has been described. ||8||

For those who possess the knowledge of ultimate reality—that is, those possessing knowledge whose object corresponds to reality—[their cognition] does not fail; it is not devoid of an object. [This was said] by Brahmā, the four-faced one.
Maheśvara is Rudra;
the two friends are Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa;
the brothers are Śatrughna and the others.
"Appropriately" means according to what is fitting. "Darśanīyatām" means loveliness.
"Śatrughna" refers to [the one named] Śatrughna.
The two holding chowries—two fly-whisks—bear [them];
there is an absence of *guṇa* in the *tasi* ending due to the rule *tviādguṇa*.
Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, fans with a palm-leaf fan (*tālavṛnta*), producing a gentle breeze.
He is both young and a king, thus "yuvarāja.
The suffix *ṭac* is applied according to the rule "rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac. He remains—that is, he abides—in his own service, meaning in service appropriate to himself.
Here, the element of the plot called "serenity" (prasāda), which consists of attendance upon [the teacher], has been described. ||9||
"Unobtainable by others" means difficult for others to attain.
"Well-pleased" means [pleased] by the wonder of their conduct— that is, by the marvel of the nature of their deeds.
Rāvaṇa, the Rākṣasa, was his very death; by him [the world] was seized, yet he brought it back to life, restored to its vital breaths.
As for the word "again": the worlds—the realms of Pātāla, Bhū, Svarga, and so forth—were born anew.
"Subjects" refers to the people; "the three Vedas" consists of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. The phrase "were born again" is to be supplied as a continuation.
By the word "etc. in the phrase "sacrifices and so forth," there is an inclusion of gifts, burnt offerings, and works of public utility (pūrta).
Here, the "addressing" (ābhāṣaṇa) which consists of the approval of an action already undertaken is stated to be a constituent element (aṅga) of the peace treaty. ||10||
The state of being an agent (*kartṛbhāva*) consists in the duty (*adhikāra*) to protect and to bring about what is desired.

"For so long" means that for this duration of time, you have continuously maintained— that is, adopted— the heroic sentiment of battle (*yuddhavīra*), which is the heroic sentiment that impels one toward combat.
The accusative case in *kālam* is used to denote continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*).

*Dharma* is that which is the means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*), as determined solely by the scriptures; *dāna* is the relinquishing of wealth to the destitute; *dayā* is the state of being pained by the suffering of others; and *vīra* refers both to the aforementioned heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) and to a hero.
These have approached you—that is, they have arrived in great abundance.
Previously, dharma and the other [aims of life] were subordinate to the hero; hereafter, however, the meaning is that the hero is subordinate to them.
The omission of dharma and the others in the first half [of the verse] is for the purpose of indicating their subordination to the hero.

In this context, the final expression "O Hero, [of] the hero" is intended to suggest that for him, dharma and the other [aims of life] are subordinate; for dharma and the rest are always inseparable from the very nature of Rāma. In some recensions, the vocative form is read. ||11||

The protection of the world itself is the sacrifice (*adhvara*); therein, all people are consecrated (*dīkṣita*) by their resolve. May they be well-disposed toward one another, with hearts intent on what is pleasing and beneficial, filled with intense joy and profound affection.
Regarding this, he states the distinction with the words beginning "May they be satisfied":

"May the virtuous—those who delight in helping others—be satisfied, that is, may they attain special joy, being honored and respected by the performance of their desired and cherished intentions. May the desire for noble deeds in the minds of the good, which is the wish to perform such deeds, always attain immediate success, that is, the accomplishment of its object at the very next moment."
"Let these twice-born ones pray for your victory and pre-eminence every morning and evening;
for the maintenance of their own welfare (*yogakṣema*) depends entirely upon you.
The sense is that, without depending on any other activity, it is always fitting for the twice-born to pray solely for your excellence."
In this context, because the effect is observed [to follow], the sequence known as "prior existence" (pūrvabhāva) is stated to be a subsidiary element of the *saṃdhi*. ||12||
Regarding the term *trailokya*:
the three worlds constitute the *trailokya*.
The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), according to the rule beginning with *cāturvaṇya*.

His welfare and happiness—that which was accomplished and brought to completion by you as the agent through effort, namely, the exertion directed toward the domain of the gods—the meaning of [the verses] beginning with "May you be happy" is clear. ||13||
Regarding the word *saujanyena*:

the state of being a good person (*sujanasya bhāvaḥ*) is goodness (*saujanyam*), which consists in having the singular nature of serving your feet. In this regard, "with a single flavor" means endowed with a passion unmixed with any other passion.
As for the definition: "Flavor (*rasa*) refers to passion, fluidity, and joy."
Accompanied by that son of Sumitrā,

Lakṣmaṇa— who was characterized by a thick, dense, steady, and firm affection, and whose mind was vigilant and undistracted in his activities pertaining to both this world and the next— he, together with him, accomplished the conduct of the virtuous— a source of joy for all— through truth (meaning speech devoted to the welfare of beings and reality), through dharma (such as non-violence and so forth), and by means of every effort directed toward those respective domains, even when not explicitly commanded.

"Acting yourself according to the manner described in such passages as 'Whatever the best person practices,' and thereby causing others to practice as well, may you become one who is praised by all good people, laudable through the excellence and highest pinnacle of a state of auspicious sovereignty (*saurājya*), illustrious, and filled with a renown for qualities difficult even for ancestors to attain. (The *loṭ* suffix is used here in the sense of a benediction. 14.
"Appointed to the position of crown prince, he has been commissioned by you. Regarding the word "sakala": it refers to the task of protecting heaven in one's own sovereignty.
According to Amara, *svaravyaya* means "the immutable heaven.
Its king is *svārāja*.
By the rule *rori*, the *r* is elided, and by the rule *ḍhralope*, a long vowel is substituted [for the preceding *a*].
Then, because *brāhmaṇa* and so forth belong to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied to form the word *kārmaṇya*. "I am established" means I am made firm. "Decided."
The meaning is that, by determining the absence of any destruction caused by Rāvaṇa, their doubt regarding ruin has ceased, and they have become objects of the certainty of eternal existence.
In the reading "niścintāḥ," the meaning is that they are free from anxiety concerning the harassment caused by Rāvaṇa.
[Regarding the word] "hṛdyān":

"From this day forward, the brahmins—the gods upon earth—will, with joyful minds, at all times and in every land, offer us on this earth pleasing sacrificial portions, parts of the oblations for sacrifice, which are dear to the heart due to the absence of fear from Rāvaṇa; that is, they will give them to us.
'Hanta' expresses joy."

You too, having performed sacrifices—namely the *rājasūyas*, so called by the etymology "in which the King (*rājā*) presses (*sūyate*) or extracts the Soma plant," and the rites designated as *aśvamedhas* because the horse is the principal element—accompanied by many and immeasurable rites worthy of kings and befitting the Kṣatriya order; having worshipped with these sacrifices, cause us to attain and reach abundant and vast bliss. ||15||
"By you"—the word "by the son" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. ||16||
"Firstly, on one hand": that which has your forest-dwelling as its root cause is described as such. "For so long a time" means for fourteen years.
The second case ending is used here to denote continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). "Now" (*idānīm*) means immediately after the coronation (*paṭṭābhiṣeka*).
"Of you" (*tava*)—[refers to the following].

While you were dwelling in the forest, during that period of exile, my heart was impaired and weakened by great sorrow—the cause of which was the boundless suffering resulting from that [separation]. Consequently, even the attainment of the status of a god, even the state of residing in heaven which is sought after by all, did not attain even the slightest natural flavor or the nature of happiness. Now that you have returned here from the forest and have come back to Ayodhyā—note that the word *punaḥ* carries the sense of the word *tu* (but/however)—[all is restored].
Even the supreme beatitude—the bliss of liberation that transcends all else—does not possess, nor does it attain, abundance or vastness within my mind filled with great joy.
The sense is that the bliss of liberation is but a trifle compared to the bliss of your arrival.
Here, the dramatic juncture (*saṃdhi*) called *samaya*, characterized by the pacification of suffering, is described. ||17||
"From this [world]" means:
through *iṣṭāpūrta*—that is, by the performance of sacrifices (*yāga*) and the construction of tanks (*taṭāka*) and so forth—one attains the eternal station, the permanent place;
as well as the accomplishment, or the fulfillment, of prosperity (*śreyas*), that is, auspiciousness, and of progeny (*saṃtāna*), that is, offspring.
"Lineages (saṃtāna), continuity (avicchitti), family line (vaṃśa), offspring (apatya), and celestial trees (suradruma) [are synonyms]," according to the *Ratnamālā*.
We "hope" (*āśāsmahe*), meaning we desire;
this is from the root *āṅ-śāsu* in the sense of "desire."
"Laṅkā," and so forth;
the meaning is "those who were allies in battle at Laṅkā. "Having honored" means having worshipped.
Regarding "by the Ādityas":
[this means] by the offspring of Āditya.
The suffix *ṇya* is applied according to the rule "dityadityāditya... and so forth.

By those [kings] who were so described—namely, those who, having maintained and practiced [the dharma] in a manner that was beautiful and pleasing, became the burden-bearers for the living beings on this great earth through their activity of securing what is desired and warding off what is undesired; and by whom [the dharma] was upheld through qualities such as heroism and other majestic powers (anubhāva) and splendors (prabhāva) that were noble—being manifested and shining forth, capable of bestowing even their very lives upon others—and who were themselves great kings, [they did so] in accordance with dharma, that is, by being endowed with the dharma prescribed in the scriptures. *Note: Amara states: "Prāptarūpa, surūpa, and abhirūpa refer to one who is wise or pleasing to the mind."*
The third case ending is used because [the word] belongs to the *prakṛtyādi* group. "Subjects" (*prajā*) means protected or guarded.
"By trustworthy persons" (*āptaiḥ*) means by those who, being perceivers as they are, speak according to reality regarding themselves (*ātmanaḥ*), that is, their own [nature].
This word "ātman" refers either to that [Self] or to Rāma;
for it is well known through reasoning and prior ascertainment that what is beneficial—even if its fulfillment occurs at a later time—results ultimately in happiness.
The suffix *caṇap* is used here in the sense of "known by him," as in the rule *tena vittaḥ*.

By the path instructed, taught, or commanded by men who carry out what has been undertaken and accomplish the tasks already begun, protect and guard the earth, extending spatially and temporally as far as the Cakravāla mountain range. 18.
"O Vasiṣṭha!"—
one must neither consult nor deliberate [with them].
"Of those two"— [refers to the aforementioned].
Maheśvara; the word "said" is to be supplied. "O Vasiṣṭha," [he said].
He whose wife is Arundhatī is referred to as such; [the vocative] of him is [the form used].
The suffix *niṅ* is applied by the rule "jāyāyā niṅ. They were joined, that is, united.
"Be untiring," meaning "be free from laziness. *Sthātam* is the second person dual of the optative (*liṅ*) in the *sārvadhātuka* category. ||19||
Those two, Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra— [the word] "said" is to be supplied as the ellipsis— [mean] "we have been favored," that is, "we have received your grace."
The form *asterlaṭyuttamapuruṣadvivacanam* refers to the second person dual of the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *as*.
"All of you, Rāma and the others; all of you, right here in Ayodhyā."
"Constant festivals" refers to activities that produce uninterrupted bliss.
As for "we," I am the four-faced Brahmā, Mahendra, and Daśaratha; each has gone to our respective abodes—Kailāsa, Satyaloka, and Svarga.
"Rāma and the others" [refers to those who have likewise departed].
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and others are included. "In a fitting manner" means in accordance with the relationship between teacher and disciple and so forth.
What further favor may I offer you?
Furthermore, the meaning is: "What else may I do that is pleasing to you?"—
that is, other than what will be stated hereafter,
namely, "they are to be killed."

The Rākṣasas, who were the cause of terror for the worlds and therefore terrifying, have been slain; they were destined for death and thus became the objects of a necessary act of killing. Furthermore, the eternal and long-enduring vow of protecting the subjects has been entered upon.
The connection is that there is nothing more dear than this.
Here, the juncture-element (saṃdhy-aṅga) called "conclusion" (upasaṃhāra), which consists of the summary of the purpose of the action, has been described. ||20||
The words of Bharata, the master of dramaturgy:

"In the literary work" means in this composition called the *Mahāvīracarita*, which is "accumulated"—that is, brought forth—by the emergence or manifestation of literature (*sāhitya*), meaning the arrangement of appropriate words; [and] by "connoisseurs" (*sahṛdayaiḥ*), meaning by persons whose hearts are endowed with the skill of poetic art and free from envy.

That whose rising or manifestation is to be honored and worshipped from all sides is so described; it is the *sārasvata*—belonging to Sarasvatī—the *sāra*, or excellent portion, which, having come together and united, triumphs, existing with supreme excellence. Such [a work] is "tremulous" (*tarala*)—meaning radiant—due to the *saṃvidhāna*, that is, the composition of the plot, which has been perfectly conceived and executed.
Alternatively, it is so called because the *saṃvidhāna* itself is the "tremulous" (*tarala*), the central gem, within it.

Among the various elements that differentiate dramas—namely rasa, substance (vastu), and hero—the element termed "substance" (vastu) is divided into the categories of well-known, invented, and mixed. Within these, the mixed variety is assigned the metaphor of "tremulousness" because it brings about a superior degree of aesthetic charm. It is "beautiful" (sundara), meaning lovely, like nectar (sudhā).

In accordance with the statement, "The account of Rāma is the reviver of living beings," may this composition called the *Mahāvīracarita*—a weaving of words that restores the dead to life like nectar—be thoroughly refined (*saṃdāyatām*) for the joy of the hearts of the wise, those learned ones inclined toward knowledge, and for the abundant happiness of the mind.
[The form *saṃdāyatām*] is derived from the root *daip* in the sense of "purifying" (*śodhane*), used in the reflexive-passive (*karmakartari*).
Because it does not end in *ghu*, the substitution of *ī* does not occur.
And there is also the reading "saṃtāyatām," meaning "let there be no interruption. The suffix *lakāra* is as before.
By the rule "tanoter yak," there is the substitution of ātva (the long vowel ā).
Here, the dramatic element named *praśasti* (eulogy), which consists of the pronouncement of auspiciousness, has been described. ||21||
Thus the drama has been described with all its constituent parts.
May she— who has attained a form through pure qualities, whose light is nourished by affection for worthy recipients,
and who illuminates the inner state of the wise like a small lamp— bestow radiance.
May the best of the Raghus— who has conquered his enemies, who acts for the pleasure of his devoted younger brothers, and who experiences boundless joy together with Queen Sītā—
grace my words by casting upon us his compassionate side-glances at every moment and by cherishing the love found in my speech as if it were nectar.
Vīrarāghava, a descendant of Vādhūla residing in Mahīsāra,
has composed the seventh act of the Mahāvīracarita.
Thus ends the seventh act in the commentary on the Mahāvīracarita, titled Bhāvaprakāśinī, composed by Vādhūla Vīrarāghava, whose name begins with the syllable Aṇṇā.
This drama is completed.
